Chen, Shi-Cheng; Hu, Ru-Bi; Liu, Yi-Fei; Shen, Chao; Li, Dan; Kang, Yu; Tian, Sheng; Teng, Peng; Hou, Ting-Jun; Pan, Pei-Chen 单位 ：未提供（基于作者姓名推断可能为中国机构，但原文未列出） 期刊/预印本平台 ：Acta Pharmacologica Sinica 年份 DOI/arXiv 号 ：10.1038/s41401-026-01957-9 代码 ：未提供 数据 ：约三百万化合物库（具体来源未提供）；基准测试数据集未提供 阅读日期 ：2026-11-14（基于 URL 访问日期推断） 在该方向中的位置 ：本文系统评估 AlphaFold2/3 预测结构在基于结构的虚拟筛选（SBVS）中的可靠性，并首次将 AlphaFold 模型应用于 CLIP1-LTK 这一无实验结构的致癌融合蛋白靶点，完成从基准测试到命中物发现的完整流程。属于「AI 结构预测 × 虚拟筛选」交叉方向，为无实验结构靶点的药物发现提供了可迁移的流程范式。 02 一句话总结 本文通过系统基准测试证明 AlphaFold2/3 预测结构可支持基于结构的虚拟筛选，并据此建立分层 VS 流程，应用于无实验结构的 CLIP1-LTK 融合蛋白，从约三百万化合物中筛选出 IC₅₀ 为 524.27 nM 的先导化合物 QL07，该化合物在细胞和异种移植模型中均显示抑癌活性。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：AlphaFold2 和 AlphaFold3 生成的蛋白质结构模型能否可靠地支持基于结构的虚拟筛选（SBVS）？如果能，如何配置最优的 VS 流程（对接 + 打分组合）？该流程能否应用于无实验结构的疾病相关靶点（如 CLIP1-LTK）并发现有效抑制剂？ 为什么重要 ：大量疾病相关蛋白缺乏实验解析结构，限制了传统 SBVS 的应用。AlphaFold 提供了结构预测的新途径，但其预测结构在 VS 中的可靠性未经系统验证，阻碍了该技术的实际应用。 现有方法不足 ：此前研究多为个案报道，缺乏对 AlphaFold2/3 模型在 VS 中系统性的适用性评估；不同对接软件和打分函数与 AlphaFold 模型的组合效果未知；尚无针对融合蛋白（如 CLIP1-LTK）的 AlphaFold 驱动 VS 案例。 精确研究问题 ：Can AlphaFold2- and AlphaFold3-derived models reliably support structure-based virtual screening, and can a hierarchical VS pipeline based on these models identify potent inhibitors against a target without experimental structures (CLIP1-LTK)? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：此脉络基于本文框架及领域常识，标注「经外部核验」部分。 阶段 代表性方法 优点 局限 本文位置 传统 SBVS 实验晶体结构 + 分子对接（DOCK、Glide、AutoDock） 结构可靠，成熟流程 依赖实验结构，靶点覆盖有限 本文对比基线 同源建模 + SBVS MODELLER、SWISS-MODEL 可覆盖无实验结构靶点 模型精度有限，VS 成功率低 本文未直接对比，但隐含优于该路线 AlphaFold2 结构预测 AF2 单链预测 高精度单链结构 多聚体/复合物预测能力有限；VS 适用性未验证 本文系统评估 AF2 模型在 VS 中的表现 AlphaFold3 结构预测 AF3 复合物/配体预测 可预测蛋白-配体复合物 新方法，VS 适用性未知 本文首次系统评估 AF3 在 VS 中的表现 分层 VS 流程 多级对接 + 打分 + 相似性搜索 提高命中率，降低假阳性 流程复杂，需系统优化 本文建立并验证分层 VS 方法 此脉络为「经外部核验」：AlphaFold2/3 的基本能力与局限为领域共识；本文在 VS 适用性评估方面为新增贡献。 05 核心痛点 痛点 表现 成因或作者解释 文中证据 无实验结构靶点的 VS 不可行 大量疾病靶点（如融合蛋白）缺乏晶体结构，传统 SBVS 无法启动 实验结构解析耗时且部分蛋白难以结晶 摘要：CLIP1-LTK 缺乏实验解析结构 AlphaFold 预测结构在 VS 中的可靠性未知 研究者不确定 AF 模型能否用于对接筛选，缺乏系统验证 AF 模型为预测结构，可能存在局部构象偏差，影响对接精度 摘要：系统评估 AF2/AF3 模型对 SBVS 表面方法 ： - 系统基准测试：将 AF2/AF3 预测结构与实验结构（已知靶点）在 VS 中的表现进行对比，评估不同对接 + 打分组合的性能。 - 建立分层 VS 流程：基于基准测试结果，设计多级筛选策略（粗筛 → 精筛 → 相似性搜索）。 - 应用案例：将流程应用于 CLIP1-LTK，筛选约三百万化合物，获得先导物 QL07。 2) 核心洞察 ： - AlphaFold 预测结构在 VS 中并非「全有或全无」，其适用性取决于靶点特性、模型置信度与 VS 流程配置的组合。 - 分层 VS 策略（而非单一对接 + 打分）可有效补偿 AF 模型的局部不精确性，提高命中率。 - AF3 的复合物预测能力可能为 VS 提供额外信息（如配体结合姿势），但需与传统对接方法结合使用。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] ： - 对于无实验结构的靶点，AI 预测结构 + 分层 VS 是一种可行的替代路径，但需针对每个靶点进行基准测试以确定最优配置。 - 融合蛋白等「非经典」靶点可通过预测结构 + 细胞验证的闭环流程实现药物发现，无需等待实验结构。 - 虚拟筛选的命中率不仅取决于结构质量，还取决于筛选策略的鲁棒性设计。 07 方法总览 输入 ：靶点氨基酸序列（CLIP1-LTK 融合蛋白序列）；约三百万化合物库；基准测试数据集（已知结构靶点 + 已知活性化合物） 输出 ：先导化合物 QL07（IC₅₀ = 524.27 nM）；VS 流程性能评估结果 模块 ： 1. 结构预测模块：AlphaFold2（单链）和 AlphaFold3（复合物/配体）生成靶点结构模型 2. 基准测试模块：评估 AF 模型在已知靶点 VS 中的表现，对比实验结构 3. 对接模块：多种对接软件（具体工具未提供）与打分函数组合 4. 分层筛选模块：多级 VS 流程（粗筛 → 精筛 → 相似性搜索） 5. 实验验证模块：细胞实验（Ba/F3-CLIP1-LTK 细胞增殖、凋亡、信号通路）+ 动物模型（异种移植） 工具 ：AlphaFold2、AlphaFold3、对接软件（未提供具体名称）、打分函数（未提供） 反馈回路 ：基准测试结果指导 VS 流程配置选择；实验验证结果反馈确认筛选命中物有效性 假设 ：AF 预测结构在 VS 中的表现可通过流程配置优化达到可用水平；CLIP1-LTK 的 AF 模型可捕捉药物结合位点 文字流程 ： 1. 对已知结构靶点，分别用 AF2/AF3 预测结构并与实验结构对比，评估不同对接 + 打分组合在 VS 中的性能（基准测试）。 2. 基于基准测试结果，选择最优的 AF 模型 + 对接/打分配置，建立分层 VS 流程。 3. 对 CLIP1-LTK 序列进行 AF2/AF3 结构预测，获得模型。 4. 将约三百万化合物库通过分层 VS 流程筛选，获得候选命中物。 5. 对候选命中物进行相似性搜索（analog searching），获得 QL07。 6. 实验验证 QL07 的活性：IC₅₀ 测定、信号通路抑制、细胞凋亡诱导、异种移植肿瘤抑制。 08 核心模块拆解 模块 功能 为何需要 输入输出 支撑证据 移除后的已知或预期影响 AlphaFold2 结构预测 相似性搜索」的流程设计，而非单一对接工具。对于本课题（蛋白质结构相关计算研究），可借鉴此思路：在结构预测质量不确定时，通过多级筛选策略（粗筛 → 精筛 → 类似物搜索）补偿结构误差，提高命中率。 可迁移方法：AF 模型适用性基准测试 。在将 AF 预测结构用于任何下游计算任务（如 MD 模拟、构象采样、分子对接）前，应先在已知结构靶点上进行基准测试，确定最优配置。此方法可直接迁移到本课题的 MD 模拟初始结构选择、构象生成验证等环节。 可迁移实验设计：从计算到实验的闭环验证 。本文展示了从虚拟筛选到细胞实验再到动物模型的完整验证链条。对于本课题的构象生成或结构设计研究，可借鉴此闭环思路：计算预测 → 体外验证 → 体内验证，确保计算结果的生物学相关性。 可迁移思路：融合蛋白靶点的处理 。CLIP1-LTK 作为融合蛋白，其结构预测可能面临特殊挑战。本课题中若涉及融合蛋白或突变体，可借鉴本文的「预测 + 筛选 + 验证」策略，而非等待实验结构。 可迁移指标：IC₅₀ 作为计算-实验桥梁 。本文以 IC₅₀ 作为最终验证指标，将计算筛选结果与生物学活性直接关联。本课题中，若计算预测（如结合自由能、构象稳定性）能与 IC₅₀ 或类似实验指标关联，将增强计算方法的可信度。 15 与已有知识连接 Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no experimental details, benchmarking data, chemical structures, or statistical analyses are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, benchmarking results, docking/scoring configurations, compound library details, chemical structures, IC50 determination protocol, signaling pathway data, apoptosis assays, xenograft study design, and statistical analyses Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially valuable application of AlphaFold models to a target lacking experimental structures, with a clear translational arc from benchmarking to hit identification to preliminary biological validation. However, the abstract alone provides insufficient evidence to assess the technical rigor of the benchmarking, the validity of the VS pipeline, or the robustness of the biological data. The claim that QL07 is a promising inhibitor is supported only by a single IC50 value and qualitative descriptions of cellular and in vivo effects, without quantitative details or statistical context. The work is of interest to the computational drug discovery community, but the case is not fully established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational chemists and structural biologists working on structure-based drug discovery, particularly those evaluating AlphaFold models for practical VS applications. Oncology researchers studying fusion kinase targets, especially CLIP1-LTK, would also be interested in the identification of a novel inhibitor scaffold. The methodological benchmarking component may appeal to method developers in the AI-for-drug-discovery space. Major strengths The study addresses a timely and important question regarding the reliability of AlphaFold models for VS. The application to a clinically relevant fusion protein without experimental structures is a compelling use case. The progression from benchmarking to prospective application to experimental validation is a logical and ambitious design. The reported IC50 in the sub-micromolar range and the inclusion of both cellular and in vivo data suggest a substantive experimental effort. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness of benchmarking Claim pointer The authors claim a systematic evaluation of AlphaFold2- and AlphaFold3-derived models for VS and the establishment of a hierarchical VS methodology based on benchmarking results. Evidence pointer Abstract only; benchmarking details not provided Concern The abstract does not describe the benchmarking dataset, the number of targets, the metrics used to evaluate VS performance, or the criteria for selecting the hierarchical pipeline. Without these details, it is impossible to assess whether the benchmarking was sufficiently comprehensive or whether the conclusions drawn from it are statistically robust. Why it matters The entire premise of the study rests on the validity of the benchmarking. If the benchmarking is flawed or limited in scope, the subsequent application to CLIP1-LTK and the generalizability of the methodology are called into question. Resolution test Provide a description of the benchmarking dataset, including target diversity, number of actives and decoys, evaluation metrics (e.g., enrichment factor, AUC), and a comparison of AlphaFold models against experimental structures where available. Statistical significance of performance differences should be reported. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence for inhibitor activity Claim pointer The authors claim QL07 exhibited an IC50 of 524.27 nM and inhibited downstream signaling, induced apoptosis, and suppressed tumor growth in xenograft models. Evidence pointer Abstract only; no experimental details or quantitative results provided Concern A single IC50 value is reported without assay details, replicates, or error estimates. The descriptions of signaling inhibition, apoptosis induction, and tumor growth suppression are qualitative and lack quantitative data such as percent inhibition, dose-response relationships, or tumor volume measurements. No statistical analyses are mentioned. Why it matters The biological validation is the key translational evidence for the utility of the VS pipeline. Without quantitative and statistically supported data, the claim that QL07 is a promising inhibitor is not established. Resolution test Provide full dose-response curves with replicates and error bars, quantitative data for signaling pathway inhibition (e.g., phosphoprotein levels), apoptosis assays (e.g., annexin V percentages), and xenograft tumor growth curves with statistical comparisons to control groups. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Selectivity and mechanism of action Claim pointer The authors imply QL07 is a specific inhibitor of CLIP1-LTK based on the VS approach and downstream signaling inhibition. Evidence pointer Abstract only; selectivity data not mentioned Concern No information is provided regarding the selectivity of QL07 against other kinases or non-kinase targets. The mechanism of binding to CLIP1-LTK is not described, and it is unclear whether QL07 binds the LTK kinase domain or the fusion interface. Why it matters Without selectivity data, off-target effects could confound the observed biological activities. Understanding the binding mode is important for medicinal chemistry optimization and for assessing the validity of the AlphaFold-derived model used for docking. Resolution test Include kinase selectivity profiling or counter-screens against related kinases, and provide structural or mutagenesis evidence supporting the proposed binding mode. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity of methodology Affected element Hierarchical VS methodology Evidence pointer Abstract only Issue The term "hierarchical VS methodology" is vague and does not convey the specific stages or decision points in the pipeline. Required correction Briefly describe the stages of the hierarchical approach, such as initial docking, rescoring, and consensus filtering, in the abstract or provide a schematic in the main text. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Compound library details Affected element Library of approximately three million compounds Evidence pointer Abstract only Issue The source and chemical diversity of the compound library are not described, which limits the reproducibility of the screening approach. Required correction Specify the library source, chemical space coverage, and any filtering criteria applied before screening. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Analog searching rationale Affected element Similarity-based analog searching leading to QL07 Evidence pointer Abstract only Issue The relationship between the initial hits and QL07 is not described, including the similarity metric used and the medicinal chemistry rationale for selecting QL07. Required correction Provide the chemical structures of the initial hits and QL07, and describe the similarity search criteria and optimization rationale. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis In vivo model relevance Affected element Xenograft models Evidence pointer Abstract only Issue The xenograft model is not described, including the cell line used, route of administration, dosing regimen, and whether the model is subcutaneous or orthotopic. Required correction Provide details of the xenograft study design, including the cell line, animal strain, dosing schedule, and tumor measurement methods. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 and R1-M2 are blocking concerns. The benchmarking methodology and the quantitative biological validation must be fully described and statistically supported before the central claims can be accepted. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The application of AlphaFold models to a fusion protein without experimental structures is a novel and timely contribution, though the general concept of AlphaFold-based VS is not entirely new. Scientific importance: The work addresses a practical bottleneck in drug discovery and could have broad implications for targeting undrugged proteins, but the significance depends on the robustness of the benchmarking and the translational validity of the biological data. Interdisciplinary readership: The topic bridges computational biology, medicinal chemistry, and oncology, and would appeal to a broad audience if the methods are clearly presented. Technical soundness: Cannot be assessed from the abstract alone; the benchmarking and biological validation require full scrutiny. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is concise and accessible, but the lack of methodological detail limits its utility for readers seeking to evaluate the approach. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The study has clear potential, but the abstract-level evidence is insufficient to establish the validity of the benchmarking or the biological claims. Full manuscript review is necessary to determine whether the case is made. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the hierarchical VS methodology is "established" based on benchmarking is unsupported without benchmarking details. The claim that QL07 is a "promising" inhibitor is supported only by a single IC50 value and qualitative biological descriptions; quantitative and statistical evidence is missing. The generalizability of the AlphaFold-based VS approach to other targets without experimental structures is implied but not demonstrated beyond the single CLIP1-LTK case. The selectivity of QL07 and its mechanism of action are not addressed and cannot be evaluated from the abstract.

boundary Claims and evidence as presented in the abstract; no access to full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report a shape-based virtual screening campaign against HDAC8 using 307,814 natural products from ZINC15, followed by docking and MM-GBSA calculations. Seven hits were tested enzymatically, yielding compound 2 (ZINC000054202375) as a promising HDAC8 inhibitor. Compound 2 showed antiproliferative effects across solid tumor cell lines, induced apoptosis-associated phenotypes, and formed a persistent interaction network in 1 microsecond molecular dynamics simulations. The authors conclude that compound 2 is a promising non-hydroxamate scaffold for HDAC-targeted anticancer drug development. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no experimental details, numerical data, statistical analyses, or methodological parameters are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, experimental protocols, compound purity and source information, assay conditions, statistical methods, MD simulation parameters, and any supplementary data Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a logically structured hit-discovery workflow with a plausible rationale for targeting HDAC8. However, the evidence base is insufficient to evaluate the validity of the central claims. Key quantitative results, assay validation details, and comparative data against known HDAC8 inhibitors are absent. The conclusion that compound 2 is a "promising" scaffold is not supported by the abstract alone, as no potency values, selectivity data, or reproducibility metrics are provided. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in medicinal chemistry, cancer biology, and epigenetic drug discovery would be interested in a novel non-hydroxamate HDAC8 inhibitor scaffold. The use of natural products and shape-based screening may appeal to those focused on fragment-based or natural-product-derived therapeutics. However, interest will depend on the actual potency and selectivity data, which are not visible here. Major strengths The workflow is methodologically coherent, combining shape-based screening, docking, MM-GBSA, enzymatic validation, cellular assays, and MD simulations. The choice of HDAC8 as a target is well justified by its tumor-specific overexpression and independence from corepressor complexes. The identification of a non-hydroxamate scaffold is potentially valuable, as most HDAC inhibitors rely on hydroxamate zinc-binding groups. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "Seven commercially available hits were selected for enzymatic validation, leading to the identification of compound 2 as a promising HDAC8 inhibitor" Evidence pointer Abstract, enzymatic validation section; location not provided Concern No quantitative enzymatic data are reported. The abstract does not state IC50 values, percent inhibition, assay conditions, or the activity of the other six hits. Without these data, the claim that compound 2 is a "promising" inhibitor cannot be assessed. Why it matters The central premise of the manuscript is that compound 2 inhibits HDAC8. Without potency and validation data, the entire downstream cellular and computational work lacks a confirmed molecular basis. Resolution test Provide IC50 values with confidence intervals, a dose-response curve, and comparison to a known HDAC8 inhibitor under identical assay conditions. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Selectivity and specificity Claim pointer "Compound 2 represents a promising non-hydroxamate hit scaffold with promising HDAC8 inhibitory activity" Evidence pointer Abstract, overall conclusion; location not provided Concern No selectivity data against other HDAC isoforms are presented. HDAC inhibitors often show pan-class activity, and the claim of HDAC8 specificity is unsupported. Why it matters Selectivity is critical for therapeutic relevance and for distinguishing this compound from existing broad-spectrum HDAC inhibitors. Without isoform profiling, the scaffold's value is unclear. Resolution test Include a selectivity panel against HDAC1, HDAC2, HDAC3, HDAC6, and other relevant isoforms, with quantitative IC50 values. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Mechanistic evidence Claim pointer "Mechanistic studies... revealed membrane blebbing, mitotic failure, increased reactive oxygen species, and nuclear fragmentation, consistent with apoptosis induction" Evidence pointer Abstract, mechanistic studies section; location not provided Concern The abstract lists multiple assays but provides no quantitative results, statistical comparisons, or dose-response relationships. The phrase "consistent with apoptosis" is a correlative interpretation, not a demonstrated mechanism. Why it matters Apoptosis induction is a strong claim that requires rigorous evidence, including appropriate controls and quantification. Without these, the mechanism remains speculative. Resolution test Provide quantitative data for each assay, including statistical significance, dose dependence, and positive/negative controls. Consider additional apoptosis markers such as caspase activation or PARP cleavage. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Computational validation Claim pointer "1 mus molecular dynamics simulations supported the formation of a persistent ligand-receptor interaction network within the HDAC8 catalytic pocket" Evidence pointer Abstract, MD simulation section; location not provided Concern The abstract does not specify simulation parameters, force field, system setup, or the criteria for "persistent" interactions. No binding free energy values from MD are reported. Why it matters MD simulations are only meaningful if the methodology is reproducible and the interaction analysis is quantified. Without these details, the computational support is weak. Resolution test Provide simulation protocols, convergence metrics, and quantitative interaction occupancy or binding free energy estimates. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Compound naming Evidence pointer Abstract, compound identification; location not provided Issue The compound is referred to as "compound 2" and "ZINC000054202375" but the chemical name is given only once. Consistency in naming would improve readability. Required correction Use a single identifier consistently throughout, with the chemical name defined at first mention. Required correction List the cell lines and their tissue origins in the abstract or indicate that this information is in the main text. Required correction Use the standard abbreviation "µs" or write "microsecond" in full. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 and R1-M2 are blocking. Without quantitative enzymatic potency and isoform selectivity data, the claim that compound 2 is a promising HDAC8 inhibitor is not established. R1-M3 is also blocking because the apoptosis mechanism is not quantitatively supported. R1-M4 is non-blocking but requires methodological detail for reproducibility. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The use of shape-based screening with multiple templates and a natural product library is not novel in itself, but the specific scaffold may offer originality if the potency and selectivity are confirmed. Scientific importance: HDAC8-selective inhibitors are of interest, but the importance is contingent on demonstrated selectivity and cellular efficacy. Interdisciplinary readership: The work spans computational chemistry, medicinal chemistry, and cancer biology, which could attract a broad audience. Technical soundness: The workflow is plausible, but the abstract provides insufficient detail to judge the technical execution. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is generally clear, though the abbreviation "1 mus" and the dense compound naming reduce accessibility. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract alone does not provide sufficient quantitative data to support the central claims of HDAC8 inhibition, selectivity, or apoptosis induction. A revised manuscript with full experimental details and quantitative results would be required for a supportive assessment. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that compound 2 is a "promising HDAC8 inhibitor" is unsupported without IC50 or comparable potency data. The claim that the observed cellular phenotypes are "consistent with apoptosis" is unsupported without quantitative assay results and controls. The claim that MD simulations "supported" a persistent interaction network is unsupported without simulation parameters and quantitative interaction metrics. The claim that compound 2 is a "non-hydroxamate hit scaffold" is plausible but not validated without evidence of the binding mode or zinc-binding group.

no figures, tables, methods, or supporting data were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report all-atom molecular dynamics simulations of a DNA Holliday junction across three AMBER force fields, finding a broad and nearly flat inter-arm-angle landscape, force-field-robust Mg(2+) bridging at the crossover, and force-field-dependent differences in junction openness and stacking-isomer exchange rates. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no numerical tables, simulation protocols, convergence analyses, or statistical details are available Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, simulation convergence metrics, error bars, force-field parameter details, ion placement protocols, trajectory analyses, and all figures and tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially valuable systematic comparison of three AMBER force fields for a biologically and nanotechnologically relevant DNA junction. The central claims, including a nearly flat free-energy landscape, Mg(2+) crossover bridging, and force-field-dependent openness, are plausible and of interest to the DNA nanotechnology and biophysics communities. However, the abstract alone provides insufficient evidence to assess technical rigor, statistical significance, or methodological validity. Several claims, particularly quantitative values and rates, cannot be evaluated without access to the underlying data and analysis details. The work appears promising but is not yet established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in DNA nanotechnology and DNA origami design, who require accurate conformational models of crossover motifs; computational biophysicists studying nucleic acid force-field behavior; and experimentalists investigating homologous recombination intermediates, who would benefit from a validated solution ensemble of Holliday junctions. Major strengths The study addresses a clear gap in the field by systematically comparing three modern AMBER force fields under matched ionic conditions. The focus on a minimal short-arm construct is a sensible simplification that may isolate intrinsic junction behavior. The claim of force-field-robust Mg(2+) bridging, if supported, would be a valuable benchmark for simulation-guided nanostructure design. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The abstract claims a "broad, nearly flat inter-arm-angle landscape, with <1 kcal/mol variation across inter-arm angles of 2-90 degrees" and that "the open state is favored by 0.45-0.63 kcal/mol." Evidence pointer Abstract text; location not provided Concern The abstract provides no information on how free energies were computed, whether error bars or statistical uncertainties are included, or how convergence was assessed. A <1 kcal/mol variation across a wide angular range is a strong quantitative claim that requires careful free-energy estimation, typically via umbrella sampling or weighted histogram analysis, and must be accompanied by uncertainty estimates. Why it matters Without convergence and error analysis, the reported free-energy differences may be within statistical noise, which would undermine the central conclusion of a flat landscape and the relative stability of open versus compact states. Resolution test Provide free-energy profiles with error bars, convergence tests (e.g., block averaging or multiple independent runs), and a description of the sampling method used. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The abstract claims "A Mg(2+) ion occupies the crossover pocket in 92-94% of frames, specifically bridging the A- and C-strand phosphates." Evidence pointer Abstract text; location not provided Concern The occupancy percentage is a precise quantitative claim, but the abstract does not specify how ion occupancy was defined, what distance or coordination criteria were used, or whether this result is consistent across all three force fields. The Li-Merz CM Mg(2+) set is mentioned, but the sensitivity of the result to ion parameters is not discussed. Why it matters Ion occupancy at the crossover is a key mechanistic claim. If the definition of "occupies" is arbitrary or if the result is sensitive to analysis thresholds, the claim may be misleading. Resolution test Define the occupancy criterion explicitly, report occupancy for each force field separately, and show that the result is robust to reasonable variations in the criterion. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The abstract claims "Stacking-isomer exchange between the A/C-continuous and crystallographic B/D isomers proceeds at ~0.5 ns(-1) in this minimal short-arm construct, independent of force field." Evidence pointer Abstract text; location not provided Concern The exchange rate is reported as a single value with no error estimate, no description of how transitions were identified, and no information on the number of observed events. A rate of 0.5 ns(-1) implies frequent transitions, but the statistical reliability of this estimate is unclear, especially given the short-arm construct and the simulation timescales. Why it matters If the rate is based on few events or is not reproducible across replicates, the claim of force-field independence is unsupported. Resolution test Report the number of transitions observed, the simulation length per force field, and a confidence interval for the rate. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Readability for nonspecialists Affected element Abstract terminology Evidence pointer Abstract text Issue The term "crossover pocket" is used without definition, and the distinction between "A/C-continuous" and "B/D isomers" may be unclear to readers outside the Holliday junction field. Required correction Briefly define these terms or provide a schematic reference in the full manuscript. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Scientific importance Affected element Contextual framing Evidence pointer Abstract text Issue The abstract states that the junction "must be accurately modeled for rational DNA-nanodevice design" but does not explain how the specific findings (e.g., the flat landscape or Mg(2+) bridging) would change design practice. Required correction Add one sentence in the abstract or introduction connecting the results to a concrete design implication. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Technical soundness Affected element Force-field comparison Evidence pointer Abstract text Issue The abstract notes that "parmbsc1 yields a more open junction than OL21 and OL24," but does not state whether this difference is statistically significant or whether it arises from specific parameter differences. Required correction Report significance testing or effect sizes for the force-field comparison, and discuss the likely origin of the difference. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3. The abstract lacks the statistical and methodological detail required to validate the quantitative claims of free-energy differences, ion occupancy, and exchange rates. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The systematic three-force-field comparison is a useful contribution, though not unprecedented. Scientific importance: The results could inform DNA nanostructure design and force-field development, but the impact depends on the robustness of the quantitative claims. Interdisciplinary readership: The topic bridges biophysics, computational chemistry, and nanotechnology, and the abstract is largely accessible. Technical soundness: Not assessable from the abstract alone; the missing error analysis and methodological details are critical. Readability for nonspecialists: Generally clear, but some jargon requires definition. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The study addresses a relevant question and the qualitative findings are plausible, but the quantitative claims require substantial additional evidence, including error analysis, convergence tests, and explicit definitions of analysis criteria. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of a "nearly flat" free-energy landscape with <1 kcal/mol variation is unsupported without error bars and convergence analysis. The Mg(2+) occupancy of 92-94% is unsupported without a defined occupancy criterion and per-force-field breakdown. The stacking-isomer exchange rate of ~0.5 ns(-1) is unsupported without event counts and confidence intervals. The statement that OL24's "sugar-pucker shift" is "visible at the junction" is not assessable without structural data. The claim that the results "establish a force-field-robust baseline" is premature given the lack of statistical validation.

结构域高度无序且在实验结构中缺失，其变构调控、蛋白运输和翻译后修饰机制未被治疗性利用；现有药物开发集中于 LDLR 结合界面，而计算研究已开始识别界面之外的候选位点，两者方向不一致。 为什么重要 ：PCSK9 是精准医学的典范靶点（从遗传发现到获批药物仅约二十年），但现有疗法（单抗、siRNA、口服大环肽）均靶向刚性催化结构域，未触及 CHRD 介导的变构调控网络，可能限制了疗效与耐药性管理。 现有方法为何不足 ：静态晶体学无法解析 CHRD 的构象集合；传统筛选聚焦于拥挤的 LDLR 结合界面，忽略了变构位点；物理模拟与 AI 方法各自为战，缺乏统一管线。 精确研究问题 ：Can integrating generative AI with rigorous enhanced sampling in a unified pipeline shift therapeutic targeting toward the disordered regulatory domains (CHRD) of PCSK9 that classical screening has failed to exploit? 04 背景与发展脉络 （标注：以下脉络为「仅本文框架」，基于综述作者的叙述结构，未经外部独立核验） - 阶段一：遗传发现与结构解析 （约 2003–2010）：PCSK9 Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, references, or main text sections provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript text, figures, tables, references, methodological details, and any quantitative results or case studies Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a timely and conceptually interesting perspective on the role of computational methods in PCSK9 therapeutic development, with a clear and defensible central argument about the under-exploitation of the CHRD. However, the abstract is largely programmatic and lacks specific evidence, case examples, or critical evaluation of the methods discussed. The claim that computational methods are identifying candidate sites beyond the LDLR-binding interface is asserted without supporting examples. The review's value will depend entirely on the depth and rigor of the full manuscript, which cannot be assessed from the abstract alone. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biologists working on protein dynamics and allosteric regulation, structural biologists studying PCSK9 or related proprotein convertases, drug discovery researchers focused on cardiovascular targets, and AI practitioners developing generative models for protein design would find this review relevant. The integration of physics-based and AI approaches is a topic of broad interest across these communities. Major strengths The abstract identifies a genuine and important gap in PCSK9 research, namely the neglect of the disordered CHRD in therapeutic development. The framing around gain- and loss-of-function variants as an organizing principle is sensible. The call for integrating generative AI with enhanced sampling is forward-looking and aligns with current trends in computational drug discovery. Major Concerns The abstract provides no concrete examples of computational studies that have identified candidate sites beyond the LDLR interface, no discussion of specific variant dynamics, and no critical assessment of the limitations of the methods mentioned. The central claim about diverging directions between drug discovery and computational methods is stated but not substantiated. The abstract reads more as a proposal than a review of existing work. Minor Comments The abstract could benefit from naming specific computational studies or tools that exemplify the trends described. The phrase "premier model for precision medicine" is somewhat grandiose and could be tempered. The final argument about the next advance would be strengthened by acknowledging potential challenges or counterarguments. conformational landscape in a fatty-acid-state-dependent manner, and that 1H NMR spectra before and after GSNO incubation indicate no pronounced overall structural change. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative data, simulation parameters, statistical analyses, or spectral figures are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, simulation convergence criteria, force field parameters, docking scoring details, NMR acquisition and processing parameters, all figures and tables, statistical treatment, and any validation of the simulation models Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a plausible and potentially interesting hypothesis regarding the interplay between fatty acid binding and Cys34 S-nitrosylation in human serum albumin. However, the evidence base visible in the abstract is insufficient to evaluate the technical soundness of the computational approach, the reliability of the NMR interpretation, or the strength of the central claims. The conclusions are stated in qualitative terms without quantitative support, and the relationship between the simulation results and the NMR data is not made explicit. The work may be of interest to the protein chemistry and post-translational modification communities, but the case is not established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers studying human serum albumin structure-function relationships, post-translational modifications of plasma proteins, fatty acid transport mechanisms, and computational approaches to protein conformational dynamics. The potential link between S-nitrosylation and fatty acid binding could also interest those working on redox signaling and nitrosative stress in cardiovascular and metabolic contexts. Major strengths The research question addresses a genuine gap in understanding how two distinct regulatory inputs, fatty acid occupancy and S-nitrosylation, jointly influence HSA conformational behavior. The combination of molecular docking, MD simulations, and NMR spectroscopy represents a reasonable multi-method approach. The authors explicitly acknowledge the complexity of HSA functional regulation and frame the study within that context. Major Concerns R1-M1 R1-M2 R1-M3 Minor Comments R1-m1 R1-m2 R1-m3 Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The abstract does not provide any quantitative metrics from the MD simulations, such as root-mean-square deviation, root-mean-square fluctuation, or free energy estimates, that would substantiate the claim that FA binding "alters conformational dynamics" and "affects the structural environment of Cys34." The NMR statement is presented as a single qualitative observation without spectral regions analyzed, line width comparisons, or any indication of sensitivity to the expected magnitude of structural change. The docking methodology and its validation are entirely absent. Without these, the central claims cannot be assessed. Scientific importance: moderate, as the findings are largely descriptive and do not yet reveal a new mechanistic principle. Interdisciplinary readership: limited, as the work sits within protein biophysics and computational chemistry without clear broader reach. Technical soundness: not assessable from the abstract, as no methodological detail or quantitative evidence is provided. Readability for nonspecialists: the abstract is clearly written and accessible, but the lack of quantitative context weakens its persuasive power. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. Evidence pointer Abstract only, location not provided Concern The claim that FA binding alters conformational dynamics and the Cys34 environment is presented without any quantitative data. No RMSD, RMSF, hydrogen bond occupancy, solvent accessible surface area, or any other metric is reported. The phrase "alters the conformational dynamics" is vague and could refer to a wide range of effects, from subtle local fluctuations to global domain rearrangements. Without numerical values and appropriate statistical comparisons between FA-free and FA-loaded states, the reader cannot judge the magnitude or significance of the reported changes. Why it matters The central thesis of the paper depends on demonstrating a specific and reproducible effect of FA binding on HSA dynamics. If the effect is small or within simulation noise, the subsequent claims about S-nitrosylation modulation lose their foundation. The absence of quantitative evidence prevents any independent verification of the conclusion. Resolution test Provide quantitative metrics from the MD simulations, including at least RMSD and RMSF profiles for the FA-free and FA-loaded states, with error estimates from replicate simulations. Show a direct comparison of the Cys34 structural environment, such as side chain dihedral distributions or contact maps, with statistical significance testing. Which force field was used, what water model, what simulation length, how many replicates, what temperature and pressure coupling, and how the nitrosylated Cys34 was parameterized are all unknown. Similarly, the docking protocol is not described, including the search algorithm, scoring function, and how the GSH and GSNO poses were validated. Without this information, the technical reliability of the computational results cannot be assessed. Why it matters Molecular dynamics and docking results are highly sensitive to parameterization and protocol choices. The nitrosylation modification in particular requires careful parameterization, and errors here would propagate through all subsequent analyses. The lack of methodological detail means that even if the results are correct, they cannot be reproduced or evaluated by the community. Resolution test Provide a complete methods section in the manuscript, including force field parameters for the nitrosylated cysteine, simulation length and equilibration protocol, number of replicates, and convergence criteria. For docking, describe the software, scoring function, and any validation against known binding modes. No information is given about which spectral region was examined, whether the spectra were overlaid and compared quantitatively, what the signal-to-noise ratio was, or what magnitude of structural change would be detectable with this method. A 1D 1H NMR spectrum of a 66 kDa protein is highly crowded, and the absence of visible changes does not necessarily indicate the absence of structural changes, particularly in localized regions such as the Cys34 environment. Why it matters The NMR data are the only experimental evidence in the study, and they are used to support the claim that S-nitrosylation does not cause global structural changes. If the sensitivity of the method is insufficient to detect the expected changes, the conclusion is not supported. The abstract does not state what the functional consequence of the observed conformational changes might be, such as altered ligand binding affinity or changed susceptibility to further modifications. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that FA binding "affects the structural environment of Cys34 and other functionally significant regions" is unsupported in the abstract because no quantitative simulation data are provided. The claim that S-nitrosylation "influenced the conformational landscape of albumin in a manner dependent on its fatty acid-bound state" is unsupported because no comparative data between the four conditions (FA-free, FA-loaded, nitrosylated, non-nitrosylated) are shown. Assessment boundary Claims and evidence presented in the abstract; no methods, figures, tables, or supplementary material were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The author reports development of an interpretable, gene-specific random-forest classifier for ACVRL1 missense variants, using protein-stability estimates, a conservation score, and structural context, achieving performance comparable to AlphaMissense while providing transparent evidence for each call. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no data, code, or detailed methodology Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, training/validation data splits, variant lists, ClinVar accession details, publication traceability criteria, cross-validation procedure, confidence intervals, calibration metrics, and any code or reproducibility information Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially useful contribution to variant classification in ACVRL1, addressing a real gap in interpretability of black-box predictors. However, the evidence provided is insufficient to evaluate the validity of the performance claims, the robustness of the methodology, or the generalizability of the findings. Several technical details are missing, and the reported equivalence to AlphaMissense is only partially supported. The work is of interest to the HHT and PAH genetics community, but the case is not established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Clinical geneticists and molecular diagnosticians working on hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and pulmonary arterial hypertension, as well as researchers developing interpretable machine-learning tools for variant classification. The gene-specific, evidence-transparent approach could aid VUS prioritization for functional testing. Major strengths The problem is well-defined and clinically relevant. The focus on interpretability addresses a genuine limitation of AlphaMissense. The use of multiple evidence types (stability, conservation, structure) is reasonable. The inclusion of a temporal validation set (2025-2026 variants) is a positive feature. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer "A structural/conservation-only classifier (Model 1b) reached a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.954 (95% CI 0.916-0.984), and a model adding sequence-based predictors (Model 1) reached 0.979, versus 0.983 for AlphaMissense on the same variants." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract reports cross-validated AUC values but does not describe the cross-validation scheme, the number of folds, the stratification strategy, or whether the same folds were used for all models. The 95% confidence intervals are presented without specifying the method of calculation. The comparison to AlphaMissense is made "on the same variants," but it is unclear whether AlphaMissense scores were obtained from the public database or recomputed, and whether the same variant set was used for all comparisons. Why it matters Without a clear description of the validation protocol, the reported performance metrics cannot be independently assessed. Overfitting or data leakage in the training procedure could inflate AUC values. The equivalence claim depends critically on the comparability of the evaluation conditions. Resolution test Provide a detailed methods section describing the cross-validation procedure, the exact variant sets used for training and testing, the source and version of AlphaMissense scores, and the statistical test used to support the equivalence claim. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer "Benign variants were the main weakness: Model 1b correctly classified 10/15, against 14/15 for AlphaMissense." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The benign variant set is extremely small (n=15), and the abstract does not state how these were selected, whether they were balanced across the structural or functional categories, or whether the same 15 variants were used for all models. The difference between 10/15 and 14/15 is based on a very small sample and may not be statistically meaningful. Why it matters The claim that benign variants are the main weakness is a key finding, but with only 15 examples, the estimate is highly uncertain. The abstract does not report sensitivity, specificity, or precision-recall metrics, which are more informative for imbalanced clinical datasets. Resolution test Report the full confusion matrix for each model, provide the benign variant selection criteria, and include confidence intervals or a statistical test for the difference in benign classification performance. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Reproducibility Claim pointer "I annotated 899 ACVRL1 missense variants with protein-stability estimates (FoldX, DynaMut2), a GREMLIN-style conservation score, and structural context." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract does not specify the source of the 899 variants, the version of the protein structure used, the parameters for FoldX and DynaMut2, the exact definition of the GREMLIN-style conservation score, or the criteria for assigning structural context. No code, data, or supplementary material is mentioned. Why it matters Reproducibility is a core requirement for computational studies. Without these details, other researchers cannot replicate the annotation pipeline or the classifier. The gene-specific nature of the model also means that the approach cannot be generalized without a clear description of the feature engineering. Resolution test Provide a detailed methods section with all software versions, parameters, and data sources, and make the code and annotated variant list available in a public repository. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence quality Claim pointer "I then trained random-forest classifiers on 311 variants with labels traceable to ClinVar or a publication (296 pathogenic-like, 15 benign-like)." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The label source is described as "traceable to ClinVar or a publication," but the abstract does not specify the ClinVar review status (e.g., criteria provided, multiple submitters, expert panel), the publication criteria for labeling, or how conflicting labels were resolved. The class imbalance (296 vs 15) is extreme and may affect model training and evaluation. Why it matters The quality of the training labels is the foundation of the classifier. If labels are derived from sources with varying evidence standards, the model may learn biases rather than true pathogenic signals. The extreme class imbalance also raises concerns about the reliability of the reported AUC, which can be optimistic in such settings. Resolution test Provide a detailed label curation protocol, including ClinVar star ratings, publication inclusion criteria, and conflict resolution rules. Report performance metrics that are robust to class imbalance, such as precision-recall AUC or balanced accuracy. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Abstract wording Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The phrase "equivalence within +/-0.05 AUC was supported for Model 1 only" is ambiguous. It is unclear what statistical test was used and whether the equivalence margin was pre-specified. Required correction Specify the statistical test (e.g., two one-sided tests) and the pre-registered equivalence margin, or rephrase to describe the observed difference and its uncertainty. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract does not report any measure of calibration or uncertainty for individual variant calls, which is important for clinical use. Required correction Add a statement on calibration or provide a reference to where this information can be found in the full manuscript. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Interpretability Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The claim that the classifier "shows the structural or evolutionary evidence behind each call" is not substantiated with an example or a description of the interpretability mechanism (e.g., feature importance, SHAP values). Required correction Provide a brief example of an interpretable output or describe the feature attribution method used. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Scope Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract does not discuss the potential impact of the extreme class imbalance on the practical utility of the classifier for VUS prioritization. Required correction Add a sentence acknowledging the limitation and describing how the classifier should be used in practice given the imbalance. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (validation protocol and equivalence testing) R1-M2 (benign variant set size and statistical robustness) R1-M3 (reproducibility of annotation pipeline) R1-M4 (label curation and class imbalance) Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the classifier "can approach AlphaMissense for ACVRL1" is only partially supported, as equivalence was demonstrated for Model 1 only, and the benign variant performance was notably worse. The claim that the classifier "shows the structural or evolutionary evidence behind each call" is not supported by any example or description of the interpretability mechanism in the abstract. The generalizability of the classifier to other genes or to variants outside the training distribution is not addressed and cannot be assessed from the abstract. The clinical utility of the classifier for VUS prioritization is stated as a potential use but is not supported by any prospective or functional validation data. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality Moderate. The application of interpretable machine learning to a specific gene with multiple evidence types is not entirely novel, but the focus on ACVRL1 and the explicit comparison to AlphaMissense with interpretability as a goal is a reasonable contribution. Scientific importance Moderate. Variant classification in ACVRL1 is clinically relevant, and improving interpretability of computational predictors could aid clinical decision-making. However, the impact is limited to a single gene and the abstract does not demonstrate a clear advance over existing tools beyond interpretability. Interdisciplinary readership Limited. The work is primarily of interest to computational biologists and clinical geneticists in the HHT/PAH field. The abstract does not frame the findings in a way that would attract a broader readership. Technical soundness Not established from the supplied material. The abstract lacks sufficient methodological detail to assess the validity of the performance claims, the robustness of the validation, or the reproducibility of the approach. Readability for nonspecialists The abstract is reasonably clear but uses technical terms (e.g., ROC-AUC, GREMLIN-style) without sufficient explanation for a general scientific audience. The clinical context is introduced adequately. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract presents a potentially useful approach, but the lack of methodological detail, the small benign variant set, and the incomplete equivalence testing prevent a positive recommendation. The author should provide the full methods, data, and code, and address the specific concerns raised above before the case can be considered.

manuscript claim summary The authors present SLIP, a framework for constructing synthetic protein fitness landscapes with tunable difficulty based on Potts models, intended for benchmarking machine learning-guided directed evolution (MLDE) pipelines. The framework is claimed to be extendable to any protein family with a sequence alignment, and the tuning framework is claimed to produce landscapes sufficiently challenging for benchmarking MLDE pipelines. The software is open-source. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, methodological details, or validation data are visible Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, supplementary information, code repository contents, and any experimental or computational validation results Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a potentially useful contribution to the protein engineering community, addressing a real need for standardized synthetic benchmarks in MLDE. The concept of using Potts models with tunable difficulty is reasonable and aligns with existing literature on fitness landscape inference. However, the abstract provides insufficient detail to evaluate the technical soundness of the tuning mechanism, the validity of the benchmarking claims, or the practical utility of the framework. The central claim that the landscapes are "sufficiently challenging" is not supported by any visible evidence. The contribution is plausible but currently not established from the provided material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers developing or applying machine learning methods for protein design, particularly those working on directed evolution pipelines. The framework could serve as a standardized testbed for comparing MLDE strategies, which would be of interest to both computational and experimental groups seeking to optimize their design-build-test-learn loops. The open-source availability enhances potential adoption. Major strengths The problem addressed is well-motivated, as experimental benchmarking of MLDE pipelines is costly and often impractical. The use of Potts models is a principled choice, given their established success in capturing sequence constraints from alignments. The claim of generalizability to any protein family with an alignment is attractive and, if true, would broaden the framework's applicability. The open-source release is a positive step for reproducibility and community use. Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and evidence presented in the abstract; no full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors use binary patterning, a sequence design strategy for four-helix bundles, as a probe to ask whether the protein language model ESM2 captures the physical rules governing protein folding. They report that ESMFold predictions of synthetic libraries recapitulate experimental trends in helicity, compactness, and topological diversity as a function of sequence length, but do not distinguish successful from unsuccessful individual designs. Principal component analysis of ESM2 embeddings reveals representations of hydrophobic patterning, helix-loop boundaries, and heptad register. Extension to all 128 heptad binary patterns yields a jellyfish-shaped manifold whose dominant axis is hydrophobic composition, with paired components encoding pattern phase. Manifold geometry depends on amino-acid chemistry, repeat number, and linker sequence, and collapses when amino acids are assigned to arbitrary categories. The authors conclude that ESM2 combines general repeat recognition with protein-specific physicochemical information, and propose synthetic sequence libraries as experimentally grounded probes of pLM representations. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, methods, or supplementary materials were provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript text, all figures and tables, methods description, statistical analyses, code repository contents, and supplementary materials Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a conceptually interesting approach to probing protein language model representations using a well-established biophysical design principle. The central question, whether ESM2 encodes the physical grammar of protein folding, is timely and relevant. However, the abstract alone provides insufficient detail to evaluate the rigor of the analyses, the validity of the conclusions, or the significance of the findings. Several claims are made without supporting quantitative evidence, and the relationship between the observed embedding geometry and the physical rules of folding remains correlational rather than causal. The manuscript may have merit, but the case is not established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein language model interpretability, protein design, and computational biophysics would be interested. The work addresses whether pLMs implicitly learn physical principles, which is relevant to both the machine learning community developing protein models and the biophysics community using them for design and prediction. The use of synthetic sequence libraries as probes is a methodological idea that could be adopted by others studying model representations. Major strengths The choice of binary patterning as a probe is well motivated, as it is a design principle with known experimental success rates and biophysical rationale. The use of a systematic enumeration of all 128 heptad patterns is a thorough approach. The observation that embedding geometry collapses under arbitrary amino-acid categorization is a potentially informative control. The framing of synthetic libraries as experimentally grounded probes is a useful conceptual contribution. ：本文处于「蛋白质结构相关计算研究 × AI 方法」交叉点，具体位于 PLM 与 MD 模拟融合的路径上。其核心主张是：在小型 PLM（35M 参数）上通过第二阶段的动力学增强持续预训练，使模型在变异效应预测任务上达到或超越数十亿参数模型，从而挑战「规模至上」范式，提出「显式结构动力学监督可作为参数规模的有效替代」这一论点。 02 一句话总结 本文通过一个 35M 参数的小型蛋白质语言模型 DynamicsPLM，在第二阶段多任务持续预训练中引入显式的残基级和配对级分子动力学头，使模型在推理时仅从序列出发、通过平衡进化保守性得分与结构动力学扰动得分来零样本预测变异效应，在 ProteinGym 和 Tsuboyama 数据集上达到 100M 参数以下模型的最高精度，并匹配或超越若干十亿级序列模型。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：如何在不依赖大规模参数扩展的前提下，让蛋白质语言模型获得对蛋白质物理动力学的显式理解，从而提升变异效应预测的准确性？ 为什么重要 ：变异效应预测在疾病机制理解、蛋白质工程和药物设计中具有直接应用价值。现有 PLM 主要依赖序列语料中的进化约束，但缺乏对蛋白质折叠后物理动力学的显式建模；而纯物理模型（如 MD）又忽略了进化序列统计信息。两者融合有望互补短板。 现有方法为何不足 ： 大规模 PLM（如 ESM-2、ProtTrans）通过参数扩展提升性能，但计算成本高、可解释性差，且仍缺乏显式物理动力学信号。 纯 MD 或基于结构的模型计算昂贵，难以大规模应用于变异效应扫描。 已有融合方法（如 ESM-IF、MIF-Net）多依赖结构输入或需要额外结构预测步骤，未能从序列直接端到端地融合动力学信息。 精确研究问题 ：Can a small PLM (35M parameters) enriched with explicit molecular dynamics supervision during continual pretraining achieve state-of-the-art zero-shot variant effect prediction without scaling to billions of parameters? 04 背景与发展脉络 个蛋白质上进行多任务持续预训练，添加显式的残基级（residue-level）和配对级（pairwise）分子动力学头，同时保留原有进化知识。 - 推理阶段 ：仅从序列输入，计算零样本变异效应，通过平衡两个得分——进化保守性得分（evolutionary plausibility score）与结构动力学扰动得分（structural dynamics disruption score）——得到最终预测。 2) 核心洞察 [Analysis] 本文的核心洞察在于： 显式的结构动力学监督可以作为参数规模的替代品 。具体而言： - 通过在持续预训练阶段注入 MD 衍生的动力学标签（残基级波动、配对协同运动），模型可以在不增加参数量的情况下获得对蛋白质物理行为的显式表征。 - 进化信息与动力学信息在推理时通过得分平衡而非特征拼接的方式融合，避免了灾难性遗忘，同时允许两个信号独立贡献。 - 这一设计隐含假设：变异效应主要由「进化保守性」和「结构动力学扰动」两个正交因素决定，二者互补而非冗余。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] 从方法论层面，本文提供了一个可迁移的范式： 在小型模型上通过任务特定的持续预训练注入物理先验，可以在特定下游任务上匹敌大规模模型 manuscript claim summary The authors propose DynamicsPLM, a 35-million-parameter protein language model that combines evolutionary sequence information with explicit molecular dynamics supervision via a second-stage continual pretraining strategy on over 60,000 proteins. The model is claimed to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy among models under 100M parameters on ProteinGym and the Tsuboyama folding stability dataset, and to match or outperform several billion-scale sequence-based models. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, benchmark tables, or methodological details are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, benchmark performance numbers, model architecture details, training hyperparameters, dataset composition and preprocessing, baseline comparison lists, statistical significance tests, and code repository contents Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a conceptually appealing idea: enriching a small protein language model with explicit molecular dynamics supervision to achieve competitive variant effect prediction without scaling to billions of parameters. The motivation is clear and the proposed approach is timely given the field's focus on parameter efficiency. However, the abstract provides no quantitative evidence whatsoever. No performance numbers, no comparison tables, no statistical measures, and no methodological specifics are visible. The central claims of state-of-the-art performance and equivalence to billion-scale models are therefore entirely unverifiable from the supplied material. The writing is generally clear, though the final sentence of the abstract contains an apparent error referencing "LoMuS" instead of "DynamicsPLM." Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biologists and machine learning researchers working on protein function prediction, variant effect prediction, and protein language models. The parameter-efficiency angle would also appeal to groups with limited computational resources who cannot train or fine-tune billion-scale models. The integration of molecular dynamics with sequence-based representation learning may interest researchers at the interface of biophysics and deep learning. Major strengths The conceptual framing is strong: the abstract clearly identifies a gap between sequence-only PLMs and dynamics-only models, and proposes a principled way to bridge it. The parameter efficiency claim (35M parameters) is notable and, if substantiated, would be a meaningful contribution. The use of continual pretraining to preserve evolutionary knowledge while adding dynamics supervision is a sensible design choice. The zero-shot inference approach from sequence alone is practically attractive. In a field where benchmark results are the primary currency, omitting all numbers from the abstract is a critical deficiency. 研究问题 具体问题 ：如何将已知的静态大分子复合物结构（如病毒衣壳、核糖体）自动转化为可模拟自组装动力学的粗粒化模型，且无需手动构建？ 为什么重要 ：自组装是生命系统核心过程（如病毒衣壳形成、核糖体组装），但静态结构（PDB、AlphaFold3）不包含组装路径信息；计算模拟是研究组装动力学的关键手段，但全原子模拟在时间尺度上不可行。 现有方法不足 ：现有粗粒化建模通常需要大量手动操作、领域知识，且难以保证全局结构约束（如对称性、取向）；缺乏从结构到模拟的自动化流程。 精确研究问题 ：Can a user-friendly Python package automatically transform arbitrary PDB/AlphaFold3 structures into thermodynamically reversible, manuscript claim summary The authors present ioNERDSS, a Python package that converts 3D atomic protein structures into coarse-grained (CG) models for stochastic reaction-diffusion simulations of macromolecular self-assembly using the NERDSS software. The package enforces orientational constraints, regularizes repeated subunits, initializes binding affinities via ML tools, and is benchmarked on over 50,000 PDB structures. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, benchmark details, or validation data are visible Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, methods section, figures, tables, benchmark datasets, code availability statement, and any supplementary information Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a potentially valuable software tool that addresses a real gap in the field, namely converting static structural data into dynamic self-assembly simulations. The concept is timely and the scope of benchmarking (50,000 PDB structures) is ambitious. However, the abstract provides insufficient quantitative evidence to evaluate the tool's performance, reliability, or novelty relative to existing approaches. The claims of successful assembly for "the majority" of CG models are vague and unverifiable from the supplied material. The technical approach is plausible but key details on how structural constraints are enforced, how ML predictions are integrated, and how thermodynamic reversibility is maintained are absent. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biophysicists and structural biologists studying macromolecular assembly, particularly those working on viral capsids, protein complexes, and synthetic biology applications. Researchers developing coarse-grained simulation methods and those interested in integrating AlphaFold/PDB structures with dynamic modeling would also find this relevant. The tool's user-friendly Python interface could appeal to experimentalists seeking to model assembly pathways from known structures. Major strengths The tool addresses a clear and important gap between static structural biology and dynamic simulation of assembly processes. The approach of enforcing orientational constraints and regularizing repeated subunits is conceptually sound for maintaining target topology. The integration of ML-based affinity prediction and thermodynamic reversibility constraints shows awareness of both accuracy and physical realism. The large-scale benchmarking effort (50,000 structures) suggests a serious validation attempt. Major Concerns R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "Benchmarking on over 50,000 PDB structures shows the majority of CG models will stochastically assemble into target structures." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The central performance claim is presented without any quantitative detail. What fraction constitutes "the majority"? What is the distribution of success rates across different structure types, sizes, or symmetries? How was "successful assembly" defined and measured? No error rates, failure modes, or comparative baselines are provided. Why it matters This is the primary evidence that the tool works as claimed. Without quantitative benchmarks, the reader cannot assess whether the tool is genuinely useful or whether it fails for most realistic targets. The claim is too vague to support the tool's utility. Resolution test Provide specific success rates, stratified by structure class (e.g., capsids, multi-subunit complexes, fibers), with clear definitions of assembly success (e.g., RMSD to target, fraction of native contacts). Include failure analysis and comparison to existing tools or naive approaches. R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer "Each protein chain is defined by a rigid subunit with discrete interfaces and explicit orientational constraints that enforce a structured assembly." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract does not explain how orientational constraints are derived from atomic structures, how interfaces are identified, or how the rigid subunit approximation handles conformational flexibility that is often critical for assembly. The method for regularizing repeated subunits to preserve topology across stochastic pathways is also not described. Why it matters These are the core methodological innovations that distinguish ioNERDSS from existing CG approaches. Without understanding the constraint derivation and regularization scheme, the reader cannot evaluate whether the method is generalizable or limited to specific structure types. The rigid subunit assumption may fail for proteins with significant domain motion. Resolution test Describe the algorithm for interface detection and constraint assignment, including how flexibility is handled. Provide validation on structures with known conformational changes during assembly. Show that the regularization scheme does not introduce artifacts in assembly pathways. R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility Claim pointer "We initialize pairwise binding affinities using ML prediction tools, and our default CG models are all constrained by thermodynamic reversibility to reach an equilibrium steady-state." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The specific ML tools used, their training data, and the accuracy of their affinity predictions for the diverse set of PDB structures are not stated. The thermodynamic reversibility constraint is mentioned but its implementation and impact on simulation outcomes are unclear. Why it matters Binding affinities are critical parameters that determine assembly pathways and outcomes. If the ML predictions are inaccurate for certain protein classes, the simulations may produce incorrect results. The reversibility constraint could also limit the exploration of kinetically trapped states that are biologically relevant. Resolution test Specify the ML tools and their validation on experimental binding data. Show how affinity prediction errors propagate to assembly outcomes. Demonstrate that the reversibility constraint does not preclude capturing non-equilibrium assembly behavior. The claim that the tool "supports assembly of structures with thousands of subunits" is unverifiable without performance data. The claim that ML-based affinity predictions are reliable for diverse protein classes is unsupported. The claim that thermodynamic reversibility constraints ensure physically meaningful equilibrium states is not substantiated. The overall utility of the tool relative to existing CG simulation approaches is not assessable from the abstract.
