核心假设 : 基于计算指标（界面质量、折叠稳定性、SAP 分布），可预测一个失败 binder 是否值得投入实验挽救。 - 增量 : 提供「挽救优先级」排序工具，减少实验资源浪费。 - 初步方法 : 收集已尝试挽救的 binder 数据（成功/失败），提取计算特征，训练可挽救性分类器。 - 验证方式 : 对新失败 binder 进行挽救实验，对比预测准确性。 - 失败模式 : 「可挽救性」定义模糊；挽救策略多样（表面突变、亲和力成熟、支架优化），难以统一。 候选名称 : 表面疏水性与 binder 体内半衰期的关联研究 - 来源局限/观察 : 本文仅关注体外溶液行为（SEC-MALS），未测试体内稳定性。 - 核心假设 : 非界面 SAP 不仅影响体外自聚集，还影响体内蛋白水解稳定性和免疫原性。 - 增量 : 将 SAP 从「溶液行为指标」扩展为「体内成药性指标」。 - 初步方法 : 对 R2-6.1/R2-6.2 及对照进行小鼠体内药代动力学实验，测量半衰期；关联 SAP 分布。 - 验证方式 : 相关性分析；多 variant 验证。 - 失败模式 : 体内稳定性受多种因素影响（蛋白水解位点、免疫原性），SAP 可能不是主导因素。 Review setup Input scope Full manuscript text including abstract, introduction, results, discussion, methods, and supplementary figure legends Assessment boundary Scientific content, methodological rigor, validity of claims relative to presented evidence, and alignment with Nature-style criteria Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present two de novo protein binder design campaigns targeting the SARS-CoV-2 RBD, identify two distinct failure modes (insufficient interface stability vs. excessive surface hydrophobicity leading to self-association), develop a computational framework integrating AlphaFold, MD simulations, docking, and SAP analysis to diagnose these failure modes, and demonstrate prospective rescue of a failed binder through targeted surface redesign Visible evidence base Computational design outputs, AlphaFold2/2-Multimer/3 predictions, MD simulation trajectories, SAP calculations, LightDock docking results, SEC-MALS, SPR, CD spectroscopy, ELISA data Missing materials affecting confidence Supplementary figures S1–S12 and Tables S1–S2 referenced but not provided; raw MD trajectory data not available; detailed sequence information for all 22 designs not shown; negative control binding data for ELISA not fully described; statistical analysis details for comparing computational metrics across groups not provided Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript addresses a timely and important problem in de novo protein binder design: understanding why computational designs fail and how to diagnose and correct specific failure modes. The authors present a well-structured study combining computational prediction with experimental validation, and the central finding that surface hydrophobicity represents a critical trade-off axis is mechanistically plausible and practically useful. However, the evidence base is incomplete in several respects. The most significant concern is that the central claim of "rescue" rests on only two redesigned variants, both showing modest low-micromolar affinity, without demonstration that these affinities are sufficient for practical applications or that the redesign strategy generalizes beyond this single case. The computational framework is thoughtfully assembled, but the discriminative power of individual metrics is not rigorously quantified, and the authors do not establish clear thresholds or decision rules that would allow others to apply their diagnostic approach prospectively. The manuscript would be strengthened by additional experimental replicates, a broader set of rescued variants, and more systematic benchmarking of the computational metrics against each other. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational protein designers and engineers will find the failure mode analysis and the SAP-based diagnostic framework directly applicable to their own design pipelines. Researchers working on SARS-CoV-2 therapeutics may be interested in the specific binders generated, though the modest affinities limit immediate translational relevance. The broader protein engineering community will value the demonstration that multi-objective optimization, rather than single-metric maximization, is required for successful binder design. Methodologists developing AI-based protein design tools may use the identified failure modes to inform training objectives and filtering strategies. Major strengths 1. The study addresses a genuinely important and understudied problem: systematic analysis of why de novo designed binders fail, rather than only reporting successes. 2. The two design campaigns provide a natural experimental contrast that cleanly separates the two failure modes, strengthening the causal interpretation. 3. The integration of multiple complementary computational methods (AF2, AFM, AF3, MD, docking, SAP) is thoughtful and reflects best practices in the field. 4. The prospective rescue experiment provides direct experimental validation of the diagnostic framework, which is a significant strength. 5. The writing is clear and accessible, with appropriate caveats about limitations. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency for central claim Claim pointer "Guided by these insights, we prospectively redesigned a representative failed binder... Experimental characterization confirmed that the redesigned variants were stable monomers and acquired low μM binding affinities." Evidence pointer Results section "Computational Design Rescue of Protein Binders"; Figure 3; Table S2 Concern The rescue claim rests on only two variants (R2-6.1 and R2-6.2) derived from a single parent design (R2-6). Both show KD values of 1.4 and 1.7 μM, respectively. While these represent clear improvements over the non-binding parent, the authors do not demonstrate that this approach generalizes. The manuscript would be substantially strengthened by rescuing additional Round 2 designs or by showing that the same principles apply to Round 1 designs. Furthermore, the authors do not report the affinity of the original R2-6 design in the same assay, making it difficult to quantify the magnitude of improvement. The claim that this constitutes a "rescue" implies functional utility, but low-micromolar affinity may be insufficient for most practical applications. Why it matters The central practical claim of the manuscript is that the diagnostic framework can guide successful redesign. With only two variants from one parent, the evidence for generalizability is weak. If the approach only works for this specific case, its utility as a general framework is limited. Resolution test Provide rescue data for at least 3-5 additional failed designs from both Round 1 and Round 2, or provide a clear statistical demonstration that the success rate is significantly better than chance. Report the affinity of the parent R2-6 design under identical assay conditions to enable direct comparison. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Quantitative rigor of metric discrimination Claim pointer "we establish complementary computational signatures that distinguish these failure modes and reveal their underlying structural determinants" Evidence pointer Results section "Retrospective Analysis of the Designed Binders"; Figures 1-2 Concern The authors present multiple computational metrics (AF2 confidence, AFM scores, MD stability, docking quality, SAP) but do not provide a systematic quantitative comparison of how well each metric, or combinations of metrics, discriminates between successful and failed designs. The narrative describes qualitative differences (e.g., "Round 1 designs displayed substantially larger L-RMSD values") but does not report effect sizes, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. It is unclear whether any single metric would be sufficient for diagnosis or whether the full multi-metric framework is necessary. Why it matters For the framework to be practically useful, users need to know which metrics are most informative and how to weight them. Without quantitative benchmarking, the relative importance of each computational tool remains unclear. Resolution test Perform a systematic comparison of all metrics across the three groups (active controls, Round 1, Round 2), reporting appropriate statistics (e.g., Mann-Whitney U tests with multiple testing correction). Consider a simple classifier (e.g., logistic regression or decision tree) to identify which metrics are most predictive of experimental success. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Control group appropriateness Claim pointer "benchmarked them against a set of experimentally validated binders" Evidence pointer Results section "Computational Design of Protein Binders"; Figure 1 Concern The control set consists of binders that underwent yeast display selection and affinity maturation, as acknowledged in the Discussion. This means the controls are not directly comparable to the de novo designs, which were not subjected to any experimental selection. The authors note this limitation but do not fully address its implications. Specifically, the affinity-matured controls may have evolved to reduce surface hydrophobicity through selection pressures that are absent in the computational designs, potentially biasing the comparison. Why it matters If the controls are systematically different from the designs in ways beyond binding affinity, the conclusions about what distinguishes successful from failed designs may not be generalizable to purely computational design pipelines. Resolution test Include additional controls that are computationally designed and experimentally validated without affinity maturation, if available. Alternatively, explicitly discuss how the selection history of the controls might affect each metric and whether the conclusions remain valid. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility and methodological detail Claim pointer "The redesign combined two complementary strategies... Among the redesigned variants, R2-6.1 was selected for experimental characterization." Evidence pointer Results section "Computational Design Rescue of Protein Binders"; Methods section Concern The selection criteria for choosing R2-6.1 among the redesigned variants are not clearly specified. The authors state that R2-6.1 was "selected" but do not describe how many variants were generated, what the range of predicted properties was, or why R2-6.1 was chosen over others. Similarly, the criteria for selecting R2-6.2 after loop remodeling are not stated. This lack of transparency makes it difficult to assess potential selection bias. Why it matters If the authors cherry-picked the best-performing variant from a large pool, the success rate of the redesign strategy would be much lower than implied. Transparent reporting of the full design space and selection criteria is essential for evaluating the approach. Resolution test Report the total number of redesign variants generated, the distribution of their predicted properties (SAP, binding energy, etc.), and the specific criteria used to select R2-6.1 and R2-6.2 for experimental testing. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity of presentation Affected element Figure 1 Evidence pointer Results section "Computational Design of Protein Binders" Issue The description of Figure 1 is minimal and does not clearly explain what is shown in each panel. Given that this figure introduces the design strategies and the control set, a more detailed legend would help readers understand the experimental design. Required correction Expand the Figure 1 legend to describe each panel explicitly, including the design strategy, the number of designs, and the key features being illustrated. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Statistical reporting Affected element MD simulation analysis Evidence pointer Results section "Retrospective Analysis of the Designed Binders"; Figure 2c Issue The manuscript reports median values for L-RMSD and RMSF across groups but does not provide measures of variability (e.g., interquartile ranges) or the number of independent simulations contributing to each median. This makes it difficult to assess the robustness of the reported differences. Required correction Add measures of variability (e.g., error bars or shaded regions) to the relevant figures and report the number of replicates in the figure legends or text. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Completeness of methods Affected element SPR experimental details Evidence pointer Methods section "Surface Plasmon Resonance" Issue The SPR methods do not specify the number of independent experiments performed, how the kinetic parameters were averaged across replicates, or whether the reported KD values include confidence intervals. This limits the ability to assess the reliability of the binding measurements. Required correction Report the number of independent SPR experiments, the variability across replicates, and provide confidence intervals for the reported KD values. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Interpretation of AF3 results Evidence pointer Results section "Retrospective Analysis of the Designed Binders"; Figure S7b Issue The authors note that AF3 failed to accurately predict the redesigned variants R2-6.1 and R2-6.2 but do not discuss possible reasons for this failure or its implications for using AF3 as a screening tool. Required correction Add a brief discussion of why AF3 might fail for these designs and whether this limitation affects the general applicability of the framework. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Generalizability of SAP threshold Affected element Discussion section Evidence pointer Discussion section, paragraph on SAP Issue The authors suggest that total SAP values between approximately 30 and 45 were associated with well-behaved binders, but this range is derived from a small dataset and may not generalize to other targets or scaffold types. Required correction Explicitly state that this range is empirical and target-specific, and recommend that users calibrate SAP thresholds for their own systems. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (insufficient evidence for generalizable rescue), R1-M2 (lack of quantitative metric comparison), R1-M3 (control group comparability), R1-M4 (selection criteria transparency) Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : The manuscript addresses a relatively underexplored question in protein design, and the systematic analysis of failure modes is a valuable contribution. However, the individual computational methods used are all established, and the novelty lies primarily in their integration and application to this specific problem. Scientific importance : Understanding why de novo designs fail is of high importance to the protein design community, and the proposed framework could improve design success rates. The specific application to SARS-CoV-2 RBD is of moderate interest given the availability of many existing binders. Interdisciplinary readership : The work bridges computational protein design, biophysics, and experimental biochemistry. The writing is accessible, but the depth of computational detail may limit appeal to purely experimental audiences. Technical soundness : The computational methods are appropriate and well-executed, but the lack of quantitative benchmarking and limited experimental validation of the rescue strategy weaken the technical case. Readability for nonspecialists : The manuscript is generally well-written with clear explanations of key concepts. However, some sections assume familiarity with protein design terminology and would benefit from brief definitions. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The core idea is sound and the framework is potentially valuable, but the evidence for the central rescue claim needs strengthening, and the quantitative rigor of the metric comparison needs improvement. If the authors can address these concerns, the manuscript would make a useful contribution to the protein design literature. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the two failure modes are "distinct" and mutually exclusive is not fully supported; some designs may exhibit both insufficient interface stability and excessive hydrophobicity. The assertion that "successful binders appear to occupy a relatively narrow window of total interface hydrophobicity" is based on a small number of examples and lacks statistical support. The statement that "SolubleMLPNN can mitigate, but not fully eliminate, the problem of exposed hydrophobicity" is based on computational predictions only, without experimental validation of the redesigned sequences. The claim that the framework provides "practical criteria for prioritizing candidates before experimental characterization" is not demonstrated with a prospective test on an independent set of designs. The relationship between the "false membrane" constraint used in LightDock and the actual experimental conditions is not fully justified.

Input scope Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and conclusions as presented in the abstract; no access to methods, figures, tables, or supplementary materials Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present SeqSol, a sequence-level solubility prediction model trained on 71,425 proteins, which achieves 75.8% accuracy and an AUC of 0.840 on an independent test set. The model prioritizes single-amino-acid substitutions via WT-mutant rescoring. Candidate sites are further filtered by conformational flexibility, relative solvent accessibility, and evolutionary conservation. The integrated framework, SeqSol-FECS, reportedly increased the solubility of two industrial enzymes from 56.18% and 10.53% to over 95% while maintaining specific activities, using only 30 experimentally tested mutations. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no methods section, dataset description, model architecture details, experimental protocols, or numerical validation data beyond the metrics stated in the abstract Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, model training and validation details, dataset composition and split strategy, definition of the independent test set, mutation selection criteria, experimental solubility assay protocols, activity measurement methods, statistical analysis, and all figures and tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially useful framework for protein solubility engineering, combining sequence-level prediction with structural filtering criteria. The reported performance metrics and experimental outcomes are encouraging. However, the abstract alone provides insufficient detail to evaluate the robustness of the model, the validity of the validation strategy, or the generalizability of the experimental results. The claim that only 30 mutations were needed to achieve the reported solubility improvements is striking but cannot be assessed without experimental replication details and statistical context. The work may be of interest to researchers in protein engineering and biomanufacturing, but the evidence base provided is too limited to establish the case. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein engineering, enzyme engineering, and biomanufacturing would be interested in a framework that combines solubility prediction with structural prioritization to reduce experimental burden. Those working on heterologous expression in E. coli and on industrial enzyme production would find the reported solubility improvements relevant. Computational biologists developing sequence-based predictors for protein properties may also be interested in the WT-mutant rescoring approach. Major strengths The integration of sequence-level prediction with structural filtering criteria is a sensible design choice that addresses the practical need to minimize activity loss. The reported use of a large training set of 71,425 proteins is a positive feature. The experimental validation on two industrial enzymes with maintained specific activities, if fully supported, would demonstrate practical utility. The claim of achieving high solubility improvements with a small number of tested mutations is potentially impactful. The claim that only 30 mutations were needed for the two enzymes is striking but cannot be assessed without information on how these 30 mutations were distributed between the two enzymes and how the selection was made. The generalizability of the framework to other proteins and expression systems is not addressed and cannot be inferred from the abstract.

Protein Chem.）——本文为 frame 差异提供了新的结构机制。 相似 ：Rainey & Goh 关于胶原模拟肽设计的综述（2004, Protein Sci.）——本文补充了 C 端封端基团的竞争性构象视角。 组合 ：本文的「末端 beta-turn 竞争」机制可与 AlphaFold 等结构预测工具结合——在预测胶原模拟肽三螺旋时，末端构象的竞争性状态可能被忽略，本文提示需显式建模末端残基的构象多态性。 冲突 ：部分文献将 C 端酰胺化视为「稳定化修饰」（通过额外氢键或电荷中和），本文提出在 POG frame 中它实际是 destabilizing 的——这提示文献中的经验规则可能依赖 frame 上下文。 可迁移领域 ：本文的「竞争性局部构象」概念可迁移到其他重复序列蛋白（如弹性蛋白、丝蛋白）的稳定性设计，以及 MD 模拟中末端效应的处理。 16 研究想法 Agent 生成的研究候选 ： 候选名称 ：末端修饰的构象偏好预测器 - 来源局限/观察 ：本文证明 C 端 amide 在 POG frame 中诱导 beta-turn，但未提供通用规则预测何种末端基团在何种 frame 中诱导竞争性构象。 - 核心假设 ：末端基团的氢键供体/受体模式与 frame 的脯氨酸位置几何共同决定 beta-turn 倾向，可通过 DFT 计算的构象能差进行预测。 - 初步方法 ：对 POG/GPO 及变体 frame 系统扫描 C 端修饰（amide、ester、N-methyl、hydrazide 等），用 DFT 计算 beta-turn vs PPII 相对能，与实验 Tm 关联。 - 验证方式 ：合成代表性肽测 Tm，检验预测准确性。 - 创新状态 ：unverified。 候选名称 ：MD 力场对脯氨酸羰基氢键描述的基准测试 - 来源局限/观察 ：本文的瞬态 CO...HN 接触定量依赖 MD 力场，但未提供力场验证。 - 核心假设 ：不同力场（AMBER ff19SB、CHARMM36m、OPLS-AA）对脯氨酸羰基作为氢键受体的描述差异显著，影响 beta-turn 占有率定量。 - 初步方法 ：用 NMR 实验 NOE 和标量耦合作为基准，比较各力场对 C 端构象群体的预测。 - 验证方式 ：计算各力场的构象群体与 NMR 实验值的 RMSD。 - 创新状态 ：unverified。 候选名称 ：胶原模拟肽末端 beta-turn 的 AlphaFold 预测能力评估 - 来源局限/观察 ：AlphaFold 等工具对单链构象多态性（特别是末端 beta-turn）的预测能力未知。 - 核心假设 ：AlphaFold 对 POG frame 肽的 C 端构象预测偏向 PPII，无法捕捉 beta-turn 竞争状态。 - 初步方法 ：用 AlphaFold2/3 预测本文肽段结构，对比 NMR/X-ray 实验构象，分析 C 端区域 pLDDT 和预测构象。 - 验证方式 ：统计 C 端预测构象与实验构象的 RMSD 和二级结构匹配率。 - 创新状态 ：unverified。 候选名称 ：末端 beta-turn 竞争对三螺旋组装动力学的 MD 研究 - 来源局限/观察 ：本文主要关注热力学稳定性（Tm），未涉及组装动力学。 - 核心假设 ：C 端 beta-turn 不仅降低 Tm，还通过减慢链间氢键成核速率影响三螺旋组装动力学。 - 初步方法 ：用粗粒化或全原子 MD 模拟三链组装过程，比较有/无 beta-turn 倾向的肽的成核时间。 - 验证方式 ：计算平均首通时间（MFPT）和组装产率。 - 创新状态 ：unverified。 候选名称 ：frame-dependent 末端效应的序列设计规则 - 来源局限/观察 ：本文只比较 POG vs GPO 两种 frame，未系统扫描 X/Y 位置残基。 - 核心假设 ：X/Y 位置的残基侧链可通过空间位阻或氢键竞争调节 C 端 beta-turn 倾向，从而提供额外的稳定性调控维度。 - 初步方法 ：对 (Gly-X-Y)n 的 X/Y 位置做饱和突变（计算 + 实验），测量 Tm 和 C 端构象。 - 验证方式 ：建立序列-稳定性-构象的三方关联模型。 - 创新状态 ：unverified。 Review setup Input scope Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and evidence as presented in the abstract; no full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose that a C-terminal beta-turn-like conformational state, stabilized by intramolecular CO...HN contacts involving the proline carbonyl, competes with interstrand hydrogen bonding and thereby controls frame-dependent stability of collagen triple helices. They report that N-methylation or esterification suppresses this state and increases stability by up to 7.5 degrees C, while the effect is frame-dependent (POG vs GPO). The mechanism is supported by DFT, NMR, X-ray crystallography, CD, and MD, and is claimed to be length-independent based on 20-22 residue peptides. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no numerical data, spectra, crystallographic parameters, or methodological details are visible Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, experimental procedures, crystallographic data, NMR assignments, DFT computational details, MD simulation parameters, and statistical analyses Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a mechanistically interesting and potentially significant hypothesis for the long-standing puzzle of frame-dependent stability in collagen triple helices. The proposed competing beta-turn-like state is a novel concept that could have broad implications for collagen mimetic peptide design. However, the abstract alone provides insufficient quantitative evidence to evaluate the robustness of the claims. The reported stability enhancement of up to 7.5 degrees C is substantial, but without visible data on the magnitude of the effect across different peptide lengths, the length-independence claim cannot be assessed. The multi-technique approach is commendable, but the abstract does not demonstrate how these techniques converge on the proposed mechanism. The claim that the beta-turn-like state "reduces availability" of the proline carbonyl for interstrand hydrogen bonding is mechanistically plausible but requires direct spectroscopic or computational evidence that is not visible in the abstract. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in collagen biochemistry, protein folding, peptide design, and biomaterials science would be interested. The work addresses a fundamental structural question about collagen stability that has implications for understanding collagen-related diseases and for designing collagen mimetic materials with tunable stability. The proposed mechanism involving competing intramolecular hydrogen bonding could also inform broader studies of beta-turn formation in proline-rich sequences. Major strengths The study addresses a well-documented but mechanistically unresolved problem in collagen biophysics. The proposed competing conformational state is a conceptually novel explanation that could unify disparate observations. The use of multiple complementary techniques (DFT, NMR, X-ray, CD, MD) is appropriate for establishing a structural mechanism. The frame-dependent comparison (POG vs GPO) provides a natural control that strengthens the causal argument. The chemical modification approach (N-methylation, esterification) is a clean way to test the proposed mechanism. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The claim that a C-terminal beta-turn-like state with intramolecular CO...HN contacts is the competing motif governing frame-dependent stability Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract asserts that the beta-turn-like state is identified and characterized, but no quantitative data are presented to demonstrate the population of this state, the occupancy of the intramolecular CO...HN contacts, or the correlation between this state and thermal stability across the peptide series. The phrase "transient intramolecular CO...HN contacts" implies a dynamic equilibrium, but no kinetic or thermodynamic parameters are reported. Why it matters The central mechanistic claim rests on the existence and functional relevance of this beta-turn-like state. Without quantitative evidence of its population and its direct competition with interstrand hydrogen bonding, the proposed mechanism remains speculative. The stability enhancement of up to 7.5 degrees C could arise from other factors such as altered solvation, steric effects, or changes in backbone conformation unrelated to the proposed beta-turn. Resolution test Provide population data (e.g., from NMR chemical shifts, NOE contacts, or MD free energy profiles) showing that the beta-turn-like state is populated in POG-frame peptides with a primary amide and suppressed upon N-methylation or esterification. Show a quantitative correlation between the population of this state and the observed melting temperature changes. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Claim support Claim pointer The claim that the mechanism is length-independent, confirmed by trends across 20-22 residue collagen-mimetic peptides Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract states that trends across 20-22 residue peptides confirm the mechanism arises from local C-terminal interactions, independent of length. However, no data are shown for the range of lengths tested, the number of peptides, or the magnitude of the stability differences across lengths. A claim of length independence requires demonstration that the effect is constant or systematically predictable across a range of lengths, and that longer peptides do not show diminishing or amplifying effects. Why it matters If the effect is truly local and length-independent, this strengthens the mechanistic interpretation and has practical implications for peptide design. If the effect varies with length, the proposed mechanism may be incomplete or may interact with other length-dependent factors such as propagation of the triple helix or fraying at the termini. Resolution test Show a table or figure with melting temperatures for peptides of at least three different lengths in both POG and GPO frames, with and without the C-terminal modification, and demonstrate that the stability difference attributable to the beta-turn is statistically indistinguishable across lengths. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Mechanistic specificity Claim pointer The claim that the beta-turn-like state "perturbs terminal polyproline II geometry, directly opposing triple-helix assembly" Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract does not specify how the perturbation of polyproline II geometry is quantified or how it directly opposes assembly. The connection between the beta-turn-like state and the disruption of triple-helix assembly is stated but not mechanistically detailed. It is unclear whether the effect is on nucleation, propagation, or both, and whether the perturbation is local to the C-terminus or propagates along the chain. Why it matters The proposed mechanism should explain not only the thermodynamic stability difference but also the kinetic or structural pathway by which the beta-turn opposes assembly. Without this detail, the mechanism is incomplete and the interpretation of the stability data could be ambiguous. Resolution test Provide structural data (e.g., from X-ray or MD) showing the conformation of the C-terminal region in the beta-turn state versus the native triple-helix state, and demonstrate how this conformation disrupts the canonical interstrand hydrogen bonding pattern or the polyproline II dihedral angles. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Evidence integration Claim pointer The claim that DFT, NMR, X-ray crystallography, CD, and MD collectively establish the structural basis Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract lists five techniques but does not describe how each contributes to the conclusion. It is not clear which technique provides the primary evidence for the beta-turn-like state, which provides the thermodynamic correlation, and which provides the structural detail. The convergence of multiple techniques is claimed but not demonstrated. Why it matters For a mechanistic claim of this specificity, it is important to understand the weight of evidence from each technique and whether any technique provides contradictory or ambiguous results. The reader cannot judge whether the techniques are truly complementary or whether some are used in a supporting role that may be less definitive. Resolution test In the full manuscript, clearly delineate the role of each technique, present the key data from each, and discuss any discrepancies or limitations. For example, specify which NMR parameters report on the beta-turn population, which crystallographic structure shows the beta-turn conformation, and how MD simulations quantify the competition between intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Definition of "frame" Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The term "frame" (POG vs GPO) is used without explicit definition. Readers unfamiliar with collagen mimetic peptide nomenclature may not understand that this refers to the amino acid sequence register relative to the Gly-X-Y repeat. Required correction Define "frame" in the abstract or introduction, for example by stating that POG and GPO refer to the sequence register of proline and hydroxyproline relative to glycine in the repeating tripeptide unit. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Quantitative reporting Affected element Stability enhancement value Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The stability enhancement is reported as "up to 7.5 degrees C" without specifying the peptide length, the exact modification, or the comparison condition. This makes it difficult to gauge the practical significance of the effect. Required correction Report the specific peptide sequence, length, and modification that yielded the maximum enhancement, and provide the melting temperature values for the modified and unmodified peptides. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element "beta-turn-like" Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The term "beta-turn-like" is used without specifying which type of beta-turn (e.g., type I, II, I', II') or the criteria used to classify it as beta-turn-like rather than a different turn or loop conformation. Required correction Specify the structural criteria used to define the beta-turn-like state, such as the distance between C-alpha atoms of the first and fourth residues, the presence of a hydrogen bond between CO(i) and NH(i+3), and the dihedral angles of the central residues. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Generalizability Affected element Scope of the conclusion Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract concludes that the findings "reveal how terminal hydrogen-bonding interactions encode competing conformations modulating peptide folding and supramolecular assembly." This is a broad statement that may overreach beyond the specific collagen mimetic peptide system studied. Required correction Qualify the conclusion to indicate that this mechanism is demonstrated in collagen mimetic peptides and may have broader relevance, rather than stating it as a general principle. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 and R1-M2 are blocking. The central mechanistic claim requires quantitative evidence of the beta-turn-like state and its population, and the length-independence claim requires data across multiple lengths. Without these, the case is not established from the provided evidence. Risk / unsupported claims The existence and functional relevance of the C-terminal beta-turn-like state as the competing motif is asserted but not quantitatively supported in the abstract. The claim that N-methylation or esterification suppresses beta-turn formation and enhances stability by up to 7.5 degrees C is reported without specific data. The claim that the mechanism is length-independent is stated without visible supporting data. The claim that the beta-turn-like state "perturbs terminal polyproline II geometry" is mechanistically plausible but not demonstrated. The convergence of five techniques on the proposed mechanism is claimed but not shown. The general conclusion about "terminal hydrogen-bonding interactions encoding competing conformations" extends beyond the specific system studied and is not supported by the abstract alone.

结构质量评估器（ARES、lociPARSE、RNA3DCNN）在三个不同训练集（含新建的 RNA3DQA）上进行全组合交叉训练，并在独立 RNA-Puzzles-Bench 基准上评估，发现训练数据特性对无参考质量评估性能的影响具有模型依赖性，且非原生数据集（RNA3DQA）可使 lociPARSE 架构达到最优的排序准确性与稳定性。 03 研究问题 具体问题 : 训练数据的组成（来源、结构多样性、质量分布、冗余度）如何影响深度学习 RNA 3D 结构质量评估器的性能与跨数据集泛化能力？ 为什么重要 : RNA 3D 结构预测方法可生成大量候选模型，无参考质量评估是筛选与排序这些模型的关键环节。若质量评估器对训练数据分布过拟合，则在实际应用中（预测未知结构）可能产生系统性偏差。理解训练数据的影响是设计可靠 QA 模型的前提。 现有方法为何不足 : 已有三种主流 QA 模型（ARES、lociPARSE、RNA3DCNN）各自使用不同的训练集，但缺乏系统性对照实验来分离「架构」与「数据」的贡献。现有比较多聚焦于架构创新与特征工程，将训练集视为固定组件，未检验训练数据分布变化对同一架构的影响。 精确研究问题 : Can the choice of training dataset (native vs. nonnative) alter the Scientific soundness, methodological rigor, validity of claims relative to provided evidence, and clarity of presentation Shared manuscript claim summary The authors systematically investigate how training data composition affects the performance of three deep learning-based RNA 3D structure quality assessment models (ARES, lociPARSE, RNA3DCNN). They introduce a new dataset, RNA3DQA, retrain each model on nonnative datasets, and evaluate on an independent RNA-Puzzles-derived benchmark. They report that training data characteristics can dominate architectural differences, with RNA3DQA-trained lociPARSE achieving the best overall performance. Visible evidence base Main text tables (Tables 1–6), figures referenced (Figs 1–4), and statistical results described in text; supplementary materials referenced but not provided Missing materials affecting confidence Supplementary tables (S1–S5), supplementary figures (S1–S16), actual figure content, detailed hyperparameter settings, and the RNA3DCNN reimplementation code were not available for verification Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript addresses a timely and important question in RNA structural bioinformatics: how training data influence deep learning-based quality assessment models. The cross-training experimental design is conceptually sound and the introduction of a new dataset (RNA3DQA) is a valuable contribution. However, several methodological details and statistical analyses are incompletely described, and some claims appear stronger than the visible evidence supports. The manuscript would benefit from clearer reporting of benchmark construction, model reimplementation fidelity, and the practical significance of observed performance differences. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers developing deep learning methods for RNA 3D structure prediction and quality assessment, computational structural biologists working on RNA modeling pipelines, and methodologists interested in dataset design for structure prediction benchmarks. The findings on training data dominance over architecture could inform future dataset construction efforts across biomolecular structure prediction fields. Major strengths 1. Systematic cross-training design that directly addresses a previously undercharacterized question 2. Introduction of a new, publicly available dataset (RNA3DQA) with clear construction criteria 3. Use of an independent benchmark (RNA-Puzzles) with explicit efforts to prevent data leakage 4. Multi-faceted evaluation including aggregate scoring schemes and per-target statistical analysis 5. Practical recommendations for dataset design grounded in observed results Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors claim that RNA3DCNN was reimplemented based on the original description, and that retrained models faithfully reproduce the original architectures. Evidence pointer Section "Cross-dataset training protocol", Table 2 Concern The RNA3DCNN reimplementation is a critical component of the study, yet no verification of reimplementation fidelity is provided. The original RNA3DCNN paper may contain ambiguities in architecture details, training procedures, or preprocessing steps that could lead to behavioral differences. Without demonstrating that the reimplemented model reproduces the original model's performance on the original training data, the validity of all RNA3DCNN-related conclusions is uncertain. Why it matters If the reimplementation differs from the original in meaningful ways, the cross-training comparisons involving RNA3DCNN may reflect implementation artifacts rather than genuine training data effects. This would undermine a core conclusion of the study. Resolution test Provide quantitative evidence that the reimplemented RNA3DCNN reproduces the original model's performance on the original training/validation split, or clearly state the limitations of the reimplementation and temper conclusions accordingly. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors state that the benchmark dataset "contains neither PDB IDs from the training sets nor any Rfam families in common" with training data. Evidence pointer Section "Benchmark set for independent evaluation" Concern The exclusion criteria are described only at the level of Rfam family membership and PDB identifiers. However, structural similarity can exist across different Rfam families, and sequence similarity below the CD-HIT thresholds used (85–88.46%) could still lead to informative leakage. Additionally, the RNA-Puzzles targets themselves may have been used in the development of some prediction methods whose outputs are included in the benchmark, potentially introducing indirect biases. The authors do not report sequence identity checks between benchmark targets and training set sequences beyond Rfam family assignment. Why it matters Incomplete leakage prevention could inflate performance estimates and weaken the claim that the benchmark provides an unbiased assessment of generalization. Resolution test Report pairwise sequence identity distributions between benchmark targets and all training set sequences, and discuss any targets with unexpectedly high similarity. If such similarity exists, either exclude those targets or demonstrate that results are robust to their removal. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor Claim pointer The authors conclude that "RNA3DQA yielding the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model" and that "the best-performing model across both evaluation protocols uses IPA and was trained on the RNA3DQA dataset." Evidence pointer Section "Results of cross-training experiment", Tables 4 and 5 Concern The aggregate scoring schemes (Top-3 and Correlation) are described only in general terms. The exact formulas, weighting schemes, and thresholds for "top-three finishes" are not fully specified in the visible text. Furthermore, the reported differences between top configurations (e.g., 26 versus 27 points in Table 5) are small, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the aggregate scores. The claim that one configuration is "best" may not be statistically distinguishable from others. Why it matters Without uncertainty quantification on the aggregate scores, the ranking of configurations may not be robust, and the central conclusion about which training dataset is most effective could be overstated. Resolution test Provide formal definitions of both scoring schemes, report bootstrap confidence intervals for aggregate scores, and perform pairwise significance tests between top configurations. If differences are not significant, state this explicitly and adjust the strength of conclusions. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility Claim pointer The authors state that "all datasets, trained models, and analysis scripts supporting this study are available in the RNA3DQA repository at Zenodo." Evidence pointer Section "Data availability" Concern While data availability is commendable, the manuscript does not specify the software versions, environment configurations, or exact commands needed to reproduce the training and evaluation pipeline. Given the known dependency issues with ARES (acknowledged by the authors), reproducibility may be challenging without a containerized environment or detailed setup instructions. Why it matters Reproducibility is a core expectation for computational studies, and incomplete documentation could prevent others from building on this work. Resolution test Provide a Dockerfile or equivalent container definition, a requirements file with pinned versions, and a step-by-step reproduction guide in the repository or supplementary materials. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Section "Evaluation protocols" Evidence pointer Location not provided Issue The two scoring schemes are introduced but their exact definitions are not fully described in the main text. The reader is left to infer how "Top-3" and "Correlation" scores are computed from the brief description. Required correction Provide explicit mathematical definitions of both scoring schemes in the main text or refer clearly to a supplementary section where they are fully specified. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Presentation Affected element Figure 3 and associated text Evidence pointer Section "Training data impact on model performance" Issue The text states that "the strongest positive effects are observed under maximum-based aggregation," but the figure is not available for verification. The description of aggregation methods (mean-, median-, minimum-, maximum-based) is not fully explained. Required correction Clarify what is being aggregated (e.g., per-target Spearman correlations) and how each aggregation method is computed. Ensure figure captions are self-contained. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Section "Case study: cross-training effect for benchmark unit PZ37" Evidence pointer Figure 4 Issue The case study is presented as illustrative, but the selection of PZ37 as the case study target is not justified. It is unclear whether PZ37 was chosen because it is representative, exceptional, or convenient. Required correction Briefly justify the selection of PZ37 or state that it was chosen as an illustrative example. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Technical detail Affected element Section "Training sets for RNA quality assessment" Evidence pointer Table 1 Issue The RNA3DCNN training set is stated to be unavailable, which limits the completeness of the cross-training analysis. The authors do not discuss the potential impact of this missing component on their conclusions. Required correction Add a sentence acknowledging this limitation and discuss how it might affect the generalizability of the findings. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (RNA3DCNN reimplementation verification), R1-M2 (leakage prevention completeness), R1-M3 (statistical significance of aggregate scores) Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The question of training data influence on RNA 3D structure quality assessment is relatively underexplored, and the systematic cross-training approach is a novel contribution. However, the individual components (the three models, the datasets, the benchmark) are all previously published, and the novelty lies primarily in their combination. Scientific importance The findings have practical implications for dataset design in RNA structure prediction and quality assessment, which is a growing field. The conclusion that training data can outweigh architecture is potentially important but needs stronger statistical support. Interdisciplinary readership The topic sits at the intersection of structural biology, machine learning, and bioinformatics. The manuscript is likely to appeal to a specialized audience within these fields, but the broader significance for general structural biology or machine learning audiences is not fully articulated. Technical soundness The experimental design is generally sound, but the concerns above regarding reimplementation fidelity, leakage prevention, and statistical rigor need to be addressed. The lack of supplementary materials for verification limits confidence. Readability for nonspecialists The manuscript is clearly written and the main concepts are accessible. However, some methodological details (e.g., scoring schemes, aggregation methods) could be explained more explicitly for readers outside the immediate subfield. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The core question is important, the experimental design is appropriate, and the new dataset is a valuable resource. However, the manuscript cannot be accepted in its current form due to the unresolved concerns about RNA3DCNN reimplementation fidelity, potential data leakage, and insufficient statistical support for the central claims. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that RNA3DQA yields "the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model" is not fully supported without confidence intervals or significance tests on aggregate scores. The claim that "training data characteristics play a dominant, model-dependent role" is supported by the data but may be overstated given the small differences between top configurations and the lack of uncertainty quantification. The assertion that the benchmark is fully independent of training data is not fully verifiable from the provided information, as sequence-level similarity checks beyond Rfam family assignment are not reported. The performance of the reimplemented RNA3DCNN relative to the original model is unverified, making all RNA3DCNN-related conclusions uncertain. The statement that "no significant difference observed in the remaining 11 contests" in the Wilcoxon test is reported without showing the actual p-values or effect sizes for those cases.

Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no numerical results beyond R = 0.9282, no figures, tables, or methodological details Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all quantitative performance metrics (RMSE, MAE values), dataset composition and source, hyperparameter settings, bootstrap details, SHAP analysis outputs, and any validation or comparison against existing methods Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a plausible and potentially useful framework for protein folding rate prediction, combining LASSO feature selection with multiple machine learning models and interpretability analysis. However, the evidence provided in the abstract is insufficient to evaluate the robustness, novelty, or generalizability of the claims. Key quantitative results are missing, and the comparative claims about model performance cannot be verified from the supplied material. The work may be of interest to the protein biophysics and computational biology communities, but the case is not established from the abstract alone. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in computational biology, protein biophysics, and machine learning applied to biological problems would be interested. The framework addresses a practical need for interpretable and accurate prediction of protein folding rates, which is relevant to understanding protein dynamics and folding mechanisms. The use of SHAP for model interpretation may appeal to those seeking explainable AI approaches in bioinformatics. Major strengths The abstract clearly identifies a specific problem (limited generalizability and multicollinearity of existing structural parameters) and proposes a coherent pipeline (feature selection, modeling, interpretation). The use of bootstrap resampling for uncertainty assessment is a positive methodological choice. The inclusion of folding-type-specific analysis and SHAP interpretation suggests attention to model behavior beyond aggregate metrics. Major Concerns R1-M1: The abstract reports only one performance metric (R = 0.9282 for SSA-BP) and does not provide the actual RMSE and MAE values for any model. Without these numbers, the comparative claim that "RF achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE" cannot be assessed. R1-M2: The claim that LASSO identified six features "from 12 structural parameters" is presented without any detail on the selection procedure, stability of selection, or validation that these features are indeed the most informative. The abstract does not state whether the same features were used across all models or whether feature selection was performed within cross-validation, which is a common source of bias. R1-M3: The abstract claims "distinct model performance patterns between two-state and multi-state proteins" but provides no quantitative support. The reader cannot determine the magnitude or direction of these differences, nor whether they are statistically significant. R1-M4: The SHAP analysis claim that "relative contributions of structural features varied across models and folding types" is not supported by any specific results. The abstract does not report which features dominated for which model or folding type, nor how these contributions were quantified. R1-M5: The training set of 145 proteins and test set of 29 proteins are mentioned, but the abstract does not state how the split was performed, whether the test set is truly independent, or whether the dataset is publicly available. This limits the reproducibility assessment. Minor Comments R1-m1: The abstract does not specify the units or definition of "folding rate" used, which is important for interpreting the RMSE and MAE values. R1-m2: The choice of the four models (RR, RF, SVM, SSA-BP) is not justified. The abstract does not explain why these particular models were selected or how they complement each other. R1-m3: The abstract mentions "bootstrap resampling used to assess performance uncertainty" but does not report any confidence intervals or uncertainty measures. The reader cannot evaluate the stability of the reported performance. R1-m4: The term "SSA-BP" is not defined in the abstract. If this is a hybrid model (e.g., sparrow search algorithm optimized backpropagation), it should be stated explicitly. R1-m5: The abstract does not compare the proposed framework against existing protein folding rate prediction methods. Without such a comparison, the added value of the approach is unclear. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M4, R1-M5. The core comparative and interpretability claims are not supported by the evidence provided in the abstract. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The combination of LASSO feature selection with multiple ML models and SHAP interpretation for protein folding rate prediction is not clearly novel from the abstract alone. Similar approaches have been used in other bioinformatics prediction tasks. The abstract does not articulate what is new compared to prior work. Scientific importance: Protein folding rate prediction is a relevant problem, but the abstract does not demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves substantially better performance or provides new biological insight beyond existing methods. Interdisciplinary readership: The work sits at the intersection of biophysics and machine learning, which could attract a broad readership. However, the abstract is written in a way that assumes familiarity with both fields, and the lack of quantitative detail limits accessibility. Technical soundness: The methodological choices (LASSO, bootstrap, SHAP) are reasonable, but the abstract does not provide enough detail to assess whether they were implemented correctly. The absence of key performance metrics is a significant technical shortcoming. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is concise but uses field-specific terms (e.g., L(eff), LRO, ACO, Sheet, H(nc), P(beta)) without definition. A nonspecialist would struggle to understand the significance of these features. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract presents a reasonable framework, but the lack of quantitative results and methodological detail prevents a supportive recommendation. The authors should provide the full manuscript with complete performance metrics, feature selection details, and SHAP outputs for a proper evaluation. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that "RF achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE" is unsupported because the actual values are not reported. The claim that "SSA-BP showed the highest correlation coefficient (R = 0.9282)" is supported only by a single number with no context (e.g., confidence interval, comparison to other models' R values). The claim of "distinct model performance patterns between two-state and multi-state proteins" is unsupported by any quantitative evidence. The claim that "SHAP analysis further showed that the relative contributions of structural features varied across models and folding types" is unsupported by specific results. The generalizability claim ("providing an interpretable approach for protein folding rate prediction") is not established because the abstract does not demonstrate performance on external or independent datasets beyond the 29-protein test set.

Introduction 第 2 段 06 核心思想 1) 表面方法 : - 从 TRACEY 数据库收集 13,941 条 SNARE TMD 序列，按亚细胞定位分为四类（Class I: ER; Class II: 高尔基; Class III: TGN/内体; Class IV: PM/分泌囊泡） - 对 28 个人类 SNARE TMD 进行全原子 MD 模拟（DMPC 和 DOPC 两种膜），用 Cα 相对脂质磷酸基团平面的位置定义膜嵌入边界 - 计算每个 TMD 的氨基酸组成、MD 定义的膜嵌入长度、脂质可及表面积（LASA） 2) 核心洞察 : - SNARE TMD 的氨基酸组成呈现清晰的二分法：早期分泌途径（ER/高尔基）富集 Phe，晚期分泌/内体途径富集 Ile。这不是简单的疏水性差异（两者疏水性相近），而是侧链体积/形状的差异——Phe 的 bulky 侧链在松散堆积的 ER/高尔基膜中能增强蛋白-脂质疏水相互作用，而 Ile 的紧凑侧链在紧密堆积的 PM/内体膜中不破坏脂质有序堆积。 - MD 模拟揭示 TMD 长度在不同区室间差异很小，挑战了「TMD 长度随膜厚度递增」的经典假说。序列预测的长度梯度主要反映的是组成差异（Phe/Ile 等）而非真实的膜嵌入长度差异。 - 单个 charged 残基（如 Vti1b 的 Glu）可显著改变 TMD 的膜内行为（诱导弯曲、水通道形成），提示 TMD 并非被动锚定结构，而是主动感知和响应膜环境的模块。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] : - 序列疏水性预测的「结构域边界」不应被当作物理边界；MD 模拟或实验确定的膜嵌入边界可能显著不同，这对所有膜蛋白的 TMD 预测和建模都有警示意义。 - 氨基酸组成（而非仅长度）是膜蛋白适应不同膜环境的主要进化变量。在设计靶向特定区室的膜蛋白或理解膜蛋白分选信号时，应更多关注组成特征（如 Phe/Ile 比例、bulky 残基分布）而非仅关注疏水核心长度。 - 单个残基的 charged 状态可对 TMD 行为产生非线性影响（水渗透、弯曲），提示在粗粒化或隐式膜模型中需谨慎处理膜内 charged 残基。 07 方法总览 输入 : 疏水性评分 （Goldman-Engelman-Steitz scale）: - 每个氨基酸赋予一个疏水性值（kcal/mol），用于从序列中识别跨膜螺旋 - 滑动窗口：15 残基加权平均，中心残基权重 1.0，向两侧线性递减至 0 - 用途：初步界定 TMD 序列范围 TMD 长度定义（MD） : - O–O 定义：Cα 原子位于两侧脂质酰基氧（acyl-oxygen）平面之间的残基数量 - P–P 定义：Cα 原子位于两侧磷酸（phosphate）平面之间的残基数量 - 直觉：O–O 更严格对应疏水核心，P–P 包含更多界面区域 LASA（Lipid-Accessible Surface Area） : - 使用探针半径 1.88 Å（模拟亚甲基基团大小）计算 TMD 残基可被脂质接触的溶剂可及表面积 - 直觉：LASA 越大，蛋白-脂质接触面越大，疏水相互作用越强 PLS-DA 二分法在所有真核谱系中均存在）可作为实验验证的补充证据，尤其适用于难以进行突变实验的系统。 Review setup Input scope Full manuscript text (abstract, introduction, results, discussion, methods, author contributions, funding, data availability) Assessment boundary Scientific content, methodological soundness, statistical rigor, interpretational validity, and alignment with stated claims. Editorial and stylistic issues are noted only where they affect scientific clarity. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors analyze approximately 14,000 SNARE transmembrane domain (TMD) sequences and perform MD simulations of 28 human SNARE TMDs to show that TMD amino acid composition, particularly Phe versus Ile content, reflects subcellular localization, with early secretory pathway SNAREs enriched in Phe and late secretory/endosomal SNAREs enriched in Ile. They further report that MD-derived TMD lengths show limited variation across compartments, contrasting with sequence-based predictions. Visible evidence base Full text including abstract, introduction, results sections (Amino Acid Composition, TMD Length, Lipid-Accessible Surface Area, C-Terminal Ends of TMDs, Conserved Charges in TMDs), discussion, methods, and references to supplementary figures (S1-S23) and alignments (S1). No figures or tables are directly viewable in the provided material. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures, tables, and supplementary materials are referenced but not provided. This includes the primary data visualizations (Figures 1-5), all supplementary figures (S1-S23), and the sequence alignment (Alignment S1). Statistical outputs, MD simulation parameters beyond those described, and the full TRACEY database contents are not directly accessible. Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript addresses a timely and important question in membrane protein biology: whether TMD composition reflects subcellular localization in the SNARE family. The authors combine a large-scale bioinformatics analysis with MD simulations, which is a powerful and appropriate approach. The central finding of a Phe/Ile dichotomy between early and late secretory pathway SNAREs is potentially significant and extends prior work by Munro. However, the manuscript has several major concerns that must be addressed before the case is fully established. These include the lack of direct statistical comparisons between classes, the limited membrane model diversity in MD simulations, the absence of functional validation, and the unclear relationship between the observed compositional differences and the proposed mechanistic role in protein sorting. The discussion is thoughtful and appropriately cautious in several places, but some claims outpace the evidence presented. Who would be interested in the results, and why Cell biologists studying membrane trafficking and organelle identity, biophysicists interested in protein-lipid interactions, computational biologists developing tools for membrane protein analysis, and evolutionary biologists studying adaptation of protein families. The findings have implications for understanding how proteins are sorted to specific membranes and how TMD sequence features relate to membrane biophysical properties. Major strengths (1) Large and well-curated dataset of approximately 14,000 SNARE TMDs from the TRACEY database, providing statistical power. (2) Combination of bioinformatics and MD simulations to address the question from complementary angles. (3) The study extends prior work by Munro to a much larger dataset and specifically to the SNARE family. (4) The authors acknowledge limitations of their model systems and discuss alternative interpretations. (5) The observation that MD-derived TMD lengths differ from sequence-based predictions is an important methodological contribution. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor Claim pointer The manuscript claims a "clear compositional dichotomy" and "pronounced difference" between Classes I/II and III/IV in Phe and Ile content, and states that these differences are "robust." Evidence pointer Results section "Amino Acid Composition", Figures 2A-C, Supplementary Figures S1-S4 Concern The manuscript describes differences in Phe and Ile content between classes but does not report any formal statistical tests (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals, permutation tests, or mixed-effects models accounting for phylogenetic non-independence). The statement that "considerable variation in individual amino acid frequency exists among TMDs within each class, resulting in substantial overlap between classes" suggests that the separation may not be as clean as implied. Without quantitative statistical support, the strength and significance of the claimed dichotomy cannot be evaluated. Why it matters The central claim of the paper rests on the statistical robustness of the compositional differences. If the overlap between classes is substantial, the biological significance of the dichotomy is weakened. Moreover, because TMD sequences within a species are not independent (shared evolutionary history), standard tests that assume independence may be inappropriate. Resolution test Provide formal statistical comparisons between class pairs for Phe and Ile content, including effect sizes and confidence intervals. Use methods that account for phylogenetic relatedness (e.g., phylogenetic generalized least squares or permutation tests that resample at the species level). Report the proportion of variance explained by class membership versus other factors. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological scope Claim pointer The manuscript states that "TMD lengths derived from MD simulations are surprisingly similar across classes" and that "differences in effective membrane-spanning length between SNARE classes are modest at best." Evidence pointer Results section "TMD Length", Figures 3B-F, Supplementary Figures S8-S10 Concern MD simulations were performed in only two lipid environments (DMPC and DOPC), both of which are thinner than most biological membranes, including the plasma membrane. The authors acknowledge this limitation but then use these simulations to draw conclusions about the lack of length variation across compartments. This is problematic because the simulations may not capture the relevant biophysical environment of thicker, cholesterol-rich membranes. The authors did perform a subset of simulations in DOPC with 40% cholesterol, but this was limited and without replicates. Why it matters The conclusion that TMD length does not vary across compartments is a key negative finding that contrasts with sequence-based predictions. If the simulations are not representative of the actual membrane environments, this conclusion is not well supported. The limited membrane model diversity undermines the generalizability of the length and LASA findings. Resolution test Perform simulations in additional lipid compositions that better represent the range of biological membranes (e.g., POPC, ER-like mixtures, plasma membrane-like mixtures with cholesterol and sphingomyelin). Include replicate simulations for the cholesterol-containing system. Alternatively, temper the conclusions to clearly state that the findings apply only to the specific lipid environments tested. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Functional validation Claim pointer The manuscript proposes that "TMD composition contributes to functional optimization by modulating energetic compatibility with specific bilayer environments and to compartmental localization." Evidence pointer Discussion section, Results sections "Lipid-Accessible Surface Area" and "Conserved Charges in TMDs" Concern The manuscript provides no experimental or functional validation of the proposed role of TMD composition in localization. The LASA calculations are purely computational and are not linked to any measurable biological outcome. The discussion of sorting mechanisms is speculative and acknowledges that "TMD-dependent partitioning could support their forward trafficking" but no direct evidence is provided. The claim that compositional differences "potentially contributing to protein localization" is appropriately hedged, but the overall framing suggests a stronger causal link than the evidence supports. Why it matters The title and abstract imply that TMD composition "reflects" localization, which is a correlational claim. However, the discussion extends this to a functional role in localization. Without experimental manipulation (e.g., swapping TMDs between SNAREs of different classes and measuring localization), the functional significance remains speculative. Resolution test Add experimental data, even preliminary, showing that swapping TMDs between early and late SNAREs alters localization, or that mutations in TMD composition affect localization. Alternatively, clearly reframe the claims as correlational and hypothesis-generating rather than functional. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Interpretational validity Claim pointer The manuscript states that "TMD lengths derived from MD simulations differ from those inferred by sequence-based approaches and show limited variation across compartments." Evidence pointer Results section "TMD Length", Figures 3D-F, Supplementary Figure S11 Concern The discrepancy between GES-based and MD-based TMD lengths is presented as a methodological insight, but the manuscript does not fully explore the implications. If GES-based boundaries are inaccurate, then the compositional analysis (which uses GES-based boundaries) may be affected. The authors do reanalyze composition with MD-based boundaries (Figure S12), but this is only for human SNAREs and the results are described as "similar overall." The potential impact of boundary choice on the central compositional findings is not thoroughly discussed. Why it matters The compositional dichotomy is the main finding. If the choice of TMD boundaries significantly affects the results, the robustness of the finding is called into question. The manuscript should more explicitly address whether the dichotomy holds regardless of boundary definition. Resolution test Provide a more detailed comparison of compositional results using GES-based versus MD-based boundaries for all classes, not just human SNAREs. Discuss the sensitivity of the findings to boundary definition. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract, first sentence Issue The phrase "necessitating adaptation to each membrane's unique environment" is vague. It is unclear what specific adaptations are being referred to. Required correction Specify the types of adaptations (e.g., length, amino acid composition, hydrophobic mismatch) in the abstract. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Statistical reporting Affected element Results section "Amino Acid Composition" Evidence pointer Results section "Amino Acid Composition", Figure 2 Issue The manuscript states that "Phe and Ile contents correlate most strongly with LASA" but does not report the correlation coefficients or their significance. Required correction Report correlation coefficients and p-values for the relationships between Phe/Ile content and LASA. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Methodological detail Affected element Methods section, MD simulations Evidence pointer Methods section, MD simulations Issue The methods state that "protein charges were kept at their default protonation states in CHARMM-GUI, corresponding to standard ionization at neutral pH." However, the pKa of the Glu residue in VtiB is discussed as potentially being shifted in the membrane environment. It is unclear whether the protonation state of this specific residue was modeled in the main simulations. Required correction Clarify whether the VtiB Glu was modeled in its charged or neutral form in the main simulations, and justify the choice. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Data presentation Affected element Results section "C-Terminal Ends of TMDs" Evidence pointer Results section "C-Terminal Ends of TMDs", Figure 5H Issue The description of the Vamp7 C-terminal region is brief. The claim that it is "highly conserved across all major eukaryotic lineages" is stated without supporting data shown in the main text. Required correction Provide the supporting alignment or conservation data, or reference the relevant supplementary figure. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Literature context Affected element Introduction and Discussion Evidence pointer Introduction, Discussion Issue The manuscript cites Munro (40) for the Phe/Ile observation but does not discuss in detail how the present findings extend or refine this earlier work beyond the larger dataset. Required correction Add a brief paragraph in the Discussion explicitly comparing the present findings to Munro's study and stating what new insights are provided. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Data Availability Statement Evidence pointer Data Availability Statement Issue The MD simulation data are stated to be "available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request." This is less transparent than depositing in a public repository. Required correction Deposit MD simulation inputs, trajectories, and analysis scripts in a public repository (e.g., Zenodo, OSF) and provide accession numbers. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that TMD composition "potentially contributing to protein localization" is presented as a functional hypothesis but is not directly tested. This is appropriately hedged in places but the title and abstract imply a stronger causal relationship. The claim that MD-derived TMD lengths "show limited variation across compartments" is based on simulations in only two lipid types, both thinner than most biological membranes. This conclusion may not generalize. The statement that "TMD composition contributes to functional optimization" is speculative and not supported by direct experimental evidence. The claim that the Phe/Ile dichotomy is "conserved across all groups" is based on PCA/PLS-DA visual inspection without formal statistical comparison across phylogenetic groups. The functional significance of the conserved charged residues in Syx5 and VtiB is inferred from MD simulations and sequence conservation but is not experimentally validated. The relationship between LASA and raft partitioning is discussed as a potential mechanism but is not directly measured or tested. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The study is original in its scale and integration of bioinformatics with MD simulations applied specifically to SNARE TMDs. The finding of a Phe/Ile dichotomy extends prior work but the systematic analysis across approximately 14,000 sequences and the MD-based length analysis provide new insights. However, the core observation is not entirely novel, as it was previously reported by Munro. Scientific importance The question of how TMDs adapt to different membrane environments is of broad importance in cell biology. The findings have implications for understanding protein sorting, membrane organization, and the evolution of membrane protein families. The potential link between TMD composition and raft partitioning is interesting but not fully developed. Interdisciplinary readership The topic is relevant to cell biologists, biophysicists, computational biologists, and evolutionary biologists. The manuscript is written in a way that is largely accessible to these groups, though some sections (e.g., PLS-DA methodology) may be challenging for non-specialists. Technical soundness The bioinformatics approach is sound, and the MD simulations are appropriate for the questions asked. However, the lack of formal statistical tests for the central compositional claims is a significant weakness. The limited diversity of membrane models in the MD simulations also limits the generalizability of the length and LASA findings. Readability for nonspecialists The manuscript is generally well-written and the logic is clear. The abstract effectively summarizes the main findings. However, some methodological details (e.g., PLS-DA, LASA calculations) may be difficult for readers without a computational background. The figures are referenced but not visible in the provided material, so their clarity cannot be assessed. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The manuscript addresses an important question with a powerful approach, and the central findings are potentially significant. However, the lack of formal statistical support for the main compositional claims, the limited membrane model diversity in MD simulations, and the absence of functional validation prevent the case from being fully established as presented. The authors should be encouraged to revise and resubmit after addressing these concerns.

01 基本信息 标题 : Functional architecture of rare protein coding variation across 786,871 exomes 作者与单位 : Hou, Kangcheng; Li, Hui; Nason, Emily; Finucane, Hilary; Sunyaev, Shamil; O'Connor, Luke J（单位未提供） 期刊/预印本平台 : medRxiv (preprint server for health sciences) 年份 : 2026-11-08 论文类型 : 预印本（方法学 + 应用研究） 领域 : 人类遗传学 / 统计遗传学 / 蛋白质结构功能预测 × 复杂性状遗传力 关键词 : rare variants, exome, heritability, protein structure, functional annotations, kernel regression, AlphaMissense DOI/arXiv 号 : 10.64898/2026.10.16.26365771 代码 : 未提供 数据 : UK Biobank 和 All of Us 外显子组数据（786,871 个体，26 个性状） 阅读日期 : 未提供 在该方向中的位置 : 本文处于「蛋白质结构相关计算研究 × 统计遗传学」交叉点，核心贡献是将蛋白质结构特征与功能预测分数整合为核函数（kernel），用于量化罕见错义变异对复杂性状遗传力的贡献。与 AlphaFold/AlphaMissense 等结构预测工具直接相关，但聚焦于群体遗传学层面的效应估计，而非单变异功能预测。 02 一句话总结 本文提出 Kernel Allelic Series Model (KASM)，将 35 种蛋白质结构与功能注释整合为基因内等位效应协方差核，应用于 786,871 例外显子组和 26 个性状，估计罕见错义遗传力至少 1.27±0.09%，并发现 3D 邻近但 1D 远距的残基对效应相关性显著增强。 03 研究问题 具体问题 : 已知的蛋白质结构特征和功能预测分数能在多大程度上解释罕见蛋白编码变异对人类复杂性状的异质性效应？ 为什么重要 : 罕见错义变异数量庞大且效应异质，若能利用结构/功能注释解释其效应模式，可提升基因发现功效、揭示疾病机制，并为药物靶点提供假设。 现有方法不足 : 传统罕见变异关联分析（如 burden test）假设基因内所有错义变异效应方向一致、大小相近，忽略结构上下文；SKAT 等方差分量方法虽允许异质性，但不利用结构/功能注释来建模效应协方差。 精确研究问题 : Can integrating protein structural features and functional scores into a kernel-based allelic series model explain the heterogeneous effects of rare missense variants on complex traits better than existing burden or variance-component approaches? 04 背景与发展脉络 （标注：以下脉络为「经外部核验」的领域常识，结合本文框架定位） 1. Burden tests（早期） : 聚合基因内罕见变异，假设同向效应。优点：简单、功效高（当假设成立时）；局限：忽略效应异质性，稀释信号。 2. Variance-component tests（SKAT 等） : 允许变异效应异质，通过核函数建模。优点：灵活；局限：核函数通常基于等位基因频率或简单注释，未利用蛋白质结构信息。 3. 功能预测器时代（PolyPhen, SIFT, CADD, AlphaMissense 等） : 单变异功能分数可提升关联分析功效，但通常作为权重或过滤条件，未建模变异间结构关系。 4. 本文位置 : KASM 将功能分数与结构特征（氨基酸化学性质、结构基序、残基接触、PPI 界面）嵌入核函数，使基因内等位效应协方差由结构/功能相似性决定，从而估计结构注释对遗传力的贡献，并识别基因特异性富集。 05 核心痛点 痛点 表现 成因或作者解释 文中证据 罕见错义变异效应高度异质 同一基因内不同错义变异对性状影响差异巨大 变异影响蛋白质结构/功能的不同方面（稳定性、结合、催化等） Abstract: manuscript claim summary The authors introduce a statistical model, KASM, that integrates multiple functional annotations to characterize how rare protein-coding variant effects covary within genes. Applying KASM to exome data from 26 traits and 786,871 individuals (UK Biobank and All of Us), they report heritability estimates for rare missense variants exceeding those for protein-truncating variants and previous burden-based estimates, identify AlphaMissense as the most enriched single predictor with a composite score doubling its enrichment, describe structural feature enrichments, characterize pairwise variant effect correlations with a 3D-structure-specific exception, and report gene-specific enrichments such as a 95-fold enrichment among PIEZO1 hydrogen bond residues. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, methods, or supplementary information were provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, all figures and tables, supplementary analyses, model specification details, trait definitions, quality control procedures, and validation results Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially important framework for integrating functional annotations into gene-level analyses of rare variant effects. The scale of the data and the breadth of annotations are impressive. However, the abstract alone does not provide sufficient detail to evaluate the statistical validity of the model, the robustness of the heritability estimates, or the biological interpretation of the reported enrichments. Several claims, particularly those involving quantitative comparisons and effect sizes, cannot be assessed without the underlying methods and results. Who would be interested in the results, and why Statistical geneticists developing methods for rare variant analysis; human geneticists studying the genetic architecture of complex traits; computational biologists working on functional annotation of protein-coding variation; and researchers interested in the contribution of missense variation to heritability. The work could inform gene discovery strategies and functional follow-up studies. Major strengths The study addresses a timely and important question about the functional architecture of rare coding variation. The integration of 35 annotations into a single modeling framework is a substantial technical effort. The use of two large biobank datasets (UK Biobank and All of Us) with nearly 800,000 exomes provides considerable statistical power. The finding that missense heritability may exceed pLoF heritability challenges current assumptions and could have broad implications. Evidence pointer Abstract, Results section (location not provided) Concern The heritability estimates are presented with standard errors, but no information is provided about the model specification, the definition of "rare" variants, the adjustment for covariates, the handling of relatedness, or the potential for confounding by population structure. The difference between the "average" and "most flexible" model estimates is substantial (1.27% vs 1.83%), and it is unclear which estimate is preferred and why. The comparison to "missense burden heritability as previously estimated" relies on an external estimate whose methodology may not be directly comparable. Why it matters The central quantitative claim of the abstract depends on the validity and comparability of these heritability estimates. Without details on model assumptions, estimation procedures, and sensitivity analyses, the claim that missense heritability exceeds pLoF heritability cannot be evaluated. If the estimates are sensitive to model choices or annotation inclusion, the conclusion may not be robust. Report sensitivity analyses varying the set of annotations, the definition of rare variants, and the inclusion of covariates.
