Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in enzyme engineering and drug development for ALL, particularly those focused on improving therapeutic proteins by reducing off-target activities. Computational biologists developing structure-based screening workflows for enzyme discovery may also find the approach relevant. Clinicians and pharmacologists interested in next-generation L-asparaginase formulations with improved safety profiles would be a secondary audience. Major strengths The study addresses a clinically meaningful problem with a clear objective. The scale of the genomic screening (~85,000 genomes) is substantial. The integration of multiple computational methods with experimental validation is a commendable design. The explicit acknowledgment of a limitation in the computational workflow (lack of binding energy correlation with catalytic efficiency) demonstrates scientific transparency. Major Concerns R1-M1 R1-M2 R1-M3 Minor Comments R1-m1 R1-m2 R1-m3 Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The lack of correlation between predicted binding energies and catalytic efficiency undermines the predictive validity of the screening workflow. Without evidence that the computational ranking reliably identifies high-performing enzymes, the claim that RhAII was identified through this workflow as a promising candidate is weakened. Additionally, the absence of experimental validation in biological models, as acknowledged by the authors, means the therapeutic potential remains speculative. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: Moderate. The combination of AlphaFold2, docking, and MD for enzyme screening is not entirely novel, but the specific application to L-asparaginase specificity is a reasonable contribution. Scientific importance: Moderate. Improving L-asparaginase specificity has clinical relevance, but the impact depends on whether RhAII performs well in biological models, which is not yet demonstrated. Interdisciplinary readership: Limited. The work bridges computational biology and enzymology, but the abstract is unlikely to attract broad interdisciplinary attention beyond these fields. Technical soundness: Not fully assessable from the abstract. Key details on computational parameters, experimental replicates, and statistical treatment are missing. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is reasonably clear, though kinetic parameters and MD terminology may be challenging for a general audience. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract presents a plausible workflow and a promising hit, but the acknowledged limitation in the computational pipeline and the lack of biological validation mean the core claims cannot be fully supported. A revised manuscript with full methods and additional validation data would be needed to assess the case more favorably. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors claim that the computational screening workflow identified RhAII as a highly specific L-asparaginase with minimal L-glutaminase co-activity. Evidence pointer Abstract, Results section; location not provided Concern The abstract states that predicted substrate binding energies did not correlate with catalytic efficiency, yet the screening workflow relied on binding-energy estimation as a key selection criterion. This internal inconsistency raises questions about how the six top-ranked enzymes were selected and whether the computational ranking had any predictive value. Without details on the selection thresholds, the ranking algorithm, or any retrospective analysis of why RhAII was correctly identified despite the poor correlation, the validity of the screening approach is unclear. Why it matters If the computational predictions do not correlate with experimental outcomes, the claim that genome-wide screening identified RhAII is weakened. The workflow may have produced a hit by chance rather than by design, which would undermine the generalizability of the approach and the scientific contribution. Resolution test Provide a detailed description of the selection criteria for the six enzymes, including any scoring functions or cutoffs. Include a retrospective analysis showing whether the computational metrics (binding energy, docking scores, MD-derived parameters) distinguished RhAII from poor performers. If no correlation exists, explain how RhAII was prioritized and whether the workflow can be expected to identify other high-specificity enzymes in future applications. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence quality Claim pointer The authors claim that RhAII shows negligible L-glutaminase activity and high specificity toward L-asparagine. Evidence pointer Abstract, Results section; location not provided Concern The abstract reports kinetic parameters for RhAII (K(M) 12 +/- 2 microM, k(cat) 34 +/- 2 s(-1)) and states negligible L-glutaminase activity, but no experimental details are provided. It is unclear how L-glutaminase activity was measured, what detection limit was used, how many replicates were performed, and whether the enzyme was purified to homogeneity. The term "negligible" is qualitative and requires a quantitative definition, such as a specific activity ratio or a detection threshold. Why it matters The central claim of the study is high substrate specificity. If the L-glutaminase assay lacked sensitivity or the enzyme preparation contained contaminants, the conclusion could be misleading. Reproducibility and comparability with existing L-asparaginases depend on rigorous kinetic characterization. Resolution test Provide full experimental methods for enzyme expression, purification, and activity assays, including substrate concentration ranges, buffer conditions, temperature, pH, number of replicates, and statistical analysis. Report the L-glutaminase activity quantitatively (e.g., specific activity or k(cat)/K(M) ratio) and state the detection limit of the assay. Include a comparison with a reference enzyme such as EcAII under identical conditions. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Claim support Claim pointer The authors claim a relationship between enzyme activity and the conformational dynamics of the flexible gating element (FGE), characterized by RMSF, and L-Asn positional fluctuations, evaluated by ligand RMSD. Evidence pointer Abstract, Results section; location not provided Concern The abstract describes a correlation between FGE dynamics and enzyme activity based on MD simulations, but no quantitative data are presented. It is unclear how many enzymes were compared, what the range of RMSF and RMSD values was, whether the correlation was statistically significant, and whether the relationship was observed across all six validated enzymes or only a subset. The mechanistic interpretation that "stable substrate positioning" leads to high activity is plausible but not substantiated without data. Why it matters The proposed structure-dynamics-function relationship is a key conceptual contribution of the study. If the correlation is weak or based on a small number of observations, the claim may be overinterpreted. This relationship also provides the rationale for why binding energies failed to predict activity, so it needs to be rigorously established. Resolution test Provide quantitative RMSF and ligand RMSD data for all validated enzymes, with statistical tests (e.g., correlation coefficients, p-values). Show that the relationship holds across multiple enzymes and is not driven by a single outlier. Include convergence analysis for the MD simulations and demonstrate that the observed dynamics are robust to simulation length and force field parameters. This limits the reproducibility of the screening scope. Required correction Specify the genome databases used (e.g., NCBI RefSeq, GenBank), the version or release date, and any filtering criteria applied before screening. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Abstract, Conclusions section Evidence pointer Abstract, Conclusions section; location not provided Issue The conclusion states that RhAII is a "promising antileukemic candidate for further validation in biological models," but no information is provided on the expected therapeutic window, potential immunogenicity, or comparison with current clinical L-asparaginases beyond the kinetic parameters. Required correction Add a brief statement on how RhAII compares to existing enzymes (e.g., EcAII or Erwinase) in terms of specificity and kinetic efficiency, and clarify what specific biological models are planned for validation. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Precision Affected element Abstract, Results section Evidence pointer Abstract, Results section; location not provided Issue The kinetic parameters for PoAII are reported as K(M) 5797 +/- 1143 microM and k(cat) 1.2 +/- 0.1 s(-1), but the units and the number of significant figures are inconsistent with those for RhAII. The large error on the K(M) value suggests high variability, which is not discussed. Required correction Report all kinetic parameters with consistent significant figures and units. Provide a brief comment on the variability observed for PoAII and whether this affects the interpretation of its poor performance. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that RhAII has "negligible L-glutaminase activity" is unsupported without quantitative data and assay detection limits. The claim of a relationship between FGE dynamics and enzyme activity is unsupported without quantitative RMSF and RMSD data and statistical analysis. The claim that the screening workflow identified RhAII as a promising candidate is weakened by the acknowledged lack of correlation between predicted binding energies and catalytic efficiency; the selection logic is not fully transparent. The therapeutic potential of RhAII as an "antileukemic candidate" is not assessable from the abstract, as no biological model data are presented. The generalizability of the computational workflow to other enzyme families or targets is not discussed and cannot be evaluated from the abstract.

MurB 是肽聚糖生物合成早期阶段的关键酶，催化 NADPH 依赖的 UNAGEP 还原为 UDP-MurNAc。抑制 MurB 可有效破坏细菌细胞壁合成。目前无临床获批的 MurB 特异性抑制剂，已报道抑制剂种类有限（4-thiazolidinone、imidazolinone、pyrazolidinedione、phenylthiazolyl urea 等），结构多样性、抗菌效力和安全性均不足。 现有方法为何不足 : 传统实验筛选成本高、周期长；已报道的 MurB 抑制剂结构类型有限，缺乏系统性筛选；纯基于对接的虚拟筛选对打分函数精度依赖高，命中率有限。 精确的「Can ... ?」研究问题 : Can a machine learning-based classification model, combined with structure-based docking and clustering, identify novel micromolar inhibitors of E. coli MurB from an in-house compound library? 04 背景与发展脉络 （标注：以下脉络为「仅本文框架」——基于本文引言与讨论中引用的文献线索构建，未逐一外部核验全部引用。） 阶段 代表性方法 快速覆盖大规模化学空间，对接提供原子级结合模式约束（特别是与关键残基 ASN A:233 的氢键），从而在保持筛选效率的同时提高命中率。 - 关键残基约束 ：基于已知共晶结构（PDB: 2Q85）中配体与 ASN A:233 的氢键相互作用作为对接筛选的硬性标准，将结构生物学知识直接嵌入筛选流程，而非仅依赖打分函数排序。 - 聚类保证多样性 ：FCFP_6 指纹聚类确保选出的候选化合物具有结构多样性，避免重复筛选同一化学骨架。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis]: - 对于缺乏大量高质量活性数据的靶标，使用小规模已知抑制剂（84 个）训练 ML 模型仍可有效预筛大规模库，关键在于选择适当的分子表征和模型评估标准（MCC + AUROC 双阈值）。 - 将已知的结构-活性关系（如关键残基相互作用）转化为可计算的筛选约束，可显著提高虚拟筛选的针对性。 Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report the use of a machine learning-guided virtual screening workflow, combined with molecular docking, to identify four compounds (Q9, Q11, Q12, Q13) with in vitro inhibitory activity against E. coli MurB (IC50 values 25.08–34.44 µM), low cytotoxicity in HepG2 cells, and computationally predicted stable binding modes. Visible evidence base Abstract, full text, tables (Tables 1–4), figures (Figures 1–9), supplementary figure references (Figure S1, S2). No raw data, model files, or supplementary material were provided for independent verification. Missing materials affecting confidence Supplementary figures (S1, S2) referenced but not provided. Raw data for enzyme inhibition assays, IC50 curve fits, and cytotoxicity data are not available. Details of the in-house compound library composition and the specific compounds Q9, Q11, Q12, Q13 (SMILES or structures) are not provided. Model training/test set splits and hyperparameters are not fully described. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript presents a straightforward application of established computational methods (machine learning, docking, MD, MM-GBSA) combined with a limited set of experimental validation assays. The identification of four micromolar inhibitors of MurB is a modest but potentially useful contribution. However, the study has several significant weaknesses that currently prevent the claims from being fully established. The most critical issues are the small training dataset (84 compounds), the lack of structural information for the hit compounds, the absence of a positive control in the enzyme assay, the unexplained discrepancy between the reported 100 ns and 200 ns MD simulations, and the lack of any attempt to demonstrate target engagement or mechanism of action beyond computational prediction. The manuscript would benefit from a more critical interpretation of the results and a clearer statement of the limitations. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in antibacterial drug discovery, particularly those focused on cell wall biosynthesis inhibitors, computational chemists applying machine learning to virtual screening, and medicinal chemists interested in novel scaffolds for MurB inhibition. The work may also be of interest to the broader community developing ML-guided screening workflows, although the methodological novelty is limited. Major strengths The study integrates a reasonable pipeline of computational and experimental methods, from ML-based screening to in vitro validation. The authors are transparent about the lack of antibacterial activity of the identified compounds, which is an important negative result. The use of multiple computational techniques (docking, MD, MM-GBSA, PCA) provides a multi-faceted view of the predicted binding modes. The manuscript is generally clearly written and the workflow is easy to follow. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors claim that "Model_2 was selected as the optimal activity-prediction model for virtual screening" based on predefined criteria (MCC > 0.5 and AUROC > 0.7). Evidence pointer Table 1, Section "Model Construction and Evaluation" Concern The training dataset consists of only 84 compounds after preprocessing. This is a very small dataset for training a robust ML classification model, especially with the "best quality" preset in AutoGluon, which is prone to overfitting. The manuscript does not report cross-validation strategies (e.g., k-fold) or external validation on a separate test set. The reported test set metrics (Table 1) are based on a single random 80/20 split, which is insufficient to demonstrate generalizability. The selection of Model_2 over Model_1 is not justified beyond the reported metrics, and the difference in performance may not be statistically significant given the small dataset size. Why it matters The entire virtual screening pipeline depends on the predictive quality of the selected ML model. If the model is overfitted or not generalizable, the prioritization of the 238 compounds is unreliable, and the subsequent experimental hits may be fortuitous. The lack of robust model validation undermines the core methodological claim of the paper. Resolution test The authors should provide a more rigorous model evaluation, including cross-validation (e.g., 5-fold or 10-fold) and, ideally, an external test set. They should also report the distribution of prediction scores and the confidence intervals for the performance metrics. If the dataset is too small for robust ML, this limitation should be explicitly acknowledged and the model selection criteria should be justified more carefully. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors state that "16 candidate compounds were selected based on their hydrogen-bond interactions with the key active-site residue ASN A:233" and that these were subsequently tested experimentally. Evidence pointer Section "Molecular Docking", Table 2 Concern The manuscript does not provide the chemical structures or identifiers (e.g., SMILES, PubChem CID) for the 16 selected compounds, nor for the four active hits (Q9, Q11, Q12, Q13). Without this information, the results are not reproducible, and the reader cannot assess the chemical novelty or drug-likeness of the identified scaffolds. Furthermore, the selection criteria for the 16 compounds are not fully described. The manuscript mentions "FCFP_6 fingerprint-based clustering to ensure structural diversity" but does not specify the clustering algorithm, similarity threshold, or how the final 16 were chosen from the 238 ML-predicted hits. The docking score cutoffs and the visual inspection criteria are also not defined. Why it matters Reproducibility is a fundamental requirement for scientific publication. The lack of compound structures and detailed selection criteria prevents other researchers from replicating the study or building upon it. The claim that these are "novel inhibitors" cannot be evaluated without knowing their structures. Resolution test The authors must provide the chemical structures (as SMILES or in a supplementary table) for all 16 tested compounds and the four active hits. They should also provide a detailed, step-by-step description of the selection process, including the clustering parameters and the docking score thresholds used. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors report IC50 values of 34.44, 31.45, 25.08, and 25.94 µM for Q9, Q11, Q12, and Q13, respectively, and state that these compounds "exhibited inhibition rates exceeding 50%" at 50 µM. Evidence pointer Section "Identification of Hits", Figure 4, Table 2 Concern The enzyme inhibition assay methodology is described in the Materials and Methods, but critical details are missing. The assay couples MurA and MurB reactions, but the authors do not specify the concentrations of MurA, MurB, UNAG, PEP, and NADPH in the final reaction. The ratio of MurA to MurB is particularly important because the assay measures NADPH consumption, which is dependent on both enzymes. The authors also do not report a positive control inhibitor (e.g., a known MurB inhibitor) to validate the assay's dynamic range and sensitivity. The IC50 values are reported with standard errors, but the number of independent experiments (stated as three) is low for a reliable estimate. Furthermore, the manuscript does not report the maximum inhibition achieved at saturating concentrations, which is important for assessing the efficacy of the compounds. Why it matters Without a properly validated assay and appropriate controls, the reported IC50 values may not accurately reflect the true inhibitory potency of the compounds. The lack of a positive control makes it difficult to compare these results with other studies. The potential for assay artifacts (e.g., compound precipitation, interference with the coupled enzyme system) cannot be ruled out. Resolution test The authors should provide a detailed description of the assay conditions, including all reagent concentrations. They should include a positive control inhibitor and report the maximum inhibition and Hill slope for each compound. Ideally, they should also confirm the inhibitory activity using an orthogonal assay (e.g., a direct binding assay or a MurB-specific assay that does not rely on MurA coupling). Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors state that "200-ns molecular dynamics simulations were performed" in the Materials and Methods, but in the Results section, they refer to "100 ns MD simulations." Evidence pointer Section "Plausible Binding Modes From Molecular Dynamics Simulations" vs. Section "Molecular Dynamics Simulation" in Materials and Methods Concern There is a direct contradiction between the simulation length reported in the Results (100 ns) and that in the Methods (200 ns). This is a critical discrepancy that affects the interpretation of the MD results. If the simulations were only 100 ns, the convergence of the systems may not have been achieved, and the conclusions about binding stability may be premature. If they were 200 ns, the Results section is incorrect. Why it matters The MD simulation results are used to support the claim that the compounds form stable complexes with MurB. An incorrect simulation length undermines the credibility of these results and raises questions about the rigor of the computational analysis. Resolution test The authors must correct this discrepancy and clearly state the actual simulation length used. They should also provide evidence of convergence (e.g., RMSD vs. time plots for the full simulation length) to support their conclusions. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Scientific importance Claim pointer The authors conclude that the identified compounds "offer promising scaffolds for further mechanistic investigation and structural optimization." Evidence pointer Conclusion, Abstract Concern The identified compounds have IC50 values in the high micromolar range (25–34 µM) and show no antibacterial activity against E. coli ATCC 25922 (MIC > 64 µg/mL). While the authors acknowledge this limitation, the claim that these are "promising scaffolds" is not strongly supported. The lack of antibacterial activity suggests poor cellular penetration or efflux, which are significant hurdles that are not addressed. The manuscript does not discuss the physicochemical properties of the compounds (e.g., LogP, molecular weight, polar surface area) that might explain the lack of whole-cell activity. The structural novelty of the scaffolds is also not discussed in the context of known MurB inhibitors. Why it matters The significance of the work depends on the potential of the identified compounds to be developed into useful antibacterial agents. Without a clear path to improving potency and cellular activity, the "promising scaffolds" claim is overstated. Resolution test The authors should temper their conclusions and provide a more critical assessment of the compounds' potential. They should discuss the physicochemical properties of the hits and propose specific medicinal chemistry strategies to improve their antibacterial activity. Alternatively, they could reposition the work as a proof-of-concept for the ML screening workflow rather than a source of drug candidates. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity and reproducibility Affected element Dataset description Evidence pointer Section "Dataset Compilation" Issue The authors state that 112 compounds were retrieved from ChEMBL and 84 remained after preprocessing. The criteria for classifying compounds as "active" or "inactive" (IC50 threshold of 50 µM) are mentioned, but the distribution of active vs. inactive compounds in the final dataset is not reported. This is important for understanding the model's performance and potential class imbalance. Required correction Report the number of active and inactive compounds in the training and test sets. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Technical soundness Affected element MM-GBSA calculations Evidence pointer Section "MM-GBSA Binding Free Energy Analysis", Table 4 Concern The MM-GBSA results are presented as a single value per compound without error estimates. It is unclear how many frames were used for the calculation and whether the results are statistically meaningful. The ranking of compounds by MM-GBSA does not correlate with the experimental IC50 values (Q9 has the most favorable ΔG bind but is not the most potent inhibitor). Required correction Provide the standard deviation or standard error of the MM-GBSA calculations and discuss the lack of correlation with experimental potency. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Clarity and reproducibility Affected element Cytotoxicity assay Evidence pointer Section "Cytotoxicity Evaluation", Figure 5 Concern The authors report cell viability data but do not state the concentration of DMSO in the assay. High DMSO concentrations can affect cell viability. The positive control (e.g., a known cytotoxic agent) is not mentioned. Required correction Specify the DMSO concentration and include a positive control in the cytotoxicity assay. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Readability for nonspecialists Affected element Introduction Evidence pointer Section "Introduction" Concern The introduction is brief and does not provide sufficient background on the MurB enzyme, its role in peptidoglycan biosynthesis, and the structural features of its active site. A reader unfamiliar with the field may struggle to understand the significance of the ASN A:233 interaction. Required correction Expand the introduction to provide more context on MurB as a drug target and the rationale for targeting ASN A:233. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1: Insufficient ML model validation (small dataset, no cross-validation). R1-M2: Missing chemical structures of the hit compounds and incomplete selection criteria. R1-M3: Incomplete enzyme assay validation (no positive control, unclear coupling conditions). R1-M4: Contradictory MD simulation lengths (100 ns vs. 200 ns). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : Low to moderate. The application of ML to virtual screening is not new, and the specific target (MurB) has been studied before. The combination of methods is standard. The identification of four new micromolar inhibitors is a modest incremental advance. Scientific importance : Low to moderate. MurB is a validated target, but the identified compounds are weak inhibitors with no antibacterial activity. The work does not provide significant new insights into MurB inhibition or the ML methods used. Interdisciplinary readership : Limited. The work is primarily of interest to computational chemists and antibacterial drug discovery researchers. The methods are not novel enough to attract a broader audience. Technical soundness : Currently not established. The ML model validation is inadequate, the experimental assay lacks key controls, and there is a critical inconsistency in the MD simulation length. These issues must be resolved before the conclusions can be accepted. Readability for nonspecialists : The manuscript is generally readable, but the introduction is too brief and the methods section is dense. The figures are not provided for review, which limits the assessment of clarity. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript has a logical workflow and the authors are transparent about the lack of antibacterial activity, which is commendable. However, the technical issues outlined above, particularly the ML model validation, the missing compound structures, the incomplete assay validation, and the MD simulation inconsistency, prevent the main claims from being supported. The authors should be encouraged to revise the manuscript to address these concerns. If the technical issues are resolved, the work could be a useful contribution to the field of computational antibacterial drug discovery, but it would likely be more suitable for a specialized journal rather than a high-impact general journal.

悖论，但景观粗糙度对折叠效率的定量影响尚未被系统理解。理解这一关系对蛋白质设计（避免误折叠）、疾病建模（错误折叠相关疾病）和折叠预测方法评估均有直接意义。 现有方法不足 ：传统 Gō-like 模型只编码天然接触，缺乏对非天然相互作用的显式建模；全原子模拟计算成本高，难以系统扫描粗糙度参数空间；实验方法难以直接测量景观粗糙度。 精确研究问题 ：Can a Gömböc-inspired 2D ：unverified Review setup Input scope Full manuscript text (abstract, introduction, computational methods, results and discussion, conclusion) for the article "When does a funnel become a trap? A Gomboc-inspired model of protein folding landscapes" by Shityakov, Skorb, and Nosonovsky. Assessment boundary Scientific content, methodological soundness, validity of claims, and internal consistency of the presented evidence. No assessment of editorial fit or journal-specific policy matters. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose a two-dimensional computational model inspired by the Gömböc shape (a convex body with one stable and one unstable equilibrium) to study how landscape ruggedness affects protein folding outcomes. They report a sharp transition from efficient folding to trapping as a ruggedness parameter r increases, and claim qualitative correspondence between model success rates and the performance of Rosetta and AlphaFold3 on the TPR1 domain. Visible evidence base Full text including equations, simulation parameters, results tables/figures referenced (Table 1, Figs 1–4, Fig S1), and benchmark comparisons against Rosetta and AlphaFold3 for the TPR1 domain (PDB 1ELW). Missing materials affecting confidence Figures and Table 1 are referenced but not provided in the submitted text. Supplementary information (Fig S1A–F) is referenced but not available. The GitHub repository link is provided but its contents were not assessed. Exact numerical values for some reported statistics (e.g., success rates at each r value) are not fully specified in the text. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript presents an interesting conceptual analogy between the Gömböc shape and protein folding landscapes, and the computational model is clearly described. However, the central claim of qualitative correspondence between model success rates and Rosetta/AF3 performance rests on a comparison of non-equivalent metrics across different systems, and the manuscript does not establish that the Gömböc-inspired model captures features beyond what standard Gō-like models already provide. The sharp transition in success rate with increasing r is presented as a key finding, but the mechanistic interpretation is underdeveloped and the apparent recovery at high r is dismissed as an artifact without rigorous demonstration. The benchmark comparison is suggestive but not quantitatively grounded. The manuscript would benefit from a clearer articulation of what specific, testable prediction the model makes that distinguishes it from existing approaches. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein folding theory, energy landscape analysis, and computational biophysics may find the Gömböc analogy conceptually appealing. The model's simplicity and computational efficiency could interest those seeking coarse-grained or conceptual frameworks for teaching or for generating hypotheses about frustration effects. The bridging of topology and folding may also appeal to mathematicians working on shape optimization or dynamical systems with applications in biophysics. Major strengths The manuscript is clearly written and the Gömböc analogy is pedagogically attractive. The computational model is simple, transparent, and reproducible in principle. The systematic sweep of the ruggedness parameter across five orders of magnitude is a reasonable approach. The use of two independent structure prediction methods (Rosetta and AF3) as benchmarks for the TPR1 domain is appropriate, and the reported energy landscape features for TPR1 are consistent with its known behavior as a well-folded domain. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Claim validity Claim pointer "These findings suggest that the Gömböc-inspired model captures essential features of folding landscape quality and may serve as a useful heuristic for comparing foldability across different systems." Evidence pointer Results and discussion, "Gömböc-inspired model reveals frustration-dependent folding behavior"; "Rosetta ab initio simulations"; "AF3 validates the TPR1 domain" Concern The central claim of qualitative correspondence between model success rates and Rosetta/AF3 performance is based on comparing fundamentally different quantities. The Gömböc model reports the fraction of optimization trajectories reaching an RMSD threshold in a 2D toy landscape, while Rosetta and AF3 report structural prediction accuracy for a real 3D protein. The numerical values (93% vs 90%, 83% vs 77%) are presented as if they were comparable, but there is no theoretical or statistical framework linking these quantities. The model success rate at r = 0 is 93%, which is claimed to correspond to AF3's 90% coverage, yet the model at r = 0 has no frustration at all, while AF3 operates on a real protein with real sequence-specific interactions. The comparison is therefore not a validation of the model but an exercise in pattern matching. Why it matters If the model is to serve as a heuristic for comparing foldability, the correspondence must be established on a principled basis, not by aligning two numbers that happen to be similar. Without a defined mapping between model parameters and physical quantities, or between model success rates and prediction confidence metrics, the claim is unfalsifiable and cannot be extended to other systems. Resolution test Provide a quantitative framework linking model success rates to physical observables (e.g., folding rates, Φ-values, or prediction confidence scores) and demonstrate predictive validity on at least two additional proteins with known frustration properties. Alternatively, clearly reframe the claim as a purely conceptual analogy with no quantitative predictive content. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer "At minimal ruggedness (10−8), the model achieves 83% success in reaching native-like states" and "At zero ruggedness (r = 0.0), the landscape acts as a near-perfect funnel, yielding an average energy drop of 129.5 ± 21.7 arbitrary units, convergence in 21 optimization steps, and a 93% success rate." Evidence pointer Abstract; Results and discussion, "Gömböc-inspired model reveals frustration-dependent folding behavior"; Table 1 (referenced, not provided) Concern The manuscript reports success rates at r = 0 (93%) and r = 10−8 (83%) but does not explain why adding even infinitesimal noise (10−8) causes a 10 percentage point drop. The energy function includes both a stochastic term (Erug) and a frustration term (Efrust), both scaled by r. At r = 10−8, the magnitude of these terms is negligible compared to the native attraction term, yet the success rate drops substantially. This is not explained mechanistically. Additionally, the text states that "the stochastic noise at extreme ruggedness values (10−4 and 10−3) causes the gradient-based optimizer to terminate prematurely; thus, the apparent recovery in the success rate is merely an artifact." This interpretation is plausible but not demonstrated. The manuscript does not report the distribution of final RMSD values, the fraction of trajectories terminating by iteration limit versus gradient tolerance, or any diagnostic to distinguish genuine folding from premature termination near the starting point. Why it matters The sharp transition between r = 10−8 and r = 10−7 is the central quantitative finding of the model. If the transition is an artifact of the optimizer terminating prematurely rather than a property of the landscape, the model's relevance to physical folding is undermined. The manuscript must distinguish between landscape trapping (a physical effect) and optimizer failure (a numerical artifact). Resolution test Report the fraction of trajectories that terminate by gradient tolerance versus iteration limit at each r value. Show the distribution of final RMSD values and energy drops. Demonstrate that the transition is robust to changes in optimizer (e.g., using a stochastic optimizer or simulated annealing) and to the choice of convergence criteria. If the transition is an optimizer artifact, the claim of landscape trapping must be revised. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Scientific importance Claim pointer "Unlike conventional Gō models that encode only native contacts, the present formulation combines a monomonostatic (single-stable-equilibrium) geometric target with an explicit, tunable Efrust that penalizes non-native long-range distances and a stochastic ruggedness term Erug that injects local energy noise." Evidence pointer Conclusion; Computational methods, "Energy function" Concern The manuscript claims novelty relative to Gō-like models, but the energy function described is a standard structure-based model with added noise and a non-native contact penalty. The Gömböc analogy is presented as the conceptual motivation, but the model itself does not appear to use any property specific to Gömböc geometry. The native state is a 2D curve generated by Fourier synthesis, not a Gömböc shape, and the energy function does not encode monomonostatic properties. The connection to Gömböc is therefore purely metaphorical. The manuscript does not demonstrate that the Gömböc analogy generates any specific, testable prediction that a generic Gō-like model with tunable frustration would not also make. Why it matters If the model is functionally equivalent to existing structure-based models with added noise, the Gömböc framing does not constitute a scientific contribution beyond the analogy itself. The manuscript must either demonstrate that the Gömböc-inspired construction leads to qualitatively different behavior than a generic Gō-like model, or reposition the work as a pedagogical or conceptual contribution rather than a novel computational method. Resolution test Compare the model's behavior to a standard Gō-like model with the same native state and the same frustration terms but without the Gömböc-inspired construction. If the behavior is identical, the Gömböc framing is decorative. Alternatively, identify a specific prediction that arises from the monomonostatic property and test it. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract, first sentence Issue The abstract states "the quantitative effects of landscape ruggedness on folding kinetics are not fully understood," but the manuscript does not measure kinetics. The model reports success rates of optimization trajectories, not folding rates or timescales. The term "kinetics" is used loosely and may mislead readers. Required correction Replace "folding kinetics" with "folding outcomes" or "folding success rates" in the abstract, or add a discussion of how the model relates to kinetic observables. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Technical clarity Affected element Computational methods, "Energy function" Evidence pointer Equations for Erug and Efrust are referenced but not fully displayed in the text Issue The equations for Erug and Efrust are described in words but the full mathematical forms are not given in the text. The equation for Erug is cut off ("according to the following equation:where N = 48") and the equation for Efrust is similarly incomplete. This makes the methods section incomplete as presented. Required correction Provide the complete equations for Erug and Efrust in the methods section. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Statistical rigor Affected element Results and discussion, "Gömböc-inspired model reveals frustration-dependent folding behavior" Evidence pointer Table 1 (referenced, not provided) Issue The manuscript reports means and standard deviations for energy drops (e.g., 129.5 ± 21.7) but does not state the number of independent simulations per condition beyond "n = 100 per condition" in the methods. It is unclear whether the reported uncertainties are standard deviations across the 100 runs or standard errors. The manuscript also does not report whether the differences between conditions are statistically significant. Required correction Clarify the uncertainty metric and report the number of simulations. Consider adding a statistical test (e.g., ANOVA or permutation test) to support claims of significant differences between ruggedness conditions. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Interpretation Affected element Results and discussion, "AF3 validates the TPR1 domain as a minimally frustrated benchmark" Evidence pointer Section text Issue The manuscript states that "High-confidence AF3 predictions (pLDdt ≥ 90) with a uniform PAE plot are characteristic of well-folded, minimally frustrated systems." This is an interpretive claim about what AF3 confidence metrics indicate about frustration. AF3 confidence reflects prediction certainty, not the physical frustration of the folding landscape. A protein with high frustration could still be predicted with high confidence if the training set contains similar folds. The claim conflates prediction confidence with biophysical properties. Required correction Soften the claim or provide a citation supporting the link between AF3 confidence metrics and physical frustration. Alternatively, reframe the AF3 results as evidence of structural predictability rather than minimal frustration. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Results and discussion, "Gömböc-inspired model reveals frustration-dependent folding behavior" Evidence pointer Section text Issue The manuscript mentions "our earlier topological bioscaling analysis of Trp-cage folding" (reference 20) and states that the two approaches "provide a quantitative bridge between monomonostatic topology and the dimensional properties of native state recovery." However, the connection between the two models is not elaborated. It is unclear how the fractional-dimensional analysis relates to the Gömböc-inspired model or what new insight the combination provides. Required correction Expand the discussion of how the two approaches complement each other, or remove the reference if it is not essential to the current work. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Computational methods, "Numerical optimization" Evidence pointer Section text Issue The manuscript states that the model is "pattern-reproducible but not bit-reproducible" and that "reruns give different individual trajectories but the same ensemble statistics." This is a useful clarification, but the manuscript does not specify the random seed policy or whether the reported results are from a single run or averaged over multiple runs with different seeds. Required correction Specify the random seed policy and report whether the results are averaged over multiple independent runs. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (claim of qualitative correspondence without a principled link between model and benchmark metrics) and R1-M2 (incomplete reporting of simulation diagnostics to distinguish landscape trapping from optimizer failure) are the primary technical issues. The incomplete equations for Erug and Efrust (R1-m2) also need correction for reproducibility. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The Gömböc analogy is novel as a conceptual framing, but the computational model itself does not demonstrate new physics or methodology beyond standard structure-based models with tunable frustration. Scientific importance: The question of how landscape ruggedness affects folding is important, but the manuscript does not establish that the toy model provides insights beyond what is already known from Gō-like models and energy landscape theory. Interdisciplinary readership: The manuscript bridges topology and biophysics in a way that could appeal to a broad audience, but the lack of quantitative rigor in the central comparison limits its impact. Technical soundness: The model is simple and clearly described, but the incomplete reporting of equations and diagnostics, and the conflation of prediction confidence with physical frustration, undermine technical rigor. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is generally well-written and accessible, with the Gömböc analogy providing an intuitive entry point. However, the abrupt transition from model results to benchmark comparisons without a clear logical bridge may confuse nonspecialist readers. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The conceptual framing is appealing and the model is simple enough to be useful as a pedagogical tool or a starting point for more rigorous work. However, the central claim of correspondence with Rosetta/AF3 performance must be either quantitatively grounded or explicitly reframed as a conceptual analogy. The simulation diagnostics must be reported to distinguish physical trapping from optimizer artifacts. If these issues are addressed, the manuscript could make a modest but useful contribution to the conceptual toolkit of protein folding research.

use molecular dynamics simulations to show that histidine tautomerism (delta vs epsilon) has minimal effect on beta-sheet propensity in PrP(106-126) A117 V monomers and dimers, but becomes decisive at the trimer and tetramer level, where specific tautomeric combinations promote beta-hairpin formation and define a nascent nucleation core. The central claims, particularly the tautomer-dependent switch at the trimer and tetramer level and the proposed two-step nucleation mechanism, cannot be evaluated without methodological detail and quantitative results. The work may be of interest to the amyloid and prion simulation community, but the current abstract alone does not establish the case. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biophysicists and physical chemists studying amyloid nucleation mechanisms, particularly those focused on prion peptides and the role of protonation and tautomeric states in protein aggregation. Researchers developing coarse-grained or atomistic models of primary nucleation would also find the proposed two-step mechanism relevant, as would experimentalists seeking testable predictions about histidine mutation effects on nucleation kinetics. Major strengths The abstract identifies a specific and understudied variable, histidine tautomerism, and proposes a clear structural hypothesis linking tautomeric state to beta-hairpin formation at specific oligomer sizes. The distinction between minimal effects at monomer and dimer level versus decisive effects at trimer and tetramer level is a testable and mechanistically meaningful claim. The proposed two-step nucleation mechanism is conceptually coherent and could guide future simulation and experimental work. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, methods, or supplementary materials provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, simulation protocols, force field parameters, system setup, convergence criteria, statistical analyses, and all figures or tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a plausible and mechanistically detailed hypothesis for how HST inhibits Abeta early aggregation, supported by REMD simulations. However, the evidence base is limited to the abstract, and several key technical details necessary to evaluate the robustness of the simulations and the validity of the mechanistic claims are absent. The conclusions are potentially significant for the antiamyloid therapeutic field, but the current evidence is insufficient to fully establish the proposed mechanism. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in computational biophysics, molecular dynamics simulation, and protein misfolding diseases, particularly those studying amyloid aggregation inhibitors and natural compounds. The work may also interest medicinal chemists developing flavonoid-based therapeutics for Alzheimer's disease, as it offers atomic-level insights into inhibitor mechanisms. Major strengths The study addresses a clinically relevant problem with a well-defined computational approach. The proposed mechanism is specific and testable, distinguishing HST from generic aggregation inhibitors. The use of REMD is appropriate for exploring conformational ensembles of Abeta dimers. The abstract clearly articulates the novelty of disrupting beta-sheet continuity rather than merely reducing aggregation. Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract does not provide any quantitative metrics for "restricted beta-strand extension" or "disruption of beta-sheet continuity." Why it matters The core conclusion hinges on this observation. If the effect is minor or within statistical noise, the proposed mechanism would be unsupported. They further claim that coarse-grained simulations lacking explicit hydrogen-bond directionality fail to maintain stable tail docking, while inclusion of selected native hydrogen-bond terms restores stability. Visible evidence base Enhanced-sampling molecular dynamics simulations, conservation-guided spatial analysis, prior allosteric network analysis, and coarse-grained modeling, all as described in the abstract only Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, simulation parameters, force field details, convergence criteria, structural figures, quantitative error estimates, statistical analyses, and any comparison with experimental validation are not provided Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a mechanistically plausible and potentially interesting hypothesis regarding sequence-specific surface docking of a disordered enzyme tail. However, the evidence base visible in the abstract is insufficient to establish the central claims. The causal link between specific interactions and allosteric function is asserted rather than demonstrated, and the coarse-grained modeling comparison, while suggestive, lacks the quantitative detail needed to assess its validity. The work may be of interest to the biophysical chemistry community, but the case is not currently established from the provided material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers studying allosteric regulation in metabolic enzymes, particularly those interested in the role of intrinsically disordered regions in enzyme function. Computational biophysicists working on enhanced-sampling methods and coarse-grained modeling of protein dynamics would also find the methodological comparison relevant. The potential generalizability of sequence-specific surface docking as a regulatory mechanism could attract a broader readership in protein science. Major strengths The study addresses a genuinely under-explored question, namely how flexible terminal segments achieve spatial precision for allosteric function. The combination of multiple computational approaches is appropriate for the problem. The explicit comparison between atomistic and coarse-grained models, with attention to hydrogen-bond directionality, is a thoughtful design that could yield mechanistic insight. abstract; no full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors describe a novel undergraduate laboratory activity using a generative AI protein design server (GeoFlow-V3) to enable students to design antiviral nanobodies targeting influenza A virus hemagglutinin. They claim this is the first use of such a platform for teaching nanobody design at the undergraduate level and extend their prior pedagogical model from siRNA design to structural protein engineering. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no data, assessment instruments, student outcomes, or platform validation results are visible Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, figures, tables, supplementary materials, student assessment data, platform output examples, and any validation of designed nanobodies Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially valuable educational innovation that addresses a real gap in undergraduate access to nanobody discovery. The pedagogical rationale is sound and the connection to prior work is appropriate. However, the abstract provides insufficient evidence to evaluate the effectiveness of the activity, the validity of the platform outputs, or the accuracy of the novelty claim. The educational impact cannot be assessed from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Educators in undergraduate biology, biotechnology, and bioinformatics programs would be interested in this work as a model for integrating generative AI into teaching laboratory curricula. Instructors seeking to expose students to structure-based protein engineering without animal or wet-lab requirements would find this activity relevant. The broader community of microbiology and immunology educators may also find value in the antiviral application context. Major strengths The activity addresses a genuine pedagogical barrier by replacing a 6 to 12 month animal-based discovery process with an accessible in silico exercise. The use of a freely available web server lowers institutional cost barriers. The extension of a previously published teaching model provides continuity and suggests iterative refinement of the authors' educational approach. The antiviral context, specifically influenza HA, gives the activity clear biomedical relevance. no access to full text, figures, tables, or supplementary materials Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report identification, heterologous expression, and characterization of Algtm3, a PL39 family alginate lyase from the thermophilic bacterium Rhodothermus profundi . They claim high thermostability, optimal activity at 70 degrees C and pH 8.0, domain essentiality for folding and activity, improved activity of a C-terminally truncated variant, structural insights from modeling and docking, and production of alginate oligosaccharides with degree of polymerization 1 to 4 via endolytic and exolytic modes. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no experimental details, numerical data beyond those stated, figures, tables, or methods are available Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, methods section, all figures and tables, supplementary data, statistical analyses, raw activity measurements, structural model validation metrics, and chromatographic or mass spectrometric data Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially useful contribution to alginate lyase engineering, particularly regarding thermostability and domain truncation effects in a PL39 family enzyme. The reported 1.98-fold activity improvement upon C-terminal truncation and the thermostability profile are of interest. However, the abstract alone does not provide sufficient experimental detail to verify the robustness of the claims. Key quantitative data, statistical treatment, and validation of structural models are absent. The work appears technically sound in outline, but the evidence base available for this review is too limited to fully establish the conclusions. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in marine biotechnology, enzyme engineering, and carbohydrate-active enzyme research would find this work relevant. Those working on alginate oligosaccharide production for pharmaceutical or nutraceutical applications would be interested in the thermostable biocatalyst aspect. The domain dissection findings may also interest structural biologists studying polysaccharide lyase family organization. Major strengths The study addresses a practical limitation of alginate lyases, namely thermostability, using a thermophilic source organism. The domain truncation approach is a logical strategy to improve heterologous expression performance. The combination of biochemical characterization, structural modeling, and product analysis provides a multi-angle perspective. The reported thermostability, retaining over 90% activity after 60 minutes at 65 degrees C, is a notable quantitative result. Interdisciplinary readership: Limited. The work is primarily of interest to enzyme biochemists and marine biotechnologists; broader appeal is not evident from the abstract. Technical soundness: Cannot be fully assessed from the abstract. The experimental design appears reasonable in outline, but the lack of statistical detail and model validation prevents verification. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is clearly written and accessible, with technical terms used appropriately, though some domain nomenclature may be unfamiliar to general readers. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract presents a plausible and potentially useful study, but the evidence base is insufficient to verify the quantitative claims, structural interpretations, and domain essentiality conclusions. A full manuscript with detailed methods, statistical analyses, and model validation would be required to assess whether the case can be made. Risk / unsupported claims The 1.98-fold activity improvement of Algtm3dc over wild-type is unsupported without replicate data and statistical analysis. The claim of "excellent thermal stability" is supported only by a single time point and temperature; broader stability data are needed. The structural interpretation that C-terminal truncation induces local changes in the substrate-binding region contributing to enhanced activity is speculative without model validation or experimental mutagenesis. The assertion that specific domains are "essential" for folding, solubility, and activity is unverifiable without systematic construct data. The endolytic and exolytic degradation modes are asserted but not quantitatively supported in the abstract. The claim of producing oligosaccharides with degree of polymerization 1 to 4 lacks quantitative product distribution data.

：在少步（few-step）生成模型中，如何在不重新训练或微调生成器的情况下，使生成样本对齐到特定奖励函数（如人类偏好、下游任务得分）？ 为什么重要 ：少步生成模型（如少步扩散模型）在推理效率上具有优势，但现有奖励对齐方法（如 RLHF、DPO）通常需要额外训练或大量采样，成本高且不适用于少步场景。 现有方法不足 ：传统对齐方法依赖梯度回传至生成器参数或需要大量 scope Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and evidence presented in the abstract; no methods, figures, tables, or supplementary material were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors claim that protein language model (pLM) embeddings can be decoded via coevolutionary analysis without supervised training to identify protein N-glycosylation sites, and that this zero-shot framework (MaskNGly) achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. They further claim that application across proteomes reveals biological insights including increased glycosylation propensity with organismal complexity, preferential glycosylation at structured and solvent-exposed regions, disease association of mutations in high-scoring motifs, and signatures of glycosylation-mediated allostery. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, methodological details, or validation data are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, methods section, all figures and tables, supplementary material, benchmark datasets, and code availability details Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents an ambitious and potentially interesting claim: that pLM embeddings can be decoded in a zero-shot manner to predict N-glycosylation sites at omics scale. The biological findings described are intriguing and would be of interest to the glycobiology and computational biology communities. However, the abstract alone provides no quantitative evidence, no methodological detail, and no validation strategy. The core claims of performance comparability to supervised predictors and the biological insights cannot be assessed from the supplied material. The manuscript may have merit, but the case is not established from the evidence provided. The claimed scalability to omics-scale analysis is practically valuable. The biological findings, if well-supported, would provide new insights into glycosylation determinants and disease associations. 模型做刚性拟合与打分，最终在 52 例蛋白质基准中达到接近参考模型的拟合质量，并在 PfA-M17 蛋白质和 Ca-raiA RNA 两个实际案例中正确鉴定目标分子。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：给定一张未鉴定的 cryoEM/cryoET 密度图（尤其来自内源复合物或未充分表征样本），如何自动确定图中分子是哪种蛋白质或 RNA？ 为什么重要 ：冷冻电镜分辨率革命使大量内源复合物、细胞提取物和原位图谱得以解析，但「图谱对应哪个分子」常需人工专家结合质谱、转录组等先验信息逐一排查，成为通量瓶颈。若能自动鉴定，将极大加速结构生物学与细胞原位结构解析。 现有方法不足 ： CryoID1 依赖传统算法特征提取，主要针对蛋白质，未覆盖 RNA，且未利用深度学习特征预测。 现有深度学习方法（DeepTracer、ModelAngelo、DeepMainmast、Cryo2Struct、CryoAtom、EMRNA）主要面向 从头建模 （de novo model building），而非 分子身份鉴定 ；它们回答「如何搭模型」，而非「这是哪个分子」。 结构库检索（如 PDB 匹配）缺乏对序列先验（质谱/转录组候选池）的整合，且对低分辨率或局部密度图鲁棒性不足。 精确研究问题（Can ... ?） ：Can a deep learning–enhanced pipeline, combining predicted structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types with sequence-based candidate ranking and rigid-body structural fitting, reliably identify both protein and RNA components from cryoEM maps given a user-supplied candidate sequence pool? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：此脉络基于本文引言与讨论，结合公开领域常识，标注为「经外部核验」部分。 冷冻电镜分辨率革命（~2015–2020） ：单颗粒 cryoEM 与 cryoET 使膜蛋白、异质复合物、细胞内源复合物的结构解析成为可能。代表：Kühlbrandt (2014) 等综述。优点：无需结晶、样本量小；局限：图谱本身不携带分子身份信息。 图谱解释的早期算法方法（~2016–2020） ：如 Phenix、Coot 等手动/半自动建模工具，依赖高分辨率侧链密度；在中等分辨率或局部密度下难以区分氨基酸类型。CryoID1（本文引文 [4]）提出从密度提取约化序列信息，用序列比对鉴定蛋白质，但限于蛋白质、依赖传统特征。 深度学习方法用于图谱解释（~2020–2024） ：DeepTracer（[13]）预测主链与残基类型；ModelAngelo（[14]）用 profile HMM 搜索鉴定蛋白质；DeepMainmast（[15]）结合 AlphaFold2 模型；Cryo2Struct（[16]）用 transformer 预测原子与残基；CryoAtom（[17]）引入 AlphaFold2 注意力机制；EMRNA（[18]）面向 RNA 建模。优点：自动化程度高；局限：聚焦建模而非身份鉴定，且多数仅覆盖蛋白质。 结构库与预测库的扩展（~2021–2025） ：AlphaFold DB 提供近乎全蛋白质组的预测结构，PDB 持续增长，使「检索候选结构并拟合到密度图」成为可行策略。但如何从序列先验（质谱/转录组）高效筛选候选并评估拟合质量仍缺乏统一框架。 本文位置 ：CryoID2 将深度学习特征预测（3D U-Net）与序列比对（BLASTp/BLASTN）和结构拟合（刚性 + 打分）整合为统一流水线，首次在同一框架内同时支持蛋白质与 RNA 鉴定，并明确区分「序列排序」与「结构验证」两个阶段，强调结构信息对序列排序结果的进一步筛选作用。 05 核心痛点 痛点 表现 成因或作者解释 文中证据 分子身份未知 内源复合物或未表征样本的 cryoEM 图谱无法直接对应到已知分子 密度图只反映电子散射，不携带序列信息；需外部先验（质谱/转录组） Introduction 第 1–2 段；SUMMARY 人工鉴定耗时且依赖专家 precision 0.16、recall 0.99 06 核心思想 表面方法 ：CryoID2 是一个四阶段流水线——(1) 三个 3D U-Net 分别从 cryoEM 密度图预测结构类（helix/sheet/coil/RNA）、关键原子位置（Cα/磷酸/糖环）和约化残基/核苷酸类型；(2) 基于预测的关键原子位置做聚类与骨架追踪，沿骨架分配约化类型，生成短序列查询；(3) 用 BLASTp（蛋白质）或最大化最小百分位策略（RNA）对用户提供的候选序列池排序；(4) 对排序靠前的候选，检索 PDB 或 AlphaFold 模型，刚性拟合到密度图，用复合打分（预测关键原子 + 预测结构类 + 实验密度）排序并输出最佳匹配。 核心洞察 ： - 约化字母表是序列与密度之间的桥梁 ：将 20 种氨基酸压缩为 6 类、4 种核苷酸压缩为 2 类，牺牲序列特异性换取对密度图预测误差的容忍度，使短查询片段仍能有效比对候选池。 - 序列排序与结构验证是互补的两阶段 ：序列排序快速缩小候选范围，但可能受假阳性干扰；结构拟合用实验密度和预测特征独立验证候选，两者结合比任一单独更可靠。 - 模块化设计允许逐步替换与扩展 ：每个 U-Net、比对策略、拟合打分均可独立优化或替换，便于适配不同分辨率、不同分子类型（如 DNA）或不同候选池来源。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] ： - 在信息不足时， 降低输出字母表的分辨率 （约化表示）可以显著提升端到端鲁棒性，这一思想可迁移到其他「从噪声观测推断序列/身份」的任务（如低分辨率质谱肽段鉴定、单细胞测序聚类）。 - 两阶段「粗筛 + 精验」策略 在计算生物学中广泛有效：先用快速方法缩小空间，再用昂贵但精确的方法验证，可平衡通量与精度。 - 对结构库（PDB/AlphaFold）的「检索 + 拟合」模式，可作为「结构预测 × 实验密度」交叉方向的通用范式，尤其适用于无先验序列但已知候选池的场景。 07 方法总览 输入 ：(1) 未鉴定的 cryoEM 密度图（3D 体素网格，重采样至 1 Å 体素大小）；(2) 用户提供的候选序列池（蛋白质为氨基酸序列，RNA 为核苷酸序列）。 输出 ：排名最高的候选分子身份（蛋白质或 RNA），以及对应的拟合后结构模型（PDB 或 AlphaFold 模型刚性放置到密度图中）。 模块 ： 1. 特征预测 ：三个独立的 3D U-Net（19 层），分别输出 voxel-wise 概率图——结构类（helix/sheet/coil/RNA/DNA/背景）、关键原子（Cα/磷酸/糖环）、约化类型（6 类氨基酸/2 类核苷酸）。 2. 骨架追踪与查询生成 ：对关键原子概率图做阈值化 + mean-shift 聚类，得到离散原子位置；用图方法（半径最近邻图）连接原子，以预测结构类为软约束，生成骨架轨迹；沿轨迹采样约化类型，生成短序列查询（FASTA 格式）。 3. 序列排序 ：蛋白质用 BLASTp-short（PAM30、word size 2、gap 15/3、E-value cutoff 1.0），RNA 用最大化最小百分位（maximin）策略——每个查询与候选比对，取所有查询中最低的百分位分数作为候选得分，强调跨查询一致性。 4. 结构检索与拟合 ：对排序靠前的候选，从 PDB（实验结构）或 AlphaFold DB（预测结构）检索对应模型；用预测关键原子和结构类生成初始放置（质心对齐 + 主成分对齐），再用 Kabsch 迭代 + Powell 优化（6 自由度刚性变换）最大化复合打分 S。 打分函数 ：S = 0.8 × 平均预测关键原子概率 + 1.2 × 平均预测结构类概率 + 0.08 × 平均实验密度 z-score（粗筛时密度权重为 0.04）。 训练 ：三个 U-Net 独立训练，使用 cryoDataBot 流程生成的 730 对 cryoEM map–model 数据（补充表 S3），加权交叉熵损失，Adam 优化器（初始学习率 1e-4，ReduceLROnPlateau 调度，batch size 16，early stopping patience 15 epoch）。 文字流程 ：输入密度图 → U-Net 预测三类特征 → 聚类 + 追踪生成骨架 → 沿骨架生成约化序列查询 → BLASTp/maximin 对候选池排序 → 检索 PDB/AlphaFold 模型 → 刚性拟合 + 打分 → 输出最佳匹配模型与身份。 08 核心模块拆解 模块 功能 为何需要 输入输出 支撑证据 移除后的已知或预期影响 3D U-Net 特征预测（结构类） 逐体素分类 helix/sheet/coil/RNA/DNA/背景 为骨架追踪提供结构约束，区分蛋白质与核酸区域 输入：64³ Å³ 密度子块；输出：6 类概率图 Results 图 3a：voxel-wise accuracy results, discussion, resource availability, and STAR methods. Assessment boundary Scientific validity, methodological soundness, clarity of claims, and alignment with stated evidence. Not assessed: code functionality, GUI usability, or reproducibility of software installation. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present cryoID2, a deep learning-enhanced pipeline for identifying proteins and RNA from cryoEM maps. The method integrates three 3D U-Nets for feature prediction, sequence-based candidate ranking, and structural evaluation. Claims include high-recall feature prediction, resolution-dependent atom clustering, near-reference fitting quality in a 52-case benchmark, and successful end-to-end identification of PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set. Visible evidence base Main text figures (Figs 1–6), supplementary figures (Supplementary Figs 1–2), supplementary tables (Supplementary Tables 1–4), and method descriptions in STAR Methods. Missing materials affecting confidence The manuscript does not provide quantitative results for the 52-case benchmark beyond mean and median Q-score differences. No per-case Q-score values are shown in the main text. The RNA proof-of-concept relies on a single case. No comparison against existing tools (e.g., ModelAngelo, DeepTracer, cryoID1) is provided. The training dataset composition and quality-control criteria are only summarized in a supplementary table without detailed statistics. The manuscript does not report runtime or computational cost. The claim of "high-recall feature prediction" is not supported by quantitative recall values in the main text. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a potentially useful extension of the cryoID approach, integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence and structural ranking for both protein and RNA identification. The modular benchmarking strategy is thoughtful, and the two end-to-end cases are illustrative. However, the evidence presented is insufficient to establish the method's general utility or superiority over existing approaches. Key quantitative results are missing or underreported, and the single-case RNA demonstration limits confidence in the RNA branch. The manuscript would benefit from more rigorous benchmarking, including comparisons to existing tools and a more detailed analysis of failure cases. Who would be interested in the results, and why Structural biologists using cryoEM/cryoET to characterize endogenous complexes or poorly characterized samples would be the primary audience. Researchers developing computational tools for cryoEM map interpretation would also be interested in the methodological contributions, particularly the integration of sequence and structural evidence. The RNA identification component may appeal to the growing cryoET community studying native RNA-protein assemblies. Major strengths The modular design of the pipeline is clear and logical, separating feature prediction, sequence ranking, and structural evaluation. The use of reduced amino acid and nucleotide alphabets is a sensible strategy for tolerating prediction uncertainty. The inclusion of a structural evaluation stage after sequence ranking is a valuable addition that can discriminate among closely related candidates. The authors are appropriately cautious in distinguishing their method from de novo model building and in acknowledging the need for direct comparisons. Major Concerns The quantitative evidence for the 52-case benchmark is thin. Only mean and median Q-score differences are reported, without per-case distributions, failure analysis, or comparison to a baseline. The RNA proof-of-concept is a single case with a heavily constrained candidate pool, limiting its generalizability. The claim of "high-recall feature prediction" is not substantiated with numbers in the main text. No comparison to existing tools (e.g., ModelAngelo, DeepTracer, cryoID1) is provided, making it difficult to assess the method's added value. The structural evaluation stage is limited to rigid-body fitting, which may not be adequate for cases with conformational differences. Minor Comments The manuscript would benefit from a more detailed description of the U-Net training data, including the distribution of resolutions and molecular weights. The choice of the 50% threshold for RNA candidate selection in the proof-of-concept is not justified. The description of the maximin scoring method could be clearer. The authors should clarify whether the 52-case benchmark includes any RNA cases. The discussion of limitations is honest but could be expanded with a more explicit statement of what the method cannot do. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The lack of quantitative feature prediction metrics in the main text. The absence of per-case results or failure analysis for the 52-case benchmark. The lack of comparison to existing methods. The single-case RNA demonstration with a length-constrained candidate pool. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: Moderate. The integration of deep learning feature prediction with sequence and structural ranking is a reasonable extension of prior work, but the individual components are not novel. Scientific importance: Moderate. The problem of molecular identification in cryoEM maps is important, but the evidence does not yet demonstrate a major advance over existing tools. Interdisciplinary readership: Limited. The manuscript is primarily of interest to cryoEM method developers and practitioners. Technical soundness: The modular benchmarking is sound in principle, but the reporting is incomplete. The lack of comparisons and quantitative details weakens the technical case. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is generally well written and accessible, though some method details are dense. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript describes a plausible and potentially useful method, but the evidence presented is insufficient to support the claims of high-recall feature prediction, near-reference fitting quality, and successful end-to-end identification. Substantial additional benchmarking and reporting are needed. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality" Evidence pointer Figure 3d, Supplementary Tables 1–2 Concern The 52-case benchmark is summarized only by mean and median Q-score differences. No per-case results, distribution plots, or failure analysis are provided. The claim of "near-reference fitting quality" is based on a mean difference of −0.0346 and a median difference of −0.0001, but the reader cannot assess how many cases had large Q-score losses or whether these correlate with resolution, molecular weight, or other factors. Why it matters Without per-case data, the reader cannot evaluate the robustness of the method or identify conditions under which it fails. The mean difference is dominated by a small number of failures, but the manuscript does not characterize these failures. This limits the ability to assess whether the method is suitable for general use. Resolution test Provide per-case Q-score differences, a histogram or scatter plot of Q-score differences versus map resolution, and a discussion of cases with large Q-score losses. If possible, compare the fitted Q-scores to those obtained by a simple baseline (e.g., fitting the deposited model without sequence ranking). Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Comparative evaluation Claim pointer "CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation" Evidence pointer Discussion, Introduction Concern The manuscript does not compare cryoID2 to existing tools for molecular identification or model building, such as ModelAngelo, DeepTracer, or the original cryoID. The authors acknowledge this in the Discussion ("Direct comparisons under matched candidate-pool and map conditions would be needed"), but the absence of any comparative data makes it impossible to assess whether cryoID2 offers a meaningful improvement. Why it matters The field already has several automated tools for map interpretation. Without a direct comparison, the reader cannot determine whether cryoID2 is a significant advance or a marginal improvement. The claim of "addressing" the bottleneck implies a solution that is at least competitive with existing approaches. Resolution test Run cryoID2 and at least one existing tool (e.g., ModelAngelo or cryoID1) on the same set of benchmark maps and candidate pools, and report identification accuracy, runtime, and Q-scores. If a direct comparison is not feasible, clearly state the limitations and provide a qualitative comparison of features and expected performance. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Generalizability of RNA branch Claim pointer "the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps" Evidence pointer Figure 6, Methods Concern The RNA proof-of-concept is a single case. The candidate pool was constructed by excluding annotated CDS regions and further constrained by the known 204-nucleotide reference length (±50%). This is a substantial prior constraint that may not be available in a real discovery scenario. The manuscript does not report how the method would perform without this length constraint or on a more diverse set of RNA structures. Why it matters The RNA branch is a key novelty of cryoID2. A single case with a heavily constrained candidate pool does not establish that the method can identify RNA in general. The length constraint, in particular, may be unrealistic for many applications. Resolution test Test the RNA branch on additional RNA cryoEM maps with different lengths, structures, and candidate pool compositions. Report performance with and without the length constraint. If additional cases are not available, clearly state this limitation and temper the claim of a "unified" route. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Quantitative feature prediction metrics Claim pointer "Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction" Evidence pointer Figure 3a–c, Methods Concern The claim of "high-recall feature prediction" is not supported by quantitative metrics in the main text. The manuscript reports voxel-wise accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 scores for the three U-Net models, but the values are only described qualitatively. The reader cannot assess whether the recall is genuinely high or whether the precision is acceptable. Why it matters Feature prediction is the foundation of the entire pipeline. If the U-Net models have low precision, the downstream steps may be overwhelmed by false positives. The manuscript should report the actual numbers and discuss the trade-off between precision and recall. Resolution test Report the numerical values for accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for each U-Net model in the main text or a clearly referenced table. Discuss the implications of the precision-recall trade-off for downstream performance. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Figure 3d Evidence pointer Figure 3d Issue The figure shows the 52-case benchmark results, but the axes and units are not described in the main text. It is unclear what is plotted and how the Q-score difference is calculated. Required correction Add a clear figure legend describing the axes, the calculation of Q-score differences, and the meaning of the plotted values. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Methodological detail Affected element RNA candidate pool construction Evidence pointer Methods Issue The manuscript states that the RNA candidate pool was constructed from the genome by excluding CDS regions, but it does not specify how the 50-nucleotide minimum length was chosen or how overlapping intervals were handled. Required correction Provide additional detail on the interval definition, including how overlapping intervals were merged or resolved, and justify the 50-nucleotide minimum. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element U-Net training Evidence pointer Methods Issue The manuscript states that 92,014 subvolumes were used for training, but does not report the number of unique maps or the distribution of resolutions in the training set. Required correction Report the number of unique maps, the resolution range, and the distribution of molecular weights in the training set. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Interpretation Affected element Discussion Evidence pointer Discussion Issue The Discussion states that "the structural benchmark should not be interpreted as an evaluation of end-to-end molecular identification across all 52 cases." This is an important caveat, but it is not reflected in the Results section, where the benchmark is presented as evidence of performance. Required correction Move or repeat this caveat in the Results section where the benchmark is first described, so that readers are not misled. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Supplementary Table 4 Evidence pointer Supplementary Table 4 Issue The illustrative example in Supplementary Table 4 is helpful, but it is not clear how the percentile scores are calculated when there are tied values. Required correction Add a brief description of the tie-handling procedure in the table legend or in the Methods section. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of "high-recall feature prediction" is not supported by quantitative metrics in the main text. The claim of "near-reference fitting quality" in the 52-case benchmark is based on summary statistics only, without per-case data or failure analysis. The claim of a "unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification" is based on a single RNA proof-of-concept case with a heavily constrained candidate pool. The claim that cryoID2 "addresses" the identification bottleneck is not supported by comparisons to existing tools. The statement that "the average decrease was dominated by a small number of failure cases" is an interpretation that is not backed by per-case data. The claim that "query sequence identity showed only a weak relationship with map resolution" is based on an R² of 0.137, but the manuscript does not report the number of data points or the confidence interval for this estimate.
