Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present a nonredundant, resolution-stratified benchmark dataset of 972 protein-chain samples from 495 cryo-EM structures resolved at 4.5–8.0 Å, with voxel-level annotations for helix, sheet, and non-periodic secondary structure (NPSS). They evaluate five deep learning architectures (U-Net, Residual U-Net, Attention U-Net, UNETR, Swin-UNETR) under standardized conditions and report that Residual U-Net achieves the highest macro-averaged foreground F1 score in all three resolution bins, with helices generally segmented more accurately than sheets or NPSS. Visible evidence base Text descriptions of dataset construction, annotation, training, and evaluation procedures. Reported numerical results in the text (e.g., F1 scores for architectures across bins, CC score distribution). References to Figures 1–5 and Tables 1–2, none of which were provided. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures and tables, including the dataset overview figure, CC score distribution figure, resolution-wise dataset composition table, training configuration table, and all results figures. No code, trained models, or supplementary material. No statistical significance testing or variance reporting. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a genuine and timely need: standardized benchmarking for secondary-structure segmentation in intermediate-resolution cryo-EM maps. The dataset construction pipeline is described in considerable detail and appears methodologically sound. However, the scientific value of the contribution cannot be fully assessed without the actual results figures and tables, which are referenced but not provided. The reported numerical results are sparse and lack statistical context. The claim that Residual U-Net is the best-performing architecture is based on mean scores without variance or significance testing. The manuscript would benefit from clearer articulation of what is genuinely novel relative to existing benchmarks and from a more critical discussion of the relatively low absolute performance values. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational structural biologists developing or applying deep learning methods for cryo-EM map interpretation. Researchers working on protein structure prediction, model building, and secondary-structure assignment from density maps. The benchmark dataset and evaluation framework would be of practical use to this community for standardized method comparison. Major strengths The dataset construction pipeline is described with unusual care, including explicit selection criteria, redundancy removal via MMseqs2 clustering, and map-to-model agreement filtering with a conservative CC threshold. The resolution-stratified design (three bins within 4.5–8.0 Å) is a thoughtful and useful contribution that addresses a real gap in the literature. The controlled evaluation framework, with fixed partitions, standardized preprocessing, and common metrics, is exactly what the field needs. The inclusion of both CNN-based and transformer-based architectures provides a reasonable initial comparison across architectural paradigms. Evidence pointer Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 4, location not provided Concern The central quantitative results of the paper are presented only as references to figures that were not provided for review. The only numerical values given in the text are a few example F1 scores from the qualitative examples (e.g., Attention U-Net achieving 0.46 Macro-FG F1 on one Bin 1 chain). Without the actual results figures and tables, it is impossible to verify the claims about architecture ranking, resolution-dependent trends, or class-specific performance. The reported mean scores lack any measure of variance, confidence intervals, or statistical significance testing, making it impossible to determine whether the observed differences between architectures are meaningful. Why it matters The primary scientific contribution of this paper is the empirical comparison of architectures under controlled conditions. If the results figures and tables are not available, the evidence base for the central claims is absent. Furthermore, without variance or significance testing, even the provided means cannot be interpreted reliably. The difference between Residual U-Net (0.386) and U-Net (0.373) in Bin 1, for example, may or may not be meaningful depending on the spread of per-chain scores. Resolution test Provide all results figures and tables. Report per-chain score distributions, standard deviations, or confidence intervals for all reported means. Conduct and report statistical significance testing (e.g., paired tests across chains) for architecture comparisons within each bin. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological validity Claim pointer The manuscript states that "voxels within a 3 Å radius of a Cα atom were assigned the secondary-structure class of the corresponding residue" and that the dataset includes "voxel-level annotations for helices, sheets, and non-periodic secondary-structure (NPSS) regions." Evidence pointer Materials and Methods, Secondary Structure Annotation, location not provided Concern The annotation procedure assigns secondary-structure labels based solely on distance to Cα atoms. This is a substantial simplification that may not accurately represent the true spatial extent of secondary-structure elements in the density map. A 3 Å fixed radius around Cα atoms will systematically under-label the volume occupied by helices and sheets, which have finite cross-sectional dimensions. The manuscript does not discuss how this annotation strategy compares to alternatives, such as using all backbone atoms or side-chain atoms, or how sensitive the results are to the choice of radius. The authors also do not report any validation of the annotation quality, such as comparison with manually curated segmentations or alternative labeling schemes. Why it matters The quality and validity of the ground-truth labels are foundational to the entire benchmark. If the labels are systematically biased or inaccurate, all subsequent performance measurements are compromised. The choice of a 3 Å Cα-based radius is a critical methodological decision that could substantially affect the measured performance of all architectures, and the manuscript does not justify this choice or assess its consequences. Resolution test Justify the 3 Å Cα-based annotation radius with reference to prior work or physical considerations. Report sensitivity analyses with different radii (e.g., 2.5 Å, 3.5 Å, 4 Å) or alternative annotation strategies. Validate the generated labels against an independent source, such as manual expert annotation on a subset of chains or comparison with segmentations from established tools. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Scientific context Claim pointer The manuscript states that "there remains a lack of standardized evaluation protocols and systematic resolution-stratified analyses" and that existing methods "were primarily designed to introduce and evaluate specific deep-learning frameworks using study-specific datasets and experimental protocols." Evidence pointer Introduction, Related Work and Research Gaps, location not provided Concern The manuscript does not provide a systematic comparison with existing benchmark datasets or evaluation protocols in the cryo-EM secondary-structure segmentation literature. While the authors correctly note that prior studies used different datasets and protocols, they do not quantify or characterize these differences in a way that would allow readers to understand what specific gap this benchmark fills. For example, the EMNIST dataset mentioned in the Related Work section is not described in terms of its size, resolution range, or annotation strategy, so the reader cannot assess how the present benchmark differs. The claim of novelty for the resolution-stratified design is plausible but not substantiated by a thorough review of existing resources. Why it matters The scientific contribution of a benchmark dataset depends on its novelty and utility relative to existing resources. Without a clear and detailed comparison to prior datasets and evaluation protocols, the reader cannot assess whether this benchmark fills a genuine gap or duplicates existing efforts with minor modifications. Resolution test Provide a detailed comparison table or section characterizing existing benchmark datasets and evaluation protocols for cryo-EM secondary-structure segmentation, including dataset size, resolution range, annotation strategy, and evaluation metrics. Explicitly state what the present benchmark adds beyond these existing resources. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Issue The abstract states the dataset "comprises 972 nonredundant protein-chain samples from 495 cryo-EM protein structures resolved at 4.5–8.0 Å" but does not mention the resolution-stratified binning in the results summary. The key finding that performance varies non-monotonically across bins is not reflected in the abstract. Required correction Add a sentence to the abstract summarizing the resolution-dependent findings, including the non-monotonic pattern and the class-specific differences. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Materials and Methods, Dataset Construction Evidence pointer Materials and Methods, location not provided Issue The manuscript states that "the database search was performed on January 16, 2026, providing a reproducible snapshot of the available data" but does not specify the exact search query, database version, or any filtering criteria applied at the database level beyond the stated selection criteria. The MMseqs2 clustering parameters are not fully specified (e.g., coverage threshold, alignment mode). Required correction Provide the full database search query, database version, and all MMseqs2 parameters used for clustering to ensure the dataset construction is fully reproducible. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Technical soundness Affected element Materials and Methods, Training Configuration Evidence pointer Table 2, location not provided Issue The manuscript states that "all five architectures were trained using the Adam optimizer with an initial learning rate of 3 × 10–4" and that "Swin-UNETR was trained with a batch size of 4 because of its higher GPU-memory requirement." The difference in batch size between Swin-UNETR and the other architectures is a potential confound, as batch size can affect optimization dynamics and final performance. The manuscript does not discuss this limitation. Required correction Acknowledge the batch size difference as a potential confound and discuss its possible impact on the comparison. Consider reporting results with Swin-UNETR trained at a smaller batch size for the other architectures as a sensitivity check, or justify why the batch size difference is unlikely to affect the conclusions. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Readability Affected element Discussion, Resolution-Dependent Segmentation Challenges Evidence pointer Discussion, location not provided Issue The discussion of why performance decreases from Bin 1 to Bin 2 but not necessarily from Bin 2 to Bin 3 is somewhat speculative. Required correction Provide quantitative characterization of the bins (e.g., average chain length, secondary-structure composition, density quality metrics) to support the interpretation of the observed performance patterns. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (results figures and tables not provided, no variance or significance testing) and R1-M2 (annotation strategy not validated or justified) are blocking. R1-M3 (insufficient comparison with existing benchmarks) is important for establishing novelty but may be addressable with additional text rather than new experiments. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: Moderate. The resolution-stratified design is a useful contribution, but the overall approach of deep learning for secondary-structure segmentation is well established. Scientific importance: Moderate. The benchmark has clear utility for the cryo-EM community, but the manuscript does not demonstrate that the benchmark enables new scientific insights beyond what existing datasets provide. Interdisciplinary readership: Limited. The manuscript is written for a specialized audience of computational structural biologists and may not be accessible to a broader readership. Technical soundness: The dataset construction pipeline is carefully described, but the annotation strategy is insufficiently justified and the results lack statistical rigor. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is clearly written but assumes substantial background in both cryo-EM and deep learning. The abstract and introduction are accessible, but the methods and results sections would be challenging for nonspecialists. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The dataset and evaluation framework are potentially valuable contributions, and the manuscript addresses a genuine need in the field. However, the blocking concerns regarding missing results evidence and annotation validation must be addressed before the scientific claims can be considered established. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that Residual U-Net achieves the highest Macro-FG F1 score in all three resolution bins is unsupported without the actual results figures and tables, and without statistical significance testing. The claim that "all five architectures achieve their highest Macro-FG F1 scores in the highest-resolution bin" is unsupported for the same reason. The claim that the dataset enables "fine-grained analysis of resolution-dependent segmentation performance" is plausible but not demonstrated without the results figures. The claim that the annotation procedure produces reliable ground-truth labels is unsupported without validation against alternative labeling schemes or manual annotation. The claim that the benchmark is "nonredundant" is supported by the described MMseqs2 clustering procedure, but the specific parameters and resulting redundancy levels are not fully reported. The claim that the dataset reflects "contemporary" cryo-EM practices is supported by the 2020–2026 release date range, but the potential impact of this restricted range on generalizability is not discussed.

01 基本信息 标题 ：Simulating Directed Evolution In Silico with an Iterative, Physics-Based Workflow 作者与单位 ：Jones, Chey M; Verma, Deeptak（单位未在提供材料中给出） 期刊/预印本平台 ：ACS Omega 年份 ：2026-10-30（按提供信息） 论文类型 ：方法学/回顾性验证研究（retrospective analysis，proof-of-concept） 领域 ：计算酶工程、定向进化、分子动力学模拟、基于结构的蛋白设计 关键词 ：directed evolution; coarse-grained molecular dynamics (CGMD); in silico mutagenesis; ketoreductase (KRED); oligomerization; protein–protein interface; AggScore; Rosetta; Martini3 DOI/arXiv 号 ：10.1021/acsomega.6c08421 代码 ：未提供 数据 ：PDB ID: 9PHG（KRED-15 dimer 晶体结构）；补充材料含 Tables S1–S10、Figures S1–S7 阅读日期 ：未提供 在课题方向中的位置 ：该文属于「蛋白质结构相关计算研究 × 物理模拟（MD/对接）」分支，具体为 基于 CGMD + 全原子 MD + Rosetta 突变建模的迭代式 in silico 定向进化工作流 ，用于蛋白质–蛋白质界面（oligomerization）的工程化设计。与 AlphaFold/AI 生成方法形成互补对照，强调显式物理模拟对构象动力学与远端效应的捕捉能力。 02 一句话总结 该文提出 ViPER——一个结合结构建模、粗粒化分子动力学（CGMD）、in silico 饱和突变与基于结构的性质评估（AggScore）的迭代工作流，通过模拟 KRED 酶从二聚体向单体方向的定向进化，在五轮内预测出 >70% 对寡聚化状态转换关键的位点，并识别出一个实验定向进化中出现的远端突变 W291Y。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：能否用一个纯物理/基于结构的迭代计算工作流，在无需大规模训练数据的前提下，模拟定向进化过程并预测调控酶寡聚化状态（dimer↔monomer）的关键突变位点与进化路径？ 为何重要 ：定向进化是酶工程的核心手段，但蛋白质设计空间巨大，实验筛选成本高；生成式 AI 方法虽能提出突变，但其「隐藏逻辑」难以揭示酶功能的基本物理细节，且对动态/远端区域可能不敏感。 现有方法不足 ：AI 方法基于序列或静态结构的学习模式提出突变，通常分散于整个酶且影响范围广；不清楚 AI 模型隐含了多少蛋白质动力学信息；对影响酶行为的远端柔性区域可能无法捕捉。 精确研究问题 ：Can a physics-based, iterative in silico workflow (CGMD + in silico mutagenesis + structure-based scoring) predict the mutations and positions that toggle the oligomerization state of a KRED enzyme, matching experimentally observed directed evolution outcomes? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：以下脉络为「仅本文框架」梳理，未经外部文献核验。 阶段一：实验定向进化 。通过迭代突变-筛选（rounds）改造酶，成功但耗时耗资源，难以同时探索多条进化路径。 阶段二：生成式 AI 方法 。基于数百至数百万同源序列的学习模式提出突变，加速了设计空间的探索，但逻辑不透明，对蛋白质动力学和远端柔性区域的隐含信息不明。 阶段三：物理/基于结构的计算方法 。利用 MD 模拟、结构建模理解酶功能物理基础，可显式捕捉纳秒-微秒尺度的动态相互作用。 本文主张的位置 ：ViPER 处于阶段三，主张物理模拟可 先验地 识别影响酶功能的动态区域，作为 AI 方法的补充而非替代；通过迭代 CGMD + in silico 突变 + AggScore 选择压力，模拟定向进化并同时探索多条路径。 05 核心痛点 痛点 表现 成因或作者解释 文中证据 蛋白质设计空间过大 难以彻底采样，实验筛选成本高 序列空间组合爆炸 Introduction AI 方法逻辑不透明 难以揭示和利用酶功能的基本物理细节 基于学习模式，隐藏逻辑 Introduction AI 对动力学信息嵌入不明 不清楚 AI 模型隐含多少蛋白质动力学信息 多数蛋白高度动态，少数突变可大幅改变构象景观 Introduction AI 突变分散且影响范围广 AI 建议的突变通常分布在整个酶上 基于家族耐受性模式聚合 Discussion 静态结构无法捕捉瞬态相互作用 无法先验预测形成瞬态蛋白-蛋白/蛋白-配体相互作用的区域 瞬态接触在静态结构中不可见 Results 开篇 实验难以并行探索多条路径 时间和资源限制 物理实验通量有限 Late-Round Evolution 06 核心思想 表面方法 ：ViPER 是一个迭代工作流——从原子结构出发，粗粒化为 CG 模型，跑 1 μs CGMD 识别界面接触残基，对这些位点做 in silico 饱和突变（Rosetta fixbb + relax），用 AggScore 评估二聚体聚集倾向，选最低者作为下一轮亲本，最多并行 5 条路径，共 5 轮。 核心洞察 ：蛋白质的瞬态动态相互作用（在纳秒-微秒尺度出现）才是决定酶功能（如寡聚化）的关键，而这些区域无法从静态结构先验预测；通过物理模拟显式捕捉这些动态接触，再结合能量可及性筛选，可以在一个聚焦的设计子空间内高效导航，甚至发现远端突变（如 W291Y）。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis]：物理模拟的「可解释性」使其能揭示 AI 方法难以暴露的机制细节；迭代 + 并行路径探索的计算框架可迁移到其他蛋白性质优化（如热稳定性、蛋白-配体相互作用），关键在于选择压力（selection pressure）需与目标性质对齐。 07 方法总览 输入 ：KRED-15 二聚体晶体结构（PDB: 9PHG） 输出 ：五轮 in silico 进化后的 isKRED 变体序列、高优先级位点列表（28 个）、预测的关键突变 模块 ： 1. 原子建模（Schrödinger Maestro + Protein Preparation，OPLS4 力场，PROPKA pH 7.4） 2. 粗粒化建模（martinize2，elastic network，insane 溶剂化，Martini3 力场） 3. Supporting Information referenced but not supplied. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the main text and the claims it makes. All Supporting Information (Figures S1–S7, Tables S1–S10) is unavailable, so any claim whose support resides primarily in the SI is treated as not independently verifiable. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present ViPER, an iterative structure- and physics-based workflow (coarse-grained MD, in silico site-saturated mutagenesis, structure-based property scoring) that retrospectively simulates directed evolution of a ketoreductase (KRED) from a dimeric state (KRED-15) toward a monomeric state. They claim ViPER predicted >70% of sites crucial for toggling oligomerization after five rounds, identified a distal mutation (W291Y) incorporated during experiment-based directed evolution, and outperformed multiple zero-shot prediction methods at identifying engineerable interfacial patches. Visible evidence base Main-text descriptions of the five-round workflow; CGMD (1 µs) and AAMD (200 ns) simulation protocols; AggScore-based selection; interface interaction energy and contact area comparisons; overlap statistics with experiment-based directed evolution (reported as 71% hydrophobic-patch capture, 42% surface-mutation capture, 62% solvent-tolerance positions); a comparison to zero-shot methods (Table S7, not shown). Missing materials affecting confidence Figures S1–S7, Tables S1–S10, benchmarking details for the elastic network model, and the zero-shot comparison table. These are load-bearing for several quantitative claims and for reproducibility. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a coherent, well-motivated physics-based workflow and applies it to a chemically relevant problem (toggling oligomerization of an industrial KRED). The narrative is clear and the iterative logic is easy to follow. However, the central quantitative claims rest heavily on Supporting Information that is not available in the supplied material, the retrospective design creates a substantial risk of hindsight bias in the reported capture rates, and the comparison against zero-shot methods is asserted without visible evidence. As presented, the work is a plausible proof-of-concept but the headline performance claims are not independently established from the supplied text. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational protein engineers and enzyme engineers interested in oligomerization and protein–protein interfaces; practitioners of MD-based and coarse-grained design workflows; groups comparing physics-based versus generative-AI mutation proposal; and biocatalysis researchers interested in solvent tolerance of ketoreductases. The retrospective framing and the interface-focused selection pressure make it most directly relevant to those already working on oligomeric enzymes. Major strengths The workflow is explicitly iterative and physics-based, which is a meaningful complement to sequence-only generative models. The use of a coarse-grained step to gain roughly 5x throughput (863 vs 182 ns/day) is a practical and clearly reported engineering choice. The authors are candid that the search space is biased toward the interface and that distal mutations are largely missed, which is an honest limitation statement. The identification of the reverse mutation W291Y at a distal surface site, if reproducible, is a genuinely non-trivial observation. The parallel-trajectory design (up to five parents per round) is a sensible way to exploit the low cost of in silico screening. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Retrospective bias and circularity of the capture-rate claim Claim pointer ViPER "successfully predicting >70% of sites that are crucial for toggling the oligomerization of this KRED enzyme (after only five rounds)" and the reported 71% hydrophobic-patch capture rate. Evidence pointer Results, "Evolutionary Space Prioritized by ViPER"; Table (final variants); Figure S6; Tables S8–S9 (not provided). Concern The study is explicitly retrospective and the selection pressure (AggScore at the dimer interface) was chosen with a priori knowledge of the engineered hydrophobic patch, as the authors state in the Discussion. The ">70%" figure is therefore computed against a target set the method was tuned to hit. No negative control, no shuffled or scrambled selection pressure, and no blinded holdout set is described in the main text. Why it matters Without a control that removes the prior knowledge, the capture rate cannot distinguish genuine predictive skill from informed target selection. This is the manuscript's headline quantitative claim. Resolution test Report capture rates under a selection pressure or scoring metric chosen without reference to the known hydrophobic patch, and/or a scrambled-target control, and show that performance degrades in a way consistent with genuine prediction rather than target leakage. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Unverifiable comparative claim against zero-shot methods Claim pointer "the ViPER workflow outperformed multiple, zero-shot prediction methods based on their ability to identify these engineerable patches at the interface." Evidence pointer Results, "Evolutionary Space Prioritized by ViPER"; Table S7 (not provided). Concern The comparison is stated in the main text but its entire evidentiary basis is Table S7, which is not in the supplied material. The identity of the zero-shot methods, the metric used, the number of methods, and whether the comparison is fair (same target set, same definition of "engineerable patch") are all unspecified in the visible text. Why it matters This is a competitive claim that positions the method against the current state of the art. It cannot be evaluated, and if the comparison is not like-for-like it would be misleading. Resolution test Provide the comparison table in the main text with named methods, the exact metric, the target set, and a statement of comparability. If the comparison is not apples-to-apples, soften or remove the claim. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Statistical support for simulation-derived conclusions Claim pointer Claims about transient versus prolonged contacts, dimer dissociation after hundreds of nanoseconds, and interface interaction energy increases of ~5–20%. Evidence pointer Results, "Late-Round Evolution" and "Modification of Structural Interactions and Properties"; Figure S3; Table S6; Table S10 (not provided). Concern The number of independent CGMD and AAMD replicas per variant is not stated in the main text. Dissociation events are described as "uncommon," and the interaction-energy shifts are small (5–20%) relative to what is typically observed across independent MD replicas. Table S10 is cited for contact-sampling statistics but is not available. Why it matters Single-trajectory observations of rare events such as dissociation, and small energy differences, are not reliable without replica statistics. The mechanistic interpretation of the workflow depends on these observations. Resolution test State the number of replicas per variant, report distributions rather than single values, and show that the reported energy and contact differences exceed replica-to-replica variability. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Validity of AggScore as a surrogate for oligomerization Claim pointer AggScore is used as the selection pressure and as the primary readout of "aggregation propensity" throughout, including the final ranking of variants. Evidence pointer Methods, "Structure-Based Variant Evaluation and Selection"; Results, "Early-Round Evolution"; Tables S1–S5 (not provided). Concern AggScore is a structure-based aggregation descriptor, and the manuscript does not present any validation that AggScore tracks the monomer/dimer equilibrium of this specific KRED, nor that it correlates with the experimental solvent-tolerance phenotype. The workflow optimizes AggScore, then reports AggScore improvements as evidence of success, which is internally consistent but not externally validated. Why it matters If AggScore is not a faithful proxy for the oligomeric state of this system, the entire selection trajectory and the final variant ranking lose their physical interpretation. Resolution test Show a correlation between AggScore and an independent measure of oligomerization (for example experimental or longer-timescale simulation-derived monomer/dimer populations) for a set of variants spanning the AggScore range. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility of the coarse-grained setup Claim pointer The CGMD protocol and the ~5x speedup claim, and the use of CGMD contacts to define mutagenesis targets. Evidence pointer Methods, "Coarse-Grained Modeling" and "Coarse-Grained Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Analysis"; Figure S7; benchmarking details in Supporting Information (not provided). Concern The elastic network model parameters, the martinize2 settings, and the benchmarking that justifies the coarse-grained representation are all placed in the Supporting Information. The main text reports a 20 fs time step for production CGMD, which is aggressive and requires justification that is not visible here. Why it matters The coarse-grained step is the throughput-enabling core of the workflow. If the representation distorts interfacial dynamics, the contact sets that drive target selection are unreliable. Resolution test Provide the elastic network and martinize2 parameters, the time-step stability evidence, and the RMSD comparison to all-atom in the main text or as a clearly summarized main-text table. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology consistency Affected element Mutation nomenclature Evidence pointer Results, "Early-Round Evolution" and "Late-Round Evolution"; Table (final variants). Issue The manuscript alternates between forward and reverse mutation nomenclature (for example P106T versus T106P, M183L versus E183M, W291Y versus Y291W) when referring to the same position across the in silico and experimental directions. This is explained in places but is easy to misread. Required correction Add a short nomenclature note or a position-indexed table clarifying directionality for each mutation discussed. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Quantitative reporting Affected element Capture-rate denominators Evidence pointer Results, "Evolutionary Space Prioritized by ViPER"; Figure S6. Issue The 71%, 62%, and 42% capture rates are reported without stating the denominator sets in the main text, and the exclusion of buried and distal positions from the 62% figure is described only in passing. Required correction State each denominator explicitly and report the excluded categories alongside each rate. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Figure and table self-containment Affected element Main-text figures Evidence pointer Results, all subsections; Figure captions. Issue Several main-text figures are referenced only by letter (for example "Figure a", "Figure b") in the supplied text, and the captions are not included, so the figures cannot be assessed for whether they support the associated claims. Required correction Ensure each figure caption states the quantity plotted, the number of replicas, and the variant set, so the figure is interpretable without the SI. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Claim scope Affected element Distal mutation interpretation Evidence pointer Results, "Late-Round Evolution"; Discussion. Issue The W291Y result is described as demonstrating "predictive capabilities," but it is a single distal event recovered in the final round, and the manuscript itself notes that distal mutations were largely not identified by the interface-biased pressure. Required correction Reframe as an anecdotal observation rather than a demonstrated capability, or provide additional distal cases. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Methods completeness Affected element AAMD protocol Evidence pointer Methods, "All-Atom Molecular Dynamics Simulations and Analysis". Issue The AAMD section does not state the number of replicas, the total aggregate sampling per variant, or how the 200 ns length was chosen relative to the 1 µs CGMD runs. Required correction Add replica counts and a brief justification for the simulation length. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (retrospective bias in the headline capture rate), R1-M2 (unverifiable zero-shot comparison), R1-M3 (replica statistics for rare events and small energy differences), R1-M4 (external validation of AggScore), R1-M5 (coarse-grained parameter and time-step justification). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is moderate. Iterative physics-based in silico directed evolution is not new in itself, but the specific combination of coarse-grained contact discovery, site-saturated Rosetta mutagenesis, and structure-based aggregation scoring applied to an oligomerization toggle is a reasonable incremental contribution. Scientific importance is currently limited by the retrospective design and the absence of prospective validation; the work is a proof-of-concept rather than a demonstrated design capability. Interdisciplinary readership is plausible, spanning computational chemistry, biocatalysis, and protein engineering, but the current evidence would need the controls above to interest a broad audience. Technical soundness is the weakest axis as presented, because the key quantitative claims depend on unavailable Supporting Information and on single-trajectory or unreplicated observations. Readability for nonspecialists is good; the workflow is explained clearly and the motivation is accessible, though the mutation-nomenclature switching and the reliance on SI figure letters will slow non-expert readers. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The workflow is coherent and the direction is promising, but the headline performance claims, the comparative claim against zero-shot methods, and the mechanistic simulation conclusions cannot be verified from the supplied material and are vulnerable to retrospective bias. Supportive if the technical concerns, in particular R1-M1 and R1-M2, are resolved with visible controls and data. Risk / unsupported claims The ">70%" site-prediction figure is not supported as an unbiased performance estimate given the retrospective, prior-informed selection pressure (R1-M1). The claim that ViPER "outperformed multiple, zero-shot prediction methods" is unsupported in the visible material; the supporting table is not provided (R1-M2). The claim that dimer dissociation "takes place after hundreds of nanoseconds" for specific variants is based on observations the manuscript itself calls uncommon, with no visible replica statistics (R1-M3). The interpretation of interface interaction energy increases of ~5–20% as evidence of interface disruption is weak without replica-level variability (R1-M3). The use of AggScore as a validated proxy for oligomerization and solvent tolerance is asserted rather than demonstrated (R1-M4). The W291Y result is presented as evidence of predictive capability from a single distal event (R1-m4). The coarse-grained speedup and representation fidelity claims depend on benchmarking placed in unavailable Supporting Information (R1-M5).

代理模型（DFT/MD 替代模型）与算法模块的组合，在 2-3 小时内生成适配体候选序列，并在梅毒螺旋体蛋白和 Tau441 两个前瞻性实验中展示了功能性结合，但未建立通用成功率或与 SELEX 的 superiority。 03 研究问题 具体问题 : 能否在不依赖 SELEX 实验筛选的情况下，仅从蛋白质三维结构出发，在数小时内设计出能够结合靶蛋白的 DNA/RNA 适配体？ 为什么重要 : SELEX 依赖靶蛋白的可溶性、纯化制备和多次筛选循环，对膜蛋白、翻译后修饰蛋白、毒性蛋白等难以制备的靶点效率低下；且筛选过程存在序列偏好和文库覆盖不足的问题。计算 de novo 设计可绕过这些限制，将适配体发现从「实验筛选」转变为「结构驱动的理性设计」。 现有方法为何不足 : 序列-only 方法（基于 HT-SELEX 数据训练的判别/生成模型）依赖已有适配体数据，对未见过的靶点泛化能力有限，且缺乏物理可解释性； 结构/物理方法（MD、对接）计算成本高，无法在筛选规模（10⁴-10⁶ 候选）下运行； AlphaFold3/RoseTTAFoldNA 等结构预测模型需要已知的核酸-蛋白复合物训练数据，对 de novo 设计（无已知复合物）不适用。 精确的「Can ... ?」研究问题 : Can a target-specific retraining? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：以下脉络基于本文框架及作者引用的外部文献，标注为「经外部核验」的部分基于文中明确引用的经典工作。 SELEX 时代（1990-2010s） ：SELEX（1990 年引入）是适配体发现的黄金标准，通过迭代筛选富集高亲和力序列。代表方法：传统 SELEX、Cell-SELEX、Capture-SELEX 等。优点：不依赖结构信息，直接实验筛选；局限：需要靶蛋白可溶性制备、多轮筛选耗时数周至数月、存在文库偏差和 PCR 扩增偏好。 序列-only 计算方法（2010s-2020s） ：利用 HT-SELEX 数据训练机器学习模型预测适配体-蛋白结合。代表方法：基于 CNN/LSTM 的判别模型、语言模型、生成模型。优点：计算快速；局限：依赖已有适配体数据，对未见靶点泛化差，缺乏物理可解释性。 结构/物理方法（2010s-2020s） ：分子对接（如 MEGADOCK、AutoDock）、MD 模拟、MM-PBSA 等用于评估核酸-蛋白相互作用。优点：物理可解释；局限：计算成本高，无法大规模筛选，力场对核酸-蛋白相互作用的准确性有限。 AI 结构预测（2020s-） ：AlphaFold2/3、RoseTTAFoldNA 等可预测核酸-蛋白复合物结构。优点：端到端结构预测；局限：依赖已知复合物训练数据，对 de novo 设计（无已知复合物）不适用，且预测精度对设计任务不足。 本文位置 ：Xelari 将问题分解为多个子任务，每个子任务用专门的代理模型（DFT/MD 替代模型）或算法模块解决，避免了对靶点特异性适配体数据的依赖。这一「分解-替代-组合」策略与蛋白质设计中的「能量函数分解 + 机器学习加速」思路一致。 Xelari 是一个九阶段流水线，将蛋白质结构作为输入，依次执行结构补全（PDBFixer/Boltz-2）、表面特异性分析（Ehrlich）、种子片段构建（DiNA + InNA）、全长适配体组装（MoNA）、折叠稳定性评估（Edgar）、复合物松弛（INGA）和亲和力排序（Valentina），最终输出适配体候选序列及复合物模型。 核心洞察 : 将 de novo 适配体设计分解为多个子问题，每个子问题用「代理模型」替代昂贵的参考计算——InNA 替代 DFT（r2SCAN-3c）计算核苷酸-氨基酸相互作用能，Edgar 替代伞形采样 MD 计算折叠自由能，Valentina 替代全原子 MD 计算结合自由能。这些代理模型在离线阶段用参考计算生成的数据训练，在线推理时只需毫秒级前向传播，从而在 2-3 小时内完成全流程。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis]: - 「分解-替代-组合」策略：将复杂设计问题分解为可独立验证的子任务，每个子任务用专门的代理模型加速，是处理「物理精度 vs 计算通量」矛盾的有效范式。这一思路可迁移到蛋白质设计（如用 GNN 替代 MM-PBSA 做突变扫描）。 - 「参考计算生成训练数据」的 self-contained 策略：不依赖实验数据或已有适配体库，而是用物理参考计算（DFT、MD）生成训练标签，使模型对未见靶点具有更好的泛化能力。这与 AlphaFold 依赖 PDB 训练数据的策略形成对比。 - 模块化设计的诊断价值：每个模块可独立 benchmark（如 DiNA 的 DCC 定位、Edgar 的折叠能、Valentina 的亲和力），失败时可定位到具体环节，而非黑箱端到端。 07 方法总览 输入 : patch，与参考蛋白库比较，识别靶蛋白的独特表面区域 3. 种子片段构建 （DiNA，算法模块 + InNA）：在选定的表面区域上构建 4-6 nt 种子片段，用 InNA 评分 4. 全长组装 （MoNA，算法模块）：将种子片段嫁接到预计算的 scaffold 库（15-45 nt），通过序列和结构过滤 5. 折叠稳定性评估 （Edgar，GNN）：预测适配体折叠自由能，过滤不稳定候选 6. 前瞻性部分 11 结论正确解读 任务范围 : 本文的结论严格限定于「从蛋白质结构出发、不依赖 SELEX 的适配体设计」这一任务。Xelari 的输入是已知或预测的蛋白质三维结构，输出是候选适配体序列。 端到端状态 : 本文展示的是「计算设计 → 合成 → 实验验证」的完整闭环，但验证规模有限（4 个适配体，2 个实验场景），且未报告阴性对照或失败案例的完整统计。 性能边界 : 表观 KD 为 0.91-2.57 μM（活细胞）和功能检测（血清 Tau41），这些数值远低于 SELEX 优化后的适配体（通常 nM 级），说明 Xelari 当前定位是「初始候选生成」而非「亲和力成熟」。 关键限定条件 : 回顾性 benchmark 的 32 条记录并非独立于校准集，且样本量小； 活细胞结合 assay 未确认与预期靶蛋白的特异性结合； Tau41 检测信号由适配体和抗体共同贡献，无法单独归因于适配体； 未报告通用成功率（即「设计 N 个适配体，M 个有功能」的完整分母）。 正确表述 : 本文证明了「从蛋白质结构出发、不依赖 SELEX 的适配体 de novo 设计」在多个模块层面（位点定位、折叠预测、亲和力排序）和两个前瞻性场景中具有可行性，但未建立通用成功率、未证明与 SELEX 的 superiority、未验证特异性结合。 12 Discussion, Materials and methods, Data and code availability, Acknowledgments, Author contributions, Declaration of interests, Supplemental information listing) Assessment boundary Single-reviewer technical and conceptual assessment of the supplied manuscript text only. No reanalysis of deposited data, no access to source code, model weights, or internal datasets, and no independent verification of the cited prospective experimental studies. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present Xelari, a modular structure-based pipeline for de novo DNA and RNA aptamer design from protein structures without target-specific SELEX data or retraining. The pipeline combines five trained models (INGA, InNA, AliNA, Edgar, ValentiNA) and three algorithmic modules (Ehrlich, DiNA, MoNA). Individual modules are benchmarked retrospectively against computational or experimental references. Prospectively, three DNA aptamers designed against Treponema pallidum proteins showed cell-associated binding in a treponeme assay (apparent KD 0.91 to 2.57 micromolar), and a fourth DNA aptamer functioned as a capture reagent for Tau441 in a serum-based hybrid assay. The authors position structure-based design as a complement to experimental selection and explicitly state that a general success rate is not established. Visible evidence base Abstract; Introduction; Results (Xelari architecture, target preparation, surface site specificity, binding-site localization, InNA, AliNA, Edgar, scaffold library, MoNA assembly, complex relaxation and affinity prediction, chemical modifications, prospective validation); Discussion; Materials and methods; Data and code availability; Acknowledgments; Author contributions; Declaration of interests; Supplemental information listing (Figure S1, Tables S1 to S15 referenced but not provided in the submission). Missing materials affecting confidence Supplemental figures and tables (S1 to S15) are referenced throughout but not included in the supplied text. Source code, model weights, and internal training datasets are explicitly not deposited. The complete denominator of candidates ranked, synthesized, and tested in the prospective studies is not reported. The two prospective experimental studies are cited rather than presented in full. The ValentiNA calibration dataset (Table S11) and retrospective affinity compilation (Table S12) are not available for inspection. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a modular, structure-first pipeline for aptamer design and reports module-level retrospective benchmarks plus two prospective applications. The framing is unusually candid about limitations, and the authors repeatedly and correctly distinguish ranking association from absolute prediction, retrospective from prospective evidence, and feasibility from success rate. The principal scientific weakness is that the central claim, that the complete workflow can generate functional aptamers against new targets without SELEX, rests on four DNA aptamers evaluated in two settings, neither of which provides purified-target 1:1 binding data for the intended protein, and neither of which reports the candidate denominator. The module benchmarks are informative but do not compose into an end-to-end accuracy estimate, and the authors acknowledge this. Several technical concerns (proprietary pipeline, non-deposited code and weights, non-homology-controlled Edgar DNA split, calibration and evaluation overlap, RNA-only MoNA benchmark, G-quadruplex exclusion) limit reproducibility and generality. The work is a credible feasibility demonstration and a useful methodological contribution if the technical concerns are addressed and the claims are held to the narrower scope the authors themselves articulate. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in aptamer discovery and nucleic-acid therapeutics, particularly groups working on targets that are difficult to produce in purified native form (membrane proteins, disordered proteins, post-translationally modified targets). Computational structural biologists and machine-learning practitioners interested in surrogate models for physics-based reference calculations across coupled design stages. Assay developers interested in aptamer-antibody hybrid formats. The work is likely to be of interest to the readership of a molecular therapy or nucleic-acid therapeutics journal, and the modular architecture may be of broader methodological interest to the molecular design community. Major strengths The problem framing is well motivated. The Introduction gives a specific and technically grounded account of SELEX constraints (target production, library coverage, amplification bias, post-selection modification) rather than a generic critique. The decomposition of de novo design into sequential subproblems, each with a stated reference method and a stated surrogate, is a coherent and inspectable architecture. The InNA benchmark is the strongest quantitative result in the manuscript. Sub-kcal/mol RMSE against r2SCAN-3c on 483,735 pair geometries, with lysine and glutamic acid held out entirely from training and validation, is a meaningful transfer result for a pairwise scoring function. The manuscript is unusually explicit about what its evidence does not show. The authors state that the cellular assay does not establish intended-target engagement, that the Tau441 study does not provide an aptamer-only affinity, that the ValentiNA panel does not establish family-independent accuracy, that the Edgar benchmark is not homology-controlled for DNA, and that the MoNA benchmark is RNA-only. The chemical-modification analysis, while limited, tests directional ranking across three distinct modification classes (C5 base, 2-prime sugar, backbone) and reports both attenuation and exaggeration of predicted effects rather than only favorable cases. The Discussion identifies concrete failure modes and a specific next test (a prospective series with predefined denominators and independent replication), which is a constructive framing. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis End-to-end validation and claim scope Claim pointer The manuscript claims that Xelari enables de novo aptamer design from protein structure without target-specific SELEX data, and that Xelari-generated candidates can retain experimental function after synthesis in more than one biological and assay setting. Evidence pointer Results, Prospective experimental validation; Results, Prospective live-cell binding; Results, Prospective application to Tau441 detection in serum; Discussion Concern The prospective evidence comprises four DNA aptamers in two settings. In the T. pallidum study, binding was measured on intact cells and was not confirmed against the purified intended lipoproteins, so engagement of the design target is not established. In the Tau441 study, the aptamer served as a capture reagent in a sandwich format in which both recognition reagents contribute to signal, and no aptamer-only 1:1 affinity or independently mapped epitope is reported. Neither study reports the complete denominator of candidates ranked, synthesized, and tested. The central claim of the manuscript therefore rests on a small number of functional successes whose target-level attribution is not established. Why it matters The headline claim is about a design capability, not about four specific sequences. Without a denominator and without target-engagement confirmation, the reader cannot distinguish a pipeline that reliably produces functional candidates from one that produced four functional sequences among an unknown number attempted. The authors acknowledge this, but the Abstract and title still carry the stronger framing. Resolution test Report the complete candidate denominator for each prospective campaign (ranked, synthesized, tested, functional). Provide purified-target binding data for at least the T. pallidum aptamers, or an epitope-mapping or competition experiment that assigns the cellular signal to the intended lipoprotein. For Tau441, provide an aptamer-only binding measurement or an epitope-mapping experiment. Alternatively, restrict the Abstract and title claims to the demonstrated scope. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Reproducibility and independent verification Claim pointer The manuscript presents Xelari as a platform whose modules are benchmarked and whose predictions are deposited for independent recalculation. Evidence pointer Data and code availability; Results, Xelari architecture; Materials and methods, Data sources, training, and test datasets Concern Source code, model weights, checkpoints, and internal training and model-development datasets are explicitly not deposited. The prediction platform is proprietary and available for academic use upon request. The deposited material permits recalculation of reported benchmark statistics from frozen predictions but does not permit re-execution of the pipeline, retraining of any model, or independent application of Xelari to a new target. The claim that the pipeline is modular and that individual failure modes are separately inspectable is therefore not independently testable by a reader. Why it matters A methods paper whose central object is a computational pipeline is difficult to evaluate or build upon if the pipeline cannot be run. The module benchmarks can be checked arithmetically from the deposit, but the composition of modules into the end-to-end workflow, which is the actual claim, cannot. This also limits the ability of the community to test the authors' own stated next step, a broader prospective series. Resolution test Deposit at minimum the inference code and frozen weights for the five trained models and the three algorithmic modules, or provide a documented execution environment sufficient to reproduce the reported prospective designs from the deposited target structures. If full release is not possible, state explicitly which claims are and are not independently reproducible from the deposit. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Benchmark independence and calibration Claim pointer ValentiNA showed MAE of 0.931 kcal/mol and Spearman rho of 0.795 across 32 retrospective records associated with 27 structural templates, and the calibrated predictions for the three T. pallidum aptamers differed from measured apparent KD values by 1.06- to 1.18-fold. Evidence pointer Results, Complex relaxation and affinity prediction; Figure 7; Materials and methods, Prediction of the complex binding free energy with ValentiNA; Materials and methods, Validation protocol; Table S11; Table S12 Concern The calibration coefficients were fitted on 17 literature records (Table S11), and the retrospective evaluation uses 32 records (Table S12). The manuscript states that separation by PDB identifier does not establish independence and that related aptamer-target systems can occur in both calibration and evaluation. The template-aggregated sensitivity analysis collapses repeated structural inputs but does not establish statistical independence. The three T. pallidum comparisons apply a global affine calibration fitted on 17 separate complexes and report 1.06- to 1.18-fold agreement, but the authors correctly note this is not an independent test of ranking accuracy. The reported accuracy metrics therefore describe correspondence within a panel that is not demonstrably independent of calibration. Why it matters The reported MAE and Spearman rho are presented as the quantitative performance of the affinity module. If calibration and evaluation records overlap at the aptamer-family or target-family level, these numbers overstate generalization. The authors flag this, but the Abstract reports the numbers without the caveat. Resolution test Report the overlap between the 17 calibration records and the 32 evaluation records at the aptamer-family and target-family level, not only by PDB identifier. Provide a held-out evaluation in which neither the aptamer family nor the target family appears in calibration. If the panel cannot support this, state the overlap explicitly in the Abstract. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Module benchmark validity Claim pointer Edgar correlated with experimental folding energies but did not reproduce their absolute scale, supporting its use as a ranking heuristic. AliNA achieved a mean F1 of 0.757 on 339 PDB-derived RNA evaluation sequences. Evidence pointer Results, Folding free energy estimation; Figure 6; Results, Predicting the secondary structure of candidate sequences; Materials and methods, Edgar folding-free-energy assessment; Materials and methods, Nucleic acid secondary structure prediction with AliNA Concern Two issues affect the interpretation of these benchmarks. First, the Edgar internal test set is not homology-controlled for DNA because sequence augmentation preceded random partitioning, so augmented variants of one parent structure can appear in more than one subset; the reported R2 of 0.958 therefore measures approximation of the simulation reference and not generalization. The authors state this. Second, the AliNA evaluation set is disjoint from training at the Rfam-family level, but the lower-similarity stratum contains only 33 sequences and the pseudoknot analysis is restricted to the higher-similarity subset (n = 86) for RNA and is not scored for the lower-similarity RNA subset (n = 14) or ssDNA (n = 4). The reported mean F1 of 0.757 aggregates strata of very different size and does not characterize performance on sequences distant from training. Why it matters Both modules are used as filters or ranking heuristics inside the pipeline, and their behavior on out-of-distribution inputs determines whether the pipeline can be expected to work on targets and sequences unlike those in training. The current benchmarks do not establish this. Resolution test For Edgar, report a homology-controlled DNA split and the corresponding metrics. For AliNA, report stratified metrics separately with confidence intervals, and state explicitly what the lower-similarity stratum can and cannot support given n = 33. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generative scope and internal consistency Claim pointer Xelari generates de novo DNA and RNA aptamers from protein structures. The current scaffold library contains approximately 12,000 RNA and 11,000 DNA single-chain scaffolds spanning 15 to 45 nt. Evidence pointer Results, Generation and structural validation of the scaffold library; Results, Assembly of full-length aptamers from the scaffold library; Discussion; Materials and methods, Scaffold library construction; Materials and methods, Assembly of the full-length aptamers from the scaffold library Concern The generative scope is narrower than the title and Abstract imply. G-quadruplex folds are not enumerated and MoNA does not generate them, yet G-quadruplex aptamers are a major and therapeutically validated class. The MoNA topology-recovery benchmark contains RNA assemblies only, so the DNA assembly path is not benchmarked at the assembly stage. The DNA branch reconstructs in RNA representation and converts to DNA, and the manuscript reports that 86.3 percent of converted chains classify as B-like after relaxation, but also states that this establishes backbone geometry and not that the tertiary fold or protein-binding energetics survive conversion. The DNA structural benchmark (median RMSD 2.52 Angstrom, median lDDT 0.724 over 58 structures) is computed over paired heavy atoms only and does not address binding competence. Why it matters The prospective validation is entirely DNA, while the assembly benchmark is entirely RNA and the reconstruction path for DNA goes through an RNA intermediate. The evidence chain for the DNA branch, which is the branch that produced the only prospective functional results, is therefore the least directly benchmarked. Resolution test Provide a DNA MoNA assembly benchmark analogous to the RNA benchmark. Report whether any of the four prospective DNA aptamers were tested for retention of the intended fold after conversion, or provide a binding-competence comparison between the RNA-intermediate model and the final DNA model for at least one case. Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis INGA reliability and downstream propagation Claim pointer INGA is used for conformational relaxation of the target and of the aptamer-protein complex, and is described as complementing conventional geometry optimization and molecular dynamics. Evidence pointer Results, Target preparation; Figure 2; Table S1; Materials and methods, Conformational relaxation using the INGA neural network model Concern The reported INGA behavior includes substantial geometric artifacts. Raw outputs increased mean potential energy by 170 to 211 eV relative to input, produced 2.51 to 14.36 unphysical bond lengths per structure on average, and up to 28 percent of outputs contained more than five unphysical bond lengths. GFN-FF refinement reduced the energy increase to 1.8 to 5.3 eV but did not resolve the bond-length artifacts, and the fail rate was slightly higher after refinement (up to 30 percent). Retention of structures already in the target cluster dropped from 96.4 percent with GFN-FF alone to 50.4 percent after the full INGA-GFN-FF step. INGA is used at two points in the pipeline, for target relaxation and for complex relaxation before ValentiNA scoring. Why it matters A relaxation module that degrades already-correct conformations and introduces unphysical geometry in a substantial fraction of outputs will propagate error into site selection, seed construction, and final affinity ranking. The manuscript reports these numbers but does not quantify the downstream consequence. Resolution test Report the effect of INGA-introduced geometry on downstream stages, for example by comparing DiNA localization or ValentiNA ranking with and without INGA relaxation on a defined subset. Report the fraction of pipeline runs in which the final complex passed a geometry sanity check. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (prospective denominator and target engagement), R1-M2 (code and weights not deposited), R1-M3 (calibration and evaluation overlap), R1-M4 (Edgar DNA split and AliNA lower-similarity stratum), R1-M5 (DNA assembly path not benchmarked), R1-M6 (INGA geometry artifacts and downstream propagation). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The individual components are largely adaptations of existing ideas: surrogate models for physics-based reference calculations, surface-patch descriptors for specificity, secondary-structure prediction, and graph-neural-network folding-energy estimation. The originality lies in the composition of these into a single structure-first pipeline for aptamer design and in the explicit decomposition of the design problem into separately benchmarked subproblems. This is a meaningful methodological contribution but not a conceptual advance of the kind associated with a broad multidisciplinary journal. Scientific importance The problem is important, and the demonstration that structure-based design can produce experimentally functional aptamers without SELEX is a useful existence proof. The importance is currently limited by the small prospective sample, the absence of target-engagement confirmation in the cellular assay, the absence of an aptamer-only affinity for Tau441, and the proprietary nature of the pipeline. The work is more likely to be of high interest to the specialized aptamer and nucleic-acid therapeutics community than to a general readership. Interdisciplinary readership The manuscript is written for a computationally literate but biologically oriented audience, and the modular framing is accessible. The relevance to adjacent fields (protein design, molecular recognition, assay development) is plausible but would be strengthened by a clearer statement of what a non-specialist should take from the results. Technical soundness The InNA benchmark is technically strong. The Ehrlich benchmarks are reasonable. The DiNA localization benchmark is reported under two aggregation schemes and the authors are explicit about the difference. The Edgar, AliNA, INGA, MoNA, and ValentiNA benchmarks each carry stated limitations that the authors disclose. The principal soundness gap is that the module benchmarks do not compose into an end-to-end accuracy estimate, and the prospective evidence does not close that gap. Readability for nonspecialists The manuscript is generally well organized and the limitations are stated clearly. The density of module names and acronyms is high, and a reader outside the field will need the architecture figure and a glossary to follow the Results. The Abstract is readable but carries several numerical claims whose scope conditions appear only later. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence for the full claim as framed in the title and Abstract. Supportive of publication in a specialized venue if the technical concerns are resolved, specifically if the prospective candidate denominator and target-engagement data are provided, if the calibration and evaluation overlap is quantified at the family level, if the DNA assembly path is benchmarked, and if the code and weights are made available or the reproducibility boundary is stated explicitly. The narrower claim, that a structure-first pipeline can produce experimentally functional DNA aptamers in two assay settings without SELEX, is supported by the supplied material. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that Xelari enables de novo aptamer design "in hours" is supported only for the computational candidate generation step on a specific GPU, excludes scaffold library construction, and excludes synthesis and experimental confirmation. The title and Abstract do not carry these exclusions. The claim that the three T. pallidum aptamers bind their intended lipoprotein targets is not supported. Binding was measured on intact cells and was not confirmed against purified intended targets. The claim that the Tau441 aptamer binds Tau441 with a defined affinity is not supported. The reported KD of 0.92 nM is a workflow prediction, and the manuscript states it is not treated as experimentally validated. The claim that ValentiNA achieves MAE of 0.931 kcal/mol and Spearman rho of 0.795 as a general performance figure is weak, because the evaluation panel is not demonstrably independent of the calibration panel at the aptamer-family or target-family level. The claim that Edgar reproduces folding free energies is not supported in absolute terms. The manuscript reports predictive R2 of minus 3.976 and a regression slope of 1.793, and correctly restricts the claim to ranking. The claim that AliNA generalizes to sequences distant from training is weak, because the lower-similarity stratum contains 33 sequences and the pseudoknot analysis is restricted to the higher-similarity subset. The claim that the DNA branch of the pipeline produces binding-competent DNA folds is not established. The reported structural benchmark covers paired heavy atoms only and the manuscript states that it does not address protein-binding energetics after conversion. The claim that the pipeline is modular and that failure modes are separately inspectable is not independently testable, because source code, model weights, and internal datasets are not deposited. The claim that the prospective studies constitute independent validation is not supported. The manuscript itself states that the T. pallidum characterization was authored predominantly by Xelari-affiliated individuals and should not be regarded as fully independent third-party validation, and that neither study constitutes fully independent third-party validation. The claim that the approach is a complement to experimental selection is a positioning statement rather than a tested proposition. No head-to-head comparison with SELEX on a matched target is reported.

Figures and figure supplements are referenced but not supplied as images. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the supplied text and the claims it makes. Figure panels, blots, micrographs, numerical source data, and supplementary files were not available for inspection, so quantitative and image-based claims cannot be independently verified. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report that the human SVEP1 CCP20 domain is the primary binding site for TIE1; that SVEP1 does not bind TIE2 in the tested binary setups; that ANG1/ANG2 enhance SVEP1-TIE1 binding; that combined SVEP1 and ANG2 stimulation of hdLECs produces TIE1 phosphorylation at pY1007 and downstream PI3K/AKT signaling readouts (pAKT, FOXO1 nuclear exclusion); and that AlphaFold-based modeling predicts a higher-order 2:2:2 SVEP1-TIE1-ANG1/2 assembly that could cluster TIE1 receptors. Visible evidence base SPR binding data (Figure 1C), negative-stain EM (Figure 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3), AlphaFold2.3/AF3 multimer predictions with PAE, ipTM and actifpTM metrics (Figure 1A-B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2, Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2, Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), ELISA binding assays (Figure 2B), co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 2C), TIE1 pY1007 phosphorylation (Figure 3A, D), pAKT with ANG2 blocking antibody and TIE1/TIE2 knockdown (Figure 3B, E), FOXO1 nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio (Figure 3C, F), and mutant binding assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-B). Missing materials affecting confidence Figure images and their quantitative source data; uncropped blots; statistics for individual panels; detailed methods for AF3 job parameters and model selection; the key resources table referenced repeatedly; the GitHub analysis scripts and BioImage Archive dataset contents; the funding information body. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a genuinely open question in vascular biology, namely how the orphan receptor TIE1 is engaged and phosphorylated, and it proposes SVEP1 as a bridging co-ligand that enables ANG2 to act on TIE1. The combination of structure prediction, biophysical binding assays, and cell-based signaling readouts is appropriate for the question. However, the central mechanistic claim, that SVEP1 enables efficient ANG2 binding to TIE1 and thereby drives TIE1 phosphorylation and downstream signaling, rests on evidence that is currently only partially visible and, in several places, internally inconsistent. The most consequential issues are the reliance on AlphaFold predictions as a primary argument for complex geometry and stoichiometry, the unresolved role of TIE2 in the observed pAKT response, the absence of direct demonstration that ANG2 is present in the ternary complex after immunoprecipitation, and the fact that the higher-order assembly model is explicitly acknowledged as unconfirmed. As presented, the core conclusion is plausible but not yet established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Vascular and lymphatic biologists working on the ANG/TIE axis, TIE1 orphan-receptor biology, and lymphangiogenesis; structural biologists using AlphaFold-multimer for ternary and higher-order complex prediction; researchers in lymphedema, glaucoma, and lymphatic malformation genetics where SVEP1 and TIE1 variants have been implicated; and cell-signaling groups interested in how extracellular matrix proteins modulate receptor tyrosine kinase activation. Major strengths The question is well motivated and builds on prior genetic and biochemical work linking SVEP1 and TIE1. The authors combine orthogonal approaches, including SPR, ELISA, co-immunoprecipitation, negative-stain EM, phosphorylation assays, knockdown, and blocking antibodies, which is the right general strategy. The use of disease-relevant human dermal LECs rather than only immortalized lines is a strength. The manuscript is candid in places about the limits of its own model, for example the statement that further experimentation is needed to confirm the multimerization model, and the discussion of the historical difficulty in detecting TIE1 phosphorylation is informative. The mutant binding experiments (SVEP1 E2568A-G2569A and TIE1 P202L-L203F) provide a useful specificity control for the proposed interface. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency for the central mechanistic claim Claim pointer SVEP1 mediates strong binding of ANG2 and TIE1, and combined SVEP1 and ANG2 stimulation leads to TIE1 phosphorylation and downstream signaling. Evidence pointer Figure 2C, Figure 3A, Figure 3D, Figure 3B, Figure 3E Concern The co-immunoprecipitation experiment intended to show ternary complex formation does not detect ANG1 or ANG2 after immunoprecipitation, and the authors state this explicitly. The claim that ANG2 is a component of the SVEP1-TIE1 complex therefore rests on an increase in co-precipitated TIE1 rather than on direct detection of the angiopoietin in the complex. In addition, the reported decrease of ANG1 and ANG2 levels in total lysate after co-transfection is not explained and could indicate altered expression, secretion, or degradation rather than complex assembly. Why it matters The bridging model is the central novelty of the manuscript. If ANG2 cannot be shown to be physically present in the SVEP1-TIE1 complex, the interpretation that SVEP1 enables ANG2 binding to TIE1 is inferential rather than demonstrated. Resolution test Provide direct detection of ANG1/ANG2 in the SVEP1 pull-down, for example by tagged angiopoietin immunoblot, mass spectrometry, or a proximity-based assay, with controls for nonspecific binding and for the observed lysate-level decrease. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Attribution of the signaling response Claim pointer TIE1 activation by SVEP1 and ANG2 enables downstream signaling, and knockdown of either TIE1 or TIE2 reduces pAKT after SVEP1-ANG2 stimulation. Evidence pointer Figure 3B, Figure 3E Concern The pAKT response requires both TIE1 and TIE2 according to the knockdown data, yet the manuscript simultaneously argues that SVEP1 does not bind TIE2 and that TIE2 is not part of the proposed complex. The authors acknowledge that whether TIE2 is necessary for TIE1 phosphorylation after SVEP1-ANG2 treatment needs further investigation. This leaves the receptor composition of the signaling unit unresolved and creates tension with the model figure. Why it matters If TIE2 is required for the pAKT readout, then the claim that SVEP1-ANG2 acts through a TIE1-centered signaling hub is not separable from a TIE1-TIE2 heteromeric mechanism, which is the pre-existing paradigm the manuscript seeks to revise. Resolution test Determine whether TIE1 phosphorylation at pY1007 after SVEP1-ANG2 stimulation persists upon TIE2 knockdown or in TIE2-negative cells, and report pAKT and pTIE1 side by side under the same knockdown conditions with knockdown efficiency documented. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Structural inference versus experimental support Claim pointer AF3 predicts a 2:2:2 SVEP1-TIE1-ANG1/2 complex in which TIE1 dimerizes and ANG1/2 cross-links SVEP1 molecules, clustering TIE1 receptors. Evidence pointer Figure 4A, Figure 4B, Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 Concern The higher-order assembly is derived entirely from prediction, and the authors state that further experimentation is needed to confirm it. The manuscript also notes that a previously reported crystallographic TIE1 Fn3 dimer was concluded to be a crystal artifact based on SAXS. The predicted TIE1 dimerization interface therefore contradicts the available solution evidence and is not experimentally tested here. Why it matters The multimerization model is presented in the abstract and discussion as a mechanistic explanation for signal amplification. Without experimental support, it functions as a hypothesis rather than a result, and the abstract wording does not fully convey this status. Resolution test Provide independent biophysical or cellular evidence for TIE1 oligomerization in the presence of SVEP1 and ANG1/2, for example size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, analytical ultracentrifugation, cross-linking, or single-molecule imaging, and reconcile the result with the prior SAXS finding. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Specificity of the SVEP1-TIE1 versus SVEP1-TIE2 distinction Claim pointer SVEP1 binds TIE1 but not TIE2 in the absence of other proteins, and CCP20 is the primary binding site for TIE1. Evidence pointer Figure 1A, Figure 1B, Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A Concern The SPR and ELISA experiments use a truncated SVEP1 construct spanning CCP15 to CCP24 rather than full-length protein, and the manuscript acknowledges that only part of the C-terminus was used. The negative result for TIE2 is therefore restricted to this fragment and to binary conditions. The AF2.3 interface metrics for TIE2 are described as weaker but the model still yields a comparable buried surface area, which weakens the qualitative claim of no binding. Why it matters The selectivity of SVEP1 for TIE1 over TIE2 is a load-bearing element of the model. A fragment-based negative result cannot exclude TIE2 engagement by other SVEP1 regions or in the presence of angiopoietins, a possibility the authors themselves raise in the discussion. Resolution test Report full-length or additional SVEP1 domain constructs in binding assays with TIE2, include quantitative affinity estimates with confidence intervals for both receptors, and state explicitly the detection limit of the assay for the TIE2 negative result. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Quantitative reporting and statistical support Claim pointer The affinity of TIE1 for SVEP1 is significantly increased by ANG1 or ANG2, and combined stimulation produces stronger pAKT and FOXO1 nuclear exclusion than either factor alone. Evidence pointer Figure 2B, Figure 3A, Figure 3B, Figure 3C, Figure 3D, Figure 3E, Figure 3F Concern KD values are reported in the text with inconsistent decimal formatting and without units, confidence intervals, or replicate counts. The claim that the combined effect exceeds the sum of individual effects is stated in the discussion but the statistical test supporting an interaction or synergy term is not described. The statistics section describes t-tests, Mann-Whitney U, and Bonferroni correction but does not specify which comparisons used which test or how synergy was assessed. Why it matters The potentiation claim is central to the interpretation of cooperative signaling. Without an explicit interaction test, an additive effect cannot be distinguished from a synergistic one. Resolution test Report KD values with units, confidence intervals, and n; specify the statistical model used to test for interaction or synergy between SVEP1 and ANG2 for pAKT and FOXO1 readouts; and provide the underlying quantitative data for each panel. Major Concerns (continued) Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility of the phosphorylation readout Claim pointer Stimulation of hdLECs with both SVEP1 and ANG2 produces robust phosphorylation of TIE1 at pY1007. Evidence pointer Figure 3A, Figure 3D Concern The manuscript notes that SVEP1 alone has a slight effect on TIE1 phosphorylation, attributed to endogenous ANG2 expression in hdLECs. This raises the possibility that the observed phosphorylation depends on endogenous ligand levels that are not controlled or measured. The prior literature cited by the authors reports that TIE1 phosphorylation was not detectable with SVEP1 or ANG2 alone, which makes the baseline and the magnitude of the combined effect important to document. Why it matters If endogenous ANG2 contributes materially, the interpretation of the SVEP1-ANG2 combination as the specific activating condition is weakened, and reproducibility across LEC batches becomes a concern. Resolution test Measure and report endogenous ANG2 and ANG1 levels in the hdLECs used, include an ANG2 depletion or blocking condition for the pY1007 readout, and show the full time course and dose response with replicate quantification. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology and consistency Affected element Receptor nomenclature throughout the manuscript Evidence pointer Introduction, Results, Discussion Issue The manuscript alternates between TIE1/TIE2 and Tie1/Tie2, and between SVEP1 and Svep1, without a stated convention for species or context. Required correction Adopt a single convention, for example human uppercase and nonhuman title case, and apply it consistently. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Numerical reporting Affected element KD values in the Results Evidence pointer Results, section on ANG1/2 strengthening binding Issue KD values are written with commas as decimal separators and without units, for example KD = 146,9 and KD = 55,6. Required correction Use decimal points and state units, for example nM, consistently. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Figure referencing Affected element Cross-references to supplementary panels Evidence pointer Results, multiple sections Issue Several claims are supported only by references to figure supplements, and the main-text description does not always state what the supplementary panel shows or how many replicates it contains. Required correction Briefly state the assay and replicate number in the main text for each supplementary-supported claim. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Methods completeness Affected element AlphaFold modeling parameters Evidence pointer Materials and methods, structure prediction section Issue The AF3 job parameters, model ranking criteria, and the basis for accepting the 2:2:2 stoichiometry are not fully specified, and the key resources table referenced for sequences is not included in the supplied text. Required correction Provide the full AF3 configuration, the number of seeds and samples, the ranking metric used, and the sequence boundaries for each chain. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Data availability Affected element Analysis scripts and imaging data Evidence pointer Data availability statement Issue The statement points to a GitHub repository and a BioImage Archive accession, but the relationship between these resources and the specific figure panels is not described. Required correction Map each deposited dataset and script to the figure panels it supports. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Internal consistency Affected element Description of TIE2 in the model Evidence pointer Results, section on higher-order complexes, and Discussion Issue The Results state that TIE2 was not predicted to co-bind stably, while the Discussion states that whether TIE2 can bind SVEP1 in the presence of angiopoietins remains an open question. The two statements are compatible but the framing shifts between sections. Required correction Align the wording so that the negative prediction and the acknowledged open question are presented consistently. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3. These concern direct detection of angiopoietin in the complex, the unresolved requirement for TIE2 in the signaling readout, and the experimental status of the higher-order assembly model. R1-M4, R1-M5, and R1-M6 are important but not by themselves blocking. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is moderate to high, since the proposal that an extracellular matrix protein acts as a bridging co-ligand for an orphan receptor tyrosine kinase is a distinct mechanistic idea, although it builds directly on the authors' prior SVEP1-TIE1 work. Scientific importance is potentially high for lymphatic and vascular biology, particularly if the TIE2-independent component of TIE1 activation can be demonstrated. Interdisciplinary readership is plausible, spanning vascular biology, structural prediction, and matrix biology, but the current reliance on predicted structures limits appeal to readers outside the modeling community. Technical soundness is mixed, with a good range of orthogonal methods but with unresolved issues in complex composition, receptor attribution, and quantitative reporting. Readability for nonspecialists is reasonable in the Introduction and Discussion, but the Results assume familiarity with AlphaFold metrics such as PAE, ipTM, and actifpTM without defining them, which will limit accessibility. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The work is potentially supportive if the technical concerns, in particular R1-M1, R1-M2, and R1-M3, are resolved with direct experimental evidence. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that ANG2 is physically present in the SVEP1-TIE1 complex is not supported by the supplied evidence, since ANG1 and ANG2 were not detected after immunoprecipitation (Figure 2C). The claim that SVEP1-ANG2 signaling proceeds through a TIE1-centered mechanism is weakened by the reported requirement for TIE2 in the pAKT readout (Figure 3B, Figure 3E). The 2:2:2 higher-order assembly and TIE1 dimerization model is a prediction without experimental confirmation, and it conflicts with prior SAXS evidence cited by the authors indicating that the crystallographic TIE1 Fn3 dimer is likely an artifact (Figure 4A-C). The claim that SVEP1 does not bind TIE2 is supported only for the CCP15-CCP24 fragment under binary conditions and cannot be generalized to full-length SVEP1 or to angiopoietin-containing conditions (Figure 1C). The claim that combined SVEP1 and ANG2 stimulation exceeds the sum of individual effects is stated in the Discussion but the supporting statistical test for interaction or synergy is not described in the supplied text. The reported KD values lack units, confidence intervals, and replicate counts, so the magnitude of the affinity change upon ANG1 or ANG2 addition cannot be evaluated (Figure 2B). The contribution of endogenous ANG2 in hdLECs to the observed TIE1 phosphorylation is acknowledged but not quantified or controlled (Figure 3A, Figure 3D).

本文通过增强构象采样、反应自由能计算、非平衡MD、进化分析和实验动力学，揭示二氢叶酸还原酶（DHFR）中一个远端别构热点残基的突变通过重新分配两个全局相似但局部关键结构差异的构象群体来调控催化活性，并据此理性设计了一个部分恢复活性的补偿性第二位点突变。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：一个远端别构热点（allosteric hot spot）的突变如何通过改变构象系综的群体分布来调控DHFR的催化活性？别构信号从远端传递到活性位点的动力学路径是什么？ 为什么重要 ：别构调控是酶催化和细胞信号转导的核心机制，但"远端扰动如何控制远端活性位点"这一基本问题长期未解。理解别构机制不仅具有基础科学意义，还为酶工程、药物设计和合成生物学中的别构调控设计提供理论指导。 现有方法为何不足 ：以往研究多聚焦于静态结构对比或单一构象的分子动力学模拟，难以捕捉别构调控中构象群体的重新分布和动态转变路径。此外，计算预测缺乏实验验证，或实验观测缺乏原子级机制解释。 精确研究问题 ：Can a distal allosteric hot spot mutation in DHFR regulate catalysis by redistributing the populations of two globally similar but locally distinct conformations, and can this mechanism be exploited to rationally engineer compensatory mutations? 04 背景与发展脉络 本文采用多方法整合策略：增强构象采样（enhanced conformational sampling）探索DHFR的构象空间；反应自由能计算（reactive free-energy calculations）量化化学步骤的能垒；扰动诱导的非平衡MD（perturbation-induced nonequilibrium MD）追踪构象转变的动态路径；进化分析（evolutionary analysis）识别功能关键残基；实验动力学（experimental kinetics）验证计算预测。 2) 核心洞察 别构热点突变并非通过改变蛋白的整体折叠或创造全新的构象来调控活性，而是 重新分配两个预先存在的、全局相似但局部关键结构不同的构象的群体比例 。其中一个构象催化competent，另一个则否。此外，突变体中的构象转变不是协同的全局运动，而是 逐步的局部结构重排序列 。这一发现将别构调控从"静态结构变化"范式转向"构象群体重分布"范式，并提供了热力学（群体比例）和动力学（转变路径）的统一视角。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] 别构效应的本质可能更多是 群体重分布 而非 新构象的创造 ——这提示在蛋白质工程中，稳定目标构象而非设计全新构象可能更可行。 构象转变的 逐步性 意味着别构信号传递可能通过一系列局部事件级联放大，而非单一协同跃迁——这对理解长程信号传递和设计别构调控有普遍意义。 计算与实验的紧密整合（计算预测→实验验证→计算再指导）是解决复杂生物物理问题的有效范式。 07 方法总览 输入 ：DHFR的蛋白序列、结构信息（推测为已知晶体结构或同源模型）、突变位点信息（别构热点突变及设计的补偿突变） 输出
