Review setup Input scope Abstract only, as provided in the submission record. Assessment boundary Evaluation is restricted to the abstract text and the associated bibliographic metadata. No full text, figures, tables, supplementary information, methods, or data files were supplied. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report that a distal allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase regulates catalysis by shifting the populations of two globally similar conformations, one catalytically competent and one not. They further report that the mutant transition between these states proceeds through stepwise local rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion, and that a rationally designed compensatory second-site mutation partially restores activity. The claimed contribution is a unified thermodynamic and kinetic account of allostery plus a general framework for engineering allosteric regulation. Visible evidence base The abstract states the use of enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics, evolutionary analysis, and experimental kinetics. No quantitative results, effect sizes, error estimates, convergence diagnostics, or experimental validation details are visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Full text, figures, tables, methods, simulation parameters, force-field and sampling details, free-energy convergence data, kinetic traces, evolutionary alignment statistics, mutation design rationale, and statistical analysis are all absent. Confidence in any technical judgment is therefore low. Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a coherent and potentially valuable multi-method study that links distal allosteric perturbation to catalytic competence through conformational population shifts and nonequilibrium relaxation pathways. The conceptual framing is clear and the combination of simulation, evolutionary analysis, and experimental kinetics is appropriate for the question. However, the supplied material is an abstract only, and it does not permit verification of the central mechanistic claims, the quantitative support for population redistribution, the convergence of the free-energy calculations, or the strength of the compensatory rescue. The work is interesting in principle but currently not established from the provided evidence. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in enzymology, protein allostery, computational biophysics, and protein engineering would be interested because the study addresses how distal perturbations propagate to active-site chemistry and proposes a mechanism-guided route to restore or tune activity. The evolutionary dimension may also interest groups studying sequence-function relationships and the evolution of latent allostery. Major strengths The abstract identifies a specific and testable mechanistic hypothesis, namely that allosteric regulation operates through population redistribution between two globally similar but catalytically distinct conformations. The integration of enhanced sampling, reactive free-energy calculations, nonequilibrium molecular dynamics, evolutionary analysis, and experimental kinetics is methodologically well matched to the question. The claim of a rationally engineered compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity, if substantiated, would provide a functional test of the proposed mechanism rather than a purely correlative account. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Mechanistic support Claim pointer A mutational perturbation at the allosteric hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations, one catalytically competent and one not. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern The abstract asserts a population redistribution between two conformational states but provides no quantitative populations, no definition of the states, no measure of the structural difference, and no demonstration that the population shift is causally linked to the observed activity change rather than merely correlated with it. Why it matters The central mechanistic claim depends on establishing that the two conformations are distinct, that their populations change upon mutation, and that this change accounts for the catalytic effect. Without this, the proposed allosteric mechanism remains an assertion. Resolution test Provide quantitative state populations for wild type and mutant, a structural metric that distinguishes the two states, and a quantitative relationship between population shift and measured catalytic activity. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness of free-energy calculations Claim pointer Reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step support the catalytic competence of one conformation and not the other. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern No information is given on the reaction coordinate, the free-energy method, convergence, statistical uncertainty, or the treatment of the chemical step. The abstract does not report whether the free-energy difference between competent and incompetent states is large enough to explain the kinetic effect. Why it matters Reactive free-energy calculations are central to the claim that one conformation is catalytically competent and the other is not. Without convergence and uncertainty data, the reported energetics cannot be evaluated. Resolution test Report the free-energy protocol, reaction coordinate, convergence diagnostics, statistical errors, and the computed barrier differences relative to experimental kinetics. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Nonequilibrium dynamics interpretation Claim pointer The transition between the two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern The abstract does not specify how the nonequilibrium relaxation simulations were initiated, how many independent trajectories were analyzed, how the stepwise sequence was identified, or how alternative concerted pathways were excluded. Why it matters The kinetic mechanism is a principal claim of the paper. Without trajectory statistics and pathway analysis, the stepwise interpretation is not distinguishable from a concerted or heterogeneous transition. Resolution test Provide the number of independent nonequilibrium trajectories, the order parameters used to define local rearrangements, and a quantitative comparison of stepwise versus concerted pathway models. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Functional validation Claim pointer A rationally engineered compensatory second-site mutation partially restores activity. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern The abstract does not report the magnitude of restoration, the assay used, the number of replicates, or whether the rescue is specific to the proposed mechanism. Partial restoration could arise from nonspecific effects. Why it matters The compensatory mutation is the main functional test of the proposed mechanism. Without quantitative rescue data and controls, the engineering claim is not established. Resolution test Report absolute and relative activity values for wild type, hot-spot mutant, and compensatory double mutant, with replicates, errors, and controls showing that rescue is mechanism specific. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Evolutionary analysis Claim pointer Evolutionary analysis contributes to the identification and interpretation of the allosteric hot spot. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern The abstract does not describe the evolutionary dataset, the conservation or coevolution metrics, or how the evolutionary signal was used to guide the mechanistic or engineering claims. Why it matters The evolutionary component is presented as part of the evidence base. Without details, its contribution to the central claims cannot be assessed. Resolution test Describe the sequence dataset, alignment, statistical tests, and the specific evolutionary predictions that were tested experimentally or computationally. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Use of the term allosteric hot spot. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Issue The abstract does not define what constitutes a hot spot in this context or how it was identified. Required correction Provide a definition and the criteria used to designate the residue or region as an allosteric hot spot. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Claim scope Affected element Claim of a general framework for engineering allosteric regulation. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Issue Generality is asserted from a single enzyme system. Required correction Either restrict the generality claim or provide evidence from additional systems or a clear argument for transferability. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Quantitative reporting Affected element Abstract reporting of activity changes. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Issue No numerical values are given for activity changes, population shifts, or rescue efficiency. Required correction Include key quantitative results in the abstract or ensure they are clearly reported in the main text. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M4. The supplied material does not allow verification of the population redistribution, the reactive free-energy calculations, the nonequilibrium pathway analysis, or the compensatory rescue. R1-M5 is non-blocking but should be addressed to support the evolutionary component. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is plausible, since the combination of population redistribution, nonequilibrium pathway analysis, and compensatory engineering in a benchmark enzyme addresses a recognized problem in allostery. Scientific importance is potentially high if the mechanism is quantitatively established, because it would connect distal perturbation to catalytic chemistry and provide a design strategy. Interdisciplinary readership is likely, spanning enzymology, biophysics, computational chemistry, and protein engineering. Technical soundness cannot be judged from the abstract alone, and the central quantitative claims are currently unsupported by visible evidence. Readability for nonspecialists is reasonable at the abstract level, but the mechanistic terminology would require clearer definition in the full text. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. Supportive if technical concerns are resolved with quantitative data on state populations, free-energy convergence, nonequilibrium pathway statistics, and compensatory rescue. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the two conformations are globally similar but differ in catalytic competence is not supported by visible structural or energetic data. The claim that the mutation redistributes conformational populations is not supported by quantitative population estimates. The claim that reactive free-energy calculations establish catalytic competence is not supported by convergence or uncertainty data. The claim that the transition proceeds through a stepwise sequence rather than a concerted motion is not supported by trajectory statistics or pathway analysis. The claim that the compensatory second-site mutation partially restores activity is not supported by quantitative activity data or controls. The claim of a general framework for engineering allosteric regulation is not supported beyond the single system described. The contribution of evolutionary analysis to the mechanistic conclusions is not evaluable from the supplied material.

Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and conclusions as presented in the abstract; no methods, figures, or supplementary data were available for evaluation Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report cryo-EM structures of human full-length UGGT1 in monomeric open and closed conformational states, with evidence for intermediate conformations from 3D variability and molecular dynamics. A density bridging the sensory TRXL2 and catalytic domains in the open state is interpreted as substrate association. A dimeric form with occluded substrate binding sites is proposed to regulate activity. Glycoproteomics of endogenous substrates shows no consensus sequence flanking modified N-glycosylation sites. Disease-associated variants are mapped onto the structure to explain functional disruption. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, methods, or supplementary information were provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, cryo-EM data quality metrics, molecular dynamics simulation details, glycoproteomics methods and datasets, variant functional assays, and any statistical analyses Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially significant advance in understanding UGGT1 substrate recognition through structural biology. The proposed conformational continuum and the observation of a substrate-associated open state are conceptually interesting. However, the evidence base available for this review is limited to the abstract, which prevents verification of the structural interpretations, the functional relevance of the dimer, and the glycoproteomics conclusions. The link between the structural data and the disease-associated variant analysis is stated but not substantiated in the provided material. The work is likely to interest the glycobiology and protein quality control communities, but the strength of the conclusions cannot be fully assessed from the abstract alone. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in glycoprotein quality control, protein folding, ER biology, and structural biology would be interested. The work also has relevance for those studying congenital disorders of glycosylation and for drug discovery efforts targeting UGGT1. The proposed conformational dynamics model may inform broader understanding of multidomain enzyme regulation. Major strengths The study addresses a long-standing question in glycoprotein quality control, namely how UGGT1 recognizes its substrates. The use of cryo-EM to capture multiple conformational states of a full-length human enzyme is technically demanding and represents a substantial advance. The integration of structural data with glycoproteomics and disease-associated variants provides a multi-layered approach. The observation of a dimeric form with occluded substrate sites offers a plausible regulatory mechanism. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The abstract claims that a density bridging the sensory TRXL2 and catalytic domains in the open state is consistent with substrate association, and that this supports a mode of binding placing the substrate near the catalytic domain. Evidence pointer Abstract text; no figure or table identifiers provided Concern The interpretation of the unassigned density as substrate is a central claim, but the abstract provides no information on the identity of the putative substrate, the resolution of the map in that region, or whether the density was validated by independent methods such as mass spectrometry or mutagenesis. Without these details, the assignment remains speculative. Why it matters If the density assignment is incorrect, the proposed binding mode and the mechanistic model built upon it would be undermined. This is the key structural observation that links the conformational states to substrate recognition. Resolution test Provide cryo-EM map quality metrics for the region of interest, show that the density is reproducible across independent reconstructions, and include orthogonal validation such as cross-linking mass spectrometry or site-directed mutagenesis with functional readouts. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Functional relevance Claim pointer The abstract states that a dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. Evidence pointer Abstract text; no figure or table identifiers provided Concern The functional significance of the dimer is inferred solely from the structural observation of occluded binding sites. No biochemical or cellular data are presented to demonstrate that dimerization occurs in solution or in cells, that it is reversible, or that it correlates with changes in enzymatic activity. Why it matters Without functional validation, the regulatory role of dimerization remains a hypothesis. If the dimer is a crystallization or grid preparation artifact, the proposed regulatory mechanism would not be supported. Resolution test Include size exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, analytical ultracentrifugation, or cellular cross-linking experiments to confirm dimer formation, and show that dimerization modulates UGGT1 activity in vitro or in cells. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Claim support Claim pointer The abstract claims that the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Evidence pointer Abstract text; no variant list or structural mapping details provided Concern The abstract does not specify which variants were analyzed, how they map onto the structure, or what functional assays were used to link structural disruption to disease. The claim of explanation is not supported by any visible data. Why it matters This claim extends the relevance of the structure to clinical genetics. Without specific variant information and functional validation, the statement is an assertion rather than a demonstrated conclusion. Resolution test Provide a table of disease-associated variants with their structural locations, predicted or measured effects on stability or activity, and functional data from cellular or biochemical assays. Required correction Briefly state the simulation approach and its role in supporting the conformational continuum model. Required correction Include the number of identified glycosylation sites and the criteria used to define the absence of a consensus sequence. The manuscript must provide the underlying data and validation for these claims. The originality is high if the structural interpretations are validated. Scientific importance: The study addresses a fundamental question in glycoprotein quality control and has potential implications for understanding congenital disorders of glycosylation. The importance is high if the functional claims are supported. Interdisciplinary readership: The topic bridges structural biology, glycobiology, cell biology, and clinical genetics. The regulatory role of UGGT1 dimerization is unsupported without biochemical or cellular evidence of dimer formation and functional consequences. Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and evidence presented in the abstract; no methods, figures, tables, or supplementary material were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose a workflow called "sequence scanning" that applies systematic constraints to improve sampling diversity in deep-learning-based cofolding models (Boltz and Protenix). They report improved accuracy in predicting antibody-antigen interface contacts and molecular glue (MG) ternary complex poses compared to previously published results, based on large benchmark sets. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, benchmark descriptions, or methodological details are available Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, methods section, benchmark dataset definitions, baseline comparisons, statistical analyses, and any figures or tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially useful methodological contribution to a recognized problem in computational structural biology, namely the limited accuracy of cofolding models for antibody-antigen and molecular glue ternary complexes. The concept of sequence scanning as a constraint-based sampling strategy is plausible and of interest to the drug discovery community. However, the abstract provides no quantitative evidence, no clear description of the scanning procedure, and no explicit comparison to the published baselines it claims to improve upon. As such, the central claims cannot be evaluated from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational structural biologists, developers of deep-learning-based protein complex prediction tools, and pharmaceutical researchers involved in antibody engineering or targeted protein degradation (molecular glue degraders) would be interested. The work addresses two clinically and industrially relevant complex types where current state-of-the-art models underperform, and a simple workflow that improves accuracy without retraining would be broadly applicable. Major strengths The problem selection is well motivated and of high practical relevance. The proposed workflow is model-agnostic (evaluated on two different architectures), which suggests potential generalizability. The use of large, diverse benchmark sets is stated, which is appropriate for assessing general performance. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "We find improved accuracy of the sequence scanning workflow in predicting antibody-antigen interface contacts and in pose prediction quality for MGs compared to previously published results." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract states improved accuracy but provides no numerical results, no effect sizes, no confidence intervals, and no explicit identification of the "previously published results" used as baselines. Without these, the magnitude and statistical significance of the improvement cannot be assessed. Why it matters The claim of improvement is the central contribution of the work. If the improvement is marginal or not statistically robust, the practical value of the workflow is unclear. The absence of quantitative support prevents any judgment on whether the method is a meaningful advance. Resolution test Provide in the abstract or manuscript explicit performance metrics (e.g., interface contact precision/recall, DockQ or similar pose quality scores) for the sequence scanning workflow and for the baseline methods on the same benchmarks, with appropriate statistical testing. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological clarity Claim pointer "We present sequence scanning, a new workflow, evaluated on Boltz and Protenix, that improves prediction accuracy in these domains by applying systematic constraints to enhance overall sampling diversity." Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract does not describe what "sequence scanning" actually does. The term is ambiguous. It is unclear whether the method involves mutating sequences, scanning residue positions, generating multiple sequence alignments, or some other procedure. The phrase "systematic constraints" is also undefined. Why it matters Without a clear description of the method, the work cannot be reproduced or evaluated for novelty. The reader cannot determine whether the approach is genuinely new or a minor variation of existing sampling strategies. Resolution test Provide a concise but specific description of the sequence scanning procedure in the abstract, or ensure the manuscript clearly defines the algorithm, its inputs, and its constraints. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Baseline validity Claim pointer "improved accuracy ... compared to previously published results" Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract does not specify which published results are used for comparison. It is unclear whether the baselines are the default Boltz and Protenix predictions on the same benchmarks, or results from other published studies using different datasets and evaluation protocols. Why it matters Comparisons across different benchmarks and evaluation pipelines can be misleading. Without a controlled comparison on identical datasets with identical metrics, the claimed improvement may be an artifact of dataset or metric differences. Resolution test State explicitly in the abstract or manuscript that the comparison is made against default Boltz and Protenix predictions on the same benchmark sets, using the same evaluation metrics. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Scope clarity Affected element Benchmark description Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract states "large, diverse benchmark sets" but gives no indication of dataset sizes, composition, or how diversity was ensured. Required correction Add brief details on the number of complexes and the criteria for diversity (e.g., sequence identity thresholds, antigen classes, MG chemotypes). Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Generalizability Affected element Model scope Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The workflow is evaluated on Boltz and Protenix, but the abstract does not state whether the method is expected to transfer to other cofolding models such as AlphaFold3. Required correction Add a sentence on the expected generalizability of the workflow to other architectures, or explicitly limit the claims to the two tested models. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Computational cost Affected element Practical utility Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue Sequence scanning likely increases the number of sampling runs, but the abstract does not mention the computational overhead relative to standard prediction. These three issues collectively prevent any assessment of whether the central claim of improved accuracy is valid. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The concept of constraint-based sampling to improve cofolding accuracy is not entirely new, but the specific application to antibody-antigen and MG ternary complexes may offer a novel angle. However, without a clear method description, originality cannot be fully assessed. Scientific importance: The problem is important for drug discovery, and a simple workflow that improves accuracy on these challenging targets would be valuable. The importance is therefore potentially high, but the evidence does not yet establish the magnitude of the contribution. Interdisciplinary readership: The work sits at the intersection of computational biology, structural biology, and medicinal chemistry. It would appeal to a broad readership if the claims are substantiated. Technical soundness: Cannot be evaluated from the abstract. The lack of methodological detail and quantitative results precludes any judgment on technical rigor. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is concise and accessible, but the undefined term "sequence scanning" and the absence of concrete results reduce clarity for nonspecialist readers. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract describes a potentially useful workflow, but the central claims of improved accuracy are unsupported by quantitative data, the method is not described with sufficient clarity, and the baselines are not identified. A revised abstract or full manuscript that addresses these gaps would be required before a supportive assessment could be made. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of "improved accuracy" in antibody-antigen interface contact prediction and MG pose quality is unsupported by any numerical data in the abstract. The claim that sequence scanning "enhances overall sampling diversity" is plausible but not demonstrated or defined. The claim of evaluation on "large, diverse benchmark sets" is unverifiable without dataset details. The comparison to "previously published results" is unverifiable because the specific baselines are not named. The generalizability of the workflow beyond Boltz and Protenix is not addressed and should not be assumed.

setup Input scope Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and evidence presented in the abstract; no methods, figures, tables, or supplementary material were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present ERIS2, an attention-convolutional deep learning framework combining contextual sequence embeddings with atomistic and residue-level structural features, trained on large-scale experimental measurements and curated ProTherm data. A 5-fold ensemble achieves Pearson correlation coefficients of 0.69 on S461, 0.51 on S669, and 0.60 on S96, with negligible anti-symmetry bias on Ssym. The tool is available as a structure-based web server without registration. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, methods, or supplementary data provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, methods description, training and test dataset details, benchmark definitions, figure panels, statistical analyses, and web server implementation details Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract reports a potentially useful deep learning platform for protein stability prediction, with competitive benchmark performance and a freely accessible web server. However, the evidence base is limited to the abstract, which prevents verification of the methodological soundness, dataset handling, benchmark rigor, and statistical claims. The reported correlations are plausible but require detailed scrutiny of training-test separation, data leakage risks, and comparison with existing methods. Who would be interested in the results, and why Protein engineers, computational biologists, and therapeutic developers interested in rapid and accurate stability prediction for variant effect assessment, rational design, and clinical variant interpretation. The web server availability without registration increases practical utility for experimental laboratories. Major strengths The integration of contextual sequence embeddings with atomistic and residue-level structural features is a reasonable design choice. The use of multiple blind-test datasets (S461, S669, S96) that are sequence-disjoint from training configurations addresses a common weakness in the field. The negligible anti-symmetry bias on Ssym is a valuable property for mutation directionality. The free web server without registration lowers access barriers. Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Concern The abstract reports simulation time but provides no details on the force field, water model, temperature/pressure coupling, equilibration protocol, or convergence assessment. The claim that systems "retained the overall prefusion architecture" is vague without structural metrics such as RMSD or RMSF. Scientific importance: The work has potential relevance for understanding antibody escape and for protein engineering, but the significance is not fully demonstrated without experimental validation. Interdisciplinary readership: The topic bridges virology and computational biophysics, which could appeal to a broad audience, but the abstract is too technical for nonspecialists without context. Technical soundness: Not assessable from the abstract alone; the lack of methodological detail is a major limitation. 01 基本信息 标题 ：Foldability Is an Intrinsic Property of Protein Sequences: A Lattice Model Study with Information-Theoretic Approach and Unsupervised Machine Learning 作者 ：Shubin Liu 单位 ：未提供 期刊/平台 ：ChemRxiv（预印本） 年份 ：2026（预印本日期 2026-10-29） 论文类型 ：理论/计算方法研究（预印本） 领域 ：蛋白质折叠理论、统计热力学、信息论、无监督机器学习 关键词 ：foldability、lattice model、information theory、variational autoencoder、random energy model、minimal frustration DOI/arXiv 号 ：10.26434/chemrxiv.15011236/v1 代码 ：未提供 数据 ：未提供（27/48/64-residue 格点杂聚物模型数据） 阅读日期 ：2026-05-13（按系统日期） 在课题方向中的位置 ：本文属于「蛋白质结构预测已基本解决，但序列可折叠性（foldability）的物理根源」这一基础理论问题。方法上结合统计热力学（物理模拟）、信息论（ITA）与无监督机器学习（VAE），研究对象为格点杂聚物（lattice heteropolymer），属于蛋白质构象采样与折叠机制的简化模型研究。对课题方向的启示在于：将可折叠性定义为序列内在属性，并用信息论量（自信息、Shannon 熵、Fisher 信息）与 VAE 潜变量作为反应坐标，为真实蛋白质的折叠预测与设计提供可迁移的度量框架。 02 一句话总结 本文用 27/48/64-residue 格点杂聚物的统计热力学、信息论（ITA）与变分自编码器（VAE），证明可折叠性是序列在给定温度与溶剂下的内在属性，并发现折叠稳定性由「天然态能量的自信息 ℐtail 超过紧凑态最大熵描述对应的 Shannon 熵 𝑆c = ln𝛺c」这一随机能量模型条件决定，且 VAE 无需标签即可从折叠系综中区分序列并重构天然态能量间隙。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：为什么给定氨基酸序列是可折叠的（foldable）？即折叠性的物理/信息论根源是什么？ 为什么重要 ：蛋白质结构预测（如 AlphaFold）已接近解决，但「序列→可折叠性」的因果机制仍不清楚。理解折叠性有助于序列设计、折叠动力学预测与错误折叠疾病研究。 现有方法为何不足 ：结构预测方法（如 AlphaFold）是判别式/端到端映射，不提供折叠性的物理解释；传统格点模型研究多关注特定序列的折叠，缺乏系统性的信息论刻画；机器学习方法多为监督式，依赖标签，难以揭示内在规律。 精确研究问题 ：Can foldability be characterized as an intrinsic, sequence-dependent property via information-theoretic measures and unsupervised learning, independent of the initial denatured ensemble? They propose an information-theoretic criterion for folding transitions, relate it to minimal frustration, and report that unsupervised variational autoencoders can distinguish folding ensembles and recover known thermodynamic quantities. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no quantitative results, statistical measures, model details, or validation procedures are visible Missing materials affecting confidence Full manuscript, all figures and tables, methods section, simulation protocols, hyperparameter choices, statistical analyses, and any comparison to prior work Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents an ambitious and potentially interesting synthesis of statistical thermodynamics, information theory, and unsupervised machine learning applied to a classic model system. However, the claims as stated substantially exceed what can be evaluated from the abstract alone. The central assertion that foldability is an intrinsic property of sequences is plausible within the lattice model framework, but the evidence base is not visible. The information-theoretic criterion relating self-information to Shannon entropy of compact states is a specific and testable claim, but its derivation and validation are not shown. The machine learning results are described in qualitative terms without any quantitative support. The manuscript may contain valuable contributions, but the case is not established from the provided material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein folding theory, statistical mechanics of biopolymers, and computational biophysics would be the primary audience. Those working on the physical principles underlying foldability, the random-energy model, and minimal frustration would find the information-theoretic reformulation of interest. The machine learning component may attract researchers at the interface of unsupervised learning and biophysical simulation, particularly those interested in learned reaction coordinates and latent representations of conformational ensembles. Major strengths The abstract addresses a fundamental and unresolved question in protein science, namely why some sequences fold while others do not. The proposed information-theoretic criterion is conceptually elegant and potentially unifying, connecting thermodynamic stability, kinetic accessibility, and the random-energy model. The use of unsupervised machine learning to recover known physical quantities without labels is a compelling approach that could demonstrate the utility of data-driven methods in biophysics. The claim that results are independent of the initial denatured ensemble is a strong reproducibility statement, if properly supported. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "Native populations, folding probabilities and free-energy surfaces are reproducible and independent of the initial denatured ensemble, so foldability is an intrinsic property of the sequence at a given temperature and solvent." Evidence pointer Location not provided Concern The abstract asserts that foldability is an intrinsic property of sequences based on reproducibility across initial denatured ensembles. However, no quantitative measures of reproducibility are provided, and the scope of the claim is unclear. The statement appears to be limited to lattice heteropolymers at specific temperatures and solvent conditions, yet the title generalizes to protein sequences broadly. The abstract does not specify how many sequences were tested, how the denatured ensembles were generated, or what statistical criteria were used to establish independence. Why it matters The central thesis of the manuscript rests on this claim. If the evidence is limited to a small number of sequences or specific simulation conditions, the generalization to protein sequences in general is not justified. The distinction between intrinsic sequence properties and environment-dependent behavior is critical for the conceptual contribution of the work. Resolution test Provide quantitative reproducibility metrics across multiple initial ensembles, specify the number and diversity of sequences tested, and clearly delineate the conditions under which the intrinsic property claim holds. If the claim is restricted to lattice models, the title and framing should be adjusted accordingly. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Theoretical derivation Claim pointer "Stability is governed by an information balance: the information content (self-information) of the native energy relative to the maximum-entropy description of compact alternatives, ℐtail, must exceed their Shannon entropy, 𝑆c = ln𝛺c. Evidence pointer Location not provided Concern The abstract presents a specific mathematical criterion for folding transitions without showing its derivation, assumptions, or validation. The connection to the random-energy model is asserted but not demonstrated. The claim that ℐtail/𝑆c fixes the ratio of folding to glass temperatures is a strong quantitative statement that requires explicit derivation and numerical verification. The recasting of minimal frustration in information units is conceptually interesting but needs a clear mapping between the information-theoretic quantities and the physical parameters of the system. The connection to the random-energy model must be made rigorous, and the predictive power of the criterion must be demonstrated on the lattice systems studied. 工程中活性-特异性权衡、结构依赖与筛选成本问题，但结论受限于高质量数据稀缺、模型可解释性不足与湿实验通量瓶颈，AI 生成候选仍需传统实验验证。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：如何系统性地组织 Cas 蛋白性能优化（PAM 兼容性、活性-特异性权衡、功能转换、小型化、物种适配）的技术路径，并明确 AI/蛋白质语言模型在其中可承担的角色与边界？ 为什么重要 ：CRISPR/Cas 临床与农业转化受 off-target、PAM 限制、NHEJ 不可控修复、大分子量递送困难四大瓶颈制约，而这些瓶颈本质上与 Cas 蛋白的分子性质相关，因此蛋白工程是通用突破口。 现有方法为何不足 ：定向进化成本高、周期长（数月至数年）、机制不清；理性设计依赖高分辨率结构、难以预测多位点协同效应、技术门槛高；整合工程仍受上游文库构建与结构解析限制，且无法创造脱离天然模板的全新骨架。 精确研究问题（Can ... ?） ：Can AI/protein language models serve as cross-layer enabling tools that reduce the cost and structural dependency of Cas protein engineering while resolving multi-objective performance trade-offs that traditional directed evolution and rational design cannot jointly solve?（本文以综述论证形式回答，非实验检验） 04 背景与发展脉络 阶段一：定向进化 + 高通量筛选（发现层） ：以综述形式建立「随机探索—精准改造—系统整合」三层递进分析框架，逐层比较定向进化、理性结构设计、整合蛋白工程的原理、优劣与互补关系，并把 AI/蛋白质语言模型定位为贯穿三层的跨层使能工具，另加 de novo 设计作为独立新范式。 核心洞察 ：三类传统策略并非替代关系而是互补递进——定向进化回答「哪些位点有工程潜力」，理性设计回答「如何在特定位点做靶向改造」，整合工程回答「如何多性状协同」；AI 的价值不在于替代湿实验，而在于压缩搜索空间（智能设计文库、预测突变效应、补足缺失结构、预测编辑结果），从而缓解传统方法难以解决的多目标耦合权衡。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] ：对任何「序列-结构-功能」多目标蛋白工程问题，可迁移的元策略是：把「广谱发现」与「精确改造」显式分层，再用预测模型做跨层桥接与预筛；同时必须承认预测模型的输出是候选而非结论，闭环验证不可省略。 07 方法总览 输入 No supplementary materials, no line numbers. Assessment boundary Evaluation is limited to the supplied manuscript text and its embedded tables and figure captions. No independent verification of cited primary literature, no access to supplementary data, no line-level referencing possible. Shared manuscript claim summary The manuscript is a narrative review proposing a three-tiered framework for Cas protein engineering (directed evolution, structure-based rational design, integrated protein engineering) and argues that AI and protein language models act as cross-layer enabling tools that, together with a de novo design paradigm, will drive development of miniaturized, broad-spectrum, high-precision editors toward clinical and industrial translation. Visible evidence base Abstract; Introduction with Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 and Tables 1 and 2; section on high-throughput screening and directed evolution with Fig. 3; section on structure-based rational design with Fig. 4; section on comprehensive protein engineering; section on AI and protein language models with Table 3; section on synergies and future trends with Table 4; Applications and prospects; Conclusion; author contributions; competing interest statement; acknowledgments. Missing materials affecting confidence No line numbers; no supplementary tables or data; no search strategy, database list, inclusion or exclusion criteria, or time window for literature selection; no PRISMA-style flow or equivalent for a review; no quantitative synthesis methods; no primary data; no figure permissions or licensing statement; no explicit statement of how references were screened or how many were excluded. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript is a broad, well-organized narrative review that maps three established Cas protein engineering paradigms and positions AI-based tools as an integrative layer. The conceptual framing (discovery layer, optimization layer, integration layer) is coherent and the tables are informative. However, as submitted, the work reads primarily as a structured synthesis of already published findings rather than a critical or systematic analysis. Several specific factual and interpretive claims are stated with more confidence than the cited evidence appears to support, at least from the material visible here. The central assertion that the review "fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field" is not demonstrated, because no systematic methodology, coverage analysis, or comparison against existing reviews is presented. The AI section is the most distinctive contribution but is largely descriptive and does not critically evaluate model performance, benchmarking, or failure modes. The manuscript is potentially useful to the field if the technical and framing concerns below are resolved. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in CRISPR tool development, protein engineering, and computational protein design; groups working on AAV-compatible miniaturized editors; translational gene therapy teams evaluating editor selection; and computational biologists interested in how protein language models are being applied to editor optimization. The comparative tables (Tables 3 and 4) may be of practical use to newcomers seeking an orientation map of the field. Major strengths The three-tier framework (directed evolution, rational design, integrated engineering) is clearly articulated and consistently applied across sections, with a corresponding summary in Table 4. Table 3 provides a reasonably structured inventory of AI tools with architecture, advantages, limitations, and applications, which is a useful reference element. The manuscript correctly emphasizes that AI-generated candidates still require wet-lab validation and does not overstate AI as a replacement for experimental work in the Conclusion. The miniaturization discussion, including Cas12f and TnpB/IscB, is a relevant and timely topic for in vivo delivery. The limitations subsections at the end of each major section are a constructive structural choice. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Originality and gap claim Claim pointer The abstract states that the review "fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field" and provides a "theoretical framework for tiered, synergistic modification." Evidence pointer Abstract; Introduction; no methods or search-strategy section anywhere in the supplied text; location not provided. Concern The manuscript asserts a gap-filling and systematic contribution but provides no methodology to substantiate either. There is no described literature search strategy, no database list, no inclusion or exclusion criteria, no time window, no screening procedure, and no comparison with existing reviews on Cas engineering or AI-assisted protein design. Without these, the claim of systematic analysis is not evaluable and the novelty relative to prior reviews cannot be assessed. Why it matters The primary claimed contribution of the manuscript is its systematic and gap-filling character. If this cannot be verified, the central justification for publication as a review is weakened, and readers cannot judge coverage completeness or selection bias. Resolution test Provide an explicit search and selection methodology (databases, query strings, date range, inclusion and exclusion criteria, number screened and included), and a short positioning statement comparing the scope of this review against at least three to five recent reviews in the same area, indicating what is added. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness of specific factual claims Claim pointer The manuscript states that engineered small Cas proteins "can achieve editing efficiencies of up to 90% in human cells without significant off-target effects or tissue toxicity," and that AsCas12f variants yham and hkra achieved "a tenfold increase in activity without increasing the risk of off-target effects." Evidence pointer Applications and prospects section; Miniaturized design subsection; location not provided. Concern These are strong quantitative and safety claims presented without accompanying qualification of the assay system, cell type, target locus, delivery format, or the specific study conditions under which the numbers were obtained. The "up to 90%" figure is not attributed to a specific variant, locus, or reference in the visible text, and "without significant off-target effects or tissue toxicity" is a safety assertion that requires defined detection methods and sensitivity limits. Similarly, the tenfold activity increase and the absence of increased off-target risk require specification of the assay and the comparison baseline. Why it matters Quantitative performance and safety claims are the most consequential statements in a translational review. Unqualified numbers can be propagated into downstream planning and grant or regulatory documents. If the underlying conditions are not stated, the claims are not verifiable and may mislead. Resolution test For each quantitative claim, state the specific variant, the cell type or organism, the target locus, the delivery method, the assay used to measure activity and off-target events, and the corresponding reference. Where the original study reported context-dependent values, report the range and conditions rather than a single maximum. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Accuracy of attribution and mechanism Claim pointer The manuscript attributes HiFiCas9 development to "Mark A. Behlke's team" using a dual positive and negative screening system in E. coli, and attributes SuperFi-Cas9 to "the University of Texas team," and the WED domain work to "the Doudna team." Evidence pointer Overcoming the activity-specificity trade-off subsection; Enhancing specificity subsection; Enhanced efficiency subsection; location not provided. Concern Attribution by team or institution rather than by the specific study and its findings is imprecise and difficult to verify. In several cases the described mechanism is compressed to the point where it may not match the primary report, for example the description of HypaCas9 mutations and the REC3 domain role, and the description of SuperFi-Cas9 as targeting "non-specific interactions at the DNA-binding interface and abnormal structural flexibility." These mechanistic summaries require direct correspondence with the cited primary literature. Why it matters Mechanistic misattribution in a review propagates errors into the field and undermines the review's value as a reference. Institutional attribution also obscures which specific study is being discussed when a group has multiple relevant publications. Resolution test Replace institutional attribution with specific study citations and verify each mechanistic statement against the primary source. Where the mechanism is contested or simplified, state so explicitly. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Critical evaluation of AI tools Claim pointer Table 3 and the AI section present AI tools as providing "computational support for optimizing Cas editors across multiple dimensions" and describe advantages such as "accurate prediction," "high-precision prediction," and "broad-spectrum prediction." Evidence pointer AI-driven Cas editor optimizes core toolchain subsection; Table 3; location not provided. Concern The AI section is largely enumerative. It does not report benchmarking results, head-to-head comparisons, performance metrics on Cas-specific tasks, or known failure modes beyond generic statements. For example, AlphaFold2 and AlphaFold3 are described as resolving "atomic-resolution 3D conformations" of Cas-sgRNA-DNA ternary complexes, but the manuscript does not address the documented limitations of these models for large, multi-component nucleic acid-protein assemblies, nor does it indicate which Cas complexes have actually been predicted with validated accuracy. Similarly, EVOLVEpro and the ESM suite are described as quantitatively ranking variant performance without reporting reported correlation with experimental measurements. Why it matters The AI section is the most distinctive part of the review. Without critical evaluation, it functions as a catalogue rather than an analysis, and readers cannot judge which tools are actually usable for which Cas engineering tasks. Resolution test Add reported performance metrics where available (for example correlation coefficients, top-k enrichment, success rates in prospective validation), specify which Cas systems each tool has been applied to and with what outcome, and explicitly discuss documented failure modes and domains where predictions are unreliable. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Internal consistency of the framework Claim pointer The manuscript states that rational design "does not require prior structural information of target proteins" in the technical workflow paragraph, while the same section and the limitations paragraph state that rational design "relies heavily on structural knowledge" and requires "high-resolution structures of protein-substrate complexes." Evidence pointer Structure-based rational design section, technical workflow paragraph and limitations paragraph; location not provided. Concern The statement that the remodeling strategy "does not require prior structural information of target proteins" appears to contradict the defining premise of structure-based rational design as presented throughout the manuscript. This may be a drafting error, but as written it creates an internal inconsistency in the core conceptual framework. Why it matters The three-tier framework depends on a clear distinction between methods that require structural knowledge and those that do not. An internal contradiction at this point undermines the framework's clarity. Resolution test Correct or clarify the statement so that the structural information requirement of rational design is stated consistently throughout. Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Evidence for the de novo design paradigm Claim pointer The manuscript states that AI can "independently generate artificial editing scaffolds without natural evolutionary templates" and cites OpenCRISPR-1 as an example of overcoming performance bottlenecks via multi-site synergistic optimization. Evidence pointer Multidimensional advantages of AI-powered Cas protein engineering subsection; Overcoming the activity-specificity trade-off subsection; location not provided. Concern The claim of fully template-free generation of functional editors is a strong one and is presented without describing the extent of experimental validation, the performance relative to natural editors, or the current limitations of such generated scaffolds. OpenCRISPR-1 is cited in a list alongside screening-derived variants without distinguishing what was AI-generated versus what was experimentally optimized. Why it matters The de novo design paradigm is presented as a new avenue for creating editors with novel functions. If the actual validated performance and remaining gaps are not described, the reader cannot assess whether this is an established capability or an early-stage aspiration. Resolution test For each de novo designed editor cited, state the design method, the experimental validation performed, the measured performance relative to a natural comparator, and the current limitations. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology consistency Affected element Classification of CRISPR systems Evidence pointer Introduction, second paragraph; location not provided. Issue The text states the system "can be classified into Type I and Type II systems based on the number of Cas proteins, and is further subdivided into seven classes (Types I-VII)," then refers to "Class I systems (Types I, III, IV, and VII)" and "Class II systems (Types II, V, and VI)." The terms Type and Class are used interchangeably in a way that is inconsistent with standard nomenclature, where Class 1 and Class 2 are the higher-level divisions and Types I through VII are the subclasses. The three-tier framework is a reasonable organizational device but overlaps substantially with existing reviews on Cas engineering. The AI section is the most potentially original element but is currently descriptive rather than analytical. The claimed gap-filling is not demonstrated. Scientific importance The topic is important and timely, particularly the integration of AI tools with editor engineering and the miniaturization problem for in vivo delivery. However, the current treatment does not advance a new argument or synthesis beyond cataloguing. Interdisciplinary readership The manuscript is potentially accessible to a broad readership across protein engineering, computational biology, and gene therapy. The tables support this. However, the density of unexplained jargon and the lack of critical framing reduce accessibility for nonspecialists. Technical soundness Several specific claims are stated without sufficient qualification or supporting detail (R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M6), and there is an internal contradiction in the framework (R1-M5). The AI section lacks benchmarking and failure-mode discussion (R1-M4). Readability for nonspecialists The prose is generally clear but frequently dense, with long compound sentences and heavy use of field-specific abbreviations. Key concepts such as PAM, NHEJ, DBTL, and PLM are used with limited or no definition at first use. The figure captions are detailed and helpful. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript requires a defined review methodology, qualification or correction of quantitative and safety claims, precise attribution of mechanistic findings, critical evaluation of AI tool performance, resolution of the internal contradiction in the framework, and stronger support for the de novo design claims before the central contribution can be assessed. Risk / unsupported claims Claim that the review "fills a gap in systematic analysis within the field" is unsupported because no systematic methodology or comparison with existing reviews is provided (R1-M1). Claim that engineered small Cas proteins achieve "editing efficiencies of up to 90% in human cells without significant off-target effects or tissue toxicity" is not evaluable without specification of variant, locus, assay, and detection sensitivity (R1-M2). Claim that AsCas12f yham and hkra achieved "a tenfold increase in activity without increasing the risk of off-target effects" is not evaluable without assay conditions and baseline definition (R1-M2). Claim that AI can "independently generate artificial editing scaffolds without natural evolutionary templates" is weakly supported because validation extent and comparative performance are not described (R1-M6). Claim that AI-driven rational design cuts "screening cycles and experimental costs by orders of magnitude" is a quantitative assertion presented without supporting measurement or citation detail (R1-M4). Claim that AI tools "resolve atomic-resolution 3D conformations of Cas monomers and Cas-sgRNA-DNA ternary complexes" overstates current demonstrated capability for large multi-component assemblies without qualification (R1-M4). Claim that the integrated strategy "represents the mainstream strategy for developing high-performance Cas editing tools today" is asserted without survey or bibliometric support. Claim that small Cas proteins as a class "combine the advantages of high editing efficiency, low immunogenicity, and a broad targeting range" generalizes variant-specific properties to a protein class (R1-m6). Statement that rational design "does not require prior structural information of target proteins" contradicts the manuscript's own framework and is unsupported as written (R1-M5).

：给定一个 DNA 结合蛋白（DBP）的结构（实验解析或计算预测），能否预测其 DNA 结合界面残基，以及每个界面残基对四种碱基（A/T/C/G）的偏好？ 为什么重要 ：蛋白质-DNA 特异性识别是基因调控、表观遗传、基因组编辑等功能的基础。但大多数 DBP 的结合基序（motif）未被实验表征，高通量实验方法（如 ChIP-seq、SELEX-seq）成本高、通量有限，且无法覆盖所有物种和蛋白家族。 现有方法不足 ： 早期方法依赖同源序列比对或已知基序数据库，无法推广到新家族。 结构-based 方法（如 DeepPBS、NA-MPNN）需要 DNA 结构作为输入，且对 apo 构象或计算预测结构敏感。 现有方法多聚焦于界面预测，缺乏残基水平的碱基偏好预测能力。 精确研究问题 ：Can a multimodal deep learning framework, trained solely on protein structure and sequence features, predict residue-level base preferences for DNA-binding proteins with sufficient accuracy to guide experimental design and protein engineering? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：此脉络基于本文 Introduction 和 Discussion 的叙述，结合外部知识标注，属于「经外部核验」的框架。 阶段 代表性方法 优点 局限 本文位置 序列同源推断 基于 PWM 数据库（JASPAR）、同源比对 简单、可解释 依赖已知家族；无法处理新蛋白 超越 核心洞察 洞察 1 ：蛋白质-DNA 识别特异性由「进化保守性 + 3D 几何 + 表面理化性质」三者共同决定，单一模态不足以捕捉完整的识别密码（recognition code）。 洞察 2 ：残基水平的碱基偏好可以通过「化学感知距离」（对氢键、疏水、盐桥赋予不同权重）从结构自动生成监督信号，无需人工标注。 洞察 3 Supplementary figures, tables, and sections are referenced but not included. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the supplied manuscript text. All claims that depend on Supporting Information (Figures S1–S9, Supplementary Methods Sections 1–3, Supplementary Results) cannot be independently verified from the material provided. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present 3M-BSIP, a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates a protein language model (SaProt), a geometric graph neural network, and a surface pointcloud encoder via cross-attention to predict, from a DBP structure alone, (i) DNA-binding interface residues, (ii) contact-strength ranking, and (iii) residue-level base preference over A/T/C/G. The authors claim state-of-the-art performance on interface and base-preference tasks, robustness to computationally modeled and conformationally flexible (apo) structures, and two real-world applications: motif prediction for an uncharacterized Streptomyces TF (51910) and computational reprogramming of BsaXI base specificity. Visible evidence base Main-text figures (Figure 1–Figure 6 and unnumbered inline references), Methods descriptions of data curation, feature extraction, model architecture, training, and evaluation metrics, and reported quantitative results in the Results section. No supplementary figures, tables, or source data files are included in the supplied material. Missing materials affecting confidence Figures S1–S9; Supplementary Methods Sections 1–3; Supplementary Results; the ntM reconstruction procedure; details of the AF3_Test_apo/holo construction; the 54-protein experimental apo/holo set composition; per-family performance breakdowns; statistical tests; code/data availability statement; and any independent validation of the BsaXI and 51910 predictions beyond the reported assays. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a technically ambitious multimodal framework for a genuinely difficult problem, namely residue-level base preference prediction from a protein structure alone. The conceptual framing, the three-modality design, and the two application case studies are attractive. However, from the supplied material, several central claims are not yet fully established. The most consequential issues are (i) the absence of a direct, quantitative comparison against the methods the authors position as the closest prior art (DeepPBS, NA-MPNN) on the base-preference task, (ii) reliance on a self-defined supervisory signal whose relationship to experimental base specificity is not independently validated, (iii) incomplete reporting of data-splitting and leakage controls, and (iv) dependence on supplementary material that is not available for verification. The work is potentially publishable if these technical concerns are resolved, but the current evidence base does not yet support the strongest claims. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational structural biologists and protein–DNA recognition researchers interested in specificity codes; machine-learning method developers working on multimodal and geometric deep learning for biomolecular interfaces; protein engineers and synthetic biologists interested in reprogramming DNA-binding specificity; and groups curating binding motifs for uncharacterized transcription factors. The residue-level base-preference formulation, if validated, would be of broad interest because most existing methods predict at the motif or interface level rather than at the per-residue base level. Major strengths The problem is well motivated and the gap in residue-level base-preference prediction is real and clearly articulated. The multimodal design is principled, and the ablation study (Figure 4D–F) provides a coherent argument that sequence, structure, and surface modalities contribute complementary information. The inclusion of apo versus holo robustness testing (Figure 5D–E) addresses a practically important failure mode for structure-based predictors. The two application case studies, particularly the BsaXI reprogramming with SPR validation, are a meaningful attempt to move beyond benchmark metrics toward functional validation. The manuscript is generally well organized and the methods are described at a level of detail that permits partial reproduction. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Benchmarking and comparative claims Claim pointer The manuscript claims "SOTA performance on both interface-residue identification and base-preference predictions" and states that 3M-BSIP "consistently outperforms the existing methods." Evidence pointer Results section "3M-BSIP Outperforms the GeoBind Method on Interface-Residue Prediction," Figure 6A–C; Introduction positioning of DeepPBS and NA-MPNN. Concern The only head-to-head quantitative comparison reported is against GeoBind, which the authors themselves note does not provide base-preference prediction. DeepPBS and NA-MPNN, which are the methods that actually predict base or motif preferences, are discussed in the Introduction but are not benchmarked against 3M-BSIP on the base-preference task in the supplied text. The SOTA claim for base-preference prediction is therefore not supported by a direct comparison. Why it matters The central novelty claim is residue-level base-preference prediction. Without a direct comparison to the closest prior methods on the same test set and the same metric, the SOTA claim is unsubstantiated and the reader cannot judge the actual advance. Resolution test Provide a head-to-head evaluation of 3M-BSIP against DeepPBS and NA-MPNN on a common, nonredundant test set using a common metric for base or motif preference, with the same input constraints (protein-only versus protein–DNA complex) clearly stated. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Validity of the supervisory signal Claim pointer The model is trained to predict a "residue-level base-preference heatmap" derived from a chemical-aware distance and a hand-designed logit formulation, and this heatmap is treated as ground truth for base preference. Evidence pointer Materials and Methods "Generation of Supervisory Signals," "Derivation of Residue Score and Base Allocation Coefficient," and "Generation of Residue-Level Base Preference Heatmap"; Results "Structural Characterizations of Protein–DNA Interface for DBPs." Concern The target label is not an experimental measurement of base preference but a deterministic function of the crystal structure geometry, with several arbitrary hyperparameters (discount factors 0.85/0.82/0.80, σ = 3.0 Å, the specific logit formulas, the 4.5 Å cutoff). The manuscript does not demonstrate that this constructed heatmap correlates with experimentally measured base preferences (for example, from PBM, SELEX, or mutation-based affinity data). The model may therefore be learning to reproduce a geometric proxy rather than biological specificity. Why it matters If the label is a proxy, all reported base-preference accuracies measure agreement with the proxy, not with biological base preference. This directly affects the interpretation of the benchmark results and the two application claims. Resolution test Show that the constructed heatmap correlates with at least one independent experimental measure of base preference on a held-out set, and report the sensitivity of the reported accuracies to the arbitrary hyperparameters in the label construction. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Data splitting and leakage control Claim pointer The model "has learned the generalizable biophysical principles of protein–DNA recognition rather than merely overfitting," supported by the deredundancy procedure and hierarchical clustering-based splitting. Evidence pointer Materials and Methods "Data Sets and Benchmarks," "Structure Preprocessing and Data Set Partitioning"; Results "Ablation Studies Validate the Necessity of Multimodal Integration," Figure 4A–C. Concern The deredundancy criterion removes structures only when both protein and DNA sequences are identical and DNA backbone RMSD is below 1.5 Å. This is a permissive criterion that can retain near-duplicate proteins with different DNA sequences. The splitting is then performed by TM-score clustering with 80/10/10 allocation within each cluster, which places structurally similar proteins in both training and test sets by design. The manuscript does not report sequence-identity-based leakage analysis between training and test sets, nor does it report performance under a strict sequence-identity or fold-level holdout. Why it matters The reported test performance, including the high MCC values at low Levenshtein distance, may be inflated by structural and sequence similarity between training and test proteins. The generalization claim depends on ruling this out. Resolution test Report a strict holdout evaluation with a defined sequence identity threshold (for example, 30 percent) and a fold-level holdout, and report the corresponding metrics alongside the current numbers. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility and reporting completeness Claim pointer Multiple results and methodological steps are stated to be detailed in Supporting Information, including the fusion strategy comparison, the ntM reconstruction, the integrated gradient attribution, and the screening pipeline. Evidence pointer References to Figure S1, Figure S2, Figure S3, Figure S4, Figure S5, Figure S6, Figure S7, Figure S8, Figure S9, Supporting Information Section 1, Supplementary Methods Sections 2–3, and Supplementary Results. Concern The supplied material does not include any supplementary content, and no code or data availability statement is present in the provided text. Several claims, including the fusion strategy comparison and the structural reconstruction that converts the heatmap into the "TTAxT" motif, cannot be evaluated. Why it matters The ntM reconstruction is the bridge between the residue-level prediction and the experimentally tested motif. Without it, the 51910 application cannot be fully assessed. Resolution test Provide all supplementary figures, tables, and methods, and include a code and data availability statement with repository identifiers. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Statistical rigor of comparative and application claims Claim pointer 3M-BSIP "surpasses GeoBind on the majority of tested samples," and the BsaXI screening is described as having a "high success rate (2/3)." Evidence pointer Results "3M-BSIP Outperforms the GeoBind Method on Interface-Residue Prediction," Figure 6A–B; Results "Reprogramming the DNA Binding Specificity of a Type IIB Restriction Endonuclease," Figure 6C–D. Concern The reported differences are small in several cases (for example, interface MCC 0.545 versus 0.523 on the full test set, and 0.518 versus 0.512 at Levenshtein distance above 5). No confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-sample paired statistics are reported. The BsaXI success rate is based on three candidates, of which one did not achieve reversal, and the specificity ratio changes are reported without error estimates or replicate numbers. Why it matters Small metric differences without uncertainty quantification cannot support a superiority claim, and a 2/3 success rate on three candidates is too small to support a general claim about the method's success rate. Resolution test Report confidence intervals or paired significance tests for all comparative metrics, and report replicate numbers and error estimates for the SPR measurements. Issue The metric is reported as a single accuracy value but its exact definition (per residue, per residue–nucleotide pair, threshold, treatment of noninterface residues) is not fully specified in the supplied text. Required correction State the exact formula and the treatment of noninterface residues and ties. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Data set description Affected element The 54-protein experimental apo/holo set. Evidence pointer Results "Well-Tolerance to 3M-BSIP toward the Structurally Flexible DBPs," Figure 5D. Issue The composition, source, and redundancy control of this set relative to the training data are not described. Required correction Describe how the 54 proteins were selected and confirm no overlap with training data. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Figure and text consistency Affected element Reference to "Figure" without a number in the Model Architecture section. Evidence pointer Materials and Methods "3M-BSIP Model Architecture," first paragraph. Issue The text refers to "(Figure )" with no figure number, and several inline figure references in the Results are unnumbered in the supplied text. Required correction Ensure all figure callouts are correctly numbered and consistent with the final figure set. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Claim scope Affected element Statement that 3M-BSIP "holds great potential in annotating the binding motifs of all DBPs." Evidence pointer Abstract; Discussion. Issue The claim of "all DBPs" is broader than the evidence, which covers a curated structural data set and two case studies. Required correction Restrict the claim to the tested scope or provide a systematic coverage analysis across DBP families. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (absence of direct comparison to DeepPBS and NA-MPNN on base preference), R1-M2 (unvalidated proxy label for base preference), R1-M3 (permissive deredundancy and similarity-based splitting without strict holdout), R1-M4 (missing supplementary material and no code/data availability), R1-M5 (no uncertainty quantification for comparative and application claims). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The residue-level base-preference formulation and the three-modality fusion are a reasonable methodological contribution. However, the originality relative to DeepPBS and NA-MPNN is not demonstrated because no direct comparison is provided. Scientific importance The problem is important and the potential impact on motif annotation and protein engineering is significant. The importance claim is weakened by the unvalidated supervisory signal and the small-scale application validation. Interdisciplinary readership The topic would interest computational biologists, protein engineers, and synthetic biologists. The current presentation assumes substantial familiarity with geometric deep learning terminology, which limits accessibility. Technical soundness The architecture and training pipeline are described in reasonable detail, but the label construction, data splitting, and comparative evaluation have unresolved issues as detailed in R1-M1 through R1-M5. Readability for nonspecialists The Abstract and Introduction are accessible. The Methods and Results contain dense jargon and several undefined metrics, which would hinder a nonspecialist reader. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The work is potentially supportive if the technical concerns R1-M1 through R1-M5 are resolved, in particular a direct benchmark against DeepPBS and NA-MPNN on base preference, validation of the supervisory signal against experimental base-preference data, and a strict holdout evaluation. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of SOTA performance on base-preference prediction is unsupported because no direct comparison to DeepPBS or NA-MPNN is provided in the supplied material. The claim that the model learns "generalizable biophysical principles" is weakened by the permissive deredundancy criterion and the similarity-based data splitting, with no strict sequence-identity or fold-level holdout reported. The claim that the residue-level base-preference heatmap represents biological base preference is not supported by any comparison to experimental base-preference measurements in the supplied text. The claim of a "high success rate (2/3)" for BsaXI reprogramming is based on three candidates and lacks replicate numbers and error estimates. The claim that 3M-BSIP can "annotate the binding motifs of all DBPs" is broader than the evidence provided. The claim that the model is robust to "profound structural rearrangements" is supported by a single detailed example (ZnF456) plus aggregate R2 values, and the aggregate analysis depends on supplementary material not provided. The claim that the ntM reconstruction reliably converts residue-level predictions into contiguous motifs cannot be evaluated because the method is in Supplementary Methods Sections 2–3, which are not supplied. The claim that the model outperforms GeoBind on "the majority of tested samples" is reported without per-sample paired statistics or confidence intervals.
