acknowledgements) as provided Assessment boundary Scientific content, methodological soundness, and claims as presented in the supplied material; no external data or supplementary figures were available for inspection Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present MINT, a computational framework combining structure-guided sequence design (ProteinMPNN) with MHC-I epitope prediction (NetMHCpan4.1) to tune CD8⁺ T cell immunogenicity of designed proteins while preserving function. Using a de novo-designed luciferase (LuxSit-i), they demonstrate in silico epitope minimization across 5 mouse and 25 human MHC-I alleles, and in vivo validation in mice showing reduced CD8⁺ T cell responses to predicted low-epitope variants. Visible evidence base Abstract, main text narrative, methods section; figures referenced but not provided (Figures 1, 2, S1, S2); no raw data, statistical analyses, or supplementary materials Missing materials affecting confidence All figures and supplementary figures; raw experimental data (flow cytometry, luminescence measurements); statistical analysis details; sequence information for designed variants; details of NetMHCpan allele selection criteria; LNP characterization data; gating strategies for flow cytometry Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a timely and important problem in protein design and adoptive cell therapy: reducing immunogenicity of therapeutic proteins without compromising function. The conceptual framework is sound and the integration of established computational tools (ProteinMPNN, NetMHCpan4.1) with in vivo validation is a logical and potentially impactful approach. However, the provided material is insufficient to fully evaluate the claims. Key experimental details, quantitative results, and figure data are absent from the supplied text. The in vivo experiments, while well-designed in concept, lack presentation of actual data. The methods section contains algorithmic descriptions but omits critical parameters and validation metrics. The claim of "function-preserving" immunogenicity minimization rests on limited functional data (luciferase activity) without comprehensive characterization. The manuscript has potential but requires substantial additional information and possibly additional experiments to establish the case convincingly. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein design and engineering, particularly those working on therapeutic proteins, cell therapy, and immunogenicity prediction. Computational biologists developing deimmunization algorithms. Immunologists studying T cell responses to engineered proteins. The broader synthetic biology community interested in designing proteins with tailored immunological properties. The work could also interest clinicians and translational researchers developing adoptive cell therapies, as reducing immunogenicity of therapeutic proteins is a major clinical barrier. Major strengths 1) Addresses a clinically relevant and technically challenging problem with a clear conceptual framework. 2) Integration of established computational tools (ProteinMPNN, NetMHCpan4.1) in a modular pipeline that can incorporate improved prediction methods. 3) In vivo validation using mRNA-LNP immunization is an appropriate and sensitive approach. 4) The "5+1" fusion design for comparing multiple variants within a shared immunization context is clever and controls for inter-animal variability. 5) The computational optimizations (caching, early rejection, allele grouping) demonstrate practical attention to scalability. 6) The demonstration of both low- and high-immunogenicity designs from the same starting protein provides a useful contrast for understanding immunogenicity determinants. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer "variants designed to have few MHC-I epitopes elicited little detectable CD8⁺ T cell response, whereas variants designed to include multiple epitopes induced robust responses" Evidence pointer Figures 2C, 2D, S2B–D; location not provided Concern The central in vivo claim is presented without any quantitative data in the provided text. No numerical values for cytokine-positive cell frequencies, no statistical comparisons, no representative flow cytometry plots, and no information on effect sizes or variability are given. The statement "minimal detectable responses" and "robust responses" are qualitative and cannot be evaluated without the underlying data. Why it matters This is the primary experimental validation of the computational approach. Without quantitative evidence, the reader cannot assess the magnitude of the immunogenicity reduction, the consistency across biological replicates, or whether the differences are statistically significant. The claim that immunogenicity can be "tuned" requires demonstration of a graded or at least reproducible binary response. Resolution test Provide quantitative data showing frequencies of cytokine-producing CD8⁺ T cells for each variant, with appropriate statistical tests (e.g., ANOVA with multiple comparison correction), effect sizes, and variability measures. Include representative flow cytometry plots and gating strategies. Ideally, show a dose-response or correlation between predicted epitope burden and measured T cell response. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Functional preservation Claim pointer "we demonstrate epitope elimination while preserving function" and "The resulting sequences exhibited substantial diversity in amino acid composition" Evidence pointer Figures 1D, S1A; location not provided Concern The claim of function preservation rests on luciferase activity measurements, but the provided text gives no quantitative activity data. The statement that low and high immunogenicity variants "retained comparable luciferase activity" is not supported by any numbers, statistical analysis, or comparison to the parent enzyme. Additionally, only a single functional readout (enzymatic activity) is used; protein stability, expression levels, and biophysical properties are not assessed. Why it matters The central premise of the work is that immunogenicity can be minimized "without compromising protein function." If the designed variants have substantially reduced activity, stability, or expression, the practical utility of the approach is diminished. The lack of quantitative functional data makes it impossible to assess the trade-off between immunogenicity reduction and functional preservation. Resolution test Provide quantitative luciferase activity measurements (e.g., relative light units normalized to expression) for parent and designed variants, with statistical comparisons. Include additional functional characterization such as thermal stability, expression yield, and kinetic parameters (Km, kcat) if feasible. Show that the activity of low-immunogenicity variants is within an acceptable range of the parent enzyme. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological completeness Claim pointer "MINT (MHC-I Immunogenicity Tuning; Figure 1A)" and the iterative optimization strategy Evidence pointer Methods section, Figure 1A; location not provided Concern The methods section describes the algorithmic framework but omits several critical parameters needed for reproducibility. The scoring function is described with equations that are incompletely specified (the actual equations are not shown in the provided text). The selection of the 25 human HLA alleles is not justified. The criteria for "zero-shot" success versus when cycling is required are not defined. The termination criteria are described but not quantified. The relationship between the described "non-cycling" and "cycling" methods and their respective performance is unclear. Why it matters Reproducibility is a fundamental requirement for computational methods. Without complete specification of the algorithm, parameters, and allele selection, other researchers cannot implement or benchmark MINT. The choice of HLA alleles is particularly important as it determines the generalizability of the approach to different human populations. Resolution test Provide complete algorithmic specifications including all equations, parameter values, and pseudocode. Justify the selection of the 25 HLA alleles (e.g., coverage of common alleles in target populations). Define clear criteria for when zero-shot design is sufficient versus when iterative cycling is needed. Provide a step-by-step example of the algorithm applied to a single design task. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generalizability Claim pointer "approaches such as MINT should be broadly applicable for reducing their immunogenicity" Evidence pointer Discussion section; location not provided Concern The manuscript validates MINT on a single protein (LuxSit-i, a luciferase). The claim of broad applicability is speculative without demonstration on multiple proteins with different folds, sizes, and functions. The choice of a small (117 residue) de novo protein may not represent the challenges of larger, more complex therapeutic proteins. Why it matters The clinical relevance of the approach depends on its applicability to diverse therapeutic proteins. A single demonstration, while valuable, does not establish generalizability. The computational cost and success rate may vary substantially with protein size and complexity. Resolution test Apply MINT to at least 2-3 additional proteins with different structural classes and functions. Report success rates, computational costs, and functional preservation across these test cases. If additional experiments are not feasible, clearly frame the current work as a proof-of-concept with explicit limitations. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Immunogenicity prediction validation Claim pointer "variants designed to have few MHC-I epitopes elicited little detectable CD8⁺ T cell response" Evidence pointer Figures 2C, 2D; location not provided Concern The in vivo validation relies on NetMHCpan4.1 predictions as the basis for design, but the correlation between predicted epitope burden and actual T cell immunogenicity is not directly assessed. The manuscript does not report whether the predicted epitopes that were removed or retained correspond to the actual T cell epitopes recognized in the mouse experiments. This is a critical validation step for the computational predictions. Why it matters NetMHCpan predictions are imperfect, and the success of the approach depends on the accuracy of these predictions for the specific protein and alleles tested. Without epitope-level validation, it is unclear whether the reduced immunogenicity results from successful epitope removal or from other unintended consequences of the sequence changes. Resolution test Perform epitope mapping studies (e.g., overlapping peptide libraries) to identify the actual T cell epitopes recognized in immunized mice. Compare these to the predicted epitopes that were targeted for removal. Report the concordance between predictions and experimental epitope identification. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Abstract Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The abstract states "efficiently tune protein immunogenicity" but the efficiency is not quantified anywhere in the provided text. The term "efficiently" is vague and could be interpreted as computational efficiency, experimental success rate, or both. Required correction Specify what is meant by "efficiently" or remove the qualifier. If computational efficiency is meant, provide runtime or cost metrics in the abstract or main text. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Statistical reporting Affected element In vivo experiments Evidence pointer Figures 2C, 2D; location not provided Issue No information is provided on the number of biological replicates, the statistical tests used, or the criteria for significance in the in vivo experiments. Required correction Include sample sizes, statistical methods, and significance thresholds in the figure legends or methods. Report exact p-values or confidence intervals for key comparisons. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element "deimmunized" and "immunized" variants Evidence pointer Methods section; location not provided Issue The terms "deimmunized" and "immunized" are used to describe the designed variants, but the criteria for these classifications are not explicitly defined. It is unclear whether these terms refer to predicted epitope counts, experimental immunogenicity, or both. Required correction Define these terms explicitly in the methods or results section. Clarify whether they are based on computational predictions, experimental measurements, or a combination. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Benchmarking Evidence pointer Benchmarking section; location not provided Issue The benchmarking section mentions comparison between non-cycling and cycling methods but does not report the results of this comparison in the provided text. The claim of improved efficiency is not supported by data. Required correction Report the benchmarking results, including computational cost, success rate, and final immunogenicity scores for both methods. If the comparison is shown in a figure, reference it explicitly and summarize the key findings in the text. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Experimental design Affected element Mouse strain choice Evidence pointer Mice and immunization section; location not provided Issue The manuscript uses C57BL/6N mice, which express H-2b MHC haplotypes. The choice of 5 mouse alleles for design is not justified in the context of the mouse strain used. It is unclear whether the designed alleles match the H-2b haplotype. Required correction Clarify the relationship between the mouse alleles used for design and the H-2b haplotype of C57BL/6N mice. If the designed alleles do not match, explain the rationale for the chosen alleles. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Computational code Evidence pointer Methods section; location not provided Issue No information is provided on code availability, software versions, or computational environment. This limits reproducibility of the computational pipeline. Required correction Provide a statement on code availability, including repository links, software versions, and any custom scripts used. Consider depositing the MINT pipeline in a public repository. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established 1) Absence of quantitative in vivo data supporting the central immunogenicity claim (R1-M1). 2) Lack of quantitative functional data for designed variants (R1-M2). 3) Incomplete specification of the computational algorithm and parameters (R1-M3). 4) No validation of predicted epitopes against experimentally identified T cell epitopes (R1-M5). 5) Benchmarking results not reported in the provided text (R1-m4). Risk / unsupported claims The claim that CD8⁺ T cell immunogenicity can be "systematically modulated" is not supported by the provided data, as no quantitative immunogenicity measurements are presented. The claim of "function-preserving" design is only weakly supported by a single functional assay (luciferase activity) with no quantitative data shown. The claim that MINT is "broadly applicable" to therapeutic proteins is speculative, as only one protein was tested. The claim of computational efficiency improvements from caching and other optimizations is not supported by benchmarking data in the provided text. The statement that "variants designed to include multiple epitopes induced robust responses" implies a positive control for immunogenicity, but the design rationale for these variants and their relationship to the low-epitope variants is not fully explained. The generalizability of the approach to human MHC alleles is based on computational predictions only, with no experimental validation in humanized models or human cells. The manuscript does not address potential off-target effects of the sequence modifications, such as altered protein stability, aggregation propensity, or changes in post-translational modification sites. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The concept of integrating structure-based protein design with immunogenicity prediction is not entirely novel, as the authors acknowledge prior work using ProteinMPNN for deimmunization. However, the systematic framework (MINT) with iterative optimization, multi-allele coverage, and in vivo validation represents a meaningful advance. The "5+1" fusion design for comparative immunogenicity assessment is a creative experimental approach. The originality is moderate to good, but the field is competitive and the incremental advance over prior work needs to be clearly articulated. Scientific importance The problem addressed is clinically important, as immunogenicity of therapeutic proteins is a major barrier to adoptive cell therapy. A reliable computational method for reducing immunogenicity while preserving function would have significant translational value. However, the importance is somewhat diminished by the limited experimental validation presented and the focus on a single model protein. The potential impact on the field is high if the method proves generalizable, but this is not yet established. Interdisciplinary readership The work bridges computational protein design, immunology, and cell therapy, which could attract readers from multiple disciplines. The conceptual framework is accessible, but the methods section is highly technical and may be challenging for non-specialists. The clinical relevance to adoptive cell therapy provides a compelling hook for a broad audience. The interdisciplinary appeal is good but could be strengthened by clearer explanations of the immunology concepts for computational readers and vice versa. Technical soundness The computational approach is based on established tools (ProteinMPNN, NetMHCpan4.1, AF3) and the algorithmic logic is reasonable. However, the incomplete specification of the algorithm, missing parameters, and absence of benchmarking data prevent a full assessment of technical soundness. The in vivo experimental design is appropriate, but the lack of quantitative data is a significant concern. The functional assay (luciferase activity) is straightforward but limited in scope. Readability for nonspecialists The abstract and introduction are clearly written and accessible. The main text is generally readable, but the methods section assumes significant expertise in both computational protein design and immunology. The discussion effectively contextualizes the work for a broad audience. The manuscript would benefit from a figure summarizing the MINT workflow in a visually accessible manner. Overall readability is adequate but could be improved with additional context for non-specialist readers. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The conceptual framework is promising and the experimental approach is well-designed, but the current manuscript does not provide sufficient evidence to establish the central claims. The authors must provide quantitative in vivo data, complete functional characterization, full algorithmic specifications, and benchmarking results. If these concerns are addressed, the work could make a valuable contribution to the field. However, as presented, the case is not fully established from the provided evidence.

在约 70% 癌症中表达异常，是重要治疗靶点；但小分子 STAT3 抑制剂临床试验失败率高，SH2 结构域在 STAT 家族中高度保守导致选择性差，DNA-binding 结构域表面大而平坦、干扰后可能影响必需基因转录。因此需要替代模态（如蛋白 binder）。 现有方法为何不足 ：小分子抑制剂选择性差、临床失败率高；SH2 与 DNA-binding 结构域各自存在成药性障碍（正文 Introduction 引 [1][4]）。 精确研究问题（Can ... ?） ：Can BindCraft design de novo miniproteins that, according to AlphaFold3 predictions, bind at or near user-specified STAT3 hotspot residues with ipTM ≥ 0.75 and pLDDT ≥ 90 over ≥ 85% of the complex, while being sequence-novel by BLASTp? 04 背景与发展脉络 声明：以下脉络为「仅本文框架」 ——本文 Introduction 只给出极简背景（STAT3 生物学 + 小分子失败），未系统综述 binder 设计方法史；下列阶段划分中，除本文明确引用者外，其余为 (Abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusion, Author Contributions, Declaration of Competing Interest, Acknowledgments). Figures and Tables are referenced but not supplied as visual content. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the supplied text. No figure images, table contents, sequence data, PAE plots, or BLASTp outputs were provided for independent inspection. No experimental data are reported. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors claim that BindCraft was used to design de novo miniprotein binders against seven selected hotspots spanning the SH2, linker, DNA-binding, and coiled-coil domains of STAT3; that 11 designs from five hotspots met a high-confidence AlphaFold3 (AF3) threshold (ipTM >= 0.75, pLDDT >= 90 for most of the complex); that these binders are predicted to dock with their intended domain and mostly within 4.5 Angstrom of at least one targeted hotspot residue; that some binder pairs are predicted to dock simultaneously without overlap and could support a sandwich assay format; and that BLASTp indicates the sequences are novel. Visible evidence base Narrative description of the computational workflow, parameter changes, hotspot selection criteria, scoring thresholds, and summarized results. All quantitative support resides in Tables 1 through 6 and Figures 1 through 6, none of which are supplied in inspectable form. No experimental binding, affinity, specificity, or functional data are presented. Missing materials affecting confidence Figure 1 (workflow), Figure 3 (AF3 models of all 11 binders), Figure 4 (simultaneous docking), Figure 5 (PAE plots), Figure 6 (numbering guide), Table 1 (BindCraft parameters), Table 2 (pipeline yield), Table 3 (ipTM values and sequences), Table 4 (BLASTp results), Table 5 (interface and overlap analysis), Table 6 (hotspot function and numbering). Absence of these prevents verification of essentially every quantitative claim. Reviewer Overall assessment This is a purely computational design report that generates and ranks minibinder candidates against STAT3 using BindCraft and AlphaFold3, with no experimental validation. The workflow is described clearly and the authors are explicit about the absence of wet-lab data. However, the central claims rest entirely on predicted confidence metrics (ipTM, pLDDT, PAE) that are not measures of binding, and the manuscript itself acknowledges this. The evidence base as supplied is insufficient to establish that any of the 11 candidates binds STAT3, that they engage the intended hotspots, or that the sandwich-assay proposal is physically realizable. The work is best characterized as a hypothesis-generating sequence disclosure rather than an established result. Several methodological choices (threshold selection, single-seed AF3 evaluation, structural superposition to construct a ternary model, BLASTp parameters) require clarification before even the computational claims can be assessed. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in computational protein design and de novo binder engineering, particularly those working with BindCraft, RFdiffusion, and AlphaFold-based scoring pipelines, may find the reported yield statistics and hotspot-selection heuristics of practical interest. Groups working on STAT3 as an oncology target and on peptide or miniprotein inhibitors of transcription factors may be interested in the disclosed sequences as starting points for experimental screening. The sandwich-assay concept, if validated, would interest assay-development groups. Because no experimental validation is presented, the immediate audience is limited to those who would independently test the designs. Major strengths The manuscript is transparent about its limitations, explicitly stating that no experimental validation was performed and that ipTM does not translate to affinity. The hotspot-selection criteria are stated concretely (three residues, within 10 Angstrom C-alpha distance, at least two hydrophobic residues, partial surface exposure, preference for secondary structure), which makes the design rationale reproducible in principle. The decision to report the negative preliminary RFdiffusion/ProteinMPNN/AF2 results for hotspots 1 through 3 is a useful disclosure. The authors provide a numbering crosswalk between AFS and PDB 6NJS schemes, which is a genuine practical contribution for anyone attempting to reproduce or extend the work. The distinction between interface contact (within 4.5 Angstrom) and visual coverage is thoughtfully discussed, and the authors note the two measures often disagree rather than collapsing them into a single favorable metric. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidentiary support for the central claim Claim pointer The manuscript claims that 11 high-confidence minibinders were designed that bind STAT3 at or near the input hotspot residues, and that these constitute promising leads for therapeutic development. Evidence pointer Abstract, Section 3.1, Section 3.2, Table 3, Figure 3, location not provided for the underlying data Concern The entire claim of binding rests on AlphaFold3 confidence metrics (ipTM, pLDDT, PAE) with no experimental binding, affinity, or specificity measurement. The authors themselves state in Section 4.3 that AF3 ipTM does not translate directly to a binding constant. AlphaFold-class models are known to produce plausible interfaces for non-binding pairs, and ipTM is a self-consistency score rather than an affinity predictor. No negative controls (for example, designed binders against an unrelated surface, or STAT3 against an unrelated miniprotein) are reported to calibrate what an ipTM of 0.75 to 0.93 means in this specific system. Why it matters The central claim of the paper is that these are STAT3 binders. Without experimental validation or at minimum a calibration of the scoring metric against known binders and non-binders, the claim is not established. The therapeutic framing in the Abstract and Conclusion amplifies a claim the evidence cannot support. Resolution test Provide experimental binding data (for example, SPR, BLI, ITC, or pull-down) for at least a subset of the 11 candidates, or provide a calibration showing that the AF3 ipTM threshold used separates known STAT3 binders from known non-binders in this system. Alternatively, substantially soften the claim throughout to "computationally predicted candidate binders requiring experimental validation" and remove therapeutic-lead framing. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Target engagement and hotspot specificity Claim pointer The manuscript claims that most binders dock within 4.5 Angstrom of one or more targeted hotspot residues and that all 11 cover their intended domain. Evidence pointer Section 3.5, Table 5, Figure 3, location not provided Concern The reported results show that only 4 of 11 binders visually cover all their input hotspot residues, 2 cover none, and one binder (Hotspot4b_l77_s720724) has no hotspot residue among its interface residues at all. The authors acknowledge that the two measures of docking location often disagree. Yet the Abstract states that "most" binders dock within 4.5 Angstrom of one or more targeted hotspot residues, which is technically true but obscures that hotspot engagement is partial or absent for a majority of candidates. The claim that all 11 cover their intended domain is based on AF3 predictions that have not been experimentally verified, and domain-level coverage is a much weaker statement than hotspot engagement. Why it matters The design intent was site-specific targeting. If binders do not engage the intended hotspot, the rationale for selecting those hotspots (biological function, druggability) does not carry over to the binders. The discrepancy between interface contact and visual coverage also raises the question of which metric, if either, is meaningful for a predicted model. Resolution test Report per-binder hotspot engagement with explicit counts and clearly separate the two metrics in the main text rather than only in table notes. State plainly how many binders engage all, some, or none of their intended hotspot residues. If hotspot engagement is the design goal, explain why binders that fail it are retained as top candidates. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Validity of the sandwich-assay claim Claim pointer The manuscript claims that several minibinders are predicted to dock simultaneously to STAT3 without overlap and that such pairs have the potential to constitute STAT3 sandwich assays. Evidence pointer Section 2.6, Section 3.2, Figure 4, location not provided Concern The simultaneous docking model was not generated by predicting a ternary complex. The authors explicitly state in Section 2.6 that they declined to submit the ternary complex to AF3 because the tool would distort folds, and instead superimposed two independently predicted binary models in ChimeraX. This is a structural alignment of two separately predicted poses, not a prediction or measurement of simultaneous binding. There is no energetic or steric assessment of whether both binders can occupy the surface at once, no consideration of linker geometry for an assay format, and no experimental demonstration of simultaneous binding. Why it matters The sandwich-assay proposal is presented as a potential application and is one of the more distinctive claims of the paper. It rests on a superposition that cannot establish co-occupancy. Presenting it as a candidate format without this caveat in the Abstract overstates what the modeling supports. Resolution test Either perform an actual ternary complex prediction with an appropriate tool and report the result, or provide a quantitative steric and energetic argument for co-occupancy, or explicitly reframe the sandwich-assay statement as a speculative hypothesis contingent on experimental demonstration of simultaneous binding. The Abstract should not present it as a supported outcome. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility of the design and scoring pipeline Claim pointer The manuscript reports specific BindCraft parameter modifications and AF3 thresholds that define the high-confidence set. Evidence pointer Section 2.3, Section 2.4, Table 1, location not provided Concern The parameter changes are described (weights_con_inter raised from 1.0 to 2.0, inter_contact_distance reduced from 20 to 10 Angstrom, inter_contact_number revised from 2 to 3), but the full parameter set is deferred to Table 1, which is not supplied. The rationale for the specific AF3 thresholds (ipTM >= 0.75, pLDDT >= 90 for >= 85% of the complex) is not justified against any benchmark. The pLDDT criterion is described as determined by visual inspection of the ribbon structure, which is not a quantitative or reproducible criterion. The number of AF3 seeds or recycles is not stated. Whether the reported ipTM values are from a single prediction or an average is not stated. Why it matters Without the full parameter set and a stated, reproducible scoring protocol, independent groups cannot reproduce the design campaign or the selection of the 11 candidates. The visual pLDDT assessment in particular is a subjective step embedded in a quantitative selection pipeline. Resolution test Provide the complete BindCraft parameter set, state the AF3 run configuration (seeds, recycles, model version), replace the visual pLDDT assessment with a quantitative per-residue criterion and report the fraction of residues meeting it, and justify the chosen thresholds against a benchmark or a sensitivity analysis. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Novelty assessment methodology Claim pointer The manuscript claims that BLASTp found no matches for six binders and only very low-significance matches for the other five, suggesting the sequences are novel and not chimeras of known proteins. Evidence pointer Section 2.7, Section 3.4, Table 4, location not provided Concern The BLASTp parameters include an E-value cutoff threshold of 10, which is unusually permissive for a novelty assessment, and a seed word size of 5, which is short and increases sensitivity to spurious short matches. The significance threshold for interpreting matches is stated separately as 10^-5 in Section 3.4, which creates an inconsistency between the search parameter and the interpretation threshold. The claim of "absolute novelty" in the Conclusion is stronger than a BLASTp search can support, since BLASTp detects sequence similarity, not structural or functional novelty, and does not exclude the possibility that a designed sequence adopts a known fold or engages an off-target partner. Why it matters The novelty claim is one of the stated hypotheses of the paper. If the search parameters are not appropriate or the interpretation threshold is inconsistent with the search threshold, the novelty conclusion is weakened. "Absolute novelty" is not a claim BLASTp can establish. Resolution test Justify the E-value cutoff of 10 and the word size of 5, or rerun with standard parameters and report both. Reconcile the search threshold with the interpretation threshold. Replace "absolutely novel" with a precise statement of what the search does and does not establish. Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Specificity and off-target risk Claim pointer The manuscript presents the binders as candidates for targeting STAT3, with the SH2 domain noted as highly conserved among STAT proteins. Evidence pointer Section 1, Section 4.3, location not provided Concern The authors acknowledge in Section 4.3 that they did not investigate binding specificity against other proteins and that evaluating interaction with other STAT proteins would be instructive. Given that the SH2 domain is explicitly described in the Introduction as highly conserved among STAT proteins, and that several binders target the SH2 domain or adjacent regions, the absence of any specificity analysis is a substantive gap. No computational cross-reactivity screen against other STAT family members or against the human proteome is reported. Why it matters Selectivity is a central concern for STAT3-targeting therapeutics, as the Introduction itself notes. A binder that engages STAT3 but also engages STAT1, STAT5, or other conserved surfaces would not address the stated limitation of existing small-molecule inhibitors. Resolution test Perform a computational specificity screen, at minimum docking or AF3 evaluation against other STAT family members and ideally against a broader set of human proteins, and report the results. If specificity is not assessed, remove or substantially qualify any implication that these binders address the selectivity problem noted in the Introduction. Required correction Standardize all binder identifiers to a single format throughout the text and tables, and correct the garbled phrase in Section 4.2. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Numerical consistency Affected element Reported ipTM ranges Evidence pointer Section 3.1 Issue The text states BindCraft ipTM values range from 0.81 to 0.94 and AF3 ipTM values range from 0.75 to 0.93. It is not stated whether these are per-binder single values or ranges across multiple predictions, and the relationship between the BindCraft (AF2) ipTM and the AF3 ipTM for the same binder is not discussed. Required correction State whether each reported value is a single prediction or an aggregate, and clarify the relationship between the two scoring stages. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Method description completeness Affected element AF3 evaluation protocol Evidence pointer Section 2.4 Issue The manuscript states that sequences were manually submitted to the AlphaFold Server but does not report the number of seeds, recycles, or the model version, nor whether any prediction was repeated. Required correction Report the AF3 run configuration and whether predictions were repeated or averaged. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Statistical interpretation Affected element BLASTp significance threshold Evidence pointer Section 2.7, Section 3.4 Issue The search uses an E-value cutoff of 10 while the interpretation uses a significance threshold of 10^-5. The two thresholds are not reconciled. Required correction Explain the relationship between the search cutoff and the interpretation threshold, or use a single consistent threshold. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Claim scope Affected element Conclusion wording Evidence pointer Section 5 Issue The Conclusion states the sequences "appear to be absolutely novel." "Absolutely" is not supportable by a BLASTp search. Required correction Replace with a precise statement of what the BLASTp results show, for example that no significant sequence similarity to known proteins was detected under the stated parameters. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Figure and table accessibility Affected element All figures and tables Evidence pointer Figures 1 through 6, Tables 1 through 6 Issue The supplied manuscript text references all figures and tables but none were provided in inspectable form, so the quantitative basis of every result could not be verified. Required correction Ensure all figures and tables are supplied with the manuscript, with legible labels and complete notes, and that Table 5 notes define both metrics unambiguously. Concern ID R1-m7 Severity Minor Axis Reference formatting Affected element In-text citations Evidence pointer Section 1, Section 2.8, Section 4.2 Issue Several citations appear with irregular spacing (for example "[ 1 ]", "[ 2 ]") and reference [20] is cited in Section 4.2 but the reference list was not supplied for verification. Required correction Standardize citation formatting and supply the full reference list. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (absence of experimental validation for the binding claim), R1-M2 (partial or absent hotspot engagement for a majority of candidates), R1-M3 (sandwich-assay claim rests on structural superposition rather than ternary prediction or measurement). R1-M4, R1-M5, and R1-M6 are non-blocking but must be resolved for the computational claims to be reproducible and for the specificity and novelty statements to be defensible. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality Moderate. The application of BindCraft to STAT3 is a new combination, and the disclosure of designed sequences against multiple STAT3 domains has some value as a community resource. However, the methodological approach (BindCraft design followed by AlphaFold3 rescoring) is an established pattern, and the manuscript does not introduce a new method, benchmark, or conceptual advance. The sandwich-assay idea is the most distinctive element but is not supported by the evidence presented. Scientific importance Currently limited. The work is hypothesis-generating and provides no experimental evidence that any candidate binds STAT3. The therapeutic framing in the Abstract and Conclusion is not matched by the evidence. Importance would increase substantially with even a small set of experimental binding measurements. Interdisciplinary readership Limited in the current form. The paper is addressed to computational design specialists. The biological and clinical framing suggests an intent to reach oncology and drug-development audiences, but without experimental data those readers have no basis to act on the results beyond treating the sequences as screening candidates. Technical soundness Partially sound but incomplete. The design pipeline is described with reasonable clarity, and the authors are candid about limitations. However, the scoring thresholds are not benchmarked, the pLDDT criterion is assessed visually, the AF3 run configuration is not reported, the BLASTp parameters are questionable and internally inconsistent, the ternary model is a superposition rather than a prediction, and no specificity analysis is performed. These are addressable but collectively they prevent the computational claims from being fully established. Readability for nonspecialists Reasonable. The Introduction provides adequate background on STAT3 and the motivation for targeting it. The Methods and Results are dense with tool-specific terminology (ipTM, pLDDT, PAE, BindCraft parameters) that is not always explained for a general audience. A brief glossary or expanded definitions at first use would help. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The computational workflow is described clearly enough to be potentially reproducible once the missing tables and parameters are supplied, and the authors are transparent about the absence of experimental validation. However, the central claims of binding, hotspot engagement, and sandwich-assay feasibility are not supported by the evidence presented, and the therapeutic framing exceeds what the data can bear. The manuscript would need experimental validation of at least a subset of candidates, or a substantial reframing as a purely computational candidate-disclosure report with all claims correspondingly qualified, before the case could be considered established. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the 11 designs are STAT3 binders is unsupported. Only predicted confidence metrics are reported, and the authors acknowledge these do not translate to binding. The claim that most binders dock within 4.5 Angstrom of a targeted hotspot residue is technically reported but obscures that only 4 of 11 visually cover all hotspot residues and 2 cover none. The claim that binder pairs could constitute STAT3 sandwich assays is unsupported. It rests on superposition of two independently predicted binary models, not on a ternary complex prediction or measurement. The claim that the sequences are "absolutely novel" is unsupported by BLASTp, which assesses sequence similarity only and cannot establish absolute novelty. The implication that these binders address the selectivity limitations of existing STAT3 inhibitors is unsupported, since no specificity analysis against other STAT proteins or off-targets was performed. The framing of the candidates as leads for preclinical drug development is unsupported by the absence of any experimental affinity, specificity, stability, or functional data. The pLDDT-based high-confidence criterion is not reproducible as described, since it depends on visual inspection of ribbon structures rather than a quantitative per-residue computation. The relationship between BindCraft (AF2) ipTM and AF3 ipTM for the same binder is not reported, so the incremental value of the AF3 rescoring step cannot be assessed.

manuscript claim summary The authors report functional and structural differences among three group-6 propane monooxygenases (PRMs) from distinct phylogenetic clusters, expressed heterologously in Mycolicibacterium smegmatis, and propose implications for propane-stimulated bioremediation of 1,4-dioxane. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no kinetic data, structural coordinates, phylogenetic trees, or experimental methods are provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, kinetic parameters, inhibition data, structural models, phylogenetic analyses, statistical details, and all figures/tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents a potentially valuable comparative study of group-6 PRMs with clear relevance to bioremediation. The central claim of functional divergence across phylogenetic clusters is plausible and interesting. However, the evidence base available for review is limited to the abstract, which precludes verification of quantitative claims, structural interpretations, and the strength of the phylogenetic and compositional analyses. The work appears technically sound in concept, but the case for the mechanistic conclusions is not fully established from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in environmental microbiology and bioremediation, particularly those working on emerging contaminants such as 1,4-dioxane, would find these results relevant. The study also speaks to enzymologists interested in monooxygenase structure-function relationships and to practitioners developing biostimulation strategies for contaminated sites. Major strengths The study addresses a clear knowledge gap regarding functional differences among group-6 PRMs. The use of heterologous expression in a defined host is a rigorous approach for comparing enzyme properties. The integration of kinetic, inhibition, and structural analyses is commendable. The potential practical relevance for propane-based biostimulation is well articulated. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The abstract claims that "variation in substrate affinity and catalytic turnover is consistent with differences in active-site pocket hydrophobicity, rigidity, and catalytic geometry." Evidence pointer Location not provided Concern The structural interpretation is presented as a key mechanistic conclusion, but no structural data, computational models, or experimental validation are described in the abstract. It is unclear whether these are based on solved crystal structures, homology models, or molecular dynamics simulations, and whether the inferred properties were quantitatively tested. Why it matters Without details on how the structural features were determined and how they correlate with the kinetic data, the mechanistic claim remains speculative. This is central to the paper's contribution beyond a descriptive comparison. Resolution test Provide the structural evidence, including model quality metrics or experimental structures, and a quantitative or statistical demonstration that the proposed structural features correlate with the observed kinetic differences. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency Claim pointer The abstract states that "phylogenetic and compositional analyses further suggested horizontal transfer in Clusters I and III." Evidence pointer Location not provided Concern The basis for inferring horizontal gene transfer is not described. It is unclear what compositional analyses were performed, what statistical support was obtained, and how alternative explanations such as gene duplication or differential loss were excluded. Why it matters This claim extends the study's significance to evolutionary biology, but without methodological detail and statistical support, it cannot be evaluated. Overinterpretation of phylogenetic signals is a common pitfall. Resolution test Describe the phylogenetic and compositional methods, report support values, and provide a formal test for recombination or horizontal transfer with appropriate controls. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Quantitative rigor Claim pointer The abstract reports qualitative differences in substrate affinity, catalytic capacity, and inhibitor sensitivity among the three PRMs. Evidence pointer Location not provided Concern No kinetic parameters, error estimates, or statistical comparisons are provided. Terms such as "low affinity but high catalytic capacity" and "high affinity but lower capacity" are relative and lack quantitative context. Why it matters Without numerical values and statistical tests, the reader cannot assess the magnitude or significance of the reported differences, which are central to the paper's conclusions. Resolution test Report kinetic constants with replicates and statistical comparisons, and provide effect sizes for the differences described. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Terminology Evidence pointer Abstract, first sentence Issue The term "propane monooxygenases" is used without specifying the enzyme family or subunit composition, which may confuse readers unfamiliar with group-6 PRMs. Required correction Define the enzyme class and subunit architecture at first mention, or provide a brief contextual description. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Strain selection rationale Evidence pointer Abstract, methods description Issue The choice of the three representative PRMs is stated but the rationale for selecting these specific strains is not explained. Required correction Briefly justify why these three PRMs are representative of their respective clusters and how they were chosen. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Interpretation Affected element Bioremediation implications Evidence pointer Abstract, final sentence Issue The claim that the results "offer mechanistic insights for optimizing microbial populations" is broad and not directly supported by the data described. Required correction Soften the claim or specify which mechanistic insights would directly inform optimization strategies. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 and R1-M2 are blocking because the structural and evolutionary claims are central to the paper's novelty and cannot be evaluated from the abstract. R1-M3, while not blocking, requires quantitative support for the core comparative claims. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The comparative approach across phylogenetic clusters is a useful contribution, though not unprecedented. Scientific importance: The topic is relevant to environmental biotechnology, but the significance is moderate and applied rather than fundamental. Interdisciplinary readership: The work will appeal primarily to environmental microbiologists and bioremediation specialists, with limited reach beyond these fields. Technical soundness: The experimental design appears reasonable, but the available evidence is insufficient to fully assess rigor. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is accessible, though some terminology could be clarified. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The core comparative kinetic study is promising, but the structural and evolutionary claims require substantial additional evidence. The manuscript may be better suited to a specialized environmental microbiology or biotechnology journal than to a broad high-impact venue. Risk / unsupported claims The structural interpretation linking active-site properties to kinetic differences is unsupported without structural data or models. The inference of horizontal gene transfer is unsupported without phylogenetic and compositional methodological details. The relative kinetic and inhibition differences are unquantified and cannot be assessed for significance. The practical implications for optimizing bioremediation are stated without direct experimental evidence.

Assessment boundary Evaluation is restricted to the abstract text and the bibliographic metadata provided. No full text, figures, tables, methods, supplementary information, or source data were available. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report a predictive workflow that couples all-atom molecular dynamics to locate mechanical soft spots, AlphaFold3 to assess feasibility of engineered metal-chelating sites, and single-molecule force spectroscopy to validate designs. Applied to two AI-designed mechanostable beta-sheet proteins from the SuperMyo series, Ni2+ coordination is claimed to yield site-dependent reinforcement, cumulative reinforcement when sites are combined, a triple-site variant with more than 110 percent gain in unfolding force, and an unfolding force above 400 pN. Visible evidence base Abstract-level statements only. No numerical distributions, replicate counts, force-loading rates, pulling geometries, ion concentrations, control constructs, structural models, or statistical tests are visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Full text, figures, tables, methods, statistics, AlphaFold3 confidence metrics, MD trajectories and force profiles, experimental force histograms, construct sequences and design coordinates, and any independent validation or negative controls. Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a conceptually coherent closed-loop strategy that links computational soft-spot identification, AI-based structural feasibility screening, and single-molecule force validation. The problem framing, namely that metal coordination has been incorporated largely empirically, is reasonable and the proposed workflow is potentially useful. However, the supplied material is an abstract only, and every quantitative and mechanistic claim is unverifiable at this level. The central assertion of predictive capability cannot be distinguished from post hoc selection of successful sites, and the reported reinforcement magnitudes lack the methodological and statistical context needed for assessment. The work is interesting in principle but currently not established from the provided evidence. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein engineering and de novo design, mechanobiology and single-molecule biophysics, computational chemistry and molecular dynamics, and groups using AlphaFold-family models for design triage. If substantiated, the workflow would interest those seeking programmable routes to tune mechanical stability in beta-sheet scaffolds, and those developing mechanostable proteins for materials or nanomechanical applications. Major strengths The abstract identifies a genuine gap, namely the absence of a rational method for choosing reinforcement sites in engineered proteins. The proposed combination of MD-derived soft-spot mapping, AF3-based feasibility assessment, and single-molecule force spectroscopy is a sensible closed-loop architecture. The reported site-dependent and cumulative effects, if supported, would be a useful demonstration that reinforcement is tunable rather than binary. The use of previously AI-designed SuperMyo scaffolds provides a defined starting point for comparison. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Predictive validity Claim pointer The workflow is described as predictive, with MD identifying mechanical soft spots and AF3 assessing structural feasibility of engineered metal-chelating sites. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern No information is given on how predictions were made before experiments, whether predicted sites were tested blindly, how many candidate sites were proposed versus tested, or what the hit rate was. Without a prospective design-test cycle, the claim of prediction cannot be separated from retrospective rationalization of sites that happened to work. Why it matters The central novelty claim is predictive capability. If site selection was informed by experimental outcomes or by trial and error, the methodological advance is not demonstrated. Resolution test Provide the prospective prediction set, the ranking or scoring rule, the number of candidates tested, the number of successes and failures, and a comparison against a naive or random site-selection baseline. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness of mechanical measurements Claim pointer Single-site variants produce substantial increases in unfolding force, and a triple-site variant achieves more than 110 percent gain with unfolding force exceeding 400 pN. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern No experimental parameters are reported, including loading rate, pulling geometry, linker and handle design, number of molecules, force distributions, or the model used to extract unfolding forces. Unfolding force in single-molecule pulling is strongly loading-rate dependent, so a bare force value cannot be interpreted or compared across constructs. Why it matters The quantitative reinforcement claims are the principal experimental support for the workflow. Without loading-rate context and distribution-level statistics, the reported gains are not evaluable. Resolution test Report force distributions with replicate counts, loading rates, pulling geometry, and the kinetic model used, and show that comparisons across variants were made at matched loading rates. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Causal attribution to metal coordination Claim pointer Ni2+ coordination produces site-dependent reinforcement and cumulative reinforcement when multiple sites are combined. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern The abstract does not state whether metal-free controls, non-coordinating mutant controls, or alternative-metal controls were performed. It also does not address whether the added chelating residues themselves, rather than the coordination bond, alter folding, stability, or the unfolding pathway. Why it matters Reinforcement is attributed specifically to metal coordination. Without appropriate controls, the effect could arise from sequence perturbation, altered local structure, or changes in unfolding pathway rather than from the coordination bond. Resolution test Include apo-state and non-coordinating-mutant controls under identical conditions, plus metal titration or competition experiments, and show that reinforcement tracks occupancy of the designed site. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Structural feasibility assessment Claim pointer AlphaFold3 was used to assess the structural feasibility of engineered metal-chelating sites. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern It is not stated how AF3 outputs were converted into a feasibility decision, whether metal ions and coordination geometry were modeled explicitly, what confidence metrics were used, or whether AF3 predictions agreed with any experimental structure or spectroscopic evidence of coordination geometry. Why it matters AF3 is used here as a design filter. Without a defined decision rule and validation of predicted coordination geometry, the role of AF3 in the workflow is not assessable. Resolution test Specify the AF3 protocol, input composition, scoring or threshold used, and provide structural or spectroscopic validation of at least one designed coordination site. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generality and scope Claim pointer The workflow enables systematic tuning of mechanical properties in beta-sheet protein scaffolds. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern The demonstration is limited to two related SuperMyo scaffolds. The abstract does not establish whether the approach transfers to unrelated beta-sheet folds, to alpha-helical or mixed folds, or to proteins with different mechanical topologies. Why it matters The generality claim extends beyond the tested system. Overreach here would misrepresent the scope of the method. Resolution test Either demonstrate application to at least one unrelated scaffold or restrict the generality claim to the SuperMyo series and state the boundary explicitly. Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Additivity mechanism Claim pointer Combining multiple coordination sites produced cumulative reinforcement. Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Concern Cumulative reinforcement is asserted without evidence on whether the combined effect is additive, synergistic, or saturating, and without evidence on whether multiple sites act on the same or distinct unfolding barriers. Why it matters The claim of cumulative reinforcement implies a specific mechanical model. Without per-site and combined quantification, the additivity statement is descriptive rather than mechanistic. Resolution test Report single-site, double-site, and triple-site values with uncertainties and test whether the combined effect deviates from the sum of individual contributions. Issue Mechanostable is used without definition or a stated quantitative criterion. Required correction Define the metric and threshold used to classify a construct as mechanostable. Issue A greater than 110 percent gain is reported without a baseline value, uncertainty, or sample size. Required correction Report baseline and variant values with uncertainties and replicate counts. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Experimental conditions Affected element Ni2+ coordination conditions Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Issue Ion concentration, buffer, pH, and incubation conditions are not stated. Required correction State the coordination conditions and confirm they are consistent across all constructs. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Nomenclature Affected element SuperMyo series description Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Issue The two SuperMyo proteins are not identified, and their prior design provenance is only briefly referenced. Required correction Identify the specific scaffolds and cite their design origin. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Claim scope Affected element Closed-loop characterization Evidence pointer Abstract only; location not provided. Issue The workflow is described as closed-loop, but the abstract does not indicate whether predictions were iterated or fed back into redesign. Required correction Clarify whether any design cycle was repeated based on experimental feedback. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3. These concern prospective predictive validation, loading-rate-resolved mechanical measurement, and control-based causal attribution to metal coordination. R1-M4, R1-M5, and R1-M6 further limit confidence in the AF3 decision rule, the generality claim, and the additivity claim. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is moderate to potentially high, since the individual components are established but their integration into a predictive reinforcement workflow is a plausible advance. Scientific importance is currently unproven because the predictive claim and the reinforcement magnitudes cannot be evaluated from the abstract. Interdisciplinary readership is plausible, spanning protein design, biophysics, and computational modeling, though the abstract does not yet demonstrate results of broad enough scope to compel a wide audience. Technical soundness is not established, as no methods, statistics, controls, or distributions are visible. Readability for nonspecialists is adequate at the abstract level, but the absence of defined metrics and conditions limits interpretation even for specialist readers. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. Supportive if technical concerns are resolved, in particular prospective prediction validation, loading-rate-resolved force measurements with controls, and a defined AF3 decision rule. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of predictive site identification is unsupported at the abstract level, since no prospective prediction set, scoring rule, or hit rate is provided. The claim that Ni2+ coordination causes reinforcement is unsupported without apo, non-coordinating mutant, or metal-substitution controls. The reported greater than 110 percent gain and unfolding force above 400 pN are not evaluable without loading rate, distributions, replicate counts, and uncertainties. The claim of cumulative reinforcement is not supported by per-site and combined quantification or by a test of additivity. The claim that the workflow enables systematic tuning across beta-sheet scaffolds is not supported beyond two related SuperMyo proteins. The role of AlphaFold3 as a feasibility filter is not assessable without a stated protocol, scoring rule, and structural or spectroscopic validation. The characterization of the strategy as closed-loop is not supported without evidence of iterative design feedback.

Input scope Abstract only, as supplied in the manuscript record Assessment boundary Evaluation is restricted to the claims and evidence visible in the abstract. No full text, figures, tables, methods, statistics, or supplementary materials were provided, so mechanistic, structural, and quantitative assertions cannot be independently verified. Shared manuscript claim summary The three human YTHDF proteins share an essentially identical m6A-RNA binding mode that requires rare protonation of m6A and a similar open-closed recognition-loop switch, yet they differ in recognition-loop flexibility and conformational preference; only YTHDF1 homodimerizes, and homodimerization prevents m6A-RNA binding; a hybrid model is proposed to reconcile the redundancy versus specificity debate. Visible evidence base Abstract-level statements referencing mutagenesis, X-ray crystallography, isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), and molecular dynamics simulations. No data values, structure identifiers, resolution limits, sample sizes, error estimates, or statistical tests are visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Full text, all figures and tables, methods, simulation parameters and force fields, crystallographic statistics, ITC raw and fitted data, mutagenesis validation, replicate information, and any supplementary material. Location not provided for every quantitative or structural claim. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a genuinely interesting and timely question, namely how highly homologous m6A reader proteins can combine near-identical binding chemistry with reported functional differentiation. The proposed hybrid model is conceptually attractive and the multi-method strategy is appropriate in principle. However, from the supplied material the central mechanistic claims are not established. The abstract asserts a protonation-dependent binding mode, a shared open-closed switch, protein-specific recognition-loop flexibility, and a homodimerization-dependent block of RNA binding, but no quantitative, structural, or statistical support is visible. The work is potentially publishable if the technical concerns below are resolved with explicit data. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in RNA epigenetics and m6A biology, structural and computational biophysicists studying protein-RNA recognition, and groups working on YTH domain function and reader-protein specificity. The results would also interest those modeling protonation-coupled or conformational-selection binding mechanisms, and scientists trying to reconcile redundancy versus specificity in paralogous protein families. Major strengths The question is well motivated and targets a real tension in the literature. The combination of experimental biophysics with molecular dynamics is a sensible way to connect structure, energetics, and dynamics. The explicit proposal of a hybrid model, together with a stated discussion of limitations and validation experiments, is a constructive framing. Comparing binding capacity, conformational change, and homodimerization within one study is a coherent design. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Mechanistic claim support Claim pointer Binding of m6A-RNA requires rare protonation of m6A. Evidence pointer Abstract statement only; location not provided Concern The claim of a protonation-dependent binding mode is asserted without any visible pKa estimate, protonation-state analysis, pH-dependent measurement, or computational free-energy support. It is unclear whether this is inferred from simulations, from ITC at a single pH, or from structural interpretation. Why it matters A rare protonation event would be a central mechanistic determinant and would need to be quantitatively consistent with measured affinities and with physiological pH. Without this, the shared binding-mode conclusion is not substantiated. Resolution test Provide pH-dependent binding data or computed protonation free energies, report the relevant pKa values with uncertainty, and show that the proposed protonated state is populated enough to account for the measured affinities. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Structural evidence Claim pointer The YTHDF proteins share an identical binding mode of m6A-RNA and a similar open-closed recognition-loop switch. Evidence pointer Abstract statement referencing X-ray crystallography; location not provided Concern No crystal structures, resolution, refinement statistics, electron density for the methylated base, or conformational states are shown. The assertion of identical binding mode and a shared switch cannot be evaluated without structural detail and without specifying which states were captured. Why it matters The identity of binding mode is the foundation for the redundancy argument. If the structures sample different loop states or lack clear m6A density, the claim is unsupported. Resolution test Present structures with data collection and refinement statistics, show electron density or omit maps for m6A and the recognition loop, and classify the observed loop conformations across the three proteins. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Quantitative support Claim pointer ITC data and crystal structures provide consistent evidence that the YTHDF proteins differ significantly in recognition-loop flexibility and conformational preferences. Evidence pointer Abstract statement referencing ITC and crystallography; location not provided Concern No ITC values, stoichiometries, dissociation constants, enthalpies, entropies, or fit quality are visible, and no measure of flexibility is defined. The word significantly is used without a statistical basis. Why it matters The distinction between shared and distinct features rests on these comparisons. Without numbers and uncertainty, the differential-flexibility claim is not testable. Resolution test Report ITC parameters with errors and replicate counts, define the flexibility metric, and provide a statistical comparison across YTHDF1-3. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Functional claim support Claim pointer Only YTHDF1 can homodimerize, which prevents binding to m6A-RNA. Evidence pointer Abstract statement; location not provided Concern The homodimerization claim and its proposed inhibitory effect on RNA binding are stated without visible oligomeric-state data, interface characterization, or a binding assay distinguishing monomer from dimer. The causal direction is asserted rather than demonstrated. Why it matters This is one of the few concrete specificity mechanisms proposed. If dimerization is not quantified or if the RNA-binding block is not separated from other effects, the hybrid model loses a key pillar. Resolution test Provide oligomeric-state measurements, identify the dimer interface, and show directly that dimerization state controls m6A-RNA binding, for example by interface mutation or concentration-dependent binding. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Computational methodology Claim pointer Molecular dynamics simulations are used to compare conformational changes and recognition-loop dynamics. Evidence pointer Abstract statement; location not provided Concern No simulation length, force field, water model, replicate count, or convergence assessment is visible. The reliability of dynamics-based conclusions about flexibility cannot be judged. Why it matters Loop flexibility and conformational preference are sensitive to sampling and force-field choice. Unconverged or single-replicate simulations would weaken the differential-flexibility claim. Resolution test Report simulation protocols, aggregate sampling per system, number of independent replicates, and convergence or uncertainty estimates for the reported observables. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Use of the term identical binding mode Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue Identical is a strong descriptor for a comparison across three proteins and is not operationally defined. Required correction Define the criteria for identical binding mode, for example shared hydrogen-bonding pattern, base stacking geometry, and comparable affinities within error. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Model framing Affected element Hybrid model reconciling redundancy and specificity Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue The model is described but its assumptions and predictive content are not stated in the visible material. Required correction State the model assumptions explicitly and list the predictions that distinguish it from the pure redundancy and pure specificity views. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Mutagenesis, ITC, crystallography, and simulation reporting Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue No construct boundaries, mutations, buffer and pH conditions, or software versions are visible. Required correction Provide construct details, experimental conditions, and software and force-field versions in the methods. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Scope of evidence Affected element Integration of available biophysical and biochemical evidence Evidence pointer Abstract; location not provided Issue It is unclear which prior evidence is integrated and how conflicts among sources are handled. Required correction Specify the sources integrated and the criteria used to weigh or reconcile them. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M4. These concern the protonation-dependent binding mechanism, the structural basis of the shared binding mode and loop switch, the quantitative basis for differential flexibility, and the homodimerization-dependent block of RNA binding. R1-M5 affects confidence in the dynamics claims and should be addressed for completeness. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is moderate to high, since the hybrid reconciliation of redundancy and specificity is a useful conceptual contribution if supported. Scientific importance is potentially significant for m6A biology, but it currently depends on unverified mechanistic claims. Interdisciplinary readership is plausible, spanning RNA biology, structural biology, and computation, though the abstract is written for a specialized audience. Technical soundness cannot be confirmed from the supplied material because no data, statistics, or methodological detail are visible. Readability for nonspecialists is limited, as terms such as recognition loop, open-closed switch, and rare protonation are used without explanation. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. Supportive if the technical concerns, in particular R1-M1 through R1-M4, are resolved with explicit quantitative, structural, and statistical support. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that m6A binding requires rare protonation of m6A is unsupported in the visible material, with no pKa, pH dependence, or free-energy evidence provided. The claim of an identical m6A-RNA binding mode across YTHDF1-3 is not verifiable without structures, density maps, and defined comparison criteria. The claim of a shared open-closed recognition-loop switch is not evaluable without conformational assignments and state populations. The claim that the proteins differ significantly in recognition-loop flexibility and conformational preferences is unsupported because no metric, values, or statistical test are visible. The claim that only YTHDF1 homodimerizes and that this prevents m6A-RNA binding is unsupported without oligomeric-state data, interface identification, and a direct binding test.
