No full text, figures, tables, schemes, supporting information, crystallographic data, NMR spectra, computational coordinates, or mutagenesis datasets were provided. Conclusions about internal validity, data quality, and reproducibility cannot be fully established. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report discovery and mechanistic characterization of a bacteria-derived sesquiterpene synthase, AceS, that converts farnesyl diphosphate to acorenol ether (1) through syn-protoetherification. They claim a unique 5/6 spiro-fused acorane skeleton with an ether ring bridging C3 and C7, elucidated by NMR and XRD of a cytochrome P450-modified derivative. Using deuterium-scanning labeling, they claim a 1,2-hydride shift from C10 to C11, a hydride shift from C6 to C10, and syn-stereochemistry of protoetherification. DFT calculations, structure-guided site-directed mutagenesis, product characterization of mutants, and protein-ligand docking are claimed to support cyclization through bisabolyl-dunnienyl cations as favored, with a carotenyl cation pathway also possible. Y186 is proposed to redirect water to trap the C7 carbocation and promote syn-protoetherification. Visible evidence base Abstract-level statements only. No primary data, spectra, structures, computational details, or statistics are visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Full text, experimental procedures, compound characterization, NMR assignments, XRD data and refinement, deuterium-scanning datasets, DFT methods and energetics, mutagenesis design and product profiles, docking protocols, sequence and phylogenetic context, enzyme kinetics, and controls. Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a potentially interesting enzyme discovery and mechanistic study on a bacterial sesquiterpene ether synthase. The central claims are mechanistically specific and testable, but the supplied material is insufficient to evaluate technical soundness. Key structural, stereochemical, and computational claims are asserted without visible supporting data. The work is not currently established from the provided evidence. Who would be interested in the results, and why Enzymologists and mechanistic biochemists studying terpene synthases, natural product chemists interested in ether-forming termination steps, synthetic and computational chemists modeling carbocation cascades, and biochemists engineering terpenoid biosynthesis. If supported, the results would inform the limited set of enzymes known to perform syn-protoetherification and expand the known acorane skeleton chemistry. Major strengths The abstract addresses a defined mechanistic gap in terpene synthase termination chemistry. The combination of isotopic labeling, DFT, mutagenesis, and docking is appropriate in principle for a mechanistic claim. The proposed role of Y186 as a water-directing residue is a concrete, testable hypothesis. The reported acorane ether scaffold, if fully characterized, would be a notable addition to sesquiterpene diversity. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Structural evidence Claim pointer The unique 5/6 spiro-fused acorane skeleton with an ether ring bridging C3 and C7 of compound 1 was elucidated based on NMR analysis and XRD of a cytochrome P450-modified derivative. Evidence pointer Abstract only; no figures, tables, or crystallographic data provided. location not provided. Concern The structural assignment of 1 rests on NMR and on XRD of a modified derivative rather than the native compound. The abstract does not state whether the P450 modification preserves the C3-C7 ether connectivity or the spiro ring system, nor does it provide crystallographic resolution, refinement statistics, or NMR assignment tables. Why it matters The entire mechanistic interpretation depends on the correct structure and connectivity of 1. If the derivative differs from 1 at the ether bridge or spiro center, the mechanistic conclusions about protoetherification are not supported. Resolution test Provide full NMR assignments, key NOE or coupling evidence for the C3-C7 ether bridge and spiro junction, XRD data for the derivative with refinement statistics, and explicit evidence that the derivative retains the native C3-C7 ether connectivity and spiro skeleton. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Stereochemical evidence Claim pointer Deuterium-scanning labeling characterized the syn-stereochemistry of the protoetherification process during cyclization. Evidence pointer Abstract only; no labeling schemes, mass spectra, or NMR data provided. location not provided. Concern The syn-stereochemistry claim is central to the novelty relative to 1,8-cineole synthase. The abstract does not show how deuterium incorporation patterns distinguish syn from anti addition, nor does it report controls for non-enzymatic or rearrangement processes. Why it matters Without direct stereochemical evidence, the claim of syn-protoetherification is not established, and the comparison to the only previously characterized syn-protoetherification enzyme is unsupported. Resolution test Provide deuterium-scanning datasets with labeling positions, quantitative incorporation, control reactions, and a clear stereochemical argument linking the observed label patterns to syn addition at the relevant carbons. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Mechanistic pathway assignment Claim pointer DFT calculations, mutagenesis, mutant product characterization, and docking suggest cyclization through bisabolyl-dunnienyl cations as the favored pathway, albeit the coexistence of a pathway through carotenyl cations is also possible. Evidence pointer Abstract only; no computational or experimental data provided. location not provided. Concern The abstract asserts a favored pathway while also allowing a competing pathway, but provides no energetic values, transition-state structures, kinetic isotope effects, or product distributions that would discriminate between them. The basis for favoring bisabolyl-dunnienyl over carotenyl cations is not visible. Why it matters The mechanistic conclusion is the core scientific claim. If the two pathways are energetically close or if mutant product profiles are ambiguous, the favored pathway assignment is not justified. Resolution test Provide DFT relative energies for all relevant intermediates and transition states, methods and functional validation, experimental product distributions for wild type and mutants, and a quantitative argument for why one pathway is favored over the other. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Residue function Claim pointer Y186 may play as a key residue to redirect water to trap the C7 carbocation and to promote the syn-protoetherification reaction. Evidence pointer Abstract only; no mutagenesis data, structures, or docking figures provided. location not provided. Concern The Y186 claim is stated with "may," which is appropriately tentative, but the abstract does not report which mutants were made, their product profiles, or whether loss of the ether product is accompanied by alternative products. Docking alone cannot establish a water-redirection function. Why it matters The proposed catalytic role of Y186 is a major mechanistic element. Without mutant product quantification and structural context, the residue-level mechanism remains speculative. Resolution test Provide site-directed mutagenesis data for Y186 and surrounding residues, quantitative product profiles, kinetic parameters where possible, and structural or computational evidence for water positioning relative to the C7 carbocation. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Enzyme discovery and assignment Claim pointer Discovery of a bacteria-derived sesquiterpene synthase AceS converting farnesyl diphosphate to acorenol ether (1). Evidence pointer Abstract only; no sequence, phylogenetic, expression, or kinetic data provided. location not provided. Concern The abstract does not describe the origin organism, sequence identity to known terpene synthases, whether AceS was heterologously expressed and purified, or whether the reaction was reconstituted in vitro with defined substrates and cofactors. Why it matters The discovery claim requires a clear link between the assigned gene and the observed enzyme activity. Without this, the identity of AceS as the responsible synthase is not established. Resolution test Provide the source organism and accession, sequence alignment or phylogenetic placement, expression and purification evidence, in vitro assay conditions, substrate specificity, and product quantification. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Use of "protoetherification" Evidence pointer Abstract, first and second sentences. location not provided. Issue The term protoetherification is used without definition in the abstract. Its relationship to water quenching and intramolecular hydroxy trapping is described but not precisely delimited. Required correction Define protoetherification explicitly and distinguish it from related termination modes at first use. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Novelty framing Affected element Comparison to 1,8-cineole synthase Evidence pointer Abstract, second sentence. location not provided. Issue The abstract states that 1,8-cineole synthase is the only characterized enzyme catalyzing syn-protoetherification, but does not specify the basis for this exclusivity or the search criteria used. Required correction Clarify the literature basis for the exclusivity claim and specify whether the comparison is mechanistic, taxonomic, or both. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Computational reporting Affected element DFT calculations Evidence pointer Abstract only. location not provided. Issue No level of theory, solvation model, or conformational sampling strategy is mentioned. Required correction Report computational methods and validation in the main text or supporting information. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Nomenclature Affected element Compound 1 and acorane skeleton Evidence pointer Abstract only. location not provided. Issue The abstract does not state whether acorenol ether (1) is a known compound or a new natural product, nor whether the acorane skeleton assignment follows established numbering. Required correction State the novelty status of 1 and provide the numbering scheme used for the acorane skeleton. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3. These are blocking because the structural assignment, the stereochemical claim, and the favored pathway assignment are the central conclusions and are not evaluable from the supplied material. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is potentially present in the reported bacterial syn-protoetherification and the acorane ether scaffold, but cannot be confirmed without full structural and literature context. Scientific importance would be moderate to high for terpene synthase mechanism and enzymology if the claims hold. Interdisciplinary readership could include enzymology, natural product chemistry, and computational chemistry, though the abstract is specialized. Technical soundness is not established from the supplied material because no primary data are visible. Readability for nonspecialists is limited by undefined terminology and dense mechanistic language. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. Supportive if technical concerns are resolved with full structural, stereochemical, and computational data. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the P450-modified derivative retains the native C3-C7 ether connectivity and spiro skeleton of 1 is not supported by the supplied material. The claim of syn-protoetherification is not supported by visible stereochemical data. The claim that bisabolyl-dunnienyl cations are the favored pathway over carotenyl cations is not supported by visible energetic or product distribution data. The proposed water-redirecting role of Y186 is speculative from the supplied material. The discovery claim for AceS is not supported by visible sequence, expression, or in vitro activity data. The exclusivity claim regarding 1,8-cineole synthase as the only characterized syn-protoetherification enzyme is not supported by a visible literature analysis.

Input scope Abstract only, as provided in the submission record. No full text, figures, tables, or Supporting Information were supplied. Assessment boundary Evaluation is restricted to the claims and evidence visible in the abstract. Mechanistic, structural, and quantitative assertions that would normally rest on figures, tables, and methods sections cannot be independently verified here. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report that ultrasound-synchronized in situ crystallization of covalent organic frameworks (COFs) around enzymes traps transient high-activity, open enzyme conformations before relaxation, yielding enhanced catalytic activity. They report a six-framework library, a 3.4-fold activity increase for horseradish peroxidase driven mainly by a reduced Michaelis constant, >70% retention over 10 cycles, molecular dynamics identification of a globally reorganized open state with displaced gating phenylalanines, 2D solid-state NMR characterization of COF-enzyme interfacial interactions, ex situ controls that fail, and extension to laccase, cytochrome c, and lipase with 3.8-fold, 2.7-fold, and 1.5-fold enhancements over conventional stirring. Visible evidence base Abstract-level statements only. No numerical tables, kinetic traces, structural models, NMR spectra, simulation parameters, synthesis details, or statistical reporting are visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Full text, all figures and tables, Methods, Supporting Information, enzyme loading and leaching data, control experiments beyond the stated ex situ comparison, simulation protocols and convergence data, NMR acquisition and assignment details, and statistical treatment. These omissions materially limit confidence in every quantitative and mechanistic claim. Reviewer Overall assessment The concept is attractive and potentially of broad interest. Coupling a transient conformational perturbation to a crystallization event that kinetically traps the perturbed state is a coherent and testable hypothesis, and the reported extension across four enzymes suggests generality. However, from the supplied material the central mechanistic claim, namely that the observed activity gains arise from locking a specific transient open conformation rather than from conventional immobilization effects such as increased local concentration, reduced aggregation, altered mass transfer, or support-induced conformational selection, is not established. The evidence is described but not shown, and several alternative explanations are not excluded by the abstract alone. The work is promising but currently unproven on the visible record. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in enzyme immobilization and biocatalysis, materials chemists working on COFs and reticular frameworks, sonochemistry and mechanochemistry groups, and structural biologists interested in cryptic sites and conformational selection. If substantiated, the approach would interest process chemists seeking stable, recyclable biocatalysts with enhanced intrinsic kinetics, and would be relevant to the broader question of whether non-equilibrium protein states can be stabilized by designed hosts. Major strengths The central hypothesis is clearly stated and mechanistically falsifiable, and the authors report an ex situ control that, if properly executed, directly tests the necessity of temporal synchrony. Use of a six-framework library with varied pore size and chemistry is an appropriate design for probing steric and nonbonded contributions. The combination of molecular dynamics and 2D solid-state NMR, if rigorously executed, is a suitable multi-technique approach to a conformational claim. Extension to laccase, cytochrome c, and lipase, if reproduced under matched conditions, would support generality beyond a single enzyme. The reframing of immobilization as conformational upgrading is a conceptually useful contribution if the mechanism holds. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Mechanistic attribution Claim pointer The captured species is a transient high-activity open enzyme conformation, and the activity enhancement is caused by locking this conformation. Evidence pointer Abstract statements referencing molecular dynamics and 2D solid-state NMR; no figures, tables, or methods provided. Location not provided. Concern The abstract asserts that the trapped species is a globally reorganized open state, but no structural data, order parameters, or population estimates are visible. It is not shown that the encapsulated enzyme differs conformationally from enzyme immobilized without synchronization, nor that the open state is the catalytically relevant species rather than a coincidental structural variant. Why it matters The entire novelty claim depends on conformational locking rather than on conventional immobilization effects. Without direct structural comparison between synchronized and non-synchronized samples, the mechanism is asserted rather than demonstrated. Resolution test Provide comparative structural data, for example solid-state NMR chemical shifts or MD-derived metrics, for enzyme in synchronized COF, non-synchronized COF, and free enzyme, showing a distinct and reproducible conformational population that correlates quantitatively with activity. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Control adequacy Claim pointer Ex situ controls in which activation precedes encapsulation fail entirely, establishing that temporal synchrony is mechanistically essential. Evidence pointer Abstract statement only. Location not provided. Concern The ex situ control is described as failing entirely, but the abstract does not specify how activation was maintained or verified before encapsulation, how long the delay was, or whether the enzyme had already relaxed. A control that fails because the perturbation was absent at the moment of encapsulation does not by itself prove that a transient state was trapped in the synchronized case. Why it matters This control is the primary mechanistic discriminator in the abstract. If its design does not isolate temporal synchrony from other differences such as enzyme concentration, mixing, or COF nucleation state, the mechanistic conclusion is unsupported. Resolution test Report the ex situ protocol with timing, the independent verification that the enzyme was activated at the point of encapsulation, and matched controls for all non-temporal variables, ideally with a time-resolved series showing loss of the effect as the delay increases. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Quantitative support Claim pointer The optimal framework increased horseradish peroxidase activity 3.4-fold, primarily through a marked reduction in the Michaelis constant, with >70% activity retained over 10 cycles. Evidence pointer Abstract statement only. Location not provided. Concern No kinetic parameters, error estimates, replicate numbers, or definitions of the comparison baseline are visible. It is unclear whether the 3.4-fold increase is relative to free enzyme, to enzyme in COF without ultrasound, or to a conventional immobilization reference, and whether the reported Km reduction is statistically robust. Why it matters The magnitude and origin of the enhancement are central to the claim of conformational upgrading. Without baseline definition and statistics, the numbers cannot be evaluated or reproduced. Resolution test Provide full kinetic parameters with confidence intervals and replicate counts, explicit definition of each comparator, and raw activity data underlying the reported fold changes and recycling retention. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Alternative explanations Claim pointer Enhanced activity is attributed to conformational locking rather than to other immobilization-related effects. Evidence pointer Abstract statements on activity, kinetics, and simulations. Location not provided. Concern The abstract does not exclude conventional contributors such as increased effective enzyme concentration, reduced autolysis or aggregation, altered substrate partitioning within the COF, changes in diffusion or mass transfer, or preferential encapsulation of a more active subpopulation. Ultrasound itself can alter enzyme activity and aggregation independently of any locking effect. Why it matters If any of these alternatives account for the effect, the mechanistic and conceptual novelty is substantially reduced. Resolution test Include controls for enzyme loading, leaching, substrate partitioning, and ultrasound-only treatment without COF formation, and show that activity per accessible enzyme molecule, not per sample, is enhanced. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generality and comparability Claim pointer Extension to laccase, cytochrome c, and lipase enhanced immobilized enzyme activity 3.8-fold, 2.7-fold, and 1.5-fold over conventional stirring. Evidence pointer Abstract statement only. Location not provided. Concern The comparison baseline is conventional stirring, which differs from the synchronized condition in multiple respects including ultrasound exposure, nucleation kinetics, and mixing. The fold changes vary widely across enzymes, and no structural or kinetic evidence is presented that the same locking mechanism operates in each case. Why it matters The claim of a general strategy requires that the mechanism, not merely the outcome, be shared across enzymes. A 1.5-fold change in particular may be within the range of ordinary immobilization effects. Resolution test Report per-enzyme structural or kinetic evidence for conformational trapping, matched controls isolating ultrasound from synchronization, and statistical comparison against appropriate immobilization references. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Use of the term locking Evidence pointer Title and abstract. Location not provided. Issue Locking implies a kinetically trapped, persistent state, but the abstract does not report the timescale over which the conformation is retained or whether it relaxes during storage or catalysis. Required correction Define locking operationally and report conformational stability over time and across catalytic cycles. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Structural specificity Affected element Gating phenylalanine displacement Evidence pointer Abstract statement on molecular dynamics. Location not provided. Issue The identity and conservation of the gating phenylalanines are not specified, and it is not stated whether their displacement is observed in simulation only or also supported experimentally. Required correction Name the residues, state the enzyme and numbering, and clarify whether the displacement is simulated, experimentally observed, or both. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Framework library description Affected element Six frameworks with varied pore size and chemistry Evidence pointer Abstract statement. Location not provided. Issue Pore sizes, chemical functionalities, and the rationale for the specific set are not given, so the structure-activity relationship cannot be assessed. Required correction Provide a table of framework identities, pore dimensions, and functional groups with the corresponding activity data. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Crystallization and enzyme integrity Affected element Sonochemical in situ crystallization Evidence pointer Abstract statement. Location not provided. Issue The abstract does not address whether ultrasound or the crystallization conditions cause enzyme denaturation, fragmentation, or partial unfolding, which would confound activity interpretation. Required correction Report enzyme integrity assays, for example activity of released enzyme and spectroscopic or electrophoretic characterization, before and after the process. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Reported fold changes and cycling retention Evidence pointer Abstract statements. Location not provided. Issue No replicate counts, variance, or batch-to-batch reproducibility data are visible. Required correction Report sample sizes, dispersion measures, and independent batch replication for all activity and stability values. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M4, R1-M5. The most critical are R1-M1 and R1-M2, since the mechanistic claim of conformational locking rests on structural differentiation and on the validity of the synchrony control. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The concept of synchronizing a transient conformational perturbation with host crystallization to trap a non-equilibrium enzyme state is distinctive and, on the visible record, not a routine extension of standard immobilization. Originality is plausible but contingent on the mechanism being demonstrated. Scientific importance Potentially high if the mechanism is substantiated, because it would provide a general route to non-equilibrium protein states. Currently the importance is asserted rather than evidenced, since the abstract does not exclude conventional explanations. Interdisciplinary readership The work sits at the intersection of biocatalysis, framework materials, sonochemistry, and protein structural dynamics, which is appropriate for a broad chemistry audience. The abstract is accessible to that audience. Technical soundness Cannot be confirmed from the supplied material. Key structural, kinetic, and control data are described but not shown, and several alternative explanations are not addressed in the visible text. Readability for nonspecialists The abstract is clearly written and the central idea is communicated effectively. Some terms, such as cryptic sites and gating residues, would benefit from brief definition for a general readership. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The concept is worth pursuing, and the assessment could become supportive if the structural differentiation, the synchrony control, and the kinetic baselines are documented with full data and appropriate statistics. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that a specific transient open conformation is captured and is responsible for the activity increase is unsupported by visible structural evidence. The claim that temporal synchrony is mechanistically essential rests on an ex situ control whose design and verification are not described. The reported fold changes and Michaelis constant reduction are not evaluable without defined baselines, replicates, and statistics. The claim of generality across laccase, cytochrome c, and lipase is not supported by per-enzyme mechanistic evidence, and the 1.5-fold lipase result may be within the range of ordinary immobilization effects. The claim that the captured state is beyond equilibrium reach is not assessable from the abstract, since no thermodynamic or kinetic stability data are provided. The assertion that 2D solid-state NMR elucidates the stabilizing interfacial interactions is not verifiable without spectra, assignments, and distance or coupling measurements.

个一致预测去稳定化的变异，并借助 AlphaFold/AlphaFold 3 结构与 PPI 工具描述其可能的结构、修饰与互作影响，结论为 算法优先级排序结果、需实验验证 ，且 PPI 相关结论受预测复合物低–中等置信度限制。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：RASSF2 的哪些错义变异最可能破坏其蛋白质稳定性、结构、翻译后修饰与蛋白–蛋白相互作用（尤其 RA 域–KRAS、SARAH 域–MST1/MST2）？ 为什么重要 ：RASSF2 是抑癌基因，通过 RA 域以 GTP 依赖方式结合 KRAS、通过 SARAH 域与 MST1(STK4)/MST2(STK3) 形成复合物行使凋亡功能；其失活与结直肠癌、肺癌、胃癌、乳腺癌、甲状腺癌相关。错义变异可改变电荷、几何与疏水性并削弱 PPI，但实验表征成本高。 现有方法为何不足 ：单一预测工具假阳性/假阴性高；作者引用文献[15]主张多工具一致性可提高准确度与性能。此外，RASSF2 的 nsSNP 此前 未被系统研究 （作者称本文为首个）。 精确研究问题（Can ... ?） ：Can an integrative in silico pipeline, requiring consensus across five pathogenicity predictors and three ΔΔG predictors, identify a small set of RASSF2 missense variants that are consistently predicted to be destabilizing and to affect RA/SARAH-domain structure and interactions?（[Analysis] provided (Simple Summary, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, Acknowledgments). Supplementary tables and figures are referenced but not supplied. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the supplied manuscript text. All supplementary items (Tables S1–S16, Figures S1A–S1D) and the primary data underlying the reported tool outputs were not available for inspection. No reanalysis of tool outputs was possible. Shared manuscript claim summary The manuscript reports an integrative in silico pipeline applied to 454 missense variants of RASSF2 retrieved from dbSNP, yielding 75 variants concordant across five pathogenicity predictors, then 19 variants concordant across three stability predictors, which are proposed as candidate destabilizing, oncogenic, and interaction-disrupting variants warranting experimental follow-up. Visible evidence base Main-text descriptions of methods and results, including reported counts, thresholds, tool versions, database access dates, and summary statistics (for example average pLDDT 77.88, ERRAT 92.4 percent, PROCHECK most-favored 83.8 percent, STRING network of 8 nodes and 19 edges). Underlying per-variant tables are referenced but not visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Tables S1–S16, Figures S1A–S1D, the full variant-level output of each predictor, the exact input files and parameter settings submitted to each server, and any code or workflow documentation. These are required to verify the reported counts and the concordance-based prioritization. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a legitimate and understudied target, RASSF2, and assembles a broad panel of established in silico predictors into a sequential filtering pipeline. The writing is generally clear and the limitations section is candid about the absence of experimental validation. However, the central contribution is a prioritized candidate list, and the evidence supporting that list cannot be verified from the supplied material because all variant-level tables are supplementary and unavailable. Several methodological choices are either internally inconsistent or insufficiently justified, and at least one reported result appears to contradict the stated selection criteria. As presented, the work is a hypothesis-generating computational survey rather than an established set of destabilizing variants. Who would be interested in the results, and why Cancer geneticists and computational biologists working on RAS effector and Hippo pathway tumor suppressors would find the candidate list of interest as a starting point for functional work. Pharmacogenomics and variant-curation groups may find the prioritization framework useful if the pipeline is made reproducible. The broader clinical oncology readership is unlikely to be served directly, because no variant is experimentally or clinically validated. Major strengths The target gene is biologically well motivated and the introduction links RASSF2 function to KRAS and MST1/MST2 signaling with appropriate citations. The use of concordance across multiple orthogonal predictors, rather than a single tool, is a reasonable design. The inclusion of AlphaMissense and AlphaFold-based structural analysis reflects current practice. The authors explicitly acknowledge that predictions are hypotheses and that experimental validation is required, and they note the low-to-moderate confidence of the RASSF2–KRAS complex. The discussion attempts to connect prioritized positions to domain architecture and to previously observed somatic positions in cBioPortal. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Verifiability and reporting completeness Claim pointer The manuscript claims that 454 missense variants were retrieved, that 75 were concordant across five tools, and that 19 were concordant across three stability tools. Evidence pointer Sections 3.1, 3.2, 3.4; Tables S1–S11 (not provided); Table 1 and Table 2 (not provided) Concern Every quantitative claim in the Results depends on supplementary tables that were not supplied. The per-tool counts, the identity of the 75 and 19 variants, and the per-variant scores cannot be checked. The main text also does not report the score distributions or the overlap structure needed to judge whether the concordance filter is doing meaningful work or simply intersecting correlated predictors. Why it matters The entire downstream analysis, including domain mapping, conservation, oncogenicity, and PPI disruption, is conditioned on the 19-variant set. If that set cannot be reconstructed, none of the secondary conclusions can be evaluated. Resolution test Provide all supplementary tables with per-variant scores for every tool, the exact input files, and a reproducible description of how multiallelic rsIDs were split and how ties or missing scores were handled. Report the full contingency structure of tool agreement. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Internal consistency of the selection criteria Claim pointer The manuscript states that only variants with ΔΔG < −0.5 in DDMut and DynaMut2 and ΔΔG > 0.5 in ThermoMPNN were prioritized, and that 19 variants met this criterion. Evidence pointer Section 2.4; Section 3.4; Table 2 and Table S11 (not provided) Concern The sign conventions as written are not mutually consistent in a way that can be verified. DDMut and DynaMut2 are described as destabilizing when the score is negative, and ThermoMPNN as destabilizing when ΔΔG is positive, which is internally coherent, but the text of Section 3.4 states that ThermoMPNN predicted 64 variants to decrease stability with ΔΔG > 0 while also stating that DDMut and DynaMut2 predicted decreases with ΔΔG < 0. Without the tables, it is impossible to confirm that the 19-variant intersection was computed with the correct signs, and the reported counts (51, 54, 64) are not reconcilable with the stated thresholds from the text alone. Why it matters A sign error or threshold misapplication would invalidate the prioritized set, which is the core output of the study. Resolution test Provide the per-variant ΔΔG values from all three tools with explicit sign conventions, and state the number of variants passing each individual threshold as well as the intersection. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Structural model validity for interface claims Claim pointer The manuscript claims that specific variants, notably V193D and Y275C, are predicted to destabilize or disrupt the RASSF2–KRAS and RASSF2–MST2 interfaces. Evidence pointer Section 3.12; Figure S1B–S1D (not provided); Table 10 (not provided) Concern The authors themselves report low-to-moderate confidence for the RASSF2–KRAS complex (pTM 0.63, ipTM 0.52) and moderate confidence for RASSF2–MST1 (pTM 0.68, ipTM 0.66) and RASSF2–MST2 (ipSAE 0.73, ipTM 0.68, pDockQ2 0.62). By the manuscript's own stated criteria, ipTM below 0.6 indicates a likely failed or low-confidence prediction. Interface-level variant effects computed on a low-confidence interface are not interpretable as evidence about binding. Why it matters The PPI disruption claims are presented in the Results and Conclusions as substantive findings, but they rest on models the authors describe as unreliable. This is a claim-evidence mismatch. Resolution test Either restrict interface claims to complexes meeting a pre-specified confidence threshold, or present them explicitly as exploratory and remove them from the Conclusions. Report per-residue confidence at the mutated positions and the distance to the interface for each variant analyzed. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Redundancy and independence of the predictor ensemble Claim pointer The manuscript treats agreement across five pathogenicity tools and across three stability tools as evidence of robustness. Evidence pointer Sections 2.2, 2.4, 3.2, 3.4 Concern Several of the tools share training data, features, or architectural lineage. SIFT, PolyPhen2, and PhD-SNPg draw on related conservation and physicochemical signals; E-SNPs&GO and AlphaMissense both use protein language model embeddings; DDMut, DynaMut2, and ThermoMPNN are all structure-based ΔΔG predictors with overlapping training sets. Concordance among correlated predictors does not provide independent support, and the manuscript does not report any measure of predictor correlation or any benchmark of the ensemble against a labeled reference set. Why it matters The strength of the central claim rests on the assumption that agreement implies reliability. If the tools are correlated, the effective number of independent tests is much smaller than stated. Resolution test Report pairwise agreement and, if possible, correlation among tool scores on the 454-variant set. Benchmark the ensemble on a held-out set of RASSF2 or RASSF-family variants with known functional or clinical labels, if any exist. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Interpretation of oncogenicity and clinical annotation Claim pointer The manuscript claims that all 19 variants are potentially oncogenic and that nine are oncogenic with high confidence, and it links these to cancer. Evidence pointer Sections 2.9, 3.8; Table 6 (not provided) Concern CScape is trained on somatic driver mutations, whereas the input here is germline dbSNP variation. The manuscript acknowledges this once in the Methods but then interprets the output in oncogenic terms throughout the Results and Discussion. In addition, the cBioPortal findings are positional coincidences at codons 235, 241, 245, 247, and 249 with different amino acid substitutions, which does not constitute evidence that the specific prioritized variants occur in tumors. The statement that no RASSF2 data are deposited in AACR GENIE is also a negative database result that should not be framed as a finding. Why it matters The oncogenicity framing may overstate the clinical relevance of germline variants that have no ClinVar classification and, in 18 of 19 cases, are extremely rare. Resolution test Reframe CScape output as a computational risk score applied out of its intended domain, separate germline from somatic evidence explicitly, and remove or clearly qualify the codon-position argument. Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Downstream analyses disconnected from the prioritized variants Claim pointer The manuscript reports muTarget expression correlations and STRING network enrichment as part of the variant analysis. Evidence pointer Sections 2.14, 2.15, 3.13, 3.14; Tables S16 (not provided); Figure 6 and Figure 7 (not provided) Concern The muTarget analysis uses RASSF2 coding mutations in COAD and LUAD cohorts and does not test the 19 prioritized variants. The STRING analysis uses the RASSF2 gene name and does not incorporate any variant. Neither analysis can support conclusions about the prioritized missense variants, yet both appear in the Results and are discussed at length as if variant-specific. Why it matters These sections inflate the apparent scope of the study without adding variant-level evidence, and they may mislead readers about what was actually tested. Resolution test Either remove these analyses or relabel them clearly as gene-level context that is not variant-specific, and remove variant-related interpretive language from those sections. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Tool version and citation accuracy Affected element Methods Sections 2.2, 2.10, 2.13 Evidence pointer Sections 2.2, 2.10, 2.13 Issue PhD-SNPg is referred to as "PhD-SNP" in Section 3.2. GPS 6.0 is introduced in Section 2.10 but the threshold is attributed to "GPS 3.0," and Section 3.9 refers to "GPS 3.0." The version used is therefore ambiguous. Required correction Use a single consistent tool name and version throughout, and state the version actually executed. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Threshold justification Affected element Methods Sections 2.2, 2.4, 2.9, 2.11 Evidence pointer Sections 2.2, 2.4, 2.9, 2.11 Issue Thresholds are stated but not justified against the tools' own recommended operating points. For example, AlphaMissense is used with a 0.5 cutoff although the developers recommend class-specific thresholds, and MutPred2 is used with 0.5 although the manuscript itself notes 0.68 and 0.80 correspond to 10 percent and 5 percent false-positive rates. Required correction Justify each threshold with a citation or a sensitivity analysis showing that the prioritized set is stable across reasonable threshold choices. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Database access dates Affected element Methods Sections 2.1 through 2.15 Evidence pointer Sections 2.1 through 2.15 Issue All access dates are in August 2026 and the manuscript date is October 2026. This is internally consistent but should be confirmed as correct, since future-dated accessions will confuse readers and reviewers. Required correction Verify and correct all access dates, or explain the dating convention. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Numerical reporting Affected element Results Sections 3.6 and 3.7 Evidence pointer Sections 3.6, 3.7 Issue Section 3.6 states that 14 variants are in the RA domain and two in the SARAH domain, and the Discussion states that 16 of 19 are in functionally important domains. Section 3.7 states that three variants showed structural changes and that "all the remaining 15 variants" were unchanged, which is consistent with 19 but should be stated explicitly. The arithmetic should be presented so readers can follow it without the supplementary tables. Required correction State the domain distribution and the structural-change counts explicitly and consistently in both Results and Discussion. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Nomenclature and typography Affected element Throughout Evidence pointer Sections 2.3, 3.13, Discussion Issue "plDDT" and "pLDDT" are used interchangeably. "NRI12" appears where NR1I2 is intended. "Also." appears as a sentence fragment in the Discussion. "ipSAE" and "pDockQ2" are introduced without citation. Required correction Standardize nomenclature, correct the gene symbol, fix the fragment, and cite the interface metrics. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Redundant and unsupported interpretive language Affected element Discussion Evidence pointer Discussion paragraphs on muTarget and STRING Issue Several statements assert mechanistic roles for downstream genes, for example that CAVIN3 upregulation may be compensatory, that KRT40 upregulation points to epithelial reprogramming, and that GPR15 is tumor-suppressive in colon cancer, without variant-level evidence and in some cases without direct citation support in the supplied text. Required correction Soften or remove mechanistic assertions that are not supported by the presented data, and ensure each claim carries an appropriate citation. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3. These concern the verifiability of the prioritized variant set, the internal consistency of the stability selection, and the use of low-confidence structural models to support interface-level claims. R1-M4, R1-M5, and R1-M6 additionally weaken the interpretive framework and should be addressed for the manuscript to be considered technically sound. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is moderate. RASSF2 missense variant prioritization has not, to the authors' knowledge, been reported previously, but the methodological approach is a conventional stacking of existing web tools rather than a new method or resource. Scientific importance is currently limited because no variant is experimentally validated and the clinical annotations are absent; the work is hypothesis-generating. Interdisciplinary readership is plausible for cancer biology and computational genomics but not for the broader audience implied by a high-impact general journal, since the findings are predictions about a single gene. Technical soundness is not established from the supplied material, because the variant-level evidence is entirely supplementary and unavailable, the stability selection criteria cannot be verified, and the interface claims rest on models the authors describe as low confidence. Readability for nonspecialists is adequate in the Introduction and Simple Summary, but the Results are dense with tool names and thresholds and would benefit from a schematic of the filtering pipeline and a clear statement of what each stage does and does not establish. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript could become supportable as a computational prioritization study if the full variant-level data are provided, the stability selection is shown to be internally consistent, interface claims are either removed or restricted to adequately confident models, and the oncogenicity and gene-level analyses are reframed to match what was actually tested. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that 19 variants are destabilizing across three tools is not verifiable from the supplied material and depends on supplementary tables that were not provided. The claim that V193D and Y275C disrupt specific protein–protein interfaces is not supported, because the underlying complexes are reported by the authors as low to moderate confidence, and the RASSF2–KRAS ipTM of 0.52 falls below the manuscript's own threshold for a likely failed prediction. The claim that all 19 variants are potentially oncogenic is weakly supported, because CScape is applied outside its somatic training domain to germline variants, and no ClinVar classification exists for any of them. The claim that codon positions 235, 241, 245, 247, and 249 are mutation-sensitive is weakly supported, because the cBioPortal observations involve different amino acid substitutions at those positions and do not demonstrate occurrence of the prioritized variants. The muTarget expression correlations and the STRING network enrichment are not variant-specific and cannot be used to support conclusions about the 19 prioritized variants. The statement that no RASSF2 data are deposited in AACR GENIE is a negative database query result and should not be presented as a finding. The assertion that this is the first study to address nsSNPs in RASSF2 is a novelty claim that cannot be independently confirmed from the supplied material.

H⁺ 泵（xenorhodopsin、schizorhodopsin）与把细菌感光 rhodopsin 改造为内向质子泵的实验共同表明 7TM 骨架支持双向（Section 2.1、Section 6.3）。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] ： - 在把新蛋白宣称为「工具」之前，应先把每个被强调的性质拆到最近缘同源物与经典对照上逐参数核验；同属内 5–7% 序列差异意味着「特色」很可能只是共享性质。 - 术语（bistable、red-shifted、slow recovery）必须绑定到可操作定义与直接测量，否则会把不同物理量（光–暗适应再平衡 vs 单次光循环时长）混为一谈。 - 制备条件（去垢剂、pH、宿主膜、温度）是被测性质的组成部分而非中性变量，跨研究比较必须显式声明这些差异。 - 对结构计算方向：本文给出的可迁移模式是「计算预测性质 → No figures, tables, or reference list were provided. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the scientific content, logical coherence, internal consistency, and evidentiary support of the narrative review as presented in the text. Claims about specific quantitative values are assessed against the internal consistency of the manuscript and the stated provenance of the data. No external verification of cited literature was performed. Shared manuscript claim summary The manuscript is a narrative review of microbial rhodopsins, focusing on structural-functional mechanisms and their application to optogenetic silencing tool design. It places particular emphasis on a newly characterized archaeorhodopsin, HeAR, from a Halorubrum strain isolated from Ejinoor Salt Lake, Inner Mongolia. The authors summarize the rhodopsin family, photocycle dynamics, and ion-pumping mechanisms, then compare HeAR quantitatively with established rhodopsins (BR, AR3, AR4), and finally review the landscape of optogenetic silencing tools and rational design strategies. A central claim is that HeAR possesses a distinctive kinetic signature (fast M-state formation/decay, slow overall photocycle, slow dark adaptation) that may have implications for low-light silencing, though the authors explicitly state this remains a hypothesis requiring direct testing. Visible evidence base The manuscript cites a body of literature (references numbered [1]–[223]) and draws on the authors' own prior work (Ref. [24]) for quantitative HeAR data. Specific quantitative values are presented for HeAR (absorption maxima, photocycle kinetics, pKa, proton extrusion rates, ATP levels) and for comparators (BR, AR3, AR4). Figures 1–3 are described but not visible. Tables 1–3 are referenced but not provided. Missing materials affecting confidence Figures 1–3, Tables 1–3, and the full reference list were not provided. This limits verification of quantitative comparisons, figure-data consistency, and citation accuracy. The absence of Table 1 is particularly significant given its central role in the HeAR comparison. Reviewer Overall assessment This is a well-structured and thoughtfully written narrative review that addresses a timely and important topic: the gap between excitatory and inhibitory optogenetic tools, and the potential of newly characterized archaeorhodopsins to fill that gap. The authors are commendably explicit about the limits of their evidence, repeatedly distinguishing measured properties from hypotheses, and clearly labeling the provenance of quantitative data. The treatment of HeAR is appropriately cautious, and the authors resist overclaiming its utility. The review is likely to be of interest to researchers in microbial rhodopsin biophysics and optogenetic tool development. However, the manuscript has several weaknesses that need to be addressed. The most significant is the tension between the stated emphasis on HeAR and the relatively thin, single-source evidence base for its distinctive properties. The review also suffers from some internal inconsistencies in quantitative claims, a tendency toward overlong and occasionally repetitive prose, and a lack of critical depth in some sections where the literature is summarized rather than interrogated. The absence of the tables and figures in the provided material makes full assessment of the comparative framework impossible. Overall, the manuscript is promising but requires revision to sharpen its claims, resolve inconsistencies, and fully deliver on its stated aims. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in optogenetics, particularly those developing or applying inhibitory tools for neural silencing; biophysicists studying microbial rhodopsin structure-function relationships, photocycle kinetics, and ion transport mechanisms; synthetic biologists interested in light-driven energy conversion modules; and neuroscientists using optogenetic tools in circuit dissection or translational research. The comparative framework for evaluating silencing tools, and the explicit discussion of what has and has not been measured for HeAR, will be valuable to these communities. Major strengths The manuscript has several notable strengths. First, the authors are exceptionally transparent about the evidentiary status of their claims, explicitly distinguishing measured properties from hypotheses and clearly labeling the provenance of quantitative data. This is a model of scientific honesty in a review context. Second, the comparative framework, particularly the quantitative comparison of HeAR with BR, AR3, and AR4, is a valuable contribution that goes beyond typical narrative reviews. Third, the authors demonstrate strong command of the historical and current literature, from foundational work in the 1970s to recent cryo-EM and machine-learning approaches. Fourth, the review is well-organized, with a logical progression from basic rhodopsin biology to tool design and application. Fifth, the authors are careful to classify tools and strategies by molecular mechanism, avoiding the conflation that often plagues this literature. Finally, the explicit statement of literature selection criteria and their limitations is commendable and should be a model for other narrative reviews. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency for central claim Claim pointer The manuscript's central emphasis is that HeAR possesses a distinctive combination of properties—fast M-state formation and decay, slow overall photocycle, slow dark adaptation, and a raised counterion pKa—that may have implications for low-light silencing. The authors state this is a hypothesis requiring direct testing, but the framing of the review gives this hypothesis substantial prominence. Evidence pointer Section 4.3, Section 6.6, Table 1 (not provided) Concern The entire case for HeAR's distinctiveness rests on a single source (Ref. [24], the authors' own work) and a single expression system (E. coli, in vitro biophysics of purified protein). The authors acknowledge this, but the review's structure gives HeAR disproportionate weight relative to the evidence base. The comparison with AR3 and AR4 is based on literature values from different laboratories, expression systems, and measurement conditions, which the authors acknowledge but do not systematically address. The absence of Table 1 in the provided material makes it impossible to assess whether the comparison is appropriately qualified. Why it matters A review that emphasizes a specific protein as a potential tool platform must establish that the protein's distinctive properties are robust and not artifacts of a single measurement context. If the HeAR data are not reproducible across expression systems or measurement conditions, the review's central emphasis is undermined. The current presentation does not allow the reader to assess this. Resolution test The authors should either (a) provide a more systematic and critical comparison of measurement conditions across studies, explicitly discussing how differences in expression system, membrane environment, pH, temperature, and detergent might affect the quantitative values, or (b) explicitly reframe the review to present HeAR as a case study in how new rhodopsins should be characterized, rather than as a protein with established distinctive properties. The latter would be more appropriate given the evidence base. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Internal consistency of quantitative claims Claim pointer The manuscript states that HeAR's slow dark adaptation "does not by itself increase per-molecule charge turnover" and that "the proposal that it improves low-light silencing therefore needs direct measurement." However, in Section 6.6, the authors list as a design implication that "the coupling between M-state kinetics and silencing efficacy merits reassessment," citing the same kinetic features. Evidence pointer Section 3.2, Section 6.6 Concern There is a tension between the cautious framing in Section 3.2, where the authors correctly note that slow dark adaptation does not imply improved silencing, and the more speculative framing in Section 6.6, where the same features are presented as design implications. The authors do not clearly resolve this tension. If slow dark adaptation does not increase per-molecule charge turnover, then its relevance to silencing is unclear, and the review should say so more directly. Why it matters The review's stated aim is to provide a comparative framework for tool design. If the implications drawn from HeAR's kinetics are not clearly grounded in the measured properties, the framework risks being misleading. Resolution test The authors should either (a) provide a more explicit mechanistic argument for why slow dark adaptation might matter for silencing, despite not increasing per-molecule charge turnover, or (b) remove or substantially qualify the design implication in Section 6.6. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Critical depth of literature review Claim pointer The review covers a broad range of topics, from rhodopsin family classification to optogenetic tool applications, but in several sections the treatment is largely descriptive rather than critical. Evidence pointer Sections 2, 5, 7 Concern In several places, the review summarizes findings without critically evaluating them. For example, the discussion of optogenetic silencing tools in Section 5 catalogs tools and their properties but does not systematically compare their relative strengths and weaknesses for specific applications. Similarly, the discussion of machine-learning approaches in Section 6.4 is brief and does not critically assess the limitations of these methods. The review would be stronger if it provided a more analytical framework, identifying open questions and controversies in the field. Why it matters A Nature-style review is expected to provide not just a summary but a critical synthesis that advances the field's understanding. The current manuscript is more descriptive than analytical in places. Resolution test The authors should add critical analysis to at least the following: (a) a systematic comparison of silencing tool performance metrics across studies, (b) a discussion of the limitations and failure modes of machine-learning approaches to rhodopsin design, and (c) an explicit statement of the most important open questions in the field. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility and provenance of quantitative data Claim pointer The manuscript presents quantitative values for HeAR (absorption maxima, photocycle kinetics, pKa, proton extrusion rates, ATP levels) and for comparators (BR, AR3, AR4) without providing sufficient detail on measurement conditions for the comparators. Evidence pointer Section 4.3, Table 1 (not provided) Concern The authors state that "excitation wavelength and intensity, pH, temperature, detergent and the fitting model all differ between these studies" for the kinetic comparison, but they do not provide a systematic account of these differences. Without this, the reader cannot assess the validity of the quantitative comparisons. The absence of Table 1, which presumably contains this information, is a significant gap in the provided material. Why it matters Quantitative comparisons across studies are only meaningful if measurement conditions are comparable or if differences are explicitly accounted for. The current presentation does not allow the reader to make this assessment. Resolution test The authors should provide a table (or expand Table 1) that systematically lists measurement conditions for each quantitative value cited, including expression system, membrane environment, pH, temperature, detergent, and fitting model. This would allow readers to assess the robustness of the comparisons. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The central case for HeAR's distinctive properties rests on a single source and a single expression system. The authors acknowledge this, but the review's structure gives HeAR disproportionate weight. The absence of Table 1 in the provided material is a significant gap. The internal tension between the cautious framing in Section 3.2 and the more speculative framing in Section 6.6 needs to be resolved. The review would benefit from a more systematic and critical comparison of measurement conditions across studies. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : The review is not entirely original in its topic, as microbial rhodopsins and optogenetics have been reviewed extensively. However, the specific emphasis on HeAR as a newly characterized archaeorhodopsin, and the explicit comparative framework for evaluating silencing tools, provides a degree of originality. The authors' transparency about the evidentiary status of their claims is also a distinctive feature. Scientific importance : The topic is of high scientific importance. The gap between excitatory and inhibitory optogenetic tools is a well-recognized problem, and the review addresses it directly. The comparative framework for evaluating silencing tools is potentially valuable. However, the importance of the HeAR-specific claims is not yet established, as the authors themselves acknowledge. Interdisciplinary readership : The review is likely to appeal to a broad interdisciplinary audience, including biophysicists, neuroscientists, synthetic biologists, and optogenetics researchers. The authors make an effort to explain concepts clearly, and the Simple Summary is accessible. However, some sections are dense and may be challenging for non-specialists. Technical soundness : The review is generally technically sound, with appropriate caveats about the limits of the evidence. However, the internal inconsistency in the kinetic comparison (M-state decay of 3.3 ms vs. 3.5 ms) and the lack of systematic accounting for measurement conditions across studies are weaknesses. The absence of Table 1 in the provided material limits assessment. Readability for nonspecialists : The Simple Summary is clear and accessible. The main text is generally well-written but is dense in places and would benefit from more careful editing to improve readability. Some sentences are overly long and complex. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The review addresses an important topic, is well-structured, and demonstrates commendable scientific honesty. However, the central emphasis on HeAR needs to be better supported by a more systematic and critical comparison of measurement conditions, and the internal inconsistency in the kinetic comparison needs to be resolved. The absence of Table 1 in the provided material makes full assessment impossible, but the text suggests the table would address many of these concerns. With these revisions, the review would be a valuable contribution to the field. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that HeAR's slow dark adaptation "may help maintain spectral and kinetic stability under extracellular environmental fluctuations" (Section 6.6) is presented as a design implication but is not directly supported by any measurement of stability under fluctuating conditions. This is an inference from the measured pKa and kinetics, and should be labeled as such. The claim that "the longer cycle lowers maximal per-molecule turnover relative to BR, so any low-light advantage must be measured rather than inferred" (Section 4.3) is appropriately cautious, but the framing in Section 6.6 that the kinetic signature is a design implication is not fully consistent with this caution. The statement that "AR4, which is 95% identical to HeAR, has been produced recombinantly in Halobacterium salinarum L33 at yields of up to 20 mg L−1 with its trimeric packing and proton-pumping kinetics retained" (Section 6.6) is presented as evidence that HeAR-based tools are feasible, but this is an inference from homology, not a direct demonstration for HeAR. The authors should clarify this. The claim that "the authors' team's work on Ejinoor Salt Lake shows that in-depth characterization of a single strain can yield a complete structural-functional parameter set with tool value" (Section 7.4) is an assertion about the value of the work that is not directly supported by the evidence presented in this review. The statement that "no archaeorhodopsin has entered clinical testing" (Section 7.3) is presented as a fact, but the source for this claim is not provided in the text.

Shared manuscript claim summary The authors use ColabFold to build models of human ferroportin (hFPN) in inward-open, occluded, and outward-open states, validate them against experimental structures via TM-align, run 1 µs MD simulations (three replicas for wild type, two for N174I, one for G80S), and interpret state-dependent salt bridges and hydrogen bonds in the context of known pathogenic mutations. They propose that a stable core (TM1, TM5, TM7b, TM8, TM10) is flanked by mobile peripheral helices, that TM1/TM5 may act as a pivot, that G323 flexibility governs TM7b movement in the final export phase, and that N174I traps the transporter in a non-functional outward-open state via loss of the N174–Q478 hydrogen bond and gain of hydrophobic contacts (L474, L170, I159).
