and Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusions, Acknowledgments). Supplementary tables and figures referenced but not supplied. Assessment boundary Assessment is limited to the supplied manuscript text. All supplementary materials (Table S1–S4, Figure S1, Table S3A–E) are referenced but unavailable, so claims that depend on them cannot be independently verified. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report untargeted peptidomic identification of 219 soy-derived peptides in a fermented soy postbiotic (GAD), describe extensive overlapping sequence families and truncation ladders, select a 10-peptide diversity panel, dock these against an approximately 5000-protein human structure library, apply GO enrichment with a Jaccard-based ranking-depth heuristic and randomized-affinity negative controls, and prioritize 180 candidate protein targets (43 Tier 1/Tier 2) across mucosal immune regulation, extracellular-matrix remodeling, epithelial turnover, and tissue restitution. The authors frame all docking outputs as hypothesis-generating prioritization rather than validated interactions. Visible evidence base Main text sections 1–5, Highlights, Abstract, and Acknowledgments. Quantitative results are reported in text for PCA, clustering sensitivity (ARI, silhouette), representative-panel coverage, randomized-affinity controls, and Peptide 4 pose-aggregation. Figure and Table callouts (Figures 1–5, Table 1, Tables S1–S4, Figure S1, Table S3A–E) are cited but their contents are not visible. Missing materials affecting confidence Table S1 (peptide-level dataset), Table S2 (candidate provenance), Table S3A–E (convergence and pose-aggregation sensitivity), Table S4 (library representation bias), Figure S1 (ranking-depth trajectories), and Figures 1–5. These are central to verifying the reported peptide counts, candidate provenance, and sensitivity analyses. Reviewer Overall assessment This is a methodologically self-aware exploratory study that characterizes a fermented soy-derived peptide fraction and uses computational docking plus GO enrichment to generate prioritized biological hypotheses. The manuscript is unusually candid about its limitations, and several internal controls (clustering sensitivity, randomized-affinity permutation, pose-aggregation sensitivity, library representation-bias analysis) are reported. However, the central biological claims rest on computational predictions that are not experimentally validated, and key supporting evidence is in supplementary materials that are not available for review. The work is best read as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than as establishing peptide–protein associations or biological activity. Several technical points require clarification before the prioritization framework can be considered robustly established. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in food-derived peptide biology, peptidomics, postbiotic and fermented-ingredient characterization, and computational structural biology / molecular docking would find the workflow relevant. Investigators studying upper-gastrointestinal mucosal defense, gastric injury, and tissue restitution may find the prioritized candidate contexts useful for hypothesis generation. The diversity-sampling and negative-control framework may also interest methodologists working on large-scale peptide–protein docking prioritization. Major strengths The peptidomic characterization reports a substantial peptide inventory (219 sequences) with explicit mapping to source proteins and documentation of truncation ladders, which is a useful descriptive contribution. The manuscript is transparent about the exploratory nature of the docking analysis and repeatedly states that predictions are not validated interactions. Multiple internal controls are reported, including clustering sensitivity (ARI across alternative representations), a 10,000-panel coverage comparison, a 500-iteration randomized-affinity permutation test per peptide, and a pose-aggregation sensitivity analysis for Peptide 4. The library representation-bias analysis (99.68% of screened accessions present in the reviewed proteome; approximately 21.4% coverage; enrichment for certain structural classes) is a valuable and honest characterization of the search space. The provenance-tracking design (PDB/chain to gene, two independent prioritization routes) is a reasonable attempt at auditability. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency for the central claim Claim pointer The manuscript claims that docking-derived rankings contain "non-random functional structure" and that prioritized biological contexts (mucosal immune regulation, extracellular-matrix remodeling, epithelial turnover, tissue restitution) are supported. Evidence pointer Section 3.3.2, Section 4, Table S2, Table S3A–E, Figure S1 (supplementary materials not provided) Concern The central biological interpretation depends on GO enrichment derived from docking scores, but no experimental validation of any peptide–protein interaction is presented. The randomized-affinity control tests only whether GO enrichment exceeds what is expected after disrupting the score-to-protein association; it does not test whether the predicted interactions are physically correct. The authors acknowledge this, but the Discussion and Conclusions still present the prioritized contexts as the principal finding, which risks overstating what the evidence supports. Why it matters Without orthogonal evidence (e.g., surface plasmon resonance, isothermal titration calorimetry, co-crystallography, or at minimum experimental binding assays for a subset), the reader cannot distinguish genuine interaction signal from artifacts of docking scoring, receptor preparation, and annotation density. Resolution test Provide experimental validation for at least a small subset of prioritized peptide–protein pairs, or explicitly reframe the conclusions to state that no biological claim is made and that the output is purely a computational prioritization list. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Reproducibility and traceability of the candidate set Claim pointer The manuscript reports 180 unique candidate protein targets (129 via GO-guided route, 51 via top-ranked docking route) and 43 Tier 1/Tier 2 candidates. Evidence pointer Section 3.3.2, Figure 5A, Figure 5B, Table S2 (not provided) Concern The candidate set and its provenance are reported only in Table S2, which is not available. The text does not provide the identity of the 10 representative peptides, the specific PDB/chain entries, the recurrent GO terms used for filtering, or the tier assignments for individual candidates. The rule-based tier classification (Section 2.13) is described but the actual assignments and the criteria thresholds are not shown. Why it matters Without the candidate list and provenance, the reader cannot assess whether the prioritization is reproducible, whether the tier assignments are consistent, or whether the 180-target count is sensitive to the many analytical choices described. Resolution test Provide Table S2 in full, including peptide identity, PDB/chain, gene, GO term, identification route, and tier, and summarize the tier-assignment rules with explicit thresholds in the main text. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Methodological validity of the ranking-depth heuristic Claim pointer The Jaccard-based convergence procedure (J ≥ 0.80 across three consecutive valid transitions) was used to select a ranking depth for downstream GO interpretation, yielding depths from N = 85 to N = 315 across the 10 peptides. Evidence pointer Section 2.9, Section 3.3, Figure S1, Table S3A–D (not provided) Concern The convergence criterion is an operational heuristic with no biological ground truth, and the manuscript acknowledges this. However, the selected depth directly determines which proteins enter the enrichment analysis and therefore which GO terms and candidates are prioritized. The sensitivity analysis reported for Peptide 4 shows that longer consecutive windows shift the selected depth, and the pose-aggregation analysis shows convergence depth varies from N = 185 to N = 375 depending on aggregation. This indicates the downstream candidate set is substantially dependent on an arbitrary parameter. Why it matters If the prioritized biological contexts change with the convergence definition, the robustness of the central interpretation is weakened. Resolution test Report the full ranking-depth trajectories (Figure S1) and demonstrate that the recurrent GO terms and Tier 1/Tier 2 candidate set are stable across a range of convergence definitions, or explicitly state the degree of instability. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Representativeness of the peptide panel Claim pointer The 10-peptide diversity panel adequately samples the 219-peptide feature space and supports the downstream docking and prioritization. Evidence pointer Section 3.3.1, Section 2.5 Concern The clustering sensitivity analysis shows only moderate agreement between alternative representations (ARI = 0.241 for PCA-only vs. submitted 10-cluster; ARI = 0.411 when constrained to 10 clusters; mean ARI = 0.659 across UMAP seeds; mean ARI = 0.553 on resampling). The coverage analysis shows the panel reduces mean nearest-representative distance by 8.30% relative to random panels, which is a modest improvement. The authors correctly interpret the panel as diversity-sampling rather than biological proxies, but the docking results are then presented as if the 10 peptides represent the broader peptidome. Why it matters If the panel captures only a modest fraction of the feature space, the 180 candidate targets may not reflect the interaction potential of the full 219-peptide mixture, and the prioritized biological contexts may be panel-specific. Resolution test Quantify what fraction of the 219-peptide feature space is within a defined distance of the panel, and discuss whether the prioritized contexts would be expected to change with a different panel. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Receptor preparation and docking validity Claim pointer Docking against the approximately 5000-protein human structure library yields meaningful relative rankings of candidate interactors. Evidence pointer Section 2.6, Section 2.7, Section 4 Concern The uniform removal of ligands, waters, ions, and cofactors, and protonation at pH 7, is acknowledged to potentially alter binding-site geometry and electrostatics. The use of a single predicted free-peptide conformation (OpenFold3) for docking is also acknowledged as a limitation. However, the manuscript does not report any validation of the docking protocol against known peptide–protein complexes (e.g., re-docking of co-crystallized peptides, or comparison with experimental binding data). Without such validation, the absolute and relative ranking performance of DiffPepDock plus PRODIGY in this specific setting is unknown. Why it matters The entire prioritization rests on the assumption that the docking scores carry useful ranking information. If the protocol has not been benchmarked, the rankings may be dominated by systematic biases (e.g., receptor size, surface charge) rather than genuine interaction propensity. Resolution test Provide a benchmark of the docking and scoring protocol against a set of experimentally characterized peptide–protein complexes, reporting rank correlation or enrichment factors. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity of statistical reporting Affected element Section 3.3.1 Evidence pointer Section 3.3.1 Issue The coverage analysis reports P values (P = 2.0 × 10−4, P = 0.0059, P = 6.0 × 10−4, P = 8.0 × 10−4) for comparisons against 10,000 random panels, but the test statistic and the null distribution are not fully described. It is unclear whether these are one-sided or two-sided and whether multiple-comparison correction was applied. Required correction State the test used, the directionality, and whether correction was applied. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Internal consistency of reported numbers Affected element Section 3.3.2 Evidence pointer Section 3.3.2 Issue The text states that for Peptide176, three of 500 randomized rankings produced at least as many significant terms as observed, yielding P = 4/501 = 0.007984. The formula P = (1 + n_null≥obs) / (B + 1) with n = 3 and B = 500 gives 4/501, which is consistent. However, the text also states that for nine of 10 peptides none of the 500 randomized rankings produced as many significant terms as observed, corresponding to P = 1/501. This is consistent with the formula. No error is apparent, but the presentation would benefit from a single consolidated table of per-peptide observed term counts, null counts, and P values. Required correction Provide a consolidated per-peptide table of observed and null enrichment counts and empirical P values. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Section 3.3 Evidence pointer Section 3.3 Issue The manuscript states that "receptor" refers to the screened protein structure and does not imply a biological receptor function. This clarification is helpful but appears only once. The term is used throughout the Results and Discussion in a way that could confuse non-specialist readers. Required correction Consider using "screened protein" or "target protein" consistently, or repeat the clarification at first use in each major section. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Reporting of the antioxidant peptide comparison Affected element Section 3.2 Evidence pointer Section 3.2 Issue Three literature-reported antioxidant sequences were identified as exact contiguous regions within longer GAD peptides. The manuscript correctly notes that activity of the longer peptides cannot be inferred. However, it does not report whether the free sequences themselves were detected in GAD, nor whether the longer peptides are predicted to release them. Required correction State explicitly whether the free antioxidant sequences were detected in the peptidomic data, and discuss the likelihood of their release. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Use of AI assistance Affected element Acknowledgments Evidence pointer Acknowledgments Issue Microsoft Copilot 365 was used to assist with terminology harmonization and consistency review of functional domains and tier classifications. The manuscript states that authors reviewed and finalized all outputs. This is appropriately disclosed, but the extent to which Copilot influenced the final tier assignments is not quantified. Required correction Clarify whether any tier assignments were changed as a result of Copilot suggestions, and if so, how many. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (lack of experimental validation for the central biological interpretation), R1-M2 (candidate set and provenance not available for verification), R1-M3 (ranking-depth heuristic sensitivity), R1-M4 (panel representativeness), R1-M5 (docking protocol not benchmarked). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The peptidomic characterization of a fermented soy postbiotic and the integration of diversity-sampling peptide selection with proteome-scale docking and GO enrichment is a reasonably novel combination, though each component (peptidomics, docking, GO enrichment) is established. The main novelty is the workflow integration and the explicit negative-control framework. Scientific importance The work is exploratory and hypothesis-generating. It does not establish biological activity or validated interactions. Its importance lies in providing a prioritized candidate list and a framework for future studies, which is a modest but legitimate contribution. Interdisciplinary readership The work spans food science, peptidomics, computational structural biology, and gastrointestinal biology. It could interest a broad readership, but the lack of experimental validation and the reliance on supplementary materials limit its immediate impact. Technical soundness The manuscript is unusually candid about limitations and includes several internal controls. However, the central technical weakness is the absence of docking-protocol benchmarking and experimental validation, and the dependence of the candidate set on an arbitrary convergence heuristic. The supplementary materials needed to verify the reported numbers are not available. Readability for nonspecialists The manuscript is generally well written and the limitations are clearly stated. However, the density of methodological detail and the use of terms like "receptor" (redefined) and "convergence depth" may challenge non-specialist readers. A clearer separation of descriptive peptidomic findings from computational predictions would improve accessibility. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The descriptive peptidomic characterization is a useful contribution, but the central biological prioritization claims rest on computational predictions that are not experimentally validated and on supplementary materials that are not available for verification. The manuscript would need to either provide experimental validation for a subset of prioritized interactions or substantially reframe its conclusions as a purely computational hypothesis-generation exercise, and provide the full supplementary data for independent assessment. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the prioritized biological contexts (mucosal immune regulation, extracellular-matrix remodeling, epithelial turnover, tissue restitution) are supported by the data is not established, because the underlying peptide–protein interactions are computational predictions without experimental validation. The claim that the docking-derived rankings contain "non-random functional structure" is supported only in the limited sense that GO enrichment exceeds a permutation null; it does not establish that the predicted interactions are physically correct. The claim that the 10-peptide panel adequately samples the 219-peptide feature space is weak, given the moderate ARI values and the modest 8.30% reduction in nearest-representative distance relative to random panels. The claim that the 180 candidate targets and 43 Tier 1/Tier 2 candidates are robust is not verifiable from the supplied material, because Table S2 and the tier-assignment details are not provided. The claim that the Jaccard-based convergence procedure identifies a meaningful ranking depth is not supported beyond its operational definition; the manuscript acknowledges this but the downstream interpretation still depends on it. The claim that the docking protocol provides useful relative rankings is not supported by any benchmark against experimentally characterized peptide–protein complexes. The claim that the antioxidant peptide sequences embedded in longer GAD peptides have any functional relevance is explicitly not established, and the manuscript correctly states this, but the finding is still presented as a notable result.

2026-11-01 在课题方向中的位置 : 本文是综述，覆盖 AI 在糖基化反应预测、糖基化位点鉴定、糖蛋白结构建模（含 AlphaFold3 评估）和糖组学数据挖掘四个环节的应用。对本课题（蛋白质结构相关计算研究 × AI/物理模拟）而言，其核心价值在于：①系统梳理了 AlphaFold3 对糖蛋白/蛋白-聚糖复合物建模的能力与局限；②展示了 AI 预测结构 + 实验验证（如 MCTS1–JAK2–IFN-γ 轴）的闭环工作流；③提出了糖蛋白构象系综建模（AlphaFLOW + MD）的可行路径。 02 一句话总结 本文系统综述了 AI 在蛋白质糖基化研究四个环节（反应预测、位点鉴定、结构建模、糖组学挖掘）的应用现状，指出 AlphaFold3 能对糖蛋白复合物进行原子级建模但存在立体化学错误且置信度指标无法检测此类错误，并主张通过多模态融合、构象系综建模和闭环实验验证推动糖蛋白研究从静态预测走向功能设计。 03 研究问题 具体问题 : AI 如何系统性地解决蛋白质糖基化研究中的三大瓶颈——糖苷键立体化学控制、糖基化位点准确鉴定、完全糖基化蛋白的天然构象建模？ 为什么重要 : 糖基化是最丰富、结构最复杂的翻译后修饰，参与蛋白折叠、免疫识别、信号转导，其异常与癌症、神经退行性疾病、先天性糖基化障碍（CDG）直接相关。但糖基化研究长期受限于实验通量低、结构数据稀缺、构象异质性大。 现有方法为何不足 : 传统化学合成依赖经验规则和 DFT 计算，难以泛化；质谱位点鉴定成本高、通量低；通用结构预测工具（如 AlphaFold2）不支持糖链；AlphaFold3 虽支持聚糖但存在立体化学错误且置信度指标无法检测；单结构预测无法反映糖蛋白的构象系综。 精确研究问题（Can ... ?） : Can AI-based methods (from predictive models to generative models) overcome the three bottlenecks of protein glycosylation research—stereochemical control, site assignment, and conformational modeling of fully glycosylated proteins—to shift the field from static prediction to functional design? 04 背景与发展脉络 → 位点鉴定 → 结构建模 → 糖组学挖掘）组织综述，逐一评估 AI 方法在各环节的进展与局限。 核心洞察 : 糖基化研究正经历从"预测"到"生成"的范式转变——AI 不再仅用于预测既有事实（如位点是否存在、反应选择性如何），而是开始生成新的化学知识（如发现新的立体选择性规则）、新的结构假设（如 AF3 建模糖蛋白复合物）和新的功能解释（如可解释 AI 挖掘调控因子）。但这一转变的关键瓶颈是 立体化学保真度 和 构象动态性 ——静态预测工具（AF3）无法保证糖链立体化学正确，单结构无法代表糖蛋白的功能构象系综。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis]: ①对含糖/修饰残基的系统，AI 结构预测的置信度指标不能替代立体化学验证——"高置信度"不等于"化学正确"；②糖基化位点预测的进步不取决于模型架构，而取决于数据质量与标准化；③从静态预测走向功能设计，必须引入构象系综（MD、flow matching）和闭环实验验证，而非依赖单一结构。 07 方法总览 输入 : 糖基化反应数据库（CAS 10,434 反应 + Barresi–Hindsgaul 734 反应）、蛋白序列（ESM-2 嵌入）、蛋白结构（AlphaFold2 预测结构）、质谱数据、凝集素结合数据、糖蛋白结构（PDB） 输出 : provided text Shared manuscript claim summary The authors argue that artificial intelligence is transforming protein glycosylation research across four domains: glycosylation reaction prediction, glycosylation site identification, glycoprotein structural modeling, and glycomics data mining. They propose a "glycan language" framework and claim that AI methods are moving the field from prediction toward generation and functional design. Visible evidence base The manuscript text includes descriptions of specific tools (GlycoPredictor, Bayesian optimization, ESM-2, AlphaFold2/3, DeepGlycanSite, CandyCrunch, DeepGlyco, GlycoCompute, GlycanGT, OneProt, AlphaFLOW, ModelAngelo, LeGenD), references to figures and tables, and case examples (MCTS1–JAK2–IFN-γ axis, CDG variant interpretation, IgG Fc glycan signatures) Missing materials affecting confidence Figures, tables, and reference list are not provided. No experimental data, benchmark results, or code are included. The manuscript is a review, so primary data are not expected, but the absence of figures and tables limits verification of the described results. Reviewer Overall assessment This is a broad, well-structured review of AI applications in protein glycosylation research. The authors cover a commendable range of topics, from chemical reaction prediction to structural biology and glycomics. The "glycan language" framing is a useful organizing principle. However, the manuscript has several significant weaknesses. The depth of technical discussion is uneven, with some sections reading as lists of tools rather than critical analyses. The treatment of AlphaFold3 is notably uncritical, and the authors do not adequately address the substantial limitations of current AI methods for glycoprotein modeling. The clinical and translational claims, particularly regarding CDG, are not well supported by the evidence presented. The manuscript would benefit from a more critical stance, clearer articulation of the field's open problems, and a more rigorous comparison of the methods discussed. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in glycobiology, glycochemistry, and glycoproteomics would find this review useful as a survey of AI tools applicable to their field. Computational biologists and machine learning researchers working on protein structure prediction or post-translational modification prediction may also be interested. The review could serve as an entry point for those seeking to apply AI methods to glycosylation-related problems. However, the lack of critical depth may limit its value for experts in either AI or glycoscience. Major strengths The manuscript covers a wide range of topics in a logical structure, from chemical synthesis to structural biology to omics data analysis. The "glycan language" framework provides a coherent narrative. The authors include recent developments (AlphaFold3, generative models) and make an effort to discuss limitations, particularly regarding data scarcity and evaluation practices. The inclusion of specific case examples, such as the CDG variant interpretation, helps ground the discussion. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors claim that AlphaFold3 can model glycoproteins with high accuracy and that it represents a significant advance for the field, citing specific examples such as the EXTL3 homodimer and OC43 spike protein. Evidence pointer Section 4.1.2, Section 4.4, Figure 4 (not provided) Concern The discussion of AlphaFold3 is overly optimistic and does not acknowledge the well-documented limitations of AF3 for glycoprotein modeling. The authors cite a few examples where AF3 performed well but do not discuss the systematic evaluation studies that show AF3 struggles with glycan conformation, anomeric configuration, and glycosidic linkage accuracy. The claim that AF3 treats glycans as "first-class molecular entities" is an overstatement; AF3's handling of glycans is still limited by training data and force field approximations. The authors also do not address the fact that AF3's confidence metrics (pLDDT, PAE) are unreliable for glycans, which they themselves note in Section 4.1.2 but do not connect to the broader claims of AF3's utility. Why it matters The manuscript's central argument is that AI is transforming glycoprotein structural biology. If the discussion of the most prominent AI tool (AF3) is uncritical and does not accurately represent its capabilities and limitations, the overall thesis is weakened. Readers may be misled about the current state of the art and make inappropriate decisions about tool selection. Resolution test The authors should provide a balanced assessment of AF3, including quantitative comparisons with experimental structures across a diverse test set, discussion of known failure modes (e.g., anomeric errors, glycan flexibility), and a clear statement of what AF3 can and cannot do for glycoprotein modeling. They should also discuss alternative approaches and their relative merits. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Support for claims Claim pointer The authors claim that "glycan language models link sequence and structure to function" and that these models are "becoming clinically actionable" for prioritizing variants in congenital disorders of glycosylation and stratifying immune disorders and tumors. Evidence pointer Section 5.3, Section 5.4, Section 5.5 Concern The claim that glycan language models are "clinically actionable" is not supported by the evidence presented. The authors describe a few examples (e.g., XGBoost classifier for PMM2-CDG with AUC 0.917, LeGenD for glycan structure prediction) but do not provide details on validation cohorts, prospective studies, or clinical implementation. The leap from computational predictions to clinical actionability is not justified. Furthermore, the authors do not discuss the regulatory, ethical, or practical challenges of deploying such models in clinical settings. Why it matters The manuscript positions AI as a transformative force in glycosylation research with clinical implications. Overstating the clinical readiness of these tools could mislead researchers and clinicians, and could undermine trust in the field if the claims are not borne out. Resolution test The authors should either temper the "clinically actionable" claim or provide concrete evidence of clinical validation, such as prospective studies, external validation cohorts, or regulatory approval. They should also discuss the specific challenges that remain before these tools can be used in clinical practice. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Completeness Claim pointer The authors state that the review covers "recent advances" in AI for glycosylation research, but the discussion of glycomics data mining is largely focused on a few specific tools and does not provide a comprehensive survey of the field. Evidence pointer Section 5 Concern The glycomics section is uneven. While the authors discuss CandyCrunch, DeepGlyco, GlycoCompute, and GlycanGT, they do not mention several other important approaches, such as the use of transformers for glycan sequence representation, graph neural networks for glycan property prediction, or the growing literature on glycan-focused foundation models. The discussion of data resources (Table 2) is brief and does not critically evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of each resource. The section on explainable AI is also thin, with only two examples discussed. Why it matters A review should provide a comprehensive and balanced survey of the field. If important approaches are omitted, the review's utility as a reference is diminished, and readers may not be aware of the full range of available tools. Resolution test The authors should expand the glycomics section to include a more comprehensive survey of AI methods, including those they may have overlooked. They should also provide a more critical evaluation of the data resources and discuss the trade-offs between different approaches. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility Claim pointer The authors describe several AI tools and their reported performance metrics (e.g., CandyCrunch top-1 accuracy 90.3%, XGBoost AUC 0.917) but do not provide sufficient details on how these metrics were obtained or whether they are reproducible. Evidence pointer Section 3.4.2, Section 5.4 Concern The manuscript does not provide details on the datasets, training/validation splits, or evaluation protocols used to obtain the reported performance metrics. This makes it difficult for readers to assess the reliability of these numbers or to reproduce the results. The authors also do not discuss potential sources of bias or overfitting in the reported results. Why it matters Reproducibility is a cornerstone of scientific research. Without clear details on evaluation methodology, the reported performance metrics cannot be independently verified, and the claims based on them are weakened. Resolution test The authors should provide more details on the evaluation protocols, including dataset descriptions, splits, and metrics. They should also discuss potential limitations and sources of bias in the reported results. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Section 2.2.1 Evidence pointer Text describing GlycoPredictor Issue The description of the GlycoPredictor model is dense and could be clearer. The authors mention "approximately 10,434 reactions" and a "734-reaction Barresi–Hindsgaul dataset" but do not explain why these specific datasets were chosen or how they differ. Required correction Provide a brief explanation of the datasets and their relevance, and consider breaking the description into smaller, more digestible paragraphs. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Section 4.1.2 Evidence pointer Text discussing AlphaFold3 Issue The term "first-class molecular entities" is vague and not standard terminology in structural biology. It is unclear what the authors mean by this phrase. Required correction Replace with a more precise description, such as "treated as explicit components of the molecular system being modeled" or similar. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Consistency Affected element Section 5.4 Evidence pointer Text discussing CDG Issue The authors mention "circulating miRNA profiles" as a biomarker for PMM2-CDG but do not explain why miRNA profiles are relevant to a disorder caused by a defect in protein glycosylation. The connection is not obvious. Required correction Add a brief explanation of the rationale for using miRNA profiles in this context, or remove the example if it is not directly relevant. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Readability Affected element Section 6 (Conclusions) Evidence pointer Text in conclusions Issue The conclusions section is largely a summary of the main sections and does not provide a forward-looking perspective or a clear statement of the most important open problems. Required correction Add a paragraph that explicitly identifies the top 3-5 challenges that need to be addressed for AI to realize its potential in glycosylation research, and suggest potential solutions or research directions. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Section 4.3.2 Evidence pointer Text discussing cryo-EM Issue The discussion of AI-assisted cryo-EM is brief and does not mention specific tools or methods beyond ModelAngelo. There are other AI-based approaches for cryo-EM map interpretation that could be mentioned. Required correction Consider adding a brief discussion of other AI-based cryo-EM tools and their applicability to glycoproteins. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The manuscript's central thesis that AI is transforming glycosylation research is plausible but not fully established. The uncritical treatment of AlphaFold3 (R1-M1) and the overstatement of clinical actionability (R1-M2) are the most significant technical failings. The lack of detail on evaluation protocols (R1-M4) also undermines the credibility of the reported performance metrics. These issues need to be addressed before the review can be considered a reliable guide to the field. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality The "glycan language" framework is a useful organizing principle, but the individual topics covered are not new. The review does not present a novel synthesis or a unique perspective that would distinguish it from other recent reviews on AI in glycosylation. Scientific importance The topic is important, as glycosylation is a ubiquitous and understudied modification with major implications for human health. A comprehensive and critical review would be valuable. However, the current manuscript does not fully deliver on this promise. Interdisciplinary readership The manuscript is likely to appeal to researchers in glycobiology and computational biology, but the lack of depth in some sections may limit its appeal to experts in either field. The writing is generally accessible but could be improved with clearer explanations of technical concepts. Technical soundness The technical soundness is mixed. The descriptions of individual tools are generally accurate, but the overall argument is weakened by the uncritical treatment of AF3 and the lack of detail on evaluation protocols. Readability for nonspecialists The manuscript is generally readable, but some sections are dense and assume prior knowledge of both glycosylation and AI. The authors could improve accessibility by providing more background and defining key terms. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The manuscript has the potential to be a useful review, but the authors need to address the concerns raised above, particularly the uncritical treatment of AlphaFold3 and the overstatement of clinical actionability. A more balanced and critical perspective would significantly strengthen the manuscript. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that glycan language models are "becoming clinically actionable" (Section 5.3) is not supported by the evidence presented. The claim that AlphaFold3 treats glycans as "first-class molecular entities" (Section 4.1.2) is an overstatement and not supported by the literature. The reported performance metrics for various tools (e.g., CandyCrunch top-1 accuracy 90.3%, XGBoost AUC 0.917) are presented without sufficient detail on evaluation methodology, making them difficult to assess. The claim that the MCTS1–JAK2–IFN-γ axis example demonstrates the utility of AI for glycoprotein structure-function analysis (Section 4.1.2) is not clearly supported, as the authors note this involves a non-glycosylated signaling axis. The statement that "AI is now laying down new methodological foundations at every link along that chain" (Section 6) is a broad generalization that is not fully supported by the specific examples discussed.

concluding remarks) as provided by the user. No supplementary figures, tables, or appendices were included in the supplied material. Assessment boundary The review is limited to the content of the provided manuscript text. Claims, figures, tables, and supplementary materials referenced but not supplied are noted as such and assessed only insofar as they are described in the text. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose a thermodynamic framework that uses spectral phasor trajectories to extract quantitative protein stability parameters (ΔG°w and m-values) from fluorescence denaturation data, explicitly accounting for changes in fluorescence quantum yield between states. The framework is validated on simulated two- and three-state data and applied to published urea-induced unfolding of E. coli OmpA and SDS-induced denaturation of A. fulgidus CopA, with the latter revealing three transitions where conventional intensity analysis resolved only two. Visible evidence base The manuscript text includes equations (1)–(22), descriptions of Figures 1–4 and S1–S7, Table 1 (referenced but not shown), and references to published datasets. No raw data, code, or full figures are available in the supplied material. Missing materials affecting confidence Supplementary figures (S1–S7), Table 1, Table S1, the Python scripts mentioned in the Acknowledgments, and the full published datasets for OmpA and AfCopA are not provided. These are essential for independent verification of the fitting results, confidence intervals, and the claimed agreement with published thermodynamic parameters. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript presents a conceptually interesting extension of spectral phasor analysis from a qualitative to a quantitative thermodynamic tool. The mathematical derivation linking phasor distances to molecular fractions via quantum yield corrections is sound in principle and addresses a real limitation of prior phasor-based approaches. The validation on simulated data is a strength, and the application to OmpA provides a useful benchmark. However, the central claim that the method resolves intermediates invisible to conventional analysis rests on a single experimental system (AfCopA) for which the full dataset, fitting details, and statistical comparisons are not fully visible in the supplied text. The manuscript would be strengthened by clearer presentation of the fitting procedures, error analysis, and the conditions under which the method fails or becomes unreliable. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in protein biophysics, particularly those studying membrane protein folding and stability, would find this work relevant. The method offers a way to extract thermodynamic parameters from fluorescence data without assuming constant quantum yield, which is a common but often unverified assumption. The ability to resolve hidden intermediates could be of interest to those working on multidomain proteins and intrinsically disordered proteins. The work may also appeal to method developers in fluorescence spectroscopy and data analysis. Major strengths The mathematical framework is clearly derived and addresses a genuine gap in the field. The use of simulated data to validate the approach before applying it to experimental systems is methodologically sound. The demonstration that ignoring quantum yield differences leads to incorrect ΔG° values is an important cautionary result. The application to a membrane protein with multiple transitions showcases the potential of the method to reveal complexity that conventional analysis misses. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors claim that the proposed formalism accurately recovers thermodynamic parameters from simulated three-state data and that phasor analysis reveals two intermediates in AfCopA denaturation that are not resolvable by conventional intensity analysis. Evidence pointer Section 2.1, Figure 2; Section 2.3, Figures 4–5; Table 1 (not provided); Table S1 (not provided) Concern The validation of the three-state model relies on simulated data with specific assumptions about spectral properties and quantum yields. The text states that a three-state model can fit the total intensity data and recover the true parameters only in the absence of error, and that 1% random error leads to substantially different estimates. This raises questions about the robustness of the method when applied to real, noisy data. For the AfCopA dataset, the authors report that the three-state intensity model shows bias at high SDS mole fractions and that a four-state model is overparameterized. The phasor analysis identifies three transitions, but the statistical significance of the improvement over the two-transition model is not quantified in the supplied text. The claim that the method resolves hidden intermediates would be substantially strengthened by a formal model comparison (e.g., AICc differences, F-tests) and by showing that the recovered parameters are stable across replicate experiments or bootstrap resampling. Why it matters The central novelty of the manuscript is the ability to resolve intermediates that conventional analysis misses. If the method is not robust to noise or if the improvement in fit is not statistically significant, the claim is not established. The manuscript currently provides insufficient evidence to distinguish between a genuine improvement in resolution and an artifact of overfitting. Resolution test Provide a formal statistical comparison between the two- and three-transition models for the AfCopA data, including AICc values, parameter uncertainties, and confidence intervals. Show that the recovered parameters are reproducible across independent experimental replicates or through bootstrap analysis. Demonstrate the method's performance on simulated data with noise levels comparable to the experimental data. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The authors state that the relative distance in phasor space equals the fraction of photons from the denatured state, and that Equation (14) relates this to the molecular fraction via quantum yields. They further claim that fitting Equation (16) without accounting for quantum yield differences leads to incorrect ΔG° values. Evidence pointer Section 2.1, Equations (7)–(16); Section 2.2, Figure 3E–F and Figure S5 (not provided) Concern The derivation of Equation (14) is referenced to Appendix A, which is not provided in the supplied material. The relationship between photon fractions and molecular fractions is critical to the entire framework, and the derivation must be shown in full to allow readers to verify its correctness. Additionally, the authors state that fitting Equation (16) with ϕN = ϕD leads to incorrect ΔG° values, but the magnitude of the error and the conditions under which this error becomes significant are not quantified. For the OmpA dataset, the authors report that the phasor-based and intensity-based analyses agree, but the text does not specify whether the quantum yield correction was applied in this case or whether the quantum yields of the native and denatured states were similar enough that the correction was negligible. Why it matters The entire method hinges on the correct conversion of phasor distances to molecular fractions. If the derivation is flawed or if the quantum yield correction is not applied correctly, the recovered thermodynamic parameters will be biased. The manuscript must provide the full derivation and demonstrate the sensitivity of the results to the quantum yield values used. Resolution test Include the full derivation from Appendix A in the main text or supplementary material. Provide a sensitivity analysis showing how the recovered ΔG° and m-values change as a function of the quantum yield ratio ϕN/ϕD. For the OmpA dataset, explicitly state whether the quantum yield correction was applied and report the quantum yield values used. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Reproducibility Claim pointer The authors state that the method was applied to published data on OmpA and to their own AfCopA data, and that the results agree with previously reported thermodynamic parameters. Evidence pointer Section 2.2, Figure 3; Section 2.3, Figures 4–5; Table 1 (not provided) Concern The manuscript does not provide sufficient detail on how the published OmpA data were digitized and processed. The text mentions that spectra were digitized, but the resolution of the digitization, the number of data points, and the wavelength range are not specified. For the AfCopA data, the fitting procedures are described in general terms, but the specific initial guesses, parameter bounds, and convergence criteria are not given. The Python scripts mentioned in the Acknowledgments are not provided, making it difficult for others to reproduce the analysis. Why it matters Reproducibility is a core requirement for method papers. Without access to the data processing scripts and detailed fitting protocols, other researchers cannot apply the method to their own data or verify the results independently. Resolution test Provide the Python scripts as supplementary material, along with a detailed description of the digitization procedure, data processing steps, and fitting protocols. Include the digitized OmpA data and the AfCopA dataset as supplementary files. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Readability Affected element Section 2.1, Equations (7)–(16) Evidence pointer Section 2.1 Issue The derivation of the relationship between phasor distance and molecular fraction is dense and would benefit from a step-by-step explanation in the main text, particularly for readers not familiar with phasor analysis. Required correction Add a brief intuitive explanation of why the phasor distance is proportional to the photon fraction, and how the quantum yield correction modifies this relationship. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Section 2.3, Figure 5 Evidence pointer Section 2.3 Issue The text states that the three transitions in AfCopA denaturation were identified from linear regions in the phasor plot, but it is not clear how the boundaries between these regions were determined objectively. Required correction Describe the criteria used to identify the linear segments in the phasor trajectory, or state that the boundaries were determined by visual inspection. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Section 3.6, Equation (20) Evidence pointer Section 3.6 Issue The quantum yield determination method is described, but the absorbance values used in Equation (20) are not reported for the OmpA and AfCopA datasets. Required correction Report the absorbance values at the excitation wavelength for the samples used for quantum yield determination, or state that these values are provided in the supplementary material. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The full derivation of Equation (14) must be provided. The statistical comparison between the two- and three-transition models for AfCopA must be quantified. The sensitivity of the results to the quantum yield correction must be demonstrated. The reproducibility of the analysis must be ensured by providing the scripts and data. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The work is original in its application of phasor analysis to quantitative thermodynamics, but the underlying mathematics is not novel. Scientific importance: The method could be useful for studying membrane protein stability, but its impact depends on the robustness of the results, which is not fully established. Interdisciplinary readership: The work is primarily of interest to biophysicists and spectroscopists; the broader interdisciplinary appeal is limited. Technical soundness: The mathematical framework is plausible, but the validation is incomplete, particularly regarding noise robustness and statistical significance. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is written for a specialist audience and assumes familiarity with phasor analysis and thermodynamic models; the introduction and methods sections are not accessible to a general scientific audience. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The core idea is promising and the simulated validation is a good start, but the manuscript does not currently provide sufficient evidence to establish the central claim of resolving hidden intermediates. The missing derivation, lack of statistical comparison, and incomplete reproducibility details must be addressed before the case is made. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that phasor analysis resolves two intermediates in AfCopA denaturation is not supported by a formal statistical comparison with the two-state model. The claim that the recovered thermodynamic parameters agree with previously published values for OmpA cannot be fully assessed without access to the digitized data and the original publication's values. The claim that the method is robust to noise is not supported, as the text states that 1% error leads to substantially different parameter estimates in the three-state simulation. The relationship between phasor distance and molecular fraction (Equation (14)) is not verifiable without the full derivation from Appendix A. The quantum yield values for the OmpA and AfCopA states are not reported, making it impossible to assess the magnitude of the correction applied.

The central proposal of water-mediated proton shuttling during sequential fluorine elimination is chemically plausible and builds on prior experimental work. However, several technical aspects require clarification and additional validation before the mechanistic conclusions can be considered fully established. The electrostatic analysis methodology, in particular, needs more rigorous justification, and the relationship between computed barriers and experimental observations should be addressed more explicitly. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in computational enzymology, medicinal chemistry, and cancer metabolism would find interest. Those working on PLP-dependent enzymes and mechanism-based inactivators would value the proposed water-assisted elimination pathway. Drug discovery groups targeting hOAT for hepatocellular carcinoma therapy would benefit from the residue-level insights for inhibitor design. Major strengths The study addresses a clinically relevant target with a clear experimental foundation. The combination of MD and QM/MM methods is appropriate for the questions posed. The identification of specific residues that promote or suppress fluorine elimination provides testable hypotheses. The water-bridge mechanism offers a novel explanation for how the elimination proceeds without high-energy direct proton transfer. Major Concerns The electrostatic analysis methodology lacks sufficient detail and validation. The relationship between computed free energy barriers and experimental kinetic data is not discussed. The QM region size and level of theory may be insufficient for accurate barrier calculations. The manuscript does not address potential alternative mechanisms or validate the chosen reaction coordinate. Minor Comments Several figure references appear without adequate in-text explanation. The Boltzmann weighting procedure is not fully described. The manuscript contains some redundancy in the results and discussion sections. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M4 Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality: The water-mediated proton-shuttle mechanism for fluorine elimination in hOAT inhibition is a novel proposal that extends prior experimental work. Scientific importance: The work has potential significance for understanding mechanism-based inactivation of PLP enzymes and for designing improved hOAT inhibitors, though the direct therapeutic impact is indirect. Interdisciplinary readership: The topic bridges enzymology, computational chemistry, and cancer biology, but the presentation is heavily computational and may not fully engage experimental or clinical readers. Technical soundness: The QM/MM methodology is standard, but several technical details require clarification and the electrostatic analysis needs stronger validation. Readability for nonspecialists: The manuscript is generally clear but assumes familiarity with QM/MM terminology and would benefit from more contextual explanation of computational methods. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The electrostatic analysis identifies Arg180 and Gly42 as promoting fluorine elimination and Phe177 as suppressing it, with the claim that these effects are significant (|ΔEi−0| > 1 kcal/mol) Evidence pointer Section 2.2, Figure 4 Concern The electrostatic decomposition method is described only by a single equation with no derivation, no validation against known systems, and no discussion of its limitations. The approach of setting residue charges to zero and recomputing barriers is a crude approximation that may not capture the full electrostatic effect, particularly for charged residues like Arg180 where charge neutralization could cause significant structural reorganization. The manuscript does not specify whether geometries were re-optimized for each residue deletion or whether single-point calculations were used, which substantially affects interpretation. Additionally, the threshold of 1 kcal/mol for significance is not justified, and no error estimates or convergence checks are provided. Why it matters The residue-specific conclusions are a central deliverable of the paper and are presented as actionable insights for drug design. If the electrostatic analysis is not robust, these conclusions may be misleading. The lack of methodological detail prevents readers from assessing the reliability of these findings. Resolution test Provide a detailed description of the electrostatic analysis protocol, including whether geometries were re-optimized, how the charge deletion was implemented, and how convergence was assessed. Validate the method on a test system with known electrostatic effects. Include error estimates or replicate calculations to demonstrate robustness. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The manuscript reports Boltzmann-weighted average energy barriers of 13.0, 10.8, 16.0, 17.7, and 24.5 kcal/mol for various steps, and states that the overall reaction energies are −10.6 and −29.9 kcal/mol for the two elimination stages Evidence pointer Sections 2.3, 2.4, 2.5, Figure 5, Figure 7 Concern The Boltzmann weighting procedure is referenced to Method S1 in the Supporting Information, but the main text does not describe how many conformations were sampled, how they were selected, or how the weighting was applied. The manuscript also does not report the range of individual barrier heights across the sampled conformations, which is critical for assessing whether the reported averages are meaningful. Furthermore, the relationship between these computed barriers and the experimental observation that approximately 8% of BCF3 proceeds to irreversible inactivation is not discussed. A computed barrier of 10.8 kcal/mol would imply very rapid reaction kinetics that may be inconsistent with the experimental yield. Why it matters The quantitative barrier heights are the primary quantitative output of the study. Without understanding the distribution of values and their relationship to experiment, readers cannot assess whether the computed mechanism is kinetically consistent with observed behavior. Resolution test Report the number of conformations used for Boltzmann averaging, the range of individual barriers, and the weighting scheme. Discuss how the computed barriers relate to the experimentally observed 8% inactivation yield and the time-dependent fluoride accumulation. If the barriers are inconsistent with experiment, explain the discrepancy. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness Claim pointer The QM/MM calculations use the M06-2x/def2-SVP//CHARMM27 level for geometry optimization and M06-2x/def2-TZVP//CHARMM27 for single-point energies, with a QM region of 87 atoms for the Fα− elimination stage Evidence pointer Section 3.2 Concern The choice of def2-SVP for geometry optimization is a relatively small basis set for a system involving fluoride elimination, where accurate description of the leaving group and any anionic character is critical. The manuscript does not provide benchmark calculations or comparisons with larger basis sets or alternative functionals to justify this choice. Additionally, the QM region of 87 atoms, while substantial, may not capture all relevant electrostatic effects from the protein environment, particularly for a reaction involving charge separation. The manuscript does not report tests of QM region size effects on the computed barriers. Why it matters The accuracy of the computed barriers and the proposed mechanism depends critically on the QM level of theory and the size of the QM region. Without validation, the quantitative conclusions are uncertain. Resolution test Provide benchmark calculations comparing def2-SVP with larger basis sets (e.g., def2-TZVP for optimization) for representative stationary points. Test the sensitivity of the computed barriers to QM region size by including additional residues or using a larger QM region. Report the effect on the key barrier heights. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Scientific importance Claim pointer The manuscript claims that the water-mediated proton-shuttle mechanism provides an atomistic explanation for the superior inhibitory potency of the bis-trifluoromethyl scaffold compared with monofluorinated or monotrifluoromethyl analogues Evidence pointer Sections 2.1, 2.3, 2.4, Conclusions Concern The manuscript does not present any comparative calculations on monofluorinated or monotrifluoromethyl analogues to support this claim. The argument appears to rest on the qualitative observation that two fluorine atoms provide two elimination steps, but no quantitative comparison of barriers or binding affinities is provided. Without such comparative data, the claim that the mechanism explains the superior potency of the bis-trifluoromethyl scaffold is speculative. Why it matters The comparative potency of different inhibitors is a key experimental observation that the computational model should explain. If the model cannot distinguish between analogues, its predictive value for drug design is limited. Resolution test Perform QM/MM calculations on the monofluorinated and monotrifluoromethyl analogues to compare their elimination barriers and binding modes with BCF3. If such calculations are not feasible, clearly state this limitation and temper the claim accordingly. curcumin、α-bromocurcumin、α-chlorocurcumin 与 Aβ1-42 的结合，发现 α-chlorocurcumin 表观亲和力最高（Kd 285 nM vs curcumin 524 nM）且伴随最大的 218 nm CD 信号衰减（1 μM 时 35%），但作者明确声明这些数据不能证明抑制寡聚化或纤维化。 03 研究问题 具体问题：α-位卤素取代（Br、Cl）如何改变 curcumin 与 Aβ1-42 的结合亲和力、结合热力学（ΔH/ΔS/ΔG）以及配体诱导的 Aβ1-42 二级结构变化？ 为什么重要：Aβ1-42 的 β-sheet 富集与寡聚/纤维化相关；curcumin 已知可结合 Aβ 并降低 β-sheet 含量，但 α-卤代衍生物的定量结合与构象效应未知（Introduction 明确写 "still unknown"）。 现有方法为何不足：已有研究多报道 curcumin 与 Aβ 的结合或抗聚集活性，但缺乏对 α-卤代衍生物的定量 Kd/Ka、化学计量 n、温度依赖热力学与 CD 构象响应的系统比较；且多数研究未区分「结合」与「抑制聚集」。 精确研究问题（Can ... ?）：Can α-halogenation of curcumin produce a derivative (specifically α-chlorocurcumin) that binds Aβ1-42 with higher affinity and induces larger secondary-structure alteration than the parent curcumin, under identical in vitro conditions? 04 背景与发展脉络 （本节脉络为「仅本文框架」，除标注处外未做外部核验） - 阶段 1：Aβ1-42 作为 AD 核心病理肽，由 APP 经 β-/γ-secretase 顺序切割产生，比短链 Aβ 更易聚集，形成可溶寡聚体与纤维（Introduction）。 - 阶段 2：curcumin 作为天然多酚，报道具抗氧化、抗炎、神经保护、抑制 NF-κB、降低 MDA/nitrite/AChE，并在体外/体内抑制 Aβ 聚集、降低 β-sheet 含量、解聚纤维（Introduction 引文 8–17）。 - 阶段 3：curcumin 类似物的结构–活性研究，包括芳香族衍生物抗聚集活性优于 curcumin（Lakey-Beitia et al.，引文 37），说明修饰位点不限于 α-位。 - 阶段 4：Pham 和 Bader（引文 27,28）合成并用单晶 X 射线衍射、UV-vis、DFT、Hirshfeld 表面分析表征 α-bromocurcumin 与 α-chlorocurcumin，显示更高热稳定性、更高分子平面性、更短 π–π 堆积距离，水溶性约与母体相当。 - 本文主张的位置：把上述合成/结构表征推进到「与 Aβ1-42 的定量结合 + 构象响应」层面，主张 α-卤代（尤其 α-氯代）调节结合与结构效应，但明确不主张抗聚集功效。 05 盲对接，比较三种 curcuminoid。 2) 核心洞察：α-位取代基的身份（Cl vs Br vs H）而非「卤代」这一类别本身决定结合优势——α-chlorocurcumin 亲和力最高（Kd 285 nM，Ka 3.66×10⁶ M⁻¹），α-bromocurcumin 反而弱于 curcumin（Kd 441 nM vs 524 nM，但 Ka 2.32×10⁶ vs 1.87×10⁶ M⁻¹，两法排序不一致）；同时 α-氯代把结合从「熵驱动为主」推向「焓驱动为主」（ΔH 从 −20.8 到 −34.0 kJ/mol，ΔS 从 43.7 到 14.3 J/mol/K）。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis]：在配体–淀粉样肽研究中，淬灭幅度、Scatchard 与非线性拟合给出的排序可能不一致，必须交叉验证；热力学分解可提示结合机制类别（焓 vs 熵）但不能定位残基；对接只应作为结构假设生成器，其分数不可替代实验亲和力。 07 方法总览 输入：Aβ1-42 单体（HFIP 处理成膜、DMSO 复溶、稀释入 20 mM HEPES/KOH pH 7.4，0.1 μM）；curcumin / α-bromocurcumin / α-chlorocurcumin（DMSO 母液 50 mM，工作浓度 0–1.0 μM）；对接用 PDB 6SZF text provided (Abstract, Introduction, Results, Discussion, Materials and Methods, Conclusions, Acknowledgments). No separate supplementary materials, raw data files, or line-numbered submission file were supplied. Assessment boundary Evaluation is limited to the claims and evidence contained in the supplied text. No independent verification of data, no access to primary spectra, fitted residuals, docking files, or statistical outputs. Assessment does not presume the manuscript belongs to any specific journal. Shared manuscript claim summary α-Halogenated curcumins (α-bromocurcumin, α-chlorocurcumin) bind Aβ1-42 with binding properties differing from parent curcumin; α-chlorocurcumin shows the highest apparent affinity (Kd ≈ 285 nM) and the most favorable binding free energy; binding is temperature-dependent and thermodynamically favorable; binding is accompanied by changes in Aβ1-42 secondary structure that are more pronounced for the halogenated derivatives; molecular docking predicts a binding pose for α-chlorocurcumin involving Glu22 and Gln15. Visible evidence base Fluorescence titration data (Figures 2, 3, 5A, 5B), Scatchard analysis (Figure 4, Table 1), temperature-dependent Kd (Table 2), Van 't Hoff and thermodynamic parameters (Figure 6, Table 3), molecular docking (Figure 7), far-UV CD spectra and deconvolution (Figures 8, 9, 10), cross-reactivity fluorescence panel (Figure 11), and Methods sections 4.1–4.9. Missing materials affecting confidence No raw fluorescence titration curves with residuals, no representative CD spectra with error bands for all ligands, no aggregation assays (ThT, TEM, AFM), no controls for ligand intrinsic fluorescence/absorbance at 280 nm, no docking validation or control docking, no replicate-level data, no statistical tables for CD comparisons, no line numbers. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a focused and potentially useful question, namely how α-halogenation of curcumin alters binding to Aβ1-42 and the associated conformational response. The topic is relevant to amyloid biology and to structure–activity exploration of curcuminoids. However, the central quantitative claims rest on fluorescence quenching and Scatchard analysis that are not fully substantiated by the presented material, and the conformational claims are weakened by internal inconsistencies between the CD narrative and the stated deconvolution approach. The docking is presented as supporting evidence but is not experimentally validated. The manuscript is generally candid about several limitations, which is a strength, but the evidence as supplied does not yet establish the core binding and structural conclusions with the rigor implied by the abstract and conclusions. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in amyloid biology, Alzheimer's disease drug discovery, and natural-product medicinal chemistry would be interested because curcuminoids are widely studied anti-amyloid scaffolds and α-halogenation is a plausible route to tune binding and conformational effects. The work would also interest groups performing ligand–peptide binding studies by fluorescence and CD, since the methodological caveats raised here are broadly relevant. Major strengths The study compares parent curcumin with two defined α-halogenated derivatives under matched conditions, which is a reasonable comparative design. The manuscript explicitly acknowledges several interpretive limits, including that quenching magnitude does not establish affinity, that ellipticity at 218 nm does not directly measure β-sheet content, and that docking scores are computational estimates. The inclusion of temperature-dependent measurements and thermodynamic analysis adds a dimension beyond simple endpoint binding. The cross-reactivity panel, while limited, is a useful attempt to assess preferential response. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / binding quantification Claim pointer α-Chlorocurcumin exhibits higher binding affinity for Aβ1-42 (Kd ≈ 285 nM) than curcumin (Kd ≈ 524 nM), with α-bromocurcumin intermediate (Kd ≈ 441 nM). Evidence pointer Figures 2, 3, 4; Tables 1 and 2; Sections 2.1, 4.3, 4.4 Concern The binding constants are derived from quenching of Aβ1-42 intrinsic fluorescence at 280 nm excitation. The ligands are curcuminoids with extended conjugated aromatic systems that absorb strongly in the 300–450 nm range and may contribute to inner-filter effects and to direct absorbance at or near the excitation/emission wavelengths. The manuscript states that absorbance at the excitation wavelength was maintained below 0.02 and that no inner-filter correction was applied, but no absorbance spectra, no ligand-only emission spectra at 280 nm excitation, and no correction verification are shown. In addition, the Scatchard analysis is applied to the same data already fitted by nonlinear regression, so the two analyses are not independent. The reported agreement between Kd and 1/Ka is therefore expected rather than confirmatory. Why it matters The central quantitative claim of differential affinity, and the specific ranking of α-chlorocurcumin > α-bromocurcumin > curcumin, depends on the validity of the quenching model and on the absence of optical artifacts. If ligand absorbance or ligand emission contributes to the measured signal, the apparent Kd values and the ranking could change. Resolution test Provide ligand-only absorbance and emission spectra under the exact assay conditions, demonstrate that inner-filter effects are negligible or apply and report a validated inner-filter correction, and show that Kd values are stable across at least two independent fitting models and across independent replicate datasets. Report residuals and confidence intervals for each fit. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / model validity Claim pointer Binding stoichiometry (n) values close to unity indicate approximately one-to-one binding for all three curcuminoids. Evidence pointer Table 1; Section 2.1; Section 4.4 Concern The reported n values are 0.89 ± 0.08, 0.92 ± 0.04, and 1.08 ± 0.06. The manuscript acknowledges deviation from unity but attributes it to variability or model limitations without testing alternative binding models. The Scatchard equation as written in Section 4.4 contains a term [R − Q][Aβ1-42]T whose dimensional consistency and derivation are not explained, and the relationship between Q, [C], and the fitted parameters is not fully specified. No simulation or goodness-of-fit comparison against a two-site or cooperative model is presented. Why it matters If binding is not one-to-one, the interpretation of Kd and Ka as intrinsic affinities is not warranted, and the comparison across compounds may reflect different binding modes rather than different affinities. Resolution test Present the full binding equation with defined units, compare fits for one-site, two-site, and cooperative models using information criteria, and report whether the data support a single-site model. Provide simulated datasets to show the expected n distribution under the stated noise level. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / structural interpretation Claim pointer α-Halogenated curcumins induce more pronounced secondary-structure changes in Aβ1-42, with α-chlorocurcumin reducing β-sheet content from 100% to 65% at 1000 nM and increasing α-helical content. Evidence pointer Figures 8, 9, 10; Sections 2.5, 4.8, 4.9 Concern There is an internal inconsistency in the CD analysis. Section 4.8 states that secondary-structure composition was estimated using CDNN deconvolution from full spectra and that ellipticity at 218 nm was not converted into β-sheet or α-helical percentages. Section 4.9 states that spectra were deconvoluted using the CONTIN algorithm on DICHROWEB. Section 2.5 reports a reduction of β-sheet content from 100% to 65% and an increase in α-helical content, which is a quantitative secondary-structure claim. The manuscript does not reconcile the use of CDNN versus CONTIN, does not present the deconvolution output tables, and does not report errors on the secondary-structure percentages. In addition, the CD samples contain curcuminoids at concentrations up to 1 μM, and the compound-only background subtraction is stated but not shown; residual ligand contributions to the far-UV CD signal are not excluded. Why it matters The claim that halogenation produces greater conformational change, and the specific β-sheet-to-α-helix interpretation, are central to the structural conclusion. Without consistent deconvolution methodology, reported percentages, and ligand artifact controls, the structural claim is not established. Resolution test State a single deconvolution method, provide full deconvolution output tables with errors for each ligand and concentration, show compound-only CD spectra at all concentrations, and demonstrate that background subtraction removes ligand contributions. Report replicate-level secondary-structure percentages and the statistical test used. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Technical soundness / computational evidence Claim pointer Molecular docking predicts that α-chlorocurcumin occupies a defined binding pocket and forms hydrogen bonds with Glu22 and Gln15, with additional π-cation, π–π stacking, and π-alkyl contacts. Evidence pointer Figure 7; Sections 2.4, 4.7 Concern Docking was performed with a blind grid covering the entire peptide, and the top-scoring pose is reported. No control docking with parent curcumin under identical conditions is presented, so the claim that α-chlorocurcumin has a specific or favorable predicted binding mode relative to curcumin is not supported. The docking score of −5.7 kcal/mol is reported without comparison to a decoy set, without redocking validation against the 6SZF structure, and without reporting the score distribution across poses. The choice of the fifth position for chlorine addition is stated but not justified relative to the synthesized compound. Why it matters Docking is used to provide a structural hypothesis for the binding preference. Without comparative docking and validation, the predicted contacts cannot be interpreted as specific to α-chlorocurcumin or as supporting the affinity ranking. Resolution test Report docking of curcumin and α-bromocurcumin under identical grid and parameter settings, report score distributions and pose clusters, validate the docking protocol by redocking a known ligand or by RMSD assessment, and confirm that the modeled chlorine position matches the synthesized α-chlorocurcumin. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Scientific importance / functional relevance Claim pointer The findings suggest that α-halogenated curcumins may modulate the structural behavior of Aβ1-42 and potentially influence its aggregation propensity. Evidence pointer Abstract; Sections 2.5, 3, 5 Concern No aggregation assay is presented. The manuscript explicitly states that the findings do not provide direct evidence for inhibition of oligomerization or fibril formation, yet the abstract and conclusions frame the results in terms of modulation of Aβ-related processes and potential influence on aggregation propensity. The link between binding, CD spectral change, and aggregation behavior is asserted as a basis for further investigation rather than demonstrated. Why it matters The stated significance of the work depends on its relevance to amyloid aggregation. Without ThT kinetics, oligomerization assays, or morphological analysis, the functional implication remains speculative. Resolution test Either add aggregation assays under matched conditions or revise the abstract and conclusions to restrict claims to binding and conformational changes, removing language that implies aggregation modulation. Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Technical soundness / specificity Claim pointer α-Chlorocurcumin shows a preferential fluorescence response to Aβ1-42 among the tested biomolecules. Evidence pointer Figure 11; Sections 2.6, 4.3 Concern The cross-reactivity panel includes free amino acids, collagen, gelatin, and BSA, but not related amyloidogenic peptides or proteins. The manuscript acknowledges this limitation. In addition, the assay uses a different fluorescence mode (excitation 430 nm, emission 537 nm) from the binding experiments (excitation 280 nm, emission 332 nm), and the relationship between the two readouts is not established. The statistical reporting is inconsistent, with ** p < 0.001 stated in Section 2.6 while Section 4.9 defines significance as p < 0.05. Why it matters The specificity claim is weak without relevant comparators, and the inconsistent significance thresholds raise concerns about statistical reporting. Resolution test Include at least one related amyloidogenic peptide or protein as a comparator, clarify the relationship between the two fluorescence readouts, and harmonize the statistical significance threshold across sections. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (binding quantification and inner-filter control), R1-M2 (binding model validity and stoichiometry), R1-M3 (CD deconvolution consistency and ligand artifact control). These are blocking because the central affinity ranking and the central structural claim cannot be established from the supplied evidence without them. R1-M4, R1-M5, and R1-M6 are non-blocking but materially weaken the specificity, computational, and functional relevance claims. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality is moderate. The comparison of α-halogenated curcumins with parent curcumin is a reasonable incremental extension of known curcumin–Aβ work, but the conceptual advance is limited and no new mechanism is established. Scientific importance is currently limited because the study reports binding and spectral changes without demonstrating functional consequences for aggregation or toxicity. Interdisciplinary readership potential is modest, as the work sits at the interface of medicinal chemistry and amyloid biophysics but does not yet provide broadly generalizable insight. Technical soundness is the main weakness, with unresolved issues in binding quantification, model selection, and CD analysis. Readability for nonspecialists is acceptable in the Introduction and Discussion, but the Results contain internal inconsistencies and undefined terms that would hinder a general audience. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript would become supportive if the binding analysis is validated with inner-filter controls and model comparison, the CD methodology is reconciled and reported with full deconvolution outputs and ligand controls, and the docking is made comparative and validated. The aggregation-related framing should be removed or supported by direct aggregation data. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that α-chlorocurcumin has higher binding affinity than curcumin is supported only by fluorescence quenching data that lack demonstrated inner-filter correction and independent confirmation. Status: weak. The claim that binding stoichiometry is approximately one-to-one is not supported by model comparison and rests on n values with overlapping errors. Status: weak. The claim that α-chlorocurcumin reduces β-sheet content from 100% to 65% and increases α-helical content is not supported by a consistent, fully reported deconvolution analysis and lacks ligand artifact controls. Status: weak. The claim that α-halogenation produces more pronounced structural alterations than curcumin is based on ellipticity changes at 218 nm that the manuscript itself states do not directly measure β-sheet content. Status: weak. The claim that α-chlorocurcumin forms specific hydrogen bonds with Glu22 and Gln15 is a computational prediction without experimental validation or comparative docking. Status: unsupported as a specific interaction claim. The claim that these compounds may modulate aggregation propensity or inhibit Aβ aggregation is not supported by any aggregation assay. Status: unsupported. The claim of preferential specificity for Aβ1-42 over other biomolecules is not supported because the comparator panel lacks related amyloidogenic peptides and proteins. Status: weak. The thermodynamic interpretation that halogenation alters enthalpic and entropic contributions is internally consistent with the Van 't Hoff analysis, but the reliability depends on the accuracy of the underlying Kd values, which are affected by R1-M1 and R1-M2. Status: conditionally supported pending resolution of binding concerns.

AI 驱动的药物重定位在抗真菌领域的效果远不如抗细菌和抗病毒领域？哪些生物物理和计算层面的瓶颈导致了这一差距？如何通过下一代计算与实验融合策略克服这些瓶颈？ 为什么重要 ：侵袭性真菌感染每年导致超过 150 万死亡，且现有抗真菌药物仅有三大类（多烯类、唑类、棘白菌素类），耐药性日益严重。传统新药研发周期超过十年且耗资数十亿美元，AI 驱动的药物重定位是加速应对耐药危机的关键路径。 现有方法为何不足 ： 现有 AI 框架（如深度学习筛选、分子对接）最初是针对细菌和病毒靶点开发和验证的，直接迁移到真菌靶点面临真核同源性问题； 真菌靶蛋白在 PDB 中的实验结构严重匮乏，配体结合复合物更少； 标准分子对接和深度学习打分函数无法有效区分真菌酶与其人类同源蛋白之间的细微活性位点差异； 现有模型忽略真菌特有的生物物理屏障（细胞壁、生物膜 EPS 基质、形态二态性）。 精确的 "Can ... ?" 1），系统对比各自的结构屏障层级、生物物理传输瓶颈和计算失效模式，并在此基础上提出下一代计算-实验融合策略。 2) 核心洞察 本文的核心洞察在于提出并系统论证了「真核悖论」（eukaryotic paradox）这一概念：真菌药物发现的根本困难不在于缺乏计算工具，而在于真菌与人类宿主之间深层的生物学相似性。这一悖论在三个层面展开： 结构层面 ：真菌必需酶（如 CYP51、Hsp90）与人类同源蛋白的结构相似性使得选择性抑制成为巨大的计算优化挑战； 物理层面 ：真菌细胞壁（几丁质-葡聚糖网络）和生物膜 EPS 基质构成多层级扩散屏障，使计算预测的靶点结合活性无法转化为实际的细胞内药物浓度； 动态层面 ：真菌的形态二态性（酵母↔菌丝）导致靶点蛋白组随感染阶段动态变化，静态结构模型从根本上无法捕捉这一动态性。 基于此，作者主张 AI 药物重定位必须从「纯靶点结合预测」转向「整合物理传输 + 动态生物学」的多尺度建模范式。 3) 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] 同源性不是二元属性而是梯度谱系 ：细菌（原核）与人类（真核）的进化距离远，使得选择性抑制相对容易；真菌与人类的进化距离近，使得选择性成为核心难题。这提示在蛋白质结构相关计算研究中，靶点可成药性评估必须将「与人类蛋白组的相似度」作为关键筛选维度，而非仅关注靶点自身的结构质量。 结构预测 ≠ 功能预测 ：AlphaFold 等工具解决了「静态结构缺失」问题，但无法解决「动态构象变化」「翻译后修饰」「配体诱导适应」等问题。对于构象采样和构象生成课题，这提示需要将结构预测与分子动力学模拟、增强采样方法结合。 计算模型的边界由物理现实决定 ：即使 AI 能完美预测靶点结合，药物分子仍需穿越细胞壁、EPS 基质等物理屏障。这提示分子对接和药物设计课题需要引入「传输感知」的评分函数，而非仅优化结合亲和力。 07 方法总览 本文为综述，无原始方法。但文章描述了 AI 驱动抗真菌药物重定位的整合流程框架： 输入 ：非抗真菌药物库（已批准药物、临床研究药物）；真菌靶蛋白序列（如 ERG11、FKS1、TAC1、CYP51、DHODH）；真菌与人类同源蛋白结构 处理模块 ： 1. 结构预测模块 ：AlphaFold/ESMFold 生成真菌靶蛋白 3D 结构（>98% 蛋白组覆盖率） 2. 虚拟筛选模块 ：分子对接 +
