Acknowledgements). Figures and Supplementary Figures are referenced but not supplied as images; figure legends are not included. Assessment boundary Assessment is restricted to the supplied text. No figure panels, supplementary figures, supplementary tables (including Table S1), raw data, or statistical reporting tables were available. Conclusions that depend on visual inspection of blots, gels, or binding curves cannot be independently verified. Shared manuscript claim summary The manuscript claims that the RNA-binding domain of human GEMIN5 is an extended surface rather than a single motif, comprising (i) a serine-rich flexible loop between helices 19 and 20 near the TPR-like dimerization module and (ii) an acidic cluster within the intrinsically disordered region of the RBS domain, and that these elements cooperatively regulate RNA binding, self-dimerization, recruitment of endogenous GEMIN5, ribosome binding, and cap-dependent translation. Visible evidence base Text describes in vitro EMSA with purified recombinant proteins (D5 and SL1 probes), RNA pulldown from total cytoplasmic extracts using a streptavidin aptamer-tagged D5 RNA, SDS-resistant oligomer analysis by immunoblot, Ni-NTA pulldown for GEMIN5-FLAG recruitment, subcellular fractionation for 80S/S30 ribosome association, luciferase reporter assays under control and GEMIN5-silenced conditions, and AlphaFold-based structural modeling. Quantitative support is asserted but the underlying figures, replicates, and statistics are not visible. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures (Fig 1 to Fig 6), all supplementary figures (Fig S1 to Fig S5), Table S1, figure legends, raw immunoblots and EMSA autoradiographs, binding curves and fitted parameters, densitometric quantification values, replicate numbers per experiment, uncropped images, and the AlphaFold model coordinates or confidence metrics. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a legitimate and interesting question, namely how non-canonical and disordered elements within the C-terminal region of GEMIN5 contribute to RNA recognition. The conceptual framing, that an extended surface including a serine-rich loop and an acidic IDR cluster cooperatively regulates RNA binding, is plausible and consistent with the cited structural literature. However, from the supplied text alone the central claims are not independently verifiable, because the evidence rests on figures that were not provided, on binding assays whose quantitative treatment is only partially described, and on AlphaFold models that are used to support mechanistic conclusions. Several claims, particularly the cooperativity of the two elements, the causal link between self-dimerization and loss of GEMIN5 recruitment, and the interpretation of the translation data, are stated more strongly than the described evidence supports. The work is potentially publishable after technical and interpretive concerns are resolved, but the case is not established from the material supplied. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in RNA biology and RNA-binding protein biochemistry, particularly those working on non-canonical RNA-binding domains, intrinsically disordered regions in RBPs, and autoinhibition or cooperative RNA recognition. Also relevant to groups studying the SMN complex, GEMIN5-associated neurodevelopmental disorders, and translation control. Structural biologists interested in how flexible loops and IDRs contribute to nucleic acid recognition in oligomeric assemblies would find the model-driven hypotheses of interest, provided the models are presented with appropriate uncertainty. Major strengths The question is well motivated and situated within a clear structural context derived from prior Cryo-EM work. The combination of in vitro binding assays with purified proteins and binding assays in the competitive environment of total cell extracts is a sensible strategy to distinguish intrinsic affinity from cellular context. The use of multiple truncation constructs (G5C, TPRα28, TPRα26, TPRα20, TPR, α18–26) provides a systematic scan of the C-terminal helical region. The attempt to connect RNA binding to downstream functional readouts (endogenous GEMIN5 recruitment, ribosome association, translation) is a strength in principle, and the inclusion of the G5C-Leu oligomerization-deficient mutant as a control is appropriate. The discussion links findings to patient variants, which is a reasonable translational framing. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency for the core claim Claim pointer The manuscript claims that the RBD of GEMIN5 is an extended binding surface in which a serine-rich loop (EGKSSSSYH, helices 19–20) and an acidic cluster within the IDR (including EE1324–1325) cooperatively regulate RNA binding. Evidence pointer Fig 1D, Fig 1E, Fig 2B, Fig 2C, Fig 3B, Fig 3C, Fig S1, Fig S2A, Fig S2B, Fig S3A, Fig S3B; figure panels and legends not provided. Concern The central claim of an extended, cooperative RNA-binding surface is asserted on the basis of figures that were not supplied. The text reports dose-dependent binding and statistically significant differences, but no binding curves, fitted dissociation constants, replicate counts, or raw quantification are visible. Cooperativity is a specific mechanistic term that requires either direct measurement of coupled binding or a quantitative comparison of single versus combined mutations; the described experiments test individual and some combined substitutions but do not appear to include a design that isolates cooperativity from additive effects. Why it matters If the two elements act additively rather than cooperatively, the mechanistic model and the abstract's wording would need revision. Without visible quantitative binding data, the reader cannot judge the magnitude or reproducibility of the reported effects. Resolution test Provide all figure panels with legends, raw and uncropped blots and gels, binding curves with fitted parameters and confidence intervals, replicate numbers, and a quantitative comparison of single, double, and combined mutants that explicitly tests whether the effects are additive or cooperative. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Specificity and interpretation of RNA-binding assays Claim pointer The manuscript claims that TPRα20 and TPRα26 bind GEMIN5 cognate targets D5 and SL1 with dose dependence, and that the serine-rich loop and acidic cluster regulate this binding. Evidence pointer Fig 1D, Fig 1E, Fig 2B, Fig 2C, Fig 3B, Fig 3C, Fig S1, Fig S2, Fig S3; Materials and Methods sections "RNA electrophoretic mobility shift assay" and "RNA binding assay in total cytoplasmic cell extracts". Concern The specificity of the reported interactions is not established from the supplied text. The manuscript does not describe control RNAs of unrelated sequence or structure, nor competition experiments with unlabeled cognate versus non-cognate RNA, nor tests with an unrelated Xpress-tagged protein to control for nonspecific bead or aptamer binding. The streptavidin aptamer pulldown measures proteins associated with the aptamer-tagged RNA, and the text does not describe an aptamer-only control. In addition, the in vitro binding buffer contains 250 mM NaCl, which is high, and the effect of ionic strength on the observed differences between constructs is not addressed. Why it matters Without specificity controls, the reported dose-dependent binding of TPRα20 and TPRα26 could reflect general nucleic acid or matrix association rather than cognate recognition, which would undermine the claim that these regions constitute a bona fide RNA-binding surface. Resolution test Include binding assays with at least one non-cognate RNA control, competition with unlabeled cognate and non-cognate RNA, an aptamer-only or empty-bead control, and an unrelated Xpress-tagged protein control. Report the effect of varying salt concentration on binding for the key constructs. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Causal inference from correlation Claim pointer The manuscript claims that mutants SSS1141–1143AAA and SY1144–1145AA are compromised in both RNA binding and oligomerization dynamics, and that this inverse correlation with self-dimerization explains diminished GEMIN5 recruitment and reduced ribosome binding. Evidence pointer Fig 4A, Fig 4B, Fig 6A, Fig 6B, Fig 6C, Fig 6D; figure panels and legends not provided. Concern The argument rests on an inverse correlation between self-dimerization intensity and GEMIN5 recruitment or ribosome association. Correlation is presented as mechanism. The manuscript does not show that disrupting dimerization directly causes loss of recruitment, for example by testing an independent oligomerization-deficient mutant in the same recruitment and ribosome assays, nor does it exclude that the substitutions alter protein folding, stability, or expression level in a way that indirectly affects all readouts. Why it matters The mechanistic conclusion that oligomerization dynamics control recruitment and ribosome binding would not be supported if the mutants are globally misfolded or differentially expressed. Resolution test Provide expression and solubility controls for all mutants, include an independent oligomerization-deficient variant in the recruitment and ribosome assays, and, if feasible, use a direct dimerization measurement rather than SDS-resistant oligomers as the primary readout. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Use of computational modeling to support mechanistic claims Claim pointer The manuscript claims that AlphaFold modeling of G5C with D5 RNA shows the RNA surrounded by S1141–1144 of one subunit and R1035 and K1061 of the other, and that TPRα26 forms an elongated dimer engulfing the RNA, supporting the involvement of the serine-rich motif in RNA binding. Evidence pointer Fig 5A, Fig 5B, Fig 5C, Fig S5; Discussion section "Dissecting RNA interaction mediated by an extended RNA-binding surface". Concern AlphaFold predictions of protein–RNA complexes are used here as mechanistic evidence rather than as hypothesis-generating models. The text does not report model confidence metrics, per-residue pLDDT or PAE values, agreement with the deposited Cryo-EM structure beyond a stated overlap, or any experimental validation of the predicted RNA-contacting residues. The claim that the RNA is "surrounded" by specific residues is a model-derived statement, not an observation. Why it matters Structural models with unresolved flexible regions and no experimental validation cannot carry the mechanistic weight assigned to them, particularly when the IDR remains unstructured in the models while the same IDR is claimed to regulate binding. Resolution test Report model confidence metrics, explicitly label all modeling as hypothesis-generating, and, where possible, validate predicted contacts by mutagenesis of the implicated residues (for example R1035, K1061, R1090) with binding assays. Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Interpretation of translation data Claim pointer The manuscript claims that SSS1141–1143AAA and SY1144–1145AA increase cap-dependent translation and that this occurs through a mechanism independent of endogenous GEMIN5. Evidence pointer Fig S4A, Fig S4B, Fig S4C, Fig S4D; Results section "RNA binding and self-dimerization negatively impact on GEMIN5 recruitment and ribosome binding". Concern The interpretation of the translation data is not fully supported by the described design. The claim of independence from endogenous GEMIN5 is inferred from the behavior of mutants under silencing conditions, but the text does not report silencing efficiency, does not show that residual GEMIN5 is functionally negligible, and does not exclude indirect effects of the overexpressed fragments on translation machinery. The direction of the effect, increased translation with reduced ribosome binding, is counterintuitive and is not mechanistically explained. Why it matters The conclusion that these mutants act independently of GEMIN5 is a strong mechanistic claim that requires direct evidence, not inference from a partial knockdown. Resolution test Report knockdown efficiency at protein level, include rescue or re-expression controls, and provide a mechanistic explanation or additional experiment that reconciles increased translation with decreased ribosome association. Major Concerns (continued) Concern ID R1-M6 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Statistical and quantitative reporting Claim pointer The manuscript reports statistically significant differences for RNA binding, recruitment, ribosome binding, and translation, with P-values indicated by asterisks. Evidence pointer Statistical analyses section; figure legends not provided. Concern The statistical methods section states that significance between two groups was determined by an unpaired two-tailed t test, but the experimental designs described involve multiple comparisons across several mutants and conditions. No correction for multiple testing is described. Replicate numbers are stated as at least three but are not specified per experiment. Effect sizes and confidence intervals are not reported. Why it matters Without correction for multiple comparisons and without per-experiment replicate reporting, the reliability of the reported significance is difficult to assess. Resolution test Specify replicate numbers for each experiment, apply and state an appropriate multiple-comparison correction, and report effect sizes with confidence intervals. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Nomenclature consistency Affected element Construct naming throughout Results and Methods Evidence pointer Results sections and Materials and Methods "Constructs" Issue The manuscript uses several overlapping naming conventions, including TPRα20, TPRα26, TPRα28, α18–26, RBS1, RBS1–1326, and RBS1–1361, and the relationship between these names and the amino acid coordinates is not always stated at first use. Required correction Provide a single consolidated table or figure mapping each construct name to its exact amino acid boundaries and parent backbone, and use these names consistently. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Methodological detail Affected element Protein purification and refolding Evidence pointer Materials and Methods "Expression and purification of proteins"; Fig S3A Issue The text states that TPRα20, α18–26, TPRα26, and mutants were purified under 8 M urea and then dialyzed, and that native and denatured-refolded TPRα26 gave similar binding. The refolding protocol, final urea carryover, and verification of folded state are not described in detail. Required correction Describe the refolding procedure, report residual urea or imidazole concentrations, and provide evidence (for example circular dichroism or a functional assay) that the refolded proteins are properly folded. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Data availability Affected element Data Availability statement Evidence pointer Data Availability section Issue The statement says data will be made available upon reasonable request, which is not consistent with current expectations for structural models, raw blots, and quantitative datasets. Required correction Deposit the AlphaFold models and any structural coordinates, provide uncropped blots and gels as supplementary material, and make source data for the quantitative figures available in a public repository. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Reference accuracy Affected element Citation of methods for SDS-resistant oligomer detection Evidence pointer Materials and Methods "Protein expression in cultured cells" Issue The text cites references (40, 41, 42) for the SDS-resistant oligomer protocol, but these numbers appear to correspond to references cited elsewhere for unrelated methods (flDPnn prediction and RNA pulldown). This may be a citation numbering error. Required correction Verify and correct the reference numbers for the SDS-resistant oligomer protocol. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Figure legend completeness Affected element All figures Evidence pointer Figure legends not provided Issue Figure legends were not included in the supplied material, so the number of replicates, statistical tests, and definitions of error bars cannot be verified. Required correction Provide complete figure legends stating n, the statistical test used, what error bars represent, and whether images are representative. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1, R1-M2, R1-M3, R1-M4, R1-M5, R1-M6. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality Moderate. The concept that disordered and flexible regions contribute to RNA binding in GEMIN5 is a reasonable extension of prior structural work, but the individual elements (serine-rich loop, acidic IDR cluster) are not unprecedented in RBP biology, and the novelty depends on demonstrating a specific cooperative mechanism that is not yet established from the supplied evidence. Scientific importance Potentially significant for the GEMIN5 and SMN complex field and for understanding non-canonical RNA-binding surfaces, but the current evidence base is insufficient to establish the mechanistic claims at the level implied by the abstract. Interdisciplinary readership Moderate. The work would interest RNA biologists, structural biologists, and clinicians studying GEMIN5-associated neurodevelopmental disorders, but the mechanistic conclusions are currently too uncertain to support broad interdisciplinary claims. Technical soundness Not established from the supplied material. Key figures, raw data, specificity controls, quantitative binding parameters, and model confidence metrics are missing. Statistical treatment of multiple comparisons is not described. Readability for nonspecialists The abstract is concise and accessible. The Introduction is well structured. The Results, however, rely heavily on construct nomenclature and on figure references that cannot be evaluated, which would make the argument difficult to follow for a nonspecialist reader without the figures. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. Supportive in principle if the technical concerns, particularly the missing figures and raw data, specificity controls, quantitative binding analysis, and model validation, are resolved. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of cooperativity between the serine-rich loop and the acidic IDR cluster is not supported by the described experimental design, which does not isolate cooperativity from additive effects. The claim that TPRα20 and TPRα26 bind cognate RNA specifically is not supported without non-cognate RNA controls, competition experiments, and aptamer-only or unrelated-protein controls. The claim that self-dimerization inversely controls GEMIN5 recruitment and ribosome binding is correlative and not supported by a direct causal test. The claim that AlphaFold models show the RNA "surrounded" by specific residues is a model-derived statement presented without confidence metrics or experimental validation. The claim that the serine-rich motif mutants increase translation through a mechanism independent of endogenous GEMIN5 is not supported without demonstrated knockdown efficiency and rescue controls. The claim that the RBD of GEMIN5 consists of an extended binding surface is plausible but not established from the supplied material, because the supporting figures and quantitative data were not provided. The statement in the Data Availability section that data will be made available upon reasonable request is inconsistent with the need for access to structural models and raw quantitative data.

representation）同样可能携带训练数据中的偏差（如对特定折叠类型的偏好），导致下游任务（如对接打分、构象采样）产生系统性误差。后处理去偏可以在不重训大模型的前提下修正这些偏差，具有实际工程价值。 现有方法不足 ：线性方法（如 orthogonal projection）过于简单，无法处理非线性偏差；对抗训练需要端到端重训，成本高；现有后处理方法未显式考虑特征空间的几何结构（如距离、测地线、等距性）。 精确研究问题 ：Can we design a post-hoc debiasing method that removes bias from pre-trained representations while preserving 是理解细胞机制、疾病发生和药物发现的基础。实验方法（如酵母双杂交）成本高、耗时长、假阳性/假阴性率高，亟需计算替代方案。现有深度学习方法虽精度高但缺乏可解释性、计算开销大、依赖大量标注数据，在数据稀缺或需要生物学洞察的场景下受限。 现有方法为何不足 ：① 深度模型（GNN、CNN、注意力机制）在黑箱预测中难以提取生物学可解释的特征；② A-B/B-A）、类别平衡（混合采样策略） 2. 特征提取 ： AC：6 种物理化学性质（疏水性、极性、极化率、侧链体积、溶剂可及表面积、侧链净电荷指数），lag 1-20，每蛋白 120 维 CT：氨基酸按侧链体积和偶极分为 7 类，统计三联体频率，每蛋白 343 维 LD：序列分为 10 个区域（A-J），每区域计算组成（C）、转变（T）、分布（D）描述符，每蛋白 910 维 3. 特征拼接 ：两蛋白特征向量拼接，共 2,626 维 4. 分类器 ：SVM（RBF 核）、RF（bagging 决策树集成）、XGBoost（梯度提升树） 5. 评估 ：分层五折交叉验证 + 独立测试集，指标包括 Accuracy、Precision、Recall、F1-score、AUROC、AUPRC 6. 可解释性分析 ：RF 和 XGBoost 的特征重要性排序 训练 ：80% 训练 / 20% 测试划分，训练部分采用分层五折交叉验证 工具 ：Scikit-learn（Python），NVIDIA RTX 6000 AD GPU（48GB VRAM），128GB RAM 文字流程 ：原始蛋白对 → 序列质量过滤 → 去重 → 类别平衡 → AC/CT/LD 特征提取 → 特征拼接（2,626 维）→ 分类器训练（五折 CV）→ 独立测试集评估 → 特征重要性分析 → 生物学解释 08 ( j ) 个物理化学描述符值 ( \bar{P}_j )：第 ( j ) 个描述符在所有 20 种标准氨基酸中的平均值 ( S_j )：第 ( j ) 个描述符的标准差 用途：将不同物理化学性质统一到零均值、单位方差，消除量纲差异 直觉：使不同性质的数值可比，避免量纲大的特征主导距离计算 2. Auto-Covariance (AC) [ AC_{j,lag} = \frac{1}{L - lag} \sum_{i=1}^{L-lag} (P'_{ij} - \bar{P}' j)(P' {i+lag,j} - \bar{P}'_j) ] ( L )：蛋白质序列长度 ( lag )：残基间距（1 到 20） ( P'_{ij} )：标准化后的第 ( i ) 个氨基酸的第 ( j ) 个物理化学性质值 ( \bar{P}'_j )：序列中第 ( j ) 个性质的均值 用途：量化序列中相距 ( lag ) 个残基的氨基酸对之间的物理化学性质协变 直觉：捕捉序列的周期性模式和短程/中程顺序依赖 维度：6 种性质 × 20 个 lag = 120 维/蛋白 3. SVM 优化目标（软间隔） [ \min_{w,b,\xi} \frac{1}{2} |w|^2 + C \sum_{i=1}^{n} \xi_i ] [ \text{s.t.} \quad y_i(w^T \phi(x_i) + b) \geq 1 - \xi_i, \quad \xi_i \geq 0 ] ( w )：权重向量 ( b )：偏置 ( \phi(x) )：特征变换函数（核函数隐式定义） ( \xi_i )：松弛变量，允许软间隔分类 ( C )：正则化参数，控制分类误差与间隔最大化的权衡 用途：寻找最大间隔超平面，处理非线性分类 4. RF 预测（bagging 平均） [ \hat{y} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} h_t(x) ] ( h_t(x) )：第 ( t ) 棵决策树的预测 ( T )：树的总数 用途：通过多棵树投票/平均降低方差，提高泛化 5. XGBoost 正则化目标 [ \mathcal{L} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, \hat{y} i) + \sum {t=1}^{T} \Omega(f_t) ] [ \Omega(f) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2} \lambda |w|^2 ] ( l(\cdot) )：损失函数（如对数损失） ( \Omega(f_t) )：第 ( t ) 棵树的正则化项 ( T )：树的叶子节点数 ( w )：叶子权重 ( \gamma, \lambda )：正则化系数 用途：控制模型复杂度，防止过拟合 6. 评估指标 [ \text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} ] [ \text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP} ] [ \text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN} ] [ F1 = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}} ] TP/TN/FP/FN：真阳性/真阴性/假阳性/假阴性 AUROC：ROC 曲线下面积，衡量阈值无关的判别能力 AUPRC：PR 曲线下面积，对类别不平衡更敏感 ：训练数据来自 Bernett et al. 的金标准序列 PPI 基准（Intra-0 子集），测试数据为独立 Human-PPI 数据集。结论不能外推到其他物种或非人类 PPI 网络。 特征边界 ：2,626 维特征全部来自序列本身，不包含结构、进化、表达或共定位信息。性能优势仅在手工业特征 + 经典 ML 的框架内成立。 模型选择 ：RF 在独立测试集上最优（99.51% 准确率），但 XGBoost 在交叉验证中最高（97.97%）。这种 CV 与测试集排名不一致表明：① 模型选择不能仅依赖 CV；② RF 的 bagging 机制在分布偏移下更稳健。 可解释性边界 ：特征重要性分析识别了极性/疏水性自协方差、三联体模式和区域组成等判别特征，但这些是相关性而非因果性。不能据此断言这些序列模式直接驱动互作。 计算成本 ：本文强调「低计算开销、无 GPU 依赖」，适用于大规模互作组筛选。但未提供具体推理时间或吞吐量数据。 不确定性 ：未报告置信区间、方差或统计显著性检验。性能数字（如 99.51%）可能受数据集特定划分影响。 与结构方法的关系 ：本文方法不依赖结构信息，与 AlphaFold 等结构预测方法互补而非竞争。Discussion 中建议未来结合结构表示（如 AlphaFold 预测）以进一步提升性能。 12 作者自认局限 局限 具体表现 availability) Assessment boundary Scientific validity, methodological rigor, reproducibility, and claims as supported by the provided text. No supplementary materials, code, or figures were available for inspection beyond those referenced in the text. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose an interpretable machine-learning framework for protein-protein interaction (PPI) prediction using three sequence-derived descriptor families (Auto-Covariance, Conjoint Triad, Local Descriptors) combined with classical classifiers (SVM, RF, XGBoost). They report high cross-validation and independent test-set performance, with Random Forest achieving 99.51% accuracy on an unseen human PPI dataset, and provide feature-importance analyses to support biological interpretability. Visible evidence base Abstract; Sections 1–4 (Introduction, Materials and Methodology, Results and Discussion, Conclusion); Tables 1–13 referenced; Figures 1–7 referenced; Data availability URLs. Missing materials affecting confidence Actual tables and figures (including feature-importance plots, ROC/PR curves, dataset statistics) were not provided. No code, hyperparameter settings, or detailed experimental configuration were included. The exact composition of the training and test datasets (e.g., number of positive/negative pairs, species origin) is not fully specified in the text. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a relevant problem in computational biology with a straightforward, interpretable approach. The reported performance metrics are strong, but several methodological ambiguities and potential data-leakage concerns need to be resolved before the claims can be fully accepted. The work is technically sound in its general design but lacks sufficient detail in key areas, particularly dataset construction, class-balancing procedures, and hyperparameter optimization. The biological interpretation of feature importance is plausible but would benefit from more rigorous validation. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in bioinformatics, computational biology, and systems biology working on PPI prediction, interactome mapping, and drug-target prioritization would find this work relevant. The emphasis on interpretability and low computational cost may appeal to groups seeking alternatives to deep learning for high-throughput screening applications. Major strengths 1) Use of well-established, biologically motivated sequence descriptors that are computationally efficient. 2) Evaluation on both cross-validation and an independent unseen dataset, which is a good practice for assessing generalization. 3) Feature-importance analysis provides interpretable insights into which sequence properties drive predictions. 4) Comparison of multiple classical classifiers offers a practical benchmark. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Data integrity and leakage prevention Claim pointer The authors claim the dataset was designed to minimize information leakage by ensuring proteins assigned to one subset were not present in other subsets, and that the independent Human-PPI test set consists of "completely unseen protein pairs." Evidence pointer Section 2.1, Table 1, Table 2 Concern The description of dataset partitioning is insufficient to verify that no protein-level overlap exists between training and test sets. The text states that the Intra-0 subset was used and that KaHIP-based partitioning minimized sequence similarity, but the exact criteria for "unseen" are not defined. If proteins in the test set share high sequence identity with training proteins, the reported generalization performance could be inflated. Additionally, the class-balancing procedure (hybrid sampling) is described only vaguely; the ratio of positive to negative samples after balancing is not reported, which affects the interpretation of accuracy and F1 scores. Why it matters PPI prediction benchmarks are highly sensitive to data leakage. Without explicit verification of sequence-level separation and clear reporting of class distributions, the reported 99.51% accuracy on the unseen test set cannot be taken at face value. This is a core issue that undermines the central claim of robust generalization. Resolution test Provide a detailed description of the dataset construction, including the number of unique proteins in training and test sets, the sequence-identity threshold used for separation, and the positive-to-negative ratio before and after balancing. Ideally, provide a supplementary figure showing the sequence-identity distribution between training and test proteins. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Methodological reproducibility Claim pointer The authors state that SVM, RF, and XGBoost were trained and evaluated, with RF selected as the final model based on test-set performance. Evidence pointer Section 2.4, Section 3.3, Tables 10 and 11 Concern No hyperparameter values, kernel types (for SVM), number of trees (for RF), learning rates or tree depths (for XGBoost), or any model selection procedure are reported. The text mentions "Scikit-learn" but does not specify whether default parameters were used or if tuning was performed. Without this information, the results cannot be reproduced, and the comparison between classifiers is not fully interpretable. Why it matters Reproducibility is a fundamental requirement for computational studies. The lack of model configuration details prevents other researchers from replicating the experiments or assessing whether the reported performance is an artifact of particular settings. Resolution test Provide a table or supplementary section listing all hyperparameters for each model, the search space if tuning was performed, and the criterion used for model selection (e.g., cross-validation score vs. test-set score). Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Evaluation methodology Claim pointer The authors report cross-validation accuracy of 97.97% for XGBoost and test-set accuracy of 99.51% for RF, and state that RF "emerged as the top-performing architecture" on the unseen dataset. Evidence pointer Section 3.3, Tables 10 and 11 Concern The selection of RF as the final model is based solely on test-set performance. This is methodologically problematic because the test set should be used only once for final evaluation, not for model selection. If the test set was used to choose between models, the reported test performance is optimistically biased. The authors should clarify whether the test set was used during model development or only for final assessment. Why it matters Using the test set for model selection violates standard evaluation protocols and can lead to overfitting to the test set, undermining the claim of generalization to unseen data. Resolution test Clarify the model selection procedure. If the test set was used to choose RF over XGBoost, the authors should either use a separate validation set for model selection or report performance with appropriate caveats. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Biological interpretation Claim pointer The authors state that feature-importance analysis revealed that short-range physicochemical correlations, regional amino-acid compositions, and specific triad patterns drive PPI discrimination, and they interpret these as biologically meaningful. Evidence pointer Section 3.3, Figures 6 and 7, Tables 12 and 13 Concern The biological interpretation is speculative and not validated against known PPI structural data or functional annotations. For example, the claim that "short-range polarity organization may contribute substantially to PPI discrimination" is plausible but not tested. The authors do not compare their identified features with known interface properties or perform any external validation (e.g., on independent datasets with known interaction mechanisms). Why it matters The interpretability claim is a key selling point of the manuscript. Without validation, the feature-importance analysis remains descriptive rather than biologically informative, weakening the contribution beyond predictive performance. Resolution test Perform additional analyses to support the biological interpretation, such as comparing top features with known interface-residue propensities, or testing the model on datasets with annotated interaction types (e.g., transient vs. permanent). Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity and completeness Affected element Section 2.3, feature extraction Evidence pointer Section 2.3, Tables 5–8 Issue The text describes the feature extraction methods but does not provide the actual formulas for normalization and autocovariance computation. The equations are referenced but not shown in the text provided. Required correction Include the full equations for normalization and autocovariance, or refer to a supplementary file where they are provided. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Statistical reporting Affected element Section 3.3, Tables 10 and 11 Evidence pointer Section 3.3 Issue The text reports mean cross-validation accuracy but does not report standard deviations or confidence intervals. Variability across folds is not discussed. Required correction Report standard deviations or confidence intervals for all cross-validation metrics. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Comparison with prior work Affected element Section 3.4, Discussion Evidence pointer Section 3.4 Issue The discussion mentions DeepPPI as a deep-learning baseline but does not provide a quantitative comparison with the proposed method or with other classical approaches. Required correction Include a table comparing the proposed method with at least one or two published baselines on the same or similar datasets. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Language and formatting Affected element Abstract, Section 1 Evidence pointer Abstract, Section 1 Issue There are minor grammatical issues and inconsistent spacing (e.g., "descriptors,specifically" in the abstract). Required correction Proofread the manuscript for grammatical errors and formatting inconsistencies. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (data leakage verification) and R1-M2 (reproducibility of model configuration) are the most critical. R1-M3 (test-set-based model selection) also needs clarification. These issues must be resolved before the reported performance can be considered reliable. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : Moderate. The combination of three established descriptor families with classical classifiers is not conceptually novel, though the systematic comparison and feature-importance analysis add some value. Scientific importance : Moderate. PPI prediction is an active field, and interpretable methods are useful, but the incremental improvement over existing approaches is not clearly demonstrated. Interdisciplinary readership : Limited. The work is primarily of interest to bioinformatics specialists; the biological insights are not deep enough to attract a broader structural biology or drug discovery audience. Technical soundness : Currently insufficient. The methodological details are incomplete, and the data-leakage concern is unresolved. Readability for nonspecialists : Acceptable. The text is generally clear, though some sections (e.g., feature extraction) assume familiarity with the descriptors. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript has potential, but the methodological ambiguities and data-integrity concerns must be addressed. I would be supportive if the authors provide detailed dataset construction information, full model configurations, and clarify the model selection procedure. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the model "avoids overfitting" is not fully supported without standard deviation reporting and a clearer description of the test-set construction. The biological interpretation of feature importance (e.g., "short-range polarity organization drives PPI discrimination") is speculative and not validated. The statement that the framework has "minimal computational overhead" is plausible but not quantified. The claim that the model is suitable for "efficient, scalable interactome screening" is not demonstrated with runtime or scalability experiments.

abstract. No full text, figures, tables, methods, supplementary information, or numerical results were provided. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present CS-SelectFold, a framework that couples generative conformational sampling (SimpleFold) with structural prescreening, chemical-shift prediction (UCBShift 2.0), and ranking against experimental excited-state chemical shifts, without retraining or fine-tuning. They claim proof-of-concept recovery of low-populated conformations for two systems, the T4 lysozyme L99A cavity mutant and the A39V/N53P/V55L Fyn SH3 domain. Visible evidence base Two benchmark systems are described. For T4 lysozyme L99A, the reported evidence is recovery of an excited-state-like local rearrangement around the engineered cavity, inward placement of Phe114, and a retrospective two-reference hotspot analysis using internal-distance RMSD (dRMSD) showing enrichment of conformations displaced from the ground-state basin toward the excited-state basin. For Fyn SH3, the reported evidence is recovery of the loss of the C-terminal beta-strand, supported by three-dimensional structural comparison and secondary-structure analysis. Missing materials affecting confidence Full text, methods, sampling parameters, candidate pool sizes, prescreening criteria, chemical-shift datasets and their uncertainty, ranking metrics, statistical tests, negative controls, baselines, figures, tables, and supplementary data are all absent. Confidence in the technical soundness and generality of the claims is therefore limited. Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a conceptually reasonable sample-and-select strategy for accessing low-populated protein conformations, and the choice of two experimentally characterized systems is appropriate for a proof-of-concept study. However, the supplied material does not allow the central claims to be independently evaluated. Key elements such as how candidates are prescreened, how chemical-shift agreement is scored, how enrichment is quantified, and how the method performs against baselines or controls are not visible. The work is potentially interesting but currently not established from the provided evidence. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers in computational structural biology, NMR spectroscopy, protein folding and misfolding, and generative protein modeling would be interested, because a reliable method to select hidden or excited conformations from generative models without retraining would be broadly useful for mechanistic and ligand-recognition studies. Major strengths The problem is well motivated and functionally relevant. The framework is modular and avoids retraining pretrained components, which is a practical advantage. The use of two distinct test systems, an excited-state cavity mutant and an aggregation-prone folding intermediate, suggests an intent to test generality. The reported use of dRMSD-based hotspot analysis is a sensible way to assess movement between basins rather than relying only on coordinate superposition. 评估预算下，能否通过多样性感知的搜索策略，发现比传统亲和力聚焦方法更广的预测互作谱？ 为什么重要 ：药物发现早期阶段需要多样化的互作假设来覆盖不同结合模式，避免过早收敛到单一化学系列；标量 score 的贪心优化会系统性丢失互作多样性。 现有方法不足 ：goal-directed 方法（如遗传算法）只优化亲和力；novelty-based random search and affinity-focused baselines, under a fixed budget of 500 docking evaluations per target, across multiple protein families? 04 背景与发展脉络 （标注： 仅本文框架 ，未经外部核验） 1. 阶段一：标量 score 贪心优化 （如经典 The central claims, particularly the distinction between global stability and local flexibility, and the causal link between observed conformational changes and hyperactivity, are not fully established from the supplied material. introduction, implementation, validation, conclusion) without figures, tables, or supplementary material Assessment boundary Scientific and technical evaluation of the described methodology, validation strategy, and reported results; software usability and reproducibility considerations Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present GroScore, an open-source Python toolkit for automated scoring of protein–protein interaction (PPI) structures using bidirectional steered molecular dynamics (SMD) with explicit solvent. The tool introduces bidirectional pulling (unbinding and rebinding), an interface-cutout mode for computational efficiency, support for three force fields, and automated handling of small molecules, noncanonical amino acids, structural ions, and crystal waters. Validation on the HADDOCK benchmark (46 complexes) shows significant correlations (Pearson r = 0.51–0.66) across force fields; on the larger PPB-Affinity dataset (2431 successful simulations), weak but significant correlations are reported (Pearson r = 0.16 overall; subset-dependent, up to r = 0.40). CAPRI Score_set testing shows improved near-native pose ranking (49 vs. 40 Top-10) compared to the unidirectional predecessor. Small-molecule ternary complex tests (19 systems) show significant stabilization for 13 cases using the CGI estimator. Visible evidence base Main text descriptions of validation results; references to Figures 1–3, Table 1, and Supplementary Figures S1–S11 and Table S1 (none of which were provided) Missing materials affecting confidence All figures, tables, and supplementary material; benchmark dataset composition details; specific correlation values with confidence intervals for individual force fields; computational cost comparisons; software documentation and test suite details Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a timely and potentially useful software tool that addresses a real need in the PPI scoring field. The bidirectional SMD approach is a sensible methodological improvement over the unidirectional predecessor, and the interface-cutout strategy for computational efficiency is pragmatic. However, the validation results as described are mixed: while the HADDOCK benchmark correlations are encouraging, the PPB-Affinity results are weak in absolute terms, and the authors' explanations for subset-dependent performance, while plausible, are not quantitatively supported in the provided text. The small-molecule ternary complex results are interesting but raise questions about the physical interpretation of the scoring scheme. The manuscript would benefit from clearer presentation of the statistical methods, more detailed reporting of benchmark results, and a more critical discussion of the limitations of the approach for absolute affinity prediction. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational structural biologists and bioinformaticians working on protein–protein interaction prediction, docking, and scoring will be the primary audience. Researchers developing or using AI-based structure prediction methods (AlphaFold, RoseTTAFold, etc.) who need post-hoc scoring functions to rank candidate complexes will find this tool relevant. The open-source, automated nature of the software and its integration with GROMACS and SLURM make it potentially attractive for high-throughput applications. The small-molecule handling may also interest researchers working on proximity-inducing compounds (molecular glues, PROTACs), though this application is less thoroughly validated. Major strengths 1. The bidirectional pulling approach directly addresses a known limitation (exponential work averaging bias) of the unidirectional predecessor, and the authors provide a clear rationale for this methodological choice. 2. The interface-cutout mode is a practical and well-motivated strategy for reducing computational cost, and the reported correlation between cutout and no-cutout scores (r = 0.87–0.96) provides evidence that this approximation preserves per-complex ranking. 3. The software is open-source, automated, and integrates with widely used tools (GROMACS, SLURM), which lowers the barrier to adoption. 4. Validation across multiple benchmarks (HADDOCK, PPB-Affinity, CAPRI Score_set) and force fields provides a reasonably broad assessment of performance. 5. The authors are transparent about the limitations of the approach, including the weak absolute correlations on heterogeneous datasets and the deliberate omission of standard-state corrections. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor and result interpretation Claim pointer "Significant positive correlations (Pearson r = 0.51–0.66) of calculated scores to experimental binding affinities were obtained for all tested force fields" (HADDOCK benchmark); "weak but significant correlation (Pearson r = 0.16, Spearman ρ = 0.24)" (PPB-Affinity overall) Evidence pointer Validation section, Figure 1, Table 1, Figures S1–S4, S10 (none provided) Concern The manuscript reports correlation coefficients without providing confidence intervals, p-values, or details on the statistical testing procedure. For the HADDOCK benchmark (n = 46), a Pearson r of 0.51–0.66 would have wide confidence intervals, and the authors do not state whether these are significantly different from each other across force fields. For the PPB-Affinity dataset, the overall r = 0.16 with n = 2431 would be statistically significant but practically weak; the authors should report the distribution of scores and residuals, not just the correlation. The subset-dependent results (r = 0.17–0.40) are presented with qualitative explanations but no statistical comparison of whether these differences are significant. Why it matters The central claim of the paper is that GroScore produces scores that correlate with experimental binding affinities. Without proper uncertainty quantification and statistical testing, the reader cannot assess the reliability of this claim or compare performance across force fields, datasets, or modes (cutout vs. no-cutout). The weak overall correlation on PPB-Affinity raises questions about the practical utility of the method for heterogeneous datasets, and the authors' explanations need quantitative support. Resolution test Provide 95% confidence intervals for all reported correlation coefficients; state the statistical test used (e.g., t-test for Pearson r) and whether correlations across force fields or datasets are significantly different; include scatter plots with regression lines and residual analysis for the PPB-Affinity subsets; report the distribution of scores for each subset to support claims about dynamic range limitations. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Validation of small-molecule ternary complex application Claim pointer "With CGI, a significant negative shift indicating ternary-complex stabilization by the small molecule was obtained for 13 of the 19 systems" and the subsequent categorization of the six nonsignificant cases Evidence pointer Validation section, Figure 3 (not provided) Concern The small-molecule ternary complex validation is presented with only 19 systems, and the authors provide qualitative explanations for the six nonsignificant cases. However, the physical interpretation of the "GroScore difference (glued – non-glued)" is unclear. The authors state that the inducer is "assigned to one of the two binding partners according to its chain identifier" and that "no restraints tether it to its host partner; its association with the host is therefore maintained only by the physical force field." This raises questions about whether the simulation setup adequately samples the inducer's dissociation from its host, and whether the scoring scheme can distinguish between specific stabilization and nonspecific effects. The categorization of the six nonsignificant cases into three groups is based on literature knowledge, but the authors do not provide quantitative criteria for these categories or a statistical framework for evaluating the sensitivity of the method. Why it matters The small-molecule application is a significant extension of the tool beyond protein-only systems, and the authors claim practical utility for molecular glue and PROTAC scoring. However, with only 19 systems and a 68% success rate, the evidence is preliminary. The physical interpretation of the scoring scheme for ternary complexes needs clarification, and the authors should demonstrate that the method can distinguish between true stabilizers and non-stabilizers with appropriate controls. Resolution test Provide a more detailed description of the simulation setup for ternary complexes, including how the inducer is positioned and how its dissociation from the host is sampled. Include control experiments with non-binding or weakly binding small molecules. Report the distribution of GroScore differences for all 19 systems with confidence intervals, and provide quantitative criteria for the categorization of nonsignificant cases. If possible, expand the validation set or clearly state the limitations of the current dataset. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Benchmark representativeness and generalizability Claim pointer "Validation on the curated HADDOCK affinity benchmark and the larger and more heterogeneous PPB-Affinity aggregate shows significant correlations with experimental binding data across diverse system classes" Evidence pointer Validation section, Table 1 (not provided) Concern The PPB-Affinity dataset is described as "much larger" but the authors report only the overall correlation (r = 0.16) and subset-specific values (r = 0.17–0.40). The subset-dependent performance varies substantially, and the authors attribute this to dataset curation quality and dynamic range. However, the manuscript does not provide details on the composition of each subset (e.g., number of complexes, range of affinities, structural diversity) or the criteria for inclusion. The HADDOCK benchmark (46 complexes) is described as "highly curated" but the overlap with the Affinity Benchmark v5.3 subset of PPB-Affinity is not discussed. The CAPRI Score_set results are presented as a ranking improvement (49 vs. 40 Top-10) but without statistical significance testing or comparison to other scoring methods. Why it matters The generalizability of GroScore across different types of PPIs is a key claim. Without detailed information on benchmark composition and subset characteristics, the reader cannot assess whether the weak overall correlation reflects method limitations or dataset heterogeneity. The CAPRI results are presented as an improvement over the predecessor but not compared to other state-of-the-art scoring functions, limiting the assessment of GroScore's competitive position. Resolution test Provide a detailed breakdown of each PPB-Affinity subset (number of complexes, affinity range, structural characteristics, source). Discuss the overlap between the HADDOCK benchmark and the Affinity Benchmark v5.3 subset. For the CAPRI results, report the statistical significance of the improvement (e.g., Wilcoxon signed-rank test) and, if possible, compare to other scoring methods on the same set. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Computational cost and practical utility Claim pointer "interface cutout for reduced computational cost" and "showcasing the scoring efficiency of GroScore on consumer-grade hardware" Evidence pointer Implementation section, Validation section (CAPRI results) Concern The manuscript claims that the interface cutout mode "dramatically reduces computational cost" and reports throughput of 56 poses/day on an NVIDIA RTX 5080 GPU, but no quantitative comparison of computational cost between cutout and no-cutout modes is provided in the text. The authors mention "small differences in the simulation wall-times without cutout mode between the force fields" but do not report actual wall-times or speedup factors. For a tool intended for high-throughput scoring, the computational cost is a critical practical consideration. Why it matters The practical utility of GroScore depends on its computational efficiency. If the cutout mode provides only marginal speedup, or if the full-system simulations are prohibitively expensive, the tool's applicability to large-scale screening would be limited. The authors should provide concrete timing data to support their efficiency claims. Resolution test Report wall-times for cutout vs. no-cutout modes for representative complexes across all force fields, including the speedup factor. Provide a breakdown of computational cost by simulation stage (equilibration, pulling, analysis). Discuss the scaling of computational cost with system size and the practical limits of the approach. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility and software documentation Affected element Software availability and documentation Evidence pointer Abstract, Implementation section Issue The manuscript states that GroScore is available on GitHub under the MIT License, but no version number, dependency list, or link to documentation is provided in the text. The description of the pipeline is high-level, and the specific parameters used for the validation simulations (e.g., pulling rate, spring constant, simulation temperature) are not stated in the main text. Required correction Provide a specific version number and a link to the documentation in the manuscript. Include a table of key simulation parameters used in the validation studies, or refer to a specific section of the SI where these are listed. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Clarity of methodological description Affected element Interface cutout procedure Evidence pointer Implementation section, Interface Cutout subsection Issue The description of the interface cutout procedure is brief. The authors state that residues within 2.0 nm of the interface are retained, but it is unclear how the "interface" is defined (e.g., based on interatomic distances, solvent-accessible surface area, or a combination). The elastic network distance restraints at chain breaks are described, but the choice of force constant (250 kJ·mol–1·nm–2) and the range (0.4–0.9 nm) are not justified. Required correction Provide a more detailed description of the interface definition and the rationale for the elastic network parameters. If this information is in the SI, refer to the specific section. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Statistical reporting Affected element CAPRI Score_set results Evidence pointer Validation section Issue The CAPRI results are reported as "49 (including 13 high-quality and 23 medium-quality) near-native poses were ranked within the Top-10 of each target, compared to 40 (including 9 high-quality and 21 medium-quality) with the original unidirectional setup." The authors do not report the total number of targets or poses, the distribution of ranks, or any statistical test for the improvement. Required correction Report the total number of targets and poses, the distribution of ranks (e.g., median, interquartile range), and the result of a paired statistical test comparing the bidirectional and unidirectional methods. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Interpretation of weak correlations Affected element PPB-Affinity results Evidence pointer Validation section Issue The authors report a weak overall correlation (r = 0.16) on the PPB-Affinity dataset and attribute this to dataset heterogeneity and dynamic range limitations. However, they do not discuss whether this level of correlation is practically useful for ranking candidate complexes in a screening context, or how it compares to other scoring methods on the same dataset. Required correction Add a brief discussion of the practical implications of the weak correlation, including a comparison to other scoring methods if available, and a statement about the expected utility of GroScore for ranking in a screening context. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Terminology and scope Affected element Title and abstract Evidence pointer Title, Abstract Issue The title states "Automated Scoring of Protein–Protein Interactions" but the validation includes small-molecule ternary complexes (molecular glues and PROTACs). The abstract mentions "automated handling of small molecules" but does not clearly state that the tool can score ternary complexes. This may be misleading for potential users. Required correction Clarify in the abstract that the tool supports scoring of ternary complexes involving small-molecule inducers, or adjust the title to reflect the broader scope. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established 1. Lack of confidence intervals and statistical tests for all reported correlation coefficients (R1-M1). 2. Insufficient detail on the small-molecule ternary complex validation, including simulation setup and controls (R1-M2). 3. Missing quantitative data on computational cost and speedup from the interface cutout mode (R1-M4). 4. No comparison to other state-of-the-art scoring methods on the same benchmarks, limiting the assessment of GroScore's competitive position. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : The bidirectional SMD approach with interface cutout is a reasonable incremental improvement over existing SMD-based scoring methods, but the core concept of using nonequilibrium work measurements for PPI scoring is not new. The combination of features (bidirectional pulling, multiple force fields, automated small-molecule handling) is somewhat novel, but the methodological advance is modest. Scientific importance : PPI scoring is an important problem in structural biology, and a reliable, automated, open-source tool would be valuable. However, the weak correlations on heterogeneous datasets suggest that the method has limited predictive power for absolute affinity prediction, and the authors themselves acknowledge this limitation. The practical utility for high-throughput screening remains to be demonstrated. Interdisciplinary readership : The work is primarily of interest to computational structural biologists and bioinformaticians. The methods and results are unlikely to attract a broad interdisciplinary audience beyond this niche. Technical soundness : The methodological choices are generally sound and well-motivated, but the statistical reporting is incomplete, and the validation on the small-molecule ternary complex set is preliminary. The lack of comparison to other methods weakens the technical case. Readability for nonspecialists : The manuscript is generally well-written and accessible to readers with a background in molecular dynamics and PPI prediction. The introduction provides a good overview of the field and the limitations of existing methods. However, some technical details (e.g., the CGI estimator) may be challenging for nonspecialists. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The manuscript describes a useful and potentially valuable software tool, and the methodological improvements over the predecessor are sensible. However, the statistical reporting needs to be strengthened, the small-molecule validation needs more detail and controls, and the computational cost claims need quantitative support. The authors should also provide a comparison to other scoring methods to establish the competitive position of GroScore. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that bidirectional pulling "overcomes the numerical bias of exponential work averaging" is not quantitatively supported in the provided text; the authors should show a direct comparison of unidirectional vs. bidirectional results on the same systems. The claim that the interface cutout mode "dramatically reduces computational cost" is not supported by quantitative data in the provided text. The categorization of the six nonsignificant small-molecule ternary complex cases into three groups is based on literature knowledge but is not quantitatively justified. The claim that "bidirectional pulling... substantially reduces the anticorrelation between scores and buried surface area" is mentioned but not quantified in the provided text. The overall PPB-Affinity correlation (r = 0.16) is described as "weak but significant," but the practical utility of this level of correlation for ranking candidate complexes is not discussed. The CAPRI Score_set improvement (49 vs. 40 Top-10) is reported without statistical significance testing or comparison to other methods.

setup Input scope Full manuscript text including abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, and concluding remarks. Figures, tables, and supplementary material referenced but not provided. Assessment boundary Scientific validity, methodological soundness, clarity of claims, and alignment with stated evidence. Assessment limited to the supplied text; figures, tables, and supplementary files were not available for direct inspection. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present gEDES-HM, a protocol that transfers conformational ensembles generated by enhanced sampling simulations of a single reference protein (E. coli adenylate kinase) to homologous family members via homology modeling using a multitemplate library. They report recovery of native-like binding modes for 92% of 26 protein-ligand complexes across 22 homologues, with performance approaching that of redocking into experimental holo structures. Visible evidence base Text descriptions of methods and results, including quantitative success rates, RMSD thresholds, correlation coefficients, and comparative performance across model sets. Specific numerical values for docking success rates and statistical correlations are reported in the text. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures, tables (including Tables S2, S4, S5, S6, S7), and supplementary figures (S1, S2, S3) are referenced but not provided. These contain the primary quantitative data supporting the claims. Without them, the accuracy of reported numbers and the validity of statistical analyses cannot be independently verified. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a conceptually appealing and potentially useful extension of the authors' prior gEDES methodology, addressing a real bottleneck in structure-based modeling of protein families. The core idea, transferring conformational ensembles from a single reference to homologues via homology modeling, is logical and the validation design is thoughtful, including appropriate controls (single-template apo and holo models, and redocking into experimental structures). However, the manuscript as presented has several significant issues. The most critical is the absence of the actual data: all figures and tables are missing from the provided material, making it impossible to verify the quantitative claims. Beyond this, there are conceptual concerns about the interpretation of the results, particularly the claim that the approach "transfers functional transitions" when the validation is based on reproducing static bound structures. The discussion of limitations is honest and well-developed, which is a strength. The writing is generally clear, though some methodological details require clarification. Overall, the idea has merit, but the evidence base as presented is insufficient to fully establish the claims. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational structural biologists, particularly those working on ensemble docking, homology modeling, and structure-based drug discovery. The protocol offers a practical way to generate conformational libraries for protein families without running expensive simulations for each member, which could be valuable for virtual screening campaigns targeting multiple homologues. Researchers studying conformational transitions in enzyme families, especially those interested in adenylate kinases, would also find the results relevant. The work may also interest method developers in the enhanced sampling community, as it demonstrates a downstream application of gEDES. Major strengths 1. The core concept is elegant and addresses a genuine practical need: reducing computational cost of generating conformational ensembles for multiple homologues. 2. The validation design is rigorous, with multiple control sets (apo-only, holo-only templates, and experimental redocking) that allow clear attribution of performance to the ensemble transfer approach. 3. The honest and detailed discussion of limitations, including the analysis of unsuccessful cases, is commendable and adds credibility. 4. The use of multiple collective coordinate systems (distances and angles) to characterize the conformational space is thorough. 5. The statistical analysis (Spearman correlations with p-values) is appropriate for the non-linear relationships being examined. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence completeness Claim pointer The manuscript claims 92.3% success in reproducing native-like binding modes across 26 complexes, and 84.6% success in generating native-like binding-site conformations. Evidence pointer Figures 1-4, Tables S2, S4, S5, S6, S7; location not provided Concern All quantitative results are presented in figures and tables that were not included in the provided material. The text alone is insufficient to verify the accuracy of the reported percentages, the distribution of RMSD values, the cluster characteristics, or the statistical correlations. Without access to the actual data, the central claims of the paper cannot be independently assessed. Why it matters The core contribution of this work is empirical: the demonstration that gEDES-HM achieves high success rates across a diverse set of homologues. If the underlying data contain errors, outliers, or are less favorable than summarized, the conclusions would be substantially weakened. The absence of the data makes the manuscript impossible to evaluate as a scientific contribution. Resolution test Provide all figures and tables with full data. The reviewer must be able to inspect the distribution of RMSD values per complex, the cluster rankings, and the correlation plots to verify the reported summary statistics. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Claim-evidence alignment Claim pointer The title and abstract state that the method enables "mapping functional transitions across protein homologues from a single simulation." Evidence pointer Abstract, Introduction, Results and Discussion; location not provided Concern The validation presented in the manuscript demonstrates that gEDES-HM can generate conformations resembling bound states, as measured by RMSD to experimental holo structures. However, this is not equivalent to mapping functional transitions. A transition implies a dynamical process or at least a characterization of the pathway between states. The manuscript does not present any analysis of transition pathways, intermediate states along a defined reaction coordinate, or kinetic/thermodynamic information about the interconversion between open and closed states. The claim of "mapping functional transitions" is therefore overstated relative to what is actually demonstrated. Why it matters The title and framing of the work promise more than the validation delivers. If the contribution is about generating binding-competent conformations for docking, that is a valuable but more modest claim. Overstating the scope could mislead readers about the method's capabilities and may invite inappropriate applications. Resolution test Either revise the title and abstract to accurately reflect that the method generates conformational libraries that include bound-like states, or add analyses that explicitly characterize transitions (e.g., transition paths, free energy profiles, or dynamical information) between the open and closed states in the transferred ensembles. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Methodological clarity Claim pointer The methods state that 101 conformational clusters from gEDES simulations were used as templates for homology modeling, and that 10 models per template were generated, yielding 1010 models per target, from which the best-scoring model per template was selected by DOPE score. Evidence pointer Methods, Homology Modeling, Model Generation; location not provided Concern The selection of the "best-scoring model" by DOPE score for each of the 101 conformations is a critical step, but the manuscript does not discuss the variability of DOPE scores across the 10 models generated per template. If the DOPE score varies substantially between models generated from the same template, the selection of a single model may introduce stochastic bias. Conversely, if the scores are tightly clustered, the selection is robust but the generation of 10 models is wasteful. The manuscript does not address this. Why it matters The reproducibility and robustness of the model selection step directly affect the reliability of the downstream docking results. If the selection is noisy, the reported success rates may not be reproducible across independent runs. This is particularly important given the authors' own acknowledgment that success depends on a small number of productive conformers surviving the selection process. Resolution test Provide an analysis of DOPE score distributions across the 10 models per template for a representative subset of targets. If variability is high, discuss the implications for reproducibility. Alternatively, demonstrate that the docking results are insensitive to the specific model selected per template. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generalizability Claim pointer The abstract and conclusion suggest that gEDES-HM "could provide a practical route to generate binding-competent structural libraries for homologues lacking experimental structures." Evidence pointer Abstract, Concluding Remarks; location not provided Concern The validation is performed exclusively on adenylate kinases, a family with a well-characterized, conserved domain motion. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the discussion, but the framing in the abstract and conclusion is more general. The key question is whether the approach would work for families with different types of conformational changes, such as loop rearrangements, domain rotations, or allosteric transitions that do not involve a simple open-to-closed motion. The manuscript provides no evidence or argument for why the approach would generalize. Why it matters The practical value of the method depends on its applicability beyond the test case. If the approach only works for families with large, well-defined domain motions similar to ADK, its utility is more limited than suggested. The authors should either temper the generalizability claims or provide a reasoned argument, based on the mechanism of the method, for why it should work more broadly. Resolution test Add a discussion of the types of conformational changes for which the approach is likely to be applicable, based on the nature of the gEDES bias and the homology modeling transfer. If possible, include a preliminary test on a family with a different type of conformational change. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Methods, Projection of Conformational Ensembles Evidence pointer Methods, Projection of Conformational Ensembles onto Collective Coordinates; location not provided Issue The manuscript states that for six short-form targets, the LID-based distance d1 is computed over 28-37% of the residue range, while the angle θ1 is computed over 12-21%. The text notes that the d1 selection is identical between models and experimental structures, but the θ1 selection is slightly smaller in the experimental structures because some residues are unresolved. This is a subtle but important detail that affects the comparability of the angle measurements. Required correction Clarify whether the θ1 values for these six targets are directly comparable to those of the long-form targets, given the different fractional coverage. If they are not directly comparable, state this explicitly in the figure captions and in the text where these values are discussed. However, the sample size (26 complexes) is modest, and the text does not report confidence intervals for the correlations. The term could be interpreted as referring to the open-to-closed conformational change, the catalytic cycle, or the ligand binding process. Required correction Define "functional transitions" explicitly in the introduction, and ensure that the usage throughout the manuscript is consistent with this definition. This may be a typographical error, or it may reflect a version numbering scheme that differs from what the community expects. Required correction Verify the software version number and correct if necessary. If the version is correct, provide a citation or reference for it. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Methods, Homology Modeling Evidence pointer Methods, Homology Modeling, Model Generation; location not provided Issue The manuscript does not specify the version of MODELLER used, nor the exact parameters for the "AutoModel" class beyond the refinement level. This limits reproducibility. Required correction Provide the MODELLER version and any non-default parameters used in the modeling protocol. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of "mapping functional transitions" (title, abstract) is not supported by the presented evidence, which demonstrates generation of bound-like conformations rather than characterization of transitions. The generalizability claim that gEDES-HM "could provide a practical route" for families beyond ADK is speculative, as validation is limited to a single family with a conserved domain motion. The reported success rates (92.3% for docking, 84.6% for binding-site generation) cannot be verified without access to the figures and tables containing the underlying data. The statement that "the accuracy obtained in docking calculations using HMgEDES is marginally higher than that recorded at the homology modeling stage" is presented as a meaningful result, but the difference (84.6% vs 92.3%) is based on a small number of cases (2 additional targets recovered) and may not be statistically robust. The claim that "every target for which a sub-2.5 Å binding-site model was available also produced a native-like pose" is presented as a positive result, but it also implies that the docking step adds no value beyond the modeling step for these cases, which is not discussed. The assertion that "failures cannot be attributed clearly to the use of transferred ensembles only" is based on the observation that the same systems fail with experimental structures, but the sample size (2 systems) is too small to draw strong conclusions.
