Results, Discussion and Conclusions, Data and Software Availability, Acknowledgements). Supplementary Material section is listed but its content is not included. Assessment boundary Evaluation is restricted to the supplied manuscript text and the claims it makes. No independent verification of code, data repositories, competition leaderboards, or cited literature was performed. Numerical values are taken as reported by the authors. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors report two open-source, physics-based entries to the ASAP-Polaris-OpenADMET antiviral pose prediction challenge based on templated molecular growth with hybrid ML/MM potentials (FEgrow). They claim their approach was among the top-performing physics-based methods, that a retrospective workflow making greater use of training data as templates achieves a 74% success rate across SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV Mpro, that building poses against an ensemble of feasible side-chain conformers (via ApoDock) improves the generation of low-RMSD poses, and that the tested scoring functions (ApoScore, gnina, short ABFE) cannot reliably select native-like poses from the generated ensemble. Visible evidence base Abstract; Introduction; Methods (prospective manual core selection, prospective MCS core selection, retrospective FEgrow plus ApoDock); Results (three subsections with references to Figures 1 to 6 and Sections S1 and S2); Discussion and Conclusions; Data and Software Availability. Figure content itself is not reproduced in the supplied text, only referenced. Missing materials affecting confidence Supplementary Material (Section S1 ABFE methods, Section S2 interaction fingerprints) is not provided. Figure panels are referenced but not included, so visual and quantitative details cannot be inspected. Competition leaderboard and organizer baseline values are cited but not reproduced. No per-ligand data tables are supplied. Reviewer Overall assessment This is a well-motivated and transparently reported account of a blind-challenge participation, with a useful negative result on pose selection from receptor ensembles. The work is strongest as a methodological case study and as a community resource. However, several central quantitative claims rest on retrospective reanalysis, on a small number of systems, and on comparisons to competition baselines that are not fully documented in the supplied text. The scoring-function and ABFE conclusions are appropriately hedged but are limited by the specific implementations tested. The manuscript is readable and the limitations are largely acknowledged, but the evidence as presented does not fully establish some of the headline performance and mechanistic claims without the missing supplementary detail and figure-level data. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational chemists and structure-based drug design practitioners interested in pose prediction, template-based molecular growth, and receptor flexibility. Developers and users of open-source docking and scoring tools (FEgrow, ApoDock, gnina). Participants and organizers of blind challenges (D3R, CACHE, CASP, ASAP-Polaris-OpenADMET) interested in benchmarking methodology and in the failure modes of scoring functions. Researchers working on Mpro antiviral design who need to understand when rigid-receptor approximations break down. Major strengths The study addresses a genuinely important and under-reported problem, namely pose selection from generated ensembles rather than pose generation alone. The prospective blind-challenge context provides an objective external benchmark. The authors report a negative result (scoring functions no better than random) that is valuable to the community. The workflow is open-source and the data and code are made available. The retrospective improvement to 74% is a concrete, testable claim. The analysis of side-chain flexibility (M165, Q189, M49 for SARS-CoV-2; Q192, L49, M25, Q167, M168 for MERS-CoV) is mechanistically informative, and the compound 2 MERS-CoV example illustrates the induced-fit argument clearly. The manuscript distinguishes generation from selection, which is a useful conceptual framing. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / claim support Claim pointer The retrospective workflow achieves a 74% success rate across SARS-CoV-2 and MERS-CoV Mpro, described as would have been the competition's top-performing physics-based method and among the best across all categories for MERS-CoV. Evidence pointer Results, subsection "FEgrow Is among the Top-Scoring Physics-Based Methods in the Prospective Pose Challenge"; Figure 3 (MCS-based retrospective); Methods, subsection "Retrospective Analysis: Combining FEgrow and ApoDock". Concern The 74% figure is derived from a retrospective procedure that uses the released crystal structures and training-set receptor structures, and it is not a prospective result. The manuscript states that apart from hindsight no information unavailable at the start of the blind competition was used, but the retrospective MERS-CoV procedure builds ligands into SARS-CoV-2 training protein structures and maps them back onto the MERS-CoV reference by backbone alignment. The dependence of the reported success rate on this specific mapping and on the choice of closest-MCS training structure is not quantified, and no uncertainty estimate or per-target breakdown with confidence intervals is given. Why it matters The headline performance claim is the main quantitative result of the paper. If it is sensitive to arbitrary retrospective choices, the claim that the method would have been top-ranked is not established. Resolution test Provide per-target success rates with confidence intervals, a sensitivity analysis over the choice of template receptor structure and mapping procedure, and an explicit statement of which steps require post-hoc information. Report the same metric under a strictly prospective-compatible protocol. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Technical soundness / statistical support Claim pointer Neither ApoScore nor gnina is significantly better than random picking for selecting low-RMSD poses from the ensemble, and short ABFE calculations do not recover the lowest-RMSD conformers better than random. Evidence pointer Results, subsection "Scoring Functions Cannot Reliably Sort Binding Poses from Decoys"; Figure 5; Figure 6; Section S1 (not provided). Concern The negative conclusion is based on a single ensemble size (20 receptor structures), a single target pair, and a subset of 27 neutral MERS-CoV ligands for ABFE. The ABFE analysis explicitly does not enforce pose-restricted sampling and relies on short simulation time to keep ligands kinetically trapped, with acknowledged substantial shifts. The claim of no significant improvement is supported by a paired bootstrap, but the power of that test is not reported, and the absence of evidence is presented close to evidence of absence. Why it matters The paper's central methodological message is that scoring is the bottleneck. If the tests are underpowered or the sampling is inadequate, the conclusion may reflect the specific protocol rather than a general property of scoring functions. Resolution test Report statistical power or effect sizes for the random-versus-scoring comparisons, expand the ABFE subset and ensemble size where feasible, and state explicitly that the conclusion is limited to the tested protocols. Provide the ABFE convergence diagnostics referenced in Section S1. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Technical soundness / reproducibility Claim pointer Building poses against an ensemble of feasible side-chain conformers is useful in generating improved binding poses, with enrichment of low-RMSD poses especially for MERS-CoV. Evidence pointer Results, subsection "Rigid Receptor Approximation Limits Achievable Accuracy"; Figure 4; Figure 5; Section S2 (not provided). Concern The enrichment claim rests on the subset of structures with the lowest ligand RMSD per compound (blue points), which is a best-case selection and therefore not a measure of prospective utility. The reported fractions (72% SARS-CoV-2, 59% MERS-CoV with pocket RMSD < 2 Å) are conditional on already having selected the best pose. The ApoDock ensemble was generated once per target rather than conditioned per ligand, which the authors acknowledge, and the per-residue RMSD distributions show ApoDock underestimates the L49 displacement in MERS-CoV. Why it matters The claim that side-chain ensembles are useful for generation is plausible but the presented metric conflates generation capacity with selection, and the ensemble may not sample the relevant conformational states. Resolution test Report generation enrichment using an unbiased metric that does not condition on the best pose, quantify how often the native-like side-chain conformation is present in the ensemble, and state the fraction of cases where the correct pose is absent from the ensemble entirely. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Claim support / comparison validity Claim pointer The approach was among the top-performing physics-based methods, and the corrected MCS-based entry would have moved alongside another template-based approach as the top-ranked open-source software entries. Evidence pointer Abstract; Results, subsection "FEgrow Is among the Top-Scoring Physics-Based Methods in the Prospective Pose Challenge"; Introduction. Concern The ranking claims depend on competition leaderboard values that are summarized in the text but not reproduced, and on a post-hoc correction of 11 misaligned structures. The effect of that correction on the reported 47% and 48% values is described qualitatively but the corrected prospective numbers are not given as a clean before-and-after table. Comparisons to POSIT, FlexX, Glide, and EasyDock/AutoDock are cited from the competition report rather than independently analyzed. Why it matters Ranking claims are relative claims and require the comparison set to be visible and consistently computed. Resolution test Provide a table of all physics-based entries with success rates as reported by the organizers, clearly mark which values are the authors' own and which are from the leaderboard, and give the corrected prospective success rates before and after the alignment fix. Major Concerns (continued) Concern ID R1-M5 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Technical soundness / method description Claim pointer The hybrid ML/MM protocol with scaled Lennard-Jones radii and charges mitigates the rigid-protein approximation, and the lowest-energy conformation is extracted as the best pose. Evidence pointer Methods, first paragraph; Introduction. Concern The scaling of Lennard-Jones radii and atomic charges is described as mitigating the rigid-protein approximation but no values, rationale, or validation are given in the supplied text. The selection of the single lowest-energy conformer as the pose is a strong assumption that is not benchmarked against alternative selection criteria within the prospective workflow. Why it matters These choices directly affect pose accuracy and reproducibility, and readers cannot assess or reproduce them from the supplied text. Resolution test State the scaling factors and their basis, and report a sensitivity analysis of pose success to the conformer selection criterion. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Reporting completeness Affected element Prospective submission results Evidence pointer Results, subsection "FEgrow Is among the Top-Scoring Physics-Based Methods in the Prospective Pose Challenge" Issue The text reports 47% and 48% before correction and 54% after correction for the MCS approach, but the corrected value for the manual core submission is not stated. Required correction Report the corrected success rate for the manual core submission alongside the MCS value. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Figure references Evidence pointer Results, multiple subsections; Figures 1 to 6 Issue Several figure references appear without panel letters in the supplied text (for example "Figure a", "Figure b"), and the mapping between claims and specific panels is sometimes ambiguous. Required correction Ensure every figure citation specifies the panel and that each quantitative claim points to a specific panel. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Terminology consistency Affected element Software naming Evidence pointer Methods and Results Issue The software is referred to as both "Apodock" and "ApoDock" in different places. Required correction Use a single consistent spelling throughout. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element ABFE protocol Evidence pointer Results, subsection "Scoring Functions Cannot Reliably Sort Binding Poses from Decoys"; Section S1 (not provided) Issue The ABFE protocol is summarized as 0.1 ns per window with five independent replicates, but the number of windows, the restraint scheme, and the convergence criteria are only in Section S1, which is not supplied. Required correction Summarize the key ABFE parameters in the main text and ensure Section S1 is available to reviewers and readers. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Claim precision Affected element Abstract and Discussion Evidence pointer Abstract; Discussion and Conclusions Issue The phrase "among the top-performing physics-based methods" is used without a defined threshold or rank. Required correction State the rank or percentile relative to the 13 physics-based entries. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established R1-M1 (retrospective 74% claim lacks sensitivity analysis and uncertainty), R1-M2 (negative scoring conclusion may be underpowered and protocol-limited), R1-M3 (enrichment metric conditions on best pose), R1-M4 (ranking claims depend on unreproduced leaderboard values and post-hoc correction), R1-M5 (ML/MM scaling and pose selection not documented). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality Moderate. The individual components (FEgrow, ApoDock, gnina, ABFE) are established. The originality lies in the blind-challenge evaluation, the generation-versus-selection framing, and the negative result on pose selection from receptor ensembles. This is a useful contribution but not a conceptual advance. Scientific importance Moderate to high for the computational drug design community. The finding that side-chain ensembles improve generation but not selection is practically important and aligns with known scoring limitations. The claim of a 74% retrospective success rate, if robust, would be of interest, but its retrospective nature limits its weight. Interdisciplinary readership Limited. The work is specialized and assumes familiarity with docking, ML/MM potentials, and free energy calculations. The conceptual message about generation versus selection could interest a broader computational audience, but the manuscript is written primarily for specialists. Technical soundness Partially established. The prospective workflow is clearly described. The retrospective analyses are plausible but under-supported in the supplied text, with missing supplementary detail, absent uncertainty estimates, and metrics that condition on best-case selection. Readability for nonspecialists Fair. The Introduction provides good context on Mpro and blind challenges. The Results are dense with method-specific terminology and would benefit from a schematic of the workflow and a clearer separation of prospective and retrospective results. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence for the headline retrospective performance and ranking claims. Supportive if technical concerns are resolved, specifically if the retrospective 74% claim is accompanied by sensitivity analysis and uncertainty, if the scoring and ABFE negative results are reported with power or effect sizes and explicit protocol limitations, and if the ranking comparisons are made fully visible. The negative result on pose selection is the most robust and valuable element and could anchor a revised manuscript. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that the retrospective workflow "would have been the competition's top-performing physics-based method" is not supported by the supplied material because the leaderboard values are summarized rather than reproduced and the retrospective protocol uses post-hoc information. The claim that the approach was "among the top-performing physics-based methods" lacks a defined rank or threshold in the supplied text. The claim that scaling Lennard-Jones radii and atomic charges "mitigate[s] to some extent the rigid-protein approximation" is asserted without values, rationale, or validation. The claim that ApoDock-generated ensembles are "similar to those observed experimentally" is based on visual comparison of distributions and is qualified by the authors as "not in perfect agreement"; it is weak as stated. The claim that scoring functions are "unable to successfully pick out native structures" is supported only for the specific implementations, ensemble size, and target pair tested, and the statistical power of the comparison is not reported. The claim that short ABFE calculations fail to enrich low-RMSD poses is limited by the acknowledged lack of pose-restricted sampling and by the small subset of 27 neutral MERS-CoV ligands. The statement that "apart from the use of hindsight, we did not use any information here that was unavailable at the start of the blind competition" is difficult to evaluate because the retrospective procedure depends on released crystal structures and training-set receptor structures, and the boundary between hindsight and available information is not precisely defined. The reported 72% and 59% pocket RMSD fractions for the lowest-ligand-RMSD subset are conditional on best-pose selection and should not be interpreted as prospective enrichment.

material were available for evaluation Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose an integrated pipeline combining Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD), a beta-variational autoencoder (betaVAE), and Markov state models (MSM) to characterize the activation landscape of FGFR3 kinase. They report that phosphorylation induces domain rearrangement and activation-loop dynamics, that coordinated movement of a molecular brake and regulatory spine governs activation, that ligand binding stabilizes the active phosphorylated state with a free energy of -19 kcal/mol, that protein structure network analysis reveals long-range allosteric pathways, and that specific loops (alphaCbeta4, beta34, beta45) represent potential allosteric intervention sites. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no figures, tables, methods descriptions, or supplementary data were provided Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, simulation parameters, convergence criteria, free energy calculation details, uncertainty estimates, validation of the machine learning components, structural figures, and any statistical analysis Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract presents an ambitious integration of physics-based and machine learning methods to address a biologically and clinically relevant question in kinase regulation. The conceptual framing is sound and the potential impact is high if the technical execution is rigorous. However, the abstract alone does not provide sufficient evidence to evaluate the validity of the central claims. Several quantitative statements, particularly the free energy value of -19 kcal/mol, lack context regarding error bars, convergence, and comparison to experimental or other computational benchmarks. The novelty relative to existing GaMD-MSM and VAE-based studies on kinases is not clearly articulated. The claim regarding "gatekeeper mutants" in the final sentence appears unsupported by any evidence described in the abstract. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational biophysicists and chemists working on enhanced sampling methods and machine learning for molecular dynamics would be interested in the methodological integration. Structural biologists studying kinase regulation, particularly FGFR family kinases, would value the mechanistic insights. Drug discovery researchers targeting FGFR3, especially those addressing resistance mutations, would find the allosteric site predictions potentially actionable. The work could also appeal to method developers interested in the combination of VAE-based dimensionality reduction with MSM construction. Major strengths The integration of three complementary computational approaches is conceptually appealing and addresses a real limitation in studying slow conformational transitions in kinases. The focus on FGFR3 is timely given its clinical relevance in cancer and skeletal disorders. The identification of specific structural elements (molecular brake, regulatory spine, specific loops) provides testable hypotheses. The stated goal of informing next-generation therapeutics is clinically meaningful. The specific application to FGFR3 and the focus on dual regulation by phosphorylation and ligand binding adds some novelty, but the abstract does not clearly distinguish the methodological advance from prior work. Scientific importance: The biological question is important, and the potential to identify allosteric sites for therapeutic intervention is significant. However, the importance of the specific findings cannot be fully assessed without quantitative validation and comparison to experimental data. Interdisciplinary readership: The work bridges computational chemistry, machine learning, structural biology, and drug discovery, which would appeal to a broad readership if the methods and results are presented accessibly. Technical soundness: Cannot be evaluated from the abstract alone. Critical details on simulation length, force field, convergence, hyperparameter selection, and model validation are absent. Readability for nonspecialists: The abstract is reasonably clear but uses specialized terminology without sufficient context. Terms such as "molecular brake" and "regulatory spine" are introduced without definition, which may hinder accessibility for readers outside the kinase field. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The abstract presents plausible claims, but the absence of methodological detail, uncertainty quantification, and validation against experimental or independent computational benchmarks prevents a supportive recommendation. A full manuscript with rigorous technical evidence could change this assessment. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Quantitative claim without uncertainty or convergence evidence Claim pointer "Ligand interaction stabilizes the active phosphorylated state with a free energy of -19 kcal/mol" Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Concern The abstract reports a specific free energy value of -19 kcal/mol for ligand stabilization of the active phosphorylated state. No information is provided regarding the statistical uncertainty of this estimate, the convergence of the free energy calculation, the method used to compute it (e.g., umbrella sampling, metadynamics, end-point methods), or the reference state for the reported value. Free energy differences of this magnitude are highly sensitive to force field parameters, simulation length, and analysis methodology. Why it matters A single free energy value without error bars or convergence assessment cannot be interpreted meaningfully. If the value is not converged or carries large uncertainty, the central thermodynamic claim of the paper is not supported. Additionally, without a clear definition of the reference state, the value is not reproducible or comparable to other studies. Resolution test Provide the free energy estimate with associated uncertainty (e.g., standard error or confidence interval), demonstrate convergence through block analysis or multiple independent simulations, specify the exact computational protocol, and compare the value to experimental binding affinities or previous computational estimates for FGFR3 or homologous kinases. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Model validation and interpretability Claim pointer "The variational autoencoder with tunable regularization was used for nonlinear dimension reduction and identifying slow collective variables. The Markov state model (MSM) was used for identifying metastable states spanning active-inactive conformations." Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Concern The abstract does not describe how the betaVAE latent space was validated as capturing physically meaningful slow collective variables, nor how the MSM was validated for statistical robustness (e.g., Chapman-Kolmogorov tests, implied timescale analysis, state population uncertainty). The choice of beta value, the number of latent dimensions, and the MSM lag time are not reported. Without these details, the metastable states and the claimed "activation landscape" cannot be assessed for reliability. Why it matters The central methodological contribution is the integration of these three methods. If the VAE latent space does not correspond to physically relevant coordinates, or if the MSM is not statistically validated, the resulting landscape and mechanistic conclusions may be artifacts of the analysis pipeline rather than genuine features of the system. Resolution test Provide validation of the VAE latent space (e.g., reconstruction error, comparison to known structural order parameters, sensitivity analysis on beta and latent dimensionality), and validate the MSM through implied timescale plots, Chapman-Kolmogorov tests, and uncertainty estimates on state populations and transition probabilities. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Unsupported translational claim Claim pointer "The integrated GaMD-betaVAE-MSM pipeline provides mechanistic insights into FGFR3 activation and may help the rational design of next-generation FGFR3-targeted therapeutics resistant to gatekeeper mutants." Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Concern The abstract makes a claim about therapeutic design "resistant to gatekeeper mutants" without any evidence that gatekeeper mutations were studied, that the identified allosteric sites are relevant to resistance mechanisms, or that the pipeline has any predictive power for drug design. This appears to be a speculative extrapolation beyond the presented scope. Why it matters Overstating translational relevance without supporting data undermines the credibility of the work. If the study did not include gatekeeper mutant simulations or drug design calculations, this claim should be removed or substantially softened. If such data exist, they must be described in the abstract or the claim should be deferred to the full manuscript. Resolution test Either remove the gatekeeper mutant claim from the abstract, or provide evidence that gatekeeper mutations were explicitly simulated and that the allosteric sites identified are mechanistically linked to resistance. If drug design is intended, demonstrate that the pipeline can discriminate between known inhibitors or generate testable predictions. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Novelty and differentiation from prior work Claim pointer "Here, we introduce an integrated GaMD-betaVAE-MSM pipeline, a hybrid physics-ML framework for studying kinase activation." Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Concern The abstract does not articulate how this pipeline differs from previously published combinations of enhanced sampling, autoencoders, and MSMs applied to kinases or other proteins. GaMD, VAE-based dimensionality reduction, and MSM are each established techniques, and their combination has been reported in various forms. The specific novelty of the betaVAE regularization choice, the integration strategy, or the application to FGFR3 is not made clear. Why it matters For a methods-oriented claim, the novelty must be explicit. If the combination is straightforward and the novelty lies only in the application to FGFR3, the framing should reflect that. If there is a methodological advance, it must be stated clearly to justify the claim of introducing a new pipeline. Resolution test In the full manuscript, clearly state what is new about the integration compared to prior GaMD-MSM and VAE-MSM studies. If the novelty is the specific application, reframe the claim accordingly. If the novelty is methodological, describe the specific advance and benchmark against existing approaches. Required correction Include these essential parameters in the abstract or indicate that they are fully described in the main text. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Statistical reporting Affected element Free energy and state populations Evidence pointer Abstract, location not provided Issue No uncertainty estimates are provided for any quantitative result, including the free energy value and the relative populations of metastable states. Required correction Report error bars or confidence intervals for all quantitative claims, or state that such estimates are provided in the main text. Required correction Clarify whether the simulations included conditions with phosphorylation alone, ligand alone, and both, and how the synergistic or additive effects were assessed. Risk / unsupported claims The free energy value of -19 kcal/mol is unsupported without uncertainty estimates, convergence analysis, and methodological detail. The claim regarding "gatekeeper mutants" is unsupported by any evidence described in the abstract. The identification of "potential regulatory sites" (alphaCbeta4, beta34, beta45 loops) is presented without structural context or validation. The statement that the pipeline "may help the rational design of next-generation FGFR3-targeted therapeutics" is speculative and not supported by the abstract content. discussion, materials and methods, and supporting information references. Assessment boundary Scientific content, methodological rigor, internal consistency, and support of claims by presented evidence. Editorial or stylistic preferences are noted only where they affect comprehension. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors propose that the A475V substitution in the SARS-CoV-2 RBD large loop (residues 475–490) attenuates ACE2 binding and viral fitness through hydrophobic remodeling and conformational reorganization, in contrast to the L455S substitution in JN.1 which primarily affects local receptor contacts. They further propose that the large loop is a structurally plastic yet functionally constrained element balancing receptor recognition, conformational stability, and antigenic diversification. Visible evidence base Cryo-EM structures of JN.4 spike in complex with ACE2 (global 2.90 Å, local 3.73 Å), biolayer interferometry binding measurements, pseudovirus infectivity assays, cell-cell fusion assays, thermal shift assays, molecular dynamics simulations, and phylogenetic analyses. Missing materials affecting confidence Raw cryo-EM maps and validation reports (half-map FSC curves, model vs map Q-scores) are not provided. Statistical details for binding measurements (number of replicates, error bars) are not fully specified. MD simulation convergence criteria and replicate information are not provided. Pseudovirus infectivity data are presented without numerical values or statistical comparisons in the text. Supporting figures (S1–S7) and tables (S1–S2) are referenced but not available for review. Reviewer Overall assessment This manuscript addresses a relevant question in SARS-CoV-2 evolution: how a hydrophobic substitution in a flexible RBD loop affects receptor engagement and viral fitness. The combination of structural, biophysical, and functional approaches is appropriate and potentially informative. However, the central claim that A475V attenuates viral fitness through a specific structural mechanism is only partially supported by the presented evidence. The structural analysis is descriptive and lacks quantitative validation of the proposed conformational differences. The functional data are presented without sufficient statistical detail, and the connection between reduced ACE2 affinity and viral fitness is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The manuscript would benefit from clearer presentation of quantitative results and a more rigorous treatment of the structural comparisons. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers studying SARS-CoV-2 evolution, spike protein structure-function relationships, and viral entry mechanisms. The work may also interest those investigating how structural flexibility in protein interfaces constrains or permits sequence diversification under immune pressure. Major strengths The study combines multiple complementary approaches (cryo-EM, BLI, pseudovirus assays, MD simulations) to address a focused question. The comparison between JN.1 and JN.4 provides a natural experiment for dissecting region-specific effects of mutations. The identification of A475 and F486 as functionally constrained hydrophobic residues within a variable loop is a potentially useful conceptual contribution. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence sufficiency for structural claims Claim pointer The authors claim that A475V induces "local remodeling of the receptor-binding motif" and "alters the RBD–ACE2 interaction geometry," and that this results in a "substantial reorganization of loop geometry" based on a distance change from 3.8 Å to 8.5 Å between residues 475 and 486. Evidence pointer Results section "Region-specific remodeling mechanisms at the RBD-ACE2 interfaces," Fig 2 Concern The structural interpretation relies on a single cryo-EM structure of JN.4 at 3.73 Å local resolution. The claim of "substantial reorganization" is based on a single distance measurement between two residues, without statistical comparison across multiple structures or states. The RMSD values reported (1.1 Å and 1.058 Å against JN.1 and BA.2.86, respectively) suggest overall structural conservation, yet the authors emphasize local differences without providing quantitative measures of local conformational change (e.g., per-residue RMSF, dihedral angle changes, or interaction energy calculations). The proposed mechanism of steric hindrance from the bulkier valine side chain is plausible but not directly demonstrated. Why it matters The central mechanistic claim of the paper rests on the structural interpretation. If the conformational differences are within the noise of the cryo-EM maps at this resolution, the proposed mechanism is not established. Resolution test Provide quantitative comparison of local conformational differences (e.g., per-residue RMSD or RMSF between structures), map-to-model validation metrics (Q-scores) for the loop region, and ideally multiple independent reconstructions or focused classification to demonstrate that the observed loop conformation is stable and not an artifact of local resolution limitations. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor of functional data Claim pointer The authors claim that A475V causes a 3.5-fold reduction in ACE2-binding affinity compared with BA.2.86, and that various mutations cause 1.3- to 1.9-fold reductions in pseudovirus infectivity. Evidence pointer Results sections "Kinetic binding analysis" and "Infectivity and fusogenicity," Figs 4 and 5 Concern The binding data are presented as KD values with standard deviations, but the number of independent replicates is not stated. The pseudovirus infectivity data are described in the text without numerical values, error bars, or statistical test results in the visible text. The statement that "all the mutations exhibited low infectivity compared to BA.2.86 (1.3- to 1.9-fold decrease; p < 0.001)" lacks specification of which statistical test was used and whether multiple comparisons were corrected for. The cell-cell fusion data are described qualitatively without quantitative metrics. Why it matters The conclusion that A475V attenuates viral fitness depends on the reliability and statistical significance of the functional measurements. Without proper statistical reporting, the reader cannot assess whether the observed differences are robust. Resolution test Provide complete statistical details: number of independent experiments, exact p-values, confidence intervals, and specification of statistical tests. Present pseudovirus infectivity and cell-cell fusion data as quantified values with error bars and statistical comparisons. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Logical connection between structural and functional observations Claim pointer The authors propose that A475V "attenuates ACE2 engagement and viral fitness" through "hydrophobic remodeling" and that this explains the limited epidemiological expansion of JN.4 compared to JN.1. Evidence pointer Abstract, Discussion Concern The manuscript does not directly demonstrate that the reduced ACE2 binding affinity of A475V translates to reduced viral fitness in a physiological context. The pseudovirus infectivity assay uses a single cell line (293T-ACE2) and does not account for other factors that influence viral fitness, such as immune evasion, replication kinetics, or stability in respiratory secretions. The connection between the in vitro measurements and the epidemiological observation that JN.4 exhibited limited expansion is speculative. Why it matters The title and abstract make a claim about viral fitness that is not directly tested. Overinterpretation of in vitro data as evidence of fitness differences in humans could mislead readers. Resolution test Either temper the claims about viral fitness to reflect the in vitro nature of the measurements, or provide additional evidence (e.g., competition assays, replication kinetics in relevant cell types, or animal models) that directly links A475V to reduced fitness. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Support for the "functionally constrained" conclusion Claim pointer The authors conclude that A475 and F486 are "functionally constrained hydrophobic residues" that "preserve the structural framework of ACE2 engagement despite extensive sequence variation within the surrounding loop." Evidence pointer Results section "Evolutionary conservation of hydrophobic anchors within the plastic large loop," Fig 3 Concern The evidence for functional constraint is based on sequence comparisons and structural observations, but the manuscript does not include a systematic mutagenesis scan of the loop region that would demonstrate which residues are functionally constrained. The text mentions "systematic mutagenesis" in the abstract but the results section does not describe such an experiment in detail. The conclusion that A475 and F486 are uniquely constrained is not supported by comparative mutagenesis data. Why it matters The claim of functional constraint is a key conceptual contribution. Without direct experimental evidence (e.g., alanine scanning or saturation mutagenesis of the loop), the conclusion is speculative. Resolution test Provide the systematic mutagenesis data referenced in the abstract, or revise the conclusion to reflect that the constraint is inferred from sequence conservation and structural analysis rather than directly demonstrated. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity of methods Affected element Materials and methods, "Protein expression and purification" Evidence pointer Location not provided Issue The methods section describes cloning of "WT-S, XAB.1.5-S, and BA.2.86-S" but the text later refers to JN.1 and JN.4 constructs. The nomenclature is inconsistent and confusing. Required correction Clarify which constructs were used for which experiments and ensure consistent naming throughout. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Completeness of figure legends Affected element Figs 4 and 5 Evidence pointer Location not provided Issue Figure legends do not specify the number of replicates, error bar definitions, or statistical tests used. Required correction Add complete statistical information to figure legends. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Internal consistency Affected element Results section "Evolutionary conservation of hydrophobic anchors" Evidence pointer Location not provided Issue The text contains a duplicated paragraph: "Despite the lack of conserved hydrophobic residues within this region, hydrophobic substitutions occur recurrently, often leading to distinct structural shifts within the 475–490 loop. Within this region, residues 475, 483, 484, 486, and 490 show particularly frequent hydrophobic substitutions across circulating variants." This information is presented twice in consecutive paragraphs. Required correction Remove the redundant paragraph. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Methodological detail Affected element Materials and methods, "Molecular Dynamics" Evidence pointer Location not provided Issue The MD simulation section states that "the V475A structure was obtained from the A475V structure" but does not specify how the mutation was introduced or whether the system was equilibrated before the production run. The simulation time (300 ns) is stated but convergence is not demonstrated. Required correction Provide details on mutation introduction, equilibration protocol, and convergence assessment (e.g., RMSD plateau, block averaging). Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Referencing Affected element Introduction and Discussion Evidence pointer Location not provided Issue Several statements about epidemiological trends (e.g., JN.4 limited expansion) are made without citations to epidemiological data. Required correction Add appropriate references to support claims about viral spread and prevalence. Risk / unsupported claims The claim that A475V "attenuates viral fitness" is not directly supported by the presented data, which are limited to in vitro binding and pseudovirus infectivity assays in a single cell line. The claim that A475 and F486 are "functionally constrained" is inferred from sequence conservation and structural analysis but is not directly tested by mutagenesis experiments, despite the abstract mentioning "systematic mutagenesis." The proposed mechanism of steric hindrance from the A475V substitution altering loop conformation and reducing ACE2 binding is plausible but not quantitatively validated. The epidemiological relevance of the findings (limited expansion of JN.4) is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in this manuscript. The MD simulation results are described qualitatively; free energy calculations are mentioned but numerical values are not provided in the visible text.

01 基本信息 标题 ：EquiDesign: a versatile computational framework for de novo protein sequence design 作者 ：Gao, Qiang; Xu, Zhongyu; Chen, Kai; Cen, Xiaochen; Yan, Ke; Liu, Jinxin; Ji, Zhiwei 单位 ：南京农业大学（Nanjing Agricultural University），作者贡献信息中提及 Bioinformatics Center, NJAU 期刊/平台 ：Briefings in Bioinformatics 年份 ：2026（在线日期 2026-10-26） 论文类型 ：方法学（深度学习框架） 领域 ：蛋白质逆折叠（inverse folding）/ 蛋白质序列设计 关键词 ：inverse folding; protein sequence design; Equiformer; geometric deep learning; SE(3) equivariance DOI/arXiv ：10.1093/bib/bbag581 代码 ：https://github.com/NJAU-CDSIC/EquiDesign 数据 ：CATH 4.4、TS50、TS500、IDRome-120、TS45（均为公开数据集） 阅读日期 ：未提供 在课题方向中的位置 ：本文属于「蛋白质结构相关计算研究 × AI 方法」中的 序列设计（inverse folding） 子方向，核心贡献是将 Equiformer（SE(3)-等变 Transformer）引入逆折叠任务，通过等变向量通道显式建模主链方向拓扑，属于几何深度学习在蛋白质设计中的应用。 02 一句话总结 本文提出 EquiDesign，一个基于 Equiformer 的深度学习框架，通过将几何特征解耦为不变标量与等变向量、结合空间 KNN 图与几何注意力，在 CATH 4.4、TS50、TS500、IDRome-120 和 TS45 五个基准上实现优于现有方法的序列恢复率，并生成经 ESMFold/AF3 验证可正确折叠的多样序列。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：给定一个目标蛋白质主链三维结构，如何设计出能折叠为该结构的氨基酸序列（蛋白质逆折叠问题）。 为什么重要 ：逆折叠是 de novo 蛋白质设计的核心瓶颈——只有先解决序列设计，才能实现功能性蛋白质的从头设计，对治疗性蛋白、工业酶、生物传感器等有直接应用价值。 现有方法为何不足 ： 物理方法（Rosetta 等）依赖经验力场，计算昂贵且精度有限； 早期统计方法受限于同源数据； 现有深度学习方法（如 ProteinMPNN、PiFold）虽有效，但多基于消息传递或不变特征，未能显式建模主链的方向性几何信息（如 N→C 方向、局部坐标系取向），导致对结构拓扑的捕捉不完整。 精确研究问题 ：Can an SE(3)-equivariant architecture with disentangled scalar-vector representations achieve higher sequence recovery and better generalization across diverse protein families than existing message-passing and invariant-feature-based inverse folding methods? Equiformer 网络 ：多层等变 Transformer 块，联合处理标量特征和向量特征，进行几何感知的消息传递 6. Assessment boundary Scientific and technical evaluation of the described framework, methodology, experimental design, reported results, and claims. No evaluation of editorial fit or journal policy. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present EquiDesign, a deep learning framework for inverse protein folding that uses an Equiformer-enhanced architecture with multistep feature extraction, spatial K-nearest neighbor graph construction, and geometric attention. They claim superior sequence recovery on standard and challenging benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art methods, along with generated sequences exhibiting high structural fidelity, folding stability, and diversity. Visible evidence base Abstract, introduction, methods (dataset preprocessing, model architecture, training, evaluation metrics, comparison baselines, ablation study, sampling strategy, simulation environment), results (ablation, benchmark comparisons, per-residue accuracy, generalization, de novo design), discussion, conclusion, data availability statement. Tables and figures referenced but not provided in full. Missing materials affecting confidence Full tables (Tables 1-8), all figures (Figs 1-4), all supplementary materials (Tables S1-S17, Figs S1-S5), detailed hyperparameter configurations, baseline implementation details, statistical test specifications, and the actual numerical results. Without these, quantitative claims cannot be independently verified. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript describes a technically plausible architecture for inverse protein folding that combines established components (Equiformer, geometric graph construction, multistep feature extraction) in a coherent manner. The methodological description is largely clear, and the evaluation strategy covers multiple benchmark types. However, the provided text lacks the quantitative results, full tables, and figures necessary to assess whether the claimed improvements are real, substantial, and statistically robust. Several claims in the abstract and results appear stronger than what the visible evidence can support. The relationship to prior work, particularly ProtseqGen, is acknowledged but the incremental contribution needs sharper delineation. The manuscript would benefit from clearer reporting of experimental conditions, baseline fairness, and statistical rigor. Who would be interested in the results, and why Computational protein designers, researchers working on inverse folding and sequence design, and developers of geometric deep learning methods for biomolecular applications. The framework addresses a recognized bottleneck in de novo protein design, and the equivariant architecture is of general interest to the machine learning for structural biology community. Practitioners seeking improved sequence recovery tools for fixed backbones would also find the work relevant. Major strengths 1. The architectural design is well motivated: separating invariant scalar and equivariant vector features is a principled approach for preserving geometric information during message passing. 2. The evaluation spans multiple benchmark types (standard, disordered, free-modeling), which is more comprehensive than many prior studies. 3. The ablation study is thoughtfully designed to isolate contributions of specific components. 4. The authors address important confounds: training-set memorization, compositional bias, and physical energy landscapes. 5. Code and data availability statements are provided, supporting reproducibility. The reader is told that EquiDesign outperforms baselines, but the magnitude of improvement, the variance across runs, and the specific comparison values are absent. Without these data, the claim of "superior" performance is unverifiable. Why it matters The primary contribution of this work is empirical: a new architecture that improves sequence recovery. If the numerical evidence is not presented, the case for the method's utility is not established. Resolution test Provide full results tables with mean and standard deviation for all methods on all benchmarks, including per-metric breakdowns. State clearly which differences are statistically significant and with what test. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Baseline fairness Claim pointer "EquiDesign is benchmarked against 16 representative baselines, categorized into five architectural families" (Methods) Evidence pointer Methods section, "Evaluation metrics" and "EquiDesign model training and calibration"; location not provided for baseline training details Concern The manuscript does not describe how baselines were trained or configured. Were all models trained on the same data splits? Were hyperparameters optimized per model or fixed? Were the same evaluation protocols used? Unequal training conditions can produce misleading comparisons. Why it matters Benchmark comparisons are only meaningful if all methods are evaluated under equivalent conditions. Without this information, observed differences could reflect tuning effort rather than architectural merit. Resolution test Describe the training and evaluation protocol for each baseline, including data splits, hyperparameter selection, and any differences in input features. State whether baselines were run with their default settings or re-tuned. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Statistical rigor Claim pointer "EquiDesign significantly outperforms the other four methods across all metrics" (Results, referring to Supplementary Table S3) Evidence pointer Supplementary Tables S3-S5; location not provided Concern The claim of statistical significance is made, but the statistical test used is not specified in the visible text. The number of paired comparisons, correction for multiple testing, and the distributional assumptions are not described. With 10 training runs per model, the effective sample size is small, and the choice of test matters. Why it matters Significance claims require transparent reporting of the test procedure. Without this, the reader cannot assess whether the reported differences are robust or could arise from chance. Resolution test Specify the statistical test used, whether it was paired or unpaired, how multiple comparisons were handled, and report effect sizes alongside p-values. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Validation depth Claim pointer "the generated sequences exhibit exceptional structural fidelity, folding stability, and sequence diversity" (Abstract); "50%–100% of the generated sequences were predicted to be foldable (scRMSD <2.0 Å) by both ESMFold and AF3" (Results) Evidence pointer Table 8, Supplementary Table S11, Fig 4; location not provided Concern The validation of designed sequences relies entirely on computational predictors (ESMFold, AF3, Rosetta). No experimental validation is presented. While this is common in computational papers, the claim of "exceptional" fidelity is strong given that computational predictors can be biased toward their training distributions. The diversity analysis is also limited to sequence-level metrics without functional assays. Why it matters The ultimate goal of protein design is functional proteins. Computational metrics are necessary but not sufficient evidence of design quality. The strength of the claims should match the evidence level. Resolution test Soften claims about "exceptional" fidelity, or add experimental validation for at least a subset of designs. If experimental data are not available, clearly state this as a limitation and frame claims accordingly. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Novelty delineation Claim pointer "The key methodological novelty lies in replacing the conventional Message Passing Neural Network (MPNN) layers with an Equiformer-driven architecture" (Discussion) Evidence pointer Discussion section; location not provided Concern The manuscript states that the initial feature extraction is inherited from ProtseqGen, and the novelty is the Equiformer replacement. However, the specific advantages of this replacement are not demonstrated through targeted experiments. The ablation study shows component contributions, but does not directly compare Equiformer against alternative equivariant or attention-based encoders. Why it matters The contribution of the work depends on showing that the Equiformer architecture provides a meaningful improvement over other possible choices, not just over the specific baselines tested. Resolution test Add an ablation that replaces Equiformer with an alternative modern encoder (e.g., a standard transformer or another equivariant network) to demonstrate the specific benefit of the chosen architecture. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Methods, "Dataset collection and preprocessing" Evidence pointer "This yielded 29 453 training, 1732 validation, and 3466 test structures [25]" Issue The reference [25] for the data split is not described. It is unclear whether this split is standard in the field or specific to this work. Required correction Describe the split procedure or cite the original source of the split. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Completeness Affected element Methods, "EquiDesign model training and calibration" Evidence pointer "Manual hyperparameter tuning (Supplementary Tables S1 and S2) precedes evaluation" Issue The hyperparameter search space and selection criterion are not described in the main text. Required correction Briefly describe the hyperparameter ranges explored and the selection criterion used. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Methods, "Simulation environment" Evidence pointer "EquiDesign was implemented in PyTorch 2.4.1 and Python 3.10.10" Issue The number of training epochs, batch size, and total training time are not reported. Required correction Add these training details to the methods section. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Terminology Affected element Abstract and throughout Evidence pointer "multistep Equiformer-enhanced architecture" Issue The term "multistep" is not clearly defined. It is unclear whether this refers to multiple Equiformer layers, multiple stages of feature extraction, or something else. Required correction Define "multistep" in the methods section when the architecture is first described. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Consistency Affected element Results, "Generalization evaluation on canonical benchmarks" Evidence pointer "After removing all overlapping proteins with the training set, the evaluation comprised 26 and 243 previously unseen samples for TS50 and TS500, respectively" Issue The original TS50 and TS500 contain 50 and 500 proteins. The reduction to 26 and 243 is substantial, but the filtering criteria are not described in the main text. Required correction Describe the overlap removal procedure and report results on both the full and filtered sets if possible. Concern ID R1-m6 Severity Minor Axis Presentation Affected element Results, "Perresidue accuracy and prediction confidence" Evidence pointer "Fig 2A" and "Fig 2B" Issue The text describes trends in the figures, but the figures are not available for review. The description is qualitative. Required correction Provide quantitative summaries of the per-residue accuracy data in the text or tables. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established 1. Missing numerical results for all benchmark comparisons (R1-M1). 2. Undescribed baseline training and evaluation protocol (R1-M2). 3. Unspecified statistical testing procedure (R1-M3). 4. No direct comparison of Equiformer against alternative modern encoders (R1-M4). 5. Computational-only validation with strong claims of "exceptional" fidelity (R1-M4). Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : Moderate. The combination of Equiformer with inverse folding is a reasonable extension of existing work, but the core idea of using equivariant networks for protein sequence design is not entirely new. The specific architectural choices and their justification are somewhat incremental. Scientific importance : Potentially relevant to the protein design community, but the importance depends on the magnitude of improvement over existing methods, which cannot be assessed from the provided text. Interdisciplinary readership : The work sits at the intersection of machine learning and structural biology. The methods section is technical and may be challenging for non-specialists, but the problem framing is accessible. Technical soundness : The architecture is plausible, and the evaluation strategy is thoughtful. However, the lack of visible numerical results and statistical details prevents a full assessment of technical soundness. Readability for nonspecialists : The abstract and introduction are readable, but the methods section assumes significant familiarity with geometric deep learning and protein design terminology. The manuscript would benefit from a brief explanation of key concepts for a broader audience. Recommendation posture Currently not established from the provided evidence. The manuscript describes a plausible and potentially useful framework, but the central quantitative claims cannot be verified without the full results tables, figures, and statistical details. The authors should be invited to provide the complete results and address the methodological reporting gaps. If the numerical evidence supports the claims, the work could be of interest to the community.

基于模型分歧（CKA）选种生成复合物做增强，仅在初始集规模较大（50%/80%）时带来小幅一致的 MCC 提升，在 20% 极端消融下增强反而有害。 03 研究问题 具体问题 ：在生物/化学领域标注数据稀缺的约束下，(1) 训练集 规模 与 分布范围（scope） 如何分别影响 pLM 的学习与泛化？(2) 能否用基于不确定性的主动学习（AL）+ 生成式 pLM（ESM-3）合成数据来补偿被移除的数据？ 为何重要 ：化学/生物数据生成成本高（需实验材料与人力），而现代模型参数量达百万至十亿级，数据需求与可获得性之间存在结构性矛盾；理解「小数据下如何构建数据集」对 pLM 落地至关重要。 现有方法为何不足 ：SMOTE/ADASYN 依赖最近邻插值，难以处理 变长样本 （如蛋白质复合物）；AL 在化学 ML 中多用于小分子/寡肽，尚未系统检验 pLM 场景；LLM 合成数据在 NLP 中有效，但蛋白质「语言」由随机进化压力驱动，与人类文本语料不同。 精确研究问题 ：Can uncertainty-based active learning with generative pLMs produce useful synthetic protein complexes that improve contact-map prediction, and how does this depend on the size and scope of the initial training set? 04 背景与发展脉络 注：以下脉络为「仅本文框架」梳理，未做外部独立核验。 - 阶段 1：数据稀缺与 AL 。AL 是 model-agnostic 方法，假设存在有限标注预算的 oracle，优先标注模型低置信度样本。代表：Smith & Roitberg 用 MLIP 集成分歧选分子训练可迁移势；An et al. 结合遗传算法与 AL 研究生物分子凝聚体。 - 阶段 2：自适应采样（adaptive sampling） 。MD 采样不足时，先跑随机轨迹，再定位欠采样区域构造新轨迹种子；Li et al. 用 MLIP 集成预测标准差排序构象做量子计算并加入训练集。本文将其类比为 AL 的迭代扩集。 - 阶段 3：过采样 。SMOTE、ADASYN 通过最近邻插值平衡类别；局限是变长样本不适用、ADASYN 不支持纯类别数据。 - 阶段 4：生成式模型作为数据增强器 。AlphaFold、ESM-3 在进化记录上训练，可模仿天然蛋白结构/序列分布，甚至充当 oracle；LLM 作为通用数据增强器（Li et al. 发现小原始集 + 合成数据有一致提升，但纯合成不如纯原始）。 - 本文主张的位置 ：把 AL 从「小分子/寡肽」推进到「蛋白质复合物接触图预测」，用 CKA 度量模型分歧选种，用 ESM-3 生成新复合物，并系统扫描数据集 size × scope 的二维条件。 05 核心痛点 痛点 表现 成因或作者解释 文中证据 化学/生物标注数据稀缺 无法像 NLP 那样利用互联网级语料 数据生成需实验室材料与熟练人力，成本高 Introduction 引文 3、4 大模型在小数据上失效 做两种消融（uniform 保分布 / targeted 窄分布）× 三种保留比例（20/50/80%）；用 AminoBERT 与 ESM-2 的 CKA 分歧挑出「难例」，掩码 ~20% 序列后用 ESM-3（pTM 引导、温度 0.3、每步解掩 3 token）生成新复合物，加入训练集再训练。 核心洞察 ：数据集的 分布范围（scope） 与 规模（size） 是两个可独立调节的轴；当只要求 in-distribution 泛化时，缩小 scope 可换取一个数量级的规模缩减；但一旦要求 out-of-distribution 泛化，窄分布反而有害。增强的有效性存在 下界 ：初始集太小则不确定性估计不可靠，合成数据有害。 可能的普适教训 [Analysis] ：在数据稀缺的科学领域，「先建一个窄而密的可信核心集，再向外扩展」可能优于「在全空间均匀稀疏采样」；生成式模型的增强能力受其自身训练分布偏置限制，需刻意设计 prompt 才能越出预训练分布。 07 方法总览 输入 ：复合物两条链的氨基酸序列（忽略 DIPS-Plus 的残基/原子级特征）。 输出 ：L₁ × L₂ 的残基-残基接触图（Cα-Cα ≤ 6 Å 定义为接触），逐位置二分类概率，阈值 0.5 二值化。 模块 ：① 双塔预训练 BERT 编码器（ESM-2 8M / AminoBERT 87M / ProtBERT 420M）；② 拼接数组 M_ij = concat(emb_i, emb_j)，尺寸 L₁×L₂×2D；③ 逐位置 MLP（单 sigmoid 输出）。 训练 ：BCE 损失 + position weight（应对接触图稀疏）；MCC 评估；Optuna 做 HPO（架构超参仅作用于 MLP），HPO 在全量训练集上做一次，最优参数复用于所有消融试验。 工具 ：Python（Pandas/NumPy/SciPy/scikit-learn）、PyTorch、Optuna、Hugging Face（ESM-2/ProtBERT 权重）、AminoBERT GitHub、ESM-3（生成）、ESM-C 6B（隐空间嵌入）。 反馈回路 ：训练 → 计算验证集 来源 ：Methods「Measuring the similarity of contact maps」。 pTM 分数（Eq. 2） ：pTM = (1/L_N) Σ_i 1/(1 + (d_i/d_0)²)，其中 L_N 为生成/天然结构残基数，L_T 为与模板对齐的残基数，d_i 为对齐残基间距离（Å），d_0 为归一化常数（Å）。 用途 ：引导 ESM-3 生成高质量结构； 直觉 Scientific claims, methodological soundness, evidence quality, and presentation as inferable from the supplied text. Figures and tables are referenced but not directly inspected. Shared manuscript claim summary The authors investigate how protein language models (pLMs) perform on limited protein-protein complex datasets, and whether targeted (distribution-narrowing) ablation and active learning (AL) with generative model (ESM-3) augmentation can improve predictive performance on residue-residue contact map prediction. Visible evidence base Text descriptions of results, figure and table references, methodological descriptions. No actual figures, tables, or numerical data were provided for direct inspection. Missing materials affecting confidence All figures (Figures 1–11, S1–S11), tables (Tables 1–3), hyperparameter details, and quantitative results. Statistical significance testing, error bars, and exact numerical values are not directly verifiable. Reviewer Overall assessment The manuscript addresses a timely and practically important question: how to train protein language models when data are scarce. The framing around dataset distribution versus dataset size is conceptually useful, and the use of generative models for augmentation is a relevant direction. However, the evidence as presented is largely qualitative, with key quantitative results and visualizations not directly available for inspection. Several claims about model performance, augmentation benefits, and distributional effects rest on descriptions that are difficult to fully evaluate without the underlying data. The manuscript would benefit from clearer reporting of effect sizes, variability, and statistical comparisons. Who would be interested in the results, and why Researchers working on protein language models, protein-protein interaction prediction, and machine learning in structural biology. The findings on data augmentation strategies and the interaction between dataset size and distribution are relevant to practitioners developing predictive models for proteins, particularly in low-data regimes. The work may also interest those studying the behavior of generative models in scientific data augmentation. Major strengths The question is well-motivated and practically relevant. The experimental design includes multiple pLM sizes, two ablation strategies (uniform vs targeted), and a clear AL pipeline. The use of ESM-3 as a generative augmenter is a current and interesting approach. The authors also acknowledge limitations and discuss potential biases in generative models. Major Concerns Concern ID R1-M1 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence quality Claim pointer The claim that targeted ablation permits an order-of-magnitude decrease in training dataset size while maintaining in-distribution generalization performance. Evidence pointer Figure 4, Figure S3, Results section "Effects of Dataset Ablation on Model Performance" Concern The central quantitative claim of an order-of-magnitude reduction in dataset size is presented without direct numerical evidence in the text. The described MCC values are qualitative ("struggle to surpass 0.2", "as high as 0.5"), and the comparison between targeted and uniform ablation at matched dataset sizes is not quantified. The claim that targeted ablation to 20% yields train/validation MCCs exceeding those on the full dataset is striking but not supported by visible data. Why it matters This is the primary finding of the paper. Without clear quantitative evidence, including effect sizes and variability across the five trials, the claim cannot be assessed for robustness or practical significance. Resolution test Provide the actual MCC values (mean and standard error) for all models, ablation types, and dataset sizes, with a direct comparison between targeted and uniform ablation at matched sizes. Include statistical tests or confidence intervals to support the order-of-magnitude claim. Concern ID R1-M2 Severity Major Blocking Yes Axis Evidence quality Claim pointer The claim that AL augmentation with ESM-3-generated complexes produces a "small but consistent increase" in both in- and out-of-distribution MCC. Evidence pointer Figure 11, Figure S11, Results section "Changes in Model Performance When Ablated Sets are Augmented With Generated Samples" Concern The reported improvements are described as "small but consistent," but no numerical values, error bars, or statistical tests are provided in the text. The claim of consistency across trials is not verifiable. Additionally, the observation that 20% ablations fail to improve or even decrease in performance upon augmentation is presented without quantitative detail. Why it matters The effectiveness of the proposed AL pipeline is a key contribution. Without quantitative evidence, the practical value of the augmentation strategy cannot be determined. Resolution test Report exact MCC values before and after augmentation for each ablation condition, with measures of variability. Include statistical comparisons (e.g., paired tests across trials) to substantiate the "consistent increase" claim. Concern ID R1-M3 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Methodological clarity Claim pointer The claim that CKA scores are a suitable measure of model disagreement for selecting uncertain complexes. Evidence pointer Methods section "Measuring the similarity of contact maps", Figure S1 Concern The choice of CKA over other similarity measures is justified only by a reference to Figure S1, which is not available for inspection. The text states that CKA exhibited "the least overlap between the train, validation, and test sets," but the basis for selecting this criterion is not explained. It is unclear why minimal overlap between sets is the desired property for a similarity measure in this context. Why it matters The AL pipeline depends critically on the reliability of the uncertainty measure. If the choice of CKA is not well justified, the validity of the entire augmentation approach is in question. Resolution test Provide the comparison of similarity measures (Figure S1) and explain the rationale for selecting CKA. Clarify why minimal overlap between train/validation/test distributions is the appropriate criterion. Concern ID R1-M4 Severity Major Blocking No Axis Generalizability Claim pointer The claim that findings are "likely applicable beyond the realm of protein sets to wide varieties of LLMs and datasets." Evidence pointer Conclusions section Concern This generalization is asserted without supporting evidence or a clear argument for why the results should transfer to other domains. The study uses a single dataset (DIPS-Plus), a specific task (contact map prediction), and a limited set of pLMs. The conditions under which the findings might generalize are not discussed. Why it matters Overclaiming generalizability can mislead readers. The scope of the conclusions should match the evidence. Resolution test Either temper the claim to reflect the specific conditions studied, or provide a reasoned argument for generalizability based on the mechanisms observed. Minor Comments Concern ID R1-m1 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Methods, "Selecting disagreed-upon protein complexes" Evidence pointer Table 2 Issue The text states that complexes are selected from the 20th percentile of CKA scores, but the number of complexes selected is only shown in Table 2, which is not available. The relationship between the percentile threshold and the number of selected complexes is unclear. Required correction State the number of selected complexes for each ablation condition in the text, or explain how the percentile threshold translates to a fixed count. Concern ID R1-m2 Severity Minor Axis Reproducibility Affected element Methods, "Generating novel protein complexes by unmasking" Evidence pointer Methods section Issue The generation parameters (temperature 0.3, 3 tokens per step) are stated, but the rationale for these choices is not given. The number of generation steps and the total compute required are not specified. Required correction Provide a brief justification for the chosen generation parameters and state the total number of generation steps or compute budget. Concern ID R1-m3 Severity Minor Axis Presentation Affected element Results, "Effects of Dataset Ablation on Model Performance" Evidence pointer Figure 4 Issue The text describes MCC differences between models and ablation types but does not report the actual values. The reader cannot assess the magnitude of the effects described. Required correction Include key numerical values in the text or refer to a table with the full results. Concern ID R1-m4 Severity Minor Axis Statistical rigor Affected element Results, "Changes in Model Performance When Ablated Sets are Augmented With Generated Samples" Evidence pointer Figure 11 Issue The claim of "consistent increase" is not supported by statistical analysis. It is unclear whether the five trials are independent and whether the observed increases are significant. Required correction Report the variability across trials and perform a statistical test (e.g., paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test) to support the claim. Concern ID R1-m5 Severity Minor Axis Clarity Affected element Methods, "Measuring distances between protein complexes in latent space" Evidence pointer Methods section Issue The choice of the ESM model with 6 billion parameters for embedding is not justified. It is unclear why this specific model was chosen over other available embedding models. Required correction Briefly explain the choice of embedding model and whether the results are sensitive to this choice. Technical failings that need to be addressed before the case is established The primary quantitative claims (order-of-magnitude dataset reduction, consistent augmentation benefit) are not supported by directly visible numerical evidence. The manuscript relies heavily on figures and tables that were not provided for review. Statistical significance and variability are not reported. The choice of CKA as the uncertainty measure requires clearer justification. Assessment against Nature-style criteria Originality : The combination of dataset distribution control with generative augmentation for pLMs is a reasonable and somewhat novel angle, though the individual components (AL, data augmentation, pLMs) are established. The originality is moderate. Scientific importance : The question of data efficiency in protein machine learning is important, and the findings could be useful for practitioners. However, the importance is somewhat limited by the narrow scope (one dataset, one task). Interdisciplinary readership : The work sits at the intersection of machine learning, structural biology, and chemistry. The framing is accessible, but the results are likely to appeal mainly to a specialized audience. Technical soundness : The experimental design is reasonable, but the lack of visible quantitative results and statistical analysis prevents a full assessment. The CKA choice needs stronger justification. Readability for nonspecialists : The manuscript is generally well-written and the concepts are explained clearly. The abstract is accessible. However, some methodological details (e.g., CKA, pTM) may be challenging for readers outside the field. Recommendation posture Supportive if technical concerns are resolved. The topic is relevant and the approach is sensible, but the evidence as presented is insufficient to fully establish the main claims. The authors should provide the underlying quantitative data, statistical analyses, and clearer justifications for methodological choices. Risk / unsupported claims The claim of an order-of-magnitude reduction in dataset size with maintained performance is not supported by visible numerical evidence. The claim of a "small but consistent increase" in MCC upon augmentation is not supported by visible numerical evidence or statistical analysis. The claim that findings generalize beyond protein sets to "wide varieties of LLMs and datasets" is unsupported. The statement that CKA is the best measure of model disagreement is not fully justified without the comparison in Figure S1. The claim that ESM-3-generated proteins are biased toward the center of ESM-3's training distribution is plausible but not directly demonstrated with quantitative comparisons.

scope Abstract only Assessment boundary Claims and evidence presented in the abstract; no methods, figures, tables, or supplementary materials were provided Shared manuscript claim summary The authors present Cooper-Beta, a chain-resolved framework that detects beta-barrel-like folds from DSSP-assigned strand connectivity using four measurements evaluated by either direct rules or logistic regression. They report high recall and specificity on held-out benchmarks, robustness to structural perturbation, and successful application to a large viral structural database, yielding candidate sequences lacking sequence homology to known matches. Visible evidence base Abstract text only; no methodological details, benchmark definitions, statistical analyses, or dataset descriptions are available Missing materials affecting confidence Full methods, benchmark construction details, classifier calibration procedures, perturbation protocol, database screening pipeline, candidate validation criteria, and all figures and tables Reviewer Overall assessment The abstract describes a potentially useful and interpretable approach for fold screening in predicted structural repositories. The reported performance metrics are encouraging, and the application to viral structural dark matter addresses a timely question. However, the abstract alone does not provide sufficient detail to assess methodological rigor, benchmark validity, or the robustness of the screening results. Several claims, particularly regarding resource efficiency and the biological significance of the candidates, cannot be evaluated from the supplied material. Who would be interested in the results, and why Structural biologists and virologists interested in discovering novel folds in undercharacterized viral proteomes; computational biologists developing interpretable tools for protein structure analysis; researchers working on the functional annotation of structural dark matter. Major strengths The approach addresses a clear gap in scalable and interpretable fold detection beyond sequence homology. The use of DSSP-assigned strand connectivity is mechanistically grounded. The inclusion of both direct and learned classifiers with comparable performance suggests methodological flexibility. The application to a large viral database with subsequent sequence-based filtering demonstrates a practical workflow.
